The authors also prove lower bounds for general spaces built from simplices: if certain cohomology classes multiply to something nonzero, the space needs at least a corresponding power-of-two count of top pieces. Spaces shaped like real, complex, or product-of-spheres projective spaces fall under that rule. Finally, they give short explicit constructions of especially small triangulations, matching the best counts previously known.
arxiv-2509-22733:
Yuting Hu and Jinjun Xiong rebuild power flow models with graph attention networks when the true grid model is flawed. A full power flow model encodes the physics of the network, and classic analysis leans on it. In practice, some parameters are wrong or missing, and grids keep changing shape. Their rebuild model constructs a new graph from the real and imaginary parts of voltage at each bus.

Attention lets the model weight neighbor information as it infers the missing structure. They compared it with two leading rebuild models on standard IEEE cases and modified variants. The attention model stayed more accurate when topology changed. It also generalized to new networks with a smaller accuracy drop.
arxiv-2509-22933: Thomas Donlon gives two short geometric proofs of the Shklovskii effect in pulsars. The effect is a slow drift in the observed period of a pulsing source. It comes from the source moving across the sky, not from any real change in spin. Donlon uses geometry and calculus that are easy to picture. He offers the short routes as a teaching aid for readers who want intuition for the topic. The note is brief and adds no new data or tests.
arxiv-2509-23033:
Uranium mononitride conducts like a bad metal, and the usual Kondo story cannot explain why. Byungkyun Kang and 4 co-authors trace the behavior to Hund's exchange instead. Their tools mix density-functional theory with dynamical mean-field theory. Two uranium 5f electrons interact inside each atom. That Hund coupling lines up local magnetic moments.

The coupling also makes quasiparticles much heavier, a strong mass boost. On this account, the compound is a 5f cousin of a Hund's metal. Such metals were known mainly among transition-metal d-electron systems. The team urge a fresh look at Mott, Kondo, and Hund forces across actinide materials.
arxiv-2509-23433:
Videos mix dull stretches with sudden moments that define the story, and uniform frame sampling misses them. Sahithya Ravi and 4 co-authors built SPIKE to find those moments by Bayesian surprise. Surprise is the belief update a new frame triggers against prior expectation. SPIKE scores localize surprise well and track human judgments on two surprise benchmarks. Zero-shot model beliefs can be weak, though.

A reinforcement variant, SPIKE-RL, sharpens the belief hypotheses with a caption-based reward. Surprise-weighted sampling then spends frames where they matter. Five downstream benchmarks gained over uniform sampling. The approach lets video models revise beliefs as evidence lands.
arxiv-2509-24133:
Pointing a computer to the right button on a screen from a plain request is harder than it sounds. Zhecheng Li and 5 co-authors built GMS, a two-part system that first scans the screen broadly, then pinpoints the target. A general vision-language model acts as the scanner and flags likely regions. A small tuned model then locates the exact spot inside those regions.

Alone, each part scored near zero on a hard professional-screen benchmark. Joined in GMS, accuracy jumped about tenfold and beat strong rival systems across settings. The split mirrors human search: eyes sweep the scene first, then focus narrows to the target. Five stages with hierarchical search link the two roles.
arxiv-2510-00033:
Muhammad and Laaksonen improve hyperspectral single-image super-resolution, the task of sharpening a satellite image that carries hundreds of narrow wavelength bands. Where restoring fine spatial detail without corrupting the spectral signatures is the hard part. Their new hybrid deep learning design adds a Spectral-Spatial Unmixing Fusion module that plugs into standard ordinary 2D convolutional networks. Combining spectral unmixing with spectral-spatial feature extraction to guide a full ResNet backbone in the work.

Training uses a custom Spatial-Spectral Gradient Loss that adds spatial and spectral gradient terms to plain mean squared error. Also pushing the reconstruction to stay faithful in both dimensions at once. On three public remote sensing hyperspectral datasets the hybrid achieves reported competitive super-resolution quality while reducing model complexity relative to heavier alternatives. Making it a genuinely practical option for real-world remote sensing pipelines in practice.
arxiv-2510-00133:
Adarsha Balaji, Sandeep Madireddy, and Prasanna Balaprakash published this 2025 paper on running language models with spiking neural networks. Spiking networks pass brief pulses, like real neurons, and can use far less energy. Turning a trained transformer model into a spiking one usually costs accuracy or speed. The team's NeuTransformer method aims to keep the conversion both accurate and scalable.

The method swaps the attention block for a spike-based version, converts the rest of the network, and fine-tunes the new block. On three sizes of the GPT-2 model, the spiking versions stayed close to the originals in quality. The spiking attention block used far less estimated energy than the standard block in their tests. Performance did degrade for models above about 300 million parameters, a limit the authors state plainly. The work matters for running AI on low-power hardware.
arxiv-2510-00233:
Siva Viknesh and Amirhossein Arzani published this 2025 paper on DIANO, a framework for compressing complex flow simulations. Engineers model blood flow and air flow with huge grids evolving over time. Machine learning can shrink that data into a few latent variables, but the shrunken picture is usually unreadable. DIANO aims for a latent space that stays physically meaningful and equation-friendly.

An autoencoding neural operator squeezes input fields down and rebuilds them on demand. A differentiable equation solver runs inside the latent space, advancing the physics there directly. Tests covered flow past a cylinder, flow through a narrowed artery model, and a patient-specific coronary artery case. Reconstructions stayed accurate while the latent variables remained interpretable. The authors present DIANO as a bridge between data-driven learning and classical physics modeling for spatiotemporal systems.
arxiv-2510-00733:
Cristofoletto, Rollo, Birolo, and Fariselli build DeepFHT in this 2025 arXiv paper, a survival analysis model with physics-based parameters. Survival analysis predicts when an event such as death or machine failure will occur, and censoring hides many event times. The standard Cox model assumes risk ratios stay constant over time, which real data often violate. DeepFHT instead treats the event as a latent diffusion process first hitting an absorbing boundary.

A neural network maps each person's features to the process parameters: starting position, drift, and diffusion strength. Those parameters yield closed-form survival and hazard curves, so risk can vary freely with time. In parameter space, patients cluster by event time, and known clinical associations reappear as geometry. On synthetic and real datasets the model matched state-of-the-art accuracy, with clear gains where effects were nonlinear. Clinicians gain predictions they can interpret as physical quantities.
arxiv-2510-00833:
Nguyen and four co-authors survey verifiable federated unlearning in this 2025 arXiv paper on privacy and machine learning. Federated learning trains one model across many clients without moving their raw data. Privacy laws such as GDPR give those clients a right to be forgotten, so their data's influence must later be removable. The catch is trust, since clients today get only metrics or notifications as proof that removal really happened.

The authors propose VeriFUL, a reference framework that defines who verifies, what goals verification must meet, and which metrics apply. They consolidate scattered earlier efforts and add new concepts for judging correctness, completeness, and timeliness together. No single technique wins on every goal, since cryptographic proofs are strong but slow. The paper maps open challenges and points to regulated fields such as healthcare as natural first users.
arxiv-2510-00933:
Strakošová, Novák, and Kadera propose PoPAN in this 2025 arXiv paper, a product-centred model for the life cycle of products. Engineering standards model production processes and resources well, but they slight the product itself and stop before end-of-life. Yet repair, remanufacturing, and upcycling decisions at end-of-life should feed back into engineering. PoPAN builds on the Product-Process-Resource paradigm with the product structure as the model's backbone.

One compact network expresses assembly and disassembly processes alike. The model travels with the product as a digital shadow inside its Asset Administration Shell. The authors define a serialization in AutomationML so tooling can exchange it. Their demonstration case disassembles an electric vehicle battery for remanufacturing into a stationary unit. Querying the model yields the right process sequence for that second life. The authors frame the work as infrastructure for genuine, rather than marketed, sustainability.
arxiv-2510-01033:
Curtis-Lake and a large team present the fourth data release of the JADES survey in this 2025 arXiv paper, the first of a release series. JADES uses the James Webb Space Telescope to take spectra of faint distant galaxies in the GOODS-North and GOODS-South fields. This release completes the survey's NIRSpec spectroscopy, covering 5,190 targets with prism and grating settings across a wide wavelength range.

Deep tiers stared at about seven hundred galaxies for more than twenty hours each, while medium tiers covered thousands more with shorter exposures. The team explains how targets were picked from photometric redshifts and colours, favouring very distant ultraviolet-selected galaxies. They secured robust redshifts for 3,297 galaxies, and 396 of them lie beyond redshift 5.7, in the early universe. Carefully defined gold subsamples and completeness estimates help other researchers use the catalogue uniformly.
arxiv-2510-01233:
Pavan and Sree build the first full computational framework for the metrical patterns of classical Telugu poetry. Chandassu, the prosody system behind centuries of verse, lives in expert memory more than in software. Preserving it digitally means teaching machines to hear light and heavy syllables as poets do.

Community collaboration produced a dataset of several thousand annotated poems. Custom tools tokenize text with prosody in mind, classify syllable weight, and check whole metrical patterns. The scoring algorithm reached strong accuracy against standards drawn from traditional literary practice. The design doubles as a template for other endangered knowledge systems. Expert validation kept the annotations faithful to living tradition. The Chandassu Score grades pattern fidelity the way critics would. Social computing frames preservation as collective work, not extraction. Digital humanities gains a worked example with real community stakes behind it.
arxiv-2510-01433:
Singh and co-authors reduce robot vision to a handful of meaningful keypoints chosen automatically from a text prompt and one image. Dense images drag in background clutter and heavy computation. Keypoint methods focus attention but usually lean on hand-made rules tied to one task.

Their three-stage pipeline filters by affordance, builds category-level points, and learns a transformer policy over them. A gating mechanism lets the policy weigh which points matter for each action. The resulting compact state trains in minutes and runs in real time. Unseen objects and backgrounds still yielded strong success rates. Eighty-two percent success greeted objects the policy had never seen. No proprioception feeds the state, only the chosen visual points. Six real-world tasks carried the experimental evaluation. Distractors and new backgrounds failed to break the focus. Fixed keypoints during inference remain the acknowledged limitation.
arxiv-2510-01633:
Zaunders and Ralph compare satellite schemes for distributing quantum entanglement over continental distances under realistic optical loss. Future quantum networks need entangled pairs delivered fast and faithfully between distant points. Fiber infrastructure at that scale is costly and lossy, while free-space satellite links dodge both problems.

Two topologies face off: three satellites in orbit, or two ground stations under one satellite. Within each, the middle satellite either relays entanglement or generates and distributes it. The authors bound achievable distribution rates for every combination. Realistic channel models keep the comparison honest for network designers. Thousand-kilometer scales are where satellite geometry wins outright. Diffraction-limited beams through vacuum model the orbital links. First-generation quantum memory assumptions enter the ground-station variant. Rate and fidelity together grade every protocol pairing. Over-the-horizon reach is the prize the schemes contest. Entanglement is infrastructure here, not experiment.
arxiv-2510-01733:
Argüelles and co-authors present a new training pipeline for neutrino telescopes in this 2025 physics paper. Such telescopes spot neutrinos using huge volumes of ice or water. Machine learning tools for them usually train on simulated events with known labels. Real data never match those simulations perfectly, and the mismatch can mislead the tools.

The team instead uses self-supervised learning on point cloud transformers with masked autoencoders. Most training then happens on real, unlabeled data from the detector itself. Their experiments show that supervised methods degrade badly when subtle unmodeled effects appear. The self-supervised methods stayed stable under the same unknown effects. Shifting training toward real data could improve event reconstruction and classification. It also cuts the systematic uncertainty that simulations bring into neutrino measurements.
arxiv-2510-01833:
Dou and eleven co-authors teach language models to plan before they reason in this 2025 paper. Chain-of-thought reasoning unfolds token by token, so models decide each step locally. Without a global plan, their reasoning can wander, repeat itself, or drift off course. Tree searches and plain reinforcement learning help, but at high cost or with mixed success.

Their framework, PTA-GRPO, works in two stages. First, strong models distill worked solutions into compact high-level guidance, and the target model learns from it. Then a guidance-aware reinforcement step improves both the final answers and the guidance itself. Tests spanned MATH, AIME, and AMC contest benchmarks across several model families and sizes. The method improved results consistently and held up across scales. The authors present planning guidance as the missing layer above step-by-step reasoning.
arxiv-2510-01933:
Catteau and six co-authors treat a famous optimization curve as an artist's brush in this 2025 paper. The central path transformed optimization in the 1980s and 1990s through its clean convergence behavior. Researchers studied it to design algorithms, almost never to admire it. In low dimensions, though, the path traces graceful curves that beg for visual exploration.

The team varies the underlying optimization models and records the paths they generate. Those paths assemble into tilings and flower-like figures across two and three dimensions. Mathematical rigor controls every stroke, so artistic modeling here literally is mathematical modeling. Heavy computing bridges the two viewpoints. The resulting patterns reach beyond screen images toward physical novelties and museum-quality pieces. The authors argue the central path deserves celebration as an aesthetic object in its own right. Future work aims to push the designs further as both mathematics and art.
arxiv-2510-02233:
Perez, Gotthelf, and Halpern show that erratic timing is normal for a quiet class of neutron stars in this 2025 astronomy paper. Central compact objects are cooling neutron stars inside supernova remnants, spinning down remarkably slowly. Their inferred surface magnetic fields seem too weak to power their X-ray hot spots. Two decades of Chandra, XMM-Newton, and NICER data now cover the three known pulsars of this class.

The two well-monitored pulsars refuse to spin down steadily. Their timing residuals fit sudden glitches in spin frequency and its derivative, or extreme timing noise. Ordinary pulsars show a clear correlation between irregularity and spin-down rate. These two objects are extreme outliers against that trend at the same spin-down rate. The third pulsar's sparse coverage could not settle its behavior. Some hidden ingredient, perhaps a buried magnetic field, must drive the noise.
arxiv-2510-02333:
Pugliese and co-authors publish two enriched datasets of human movement for other researchers. Their resource paper builds on public GPS traces from OpenStreetMap. Raw traces only say where someone went. The datasets add layers of meaning on top. Each trip gains stops, moves, and visited places. Inferred travel modes say whether someone walked or rode. Weather records add the conditions of each journey. A novel layer adds synthetic social media posts. Language models wrote those posts to feel realistic.

The paper also releases the full building pipeline. Other teams can rebuild or extend the datasets freely. Mobility data with context supports richer questions. Analysts can ask how weather shapes daily travel. Language tools can answer plain questions over the data. The resource targets interpretable, context aware behavior research. Shared enriched data lowers the entry cost for everyone.
arxiv-2510-02433:
Duque and co-authors compute how accretion discs push on small black holes spiraling inward. Their 2025 astrophysics paper studies extreme-mass-ratio inspirals, called EMRIs. A stellar mass object circles a giant black hole for years. Gas discs around the giant exert Lindblad torques on the orbiter. Newtonian estimates made those torques look modest. Full relativity changes the picture sharply. Near the black hole, torque strength grows by orders of magnitude. The torque can even flip direction near the innermost stable orbit. Black hole spin moves that flip point and reshapes the radial pattern.

Simple power law fits struggle to capture the behavior. Slopes vary strongly with spin and disc type. Future space detectors like LISA will hear these inspirals. Disc effects in the signal could reveal disc properties. Accurate torque physics is needed to read those signals. The work supplies relativistic corrections for that task.
arxiv-2510-03033:
Rabelo and Seade study singularities of maps that mix complex variables with their conjugates. Such mixed maps appear in real analytic geometry. Their bad points can form isolated complete intersection singularities. The authors give two natural families of those singularities. A notion of partial non-degeneracy sorts the well-behaved cases. Under the right conditions, those cases are genuine singular intersections. They also carry a local Milnor fibration, a layered view near the bad point.

Building on work by Oka, the authors go further. Certain mixed links gain natural contact structures from the construction. An open book decomposition fits those contact structures neatly. Some mixed links turn out to match holomorphic ones in shape. Comparing their contact structures then becomes the subtle task. The paper closes by setting up that comparison problem. The results enrich the topology of real singularities.
arxiv-2510-03433:
Kovács, Hermosilla, and Raidou, at TU Wien in Austria, present a 2025 arXiv paper on restyling 3D objects with guidance from the artist. Style transfer paints a mesh in the look of a chosen image, but older tools give users little say over where patterns run. Their tool, Style Brush, takes a textured mesh, a guide texture with drawn contours, and one or more style images. A new loss function reads the direction of style features, not just their content.

The system rewrites the texture so brush patterns follow the user's contours. Several styles can blend across one object with smooth transitions between them. Tests on many meshes and styles produced textures in just a few minutes per object. The authors say no earlier method offered this kind of directional control for 3D objects. Game and film artists could restyle prop libraries while keeping a hand in the look.
arxiv-2510-03633:
Vuong and Gauch present a 2025 arXiv paper predicting next day stock moves by adding tweet emotion features, sharpened by a language model, to price history. Markets react to investor mood, and posts carry that mood. The team used Meta's Llama model to enrich emotion signals drawn from three analyzers: a transformer classifier and two lexicon based methods. Those features joined the day's prices as inputs to a recurrent network. Tests covered Tesla, Apple, and Amazon shares.

Every emotion method improved accuracy over the price only baseline, which managed about thirteen and a half percent. The transformer classifier performed best once the language model enhanced its features. Its accuracy climbed from about twenty three and a half percent to about thirty eight and a half percent. The gains show that preprocessing text with a model makes emotion signals more useful. Short term traders live on these move forecasts.
arxiv-2510-03733:
Gupta, Hegde, and Huang present a 2025 arXiv paper running logic circuits on plasmonic wires driven by a single laser beam, with no control signals. Plasmonic circuits promise ultrafast, nanoscale computing, but most designs need interferometers or extra beams to steer them. This scheme builds a single global threshold into two wire transmission lines. Polarization states of the one beam carry the control information, and geometric tuning shapes the response. Six deterministic polarization states do the encoding.

The team demonstrated a two bit comparator, parity checkers, and encoder and decoder circuits on the platform. Their footprint shrank by about sixty seven percent relative to designs. Power consumption fell by about half. The transition where both inputs are off still produced an on output, a stumbling block. Collapsing control and computation into one beam makes plasmonic logic easier to cascade. Denser optical processors and hybrid photonic electronic accelerators are the target applications.
arxiv-2510-04033:
Noori and a large group of co-authors present this 2025 arXiv paper proposing a global event log for medical artificial intelligence. Computer systems rely on syslog, a universal protocol that records every critical event. Hospitals are adopting clinical AI tools quickly, yet no shared standard records each model is used. Without such records, real-world performance, adverse events, and bias drift stay hard to detect.

The authors propose a logging protocol in the spirit of syslog for every clinical AI invocation. Each record carries nine fields, covering the model, the user, the target, inputs, outputs, outcomes, and feedback. To keep the burden low, the design supports risk-based sampling, retention rules by lifecycle stage, and delayed writing. The authors argue such logs would enable continuous surveillance and auditing of medical AI. They frame the long-term payoff as a new digital epidemiology for clinical algorithms.
arxiv-2510-04133:
Guo and Weng present this 2025 arXiv paper on time series in the frequency domain instead of the time domain. Neural ordinary differential equations handle continuous dynamics, but time-domain representations hide long-term and periodic structure. Their continuous formulation also grinds against the discrete sampling of real data. Many series, from energy demand to health signals, are dominated by exactly those periodic patterns.

Their model, FODE, first transforms the series with a fast Fourier transform. Learning dynamics among frequency components exposes global periodic behavior. A element-wise filter then aligns the continuous model output with discrete observations, preserving fine detail. Experiments on various time series datasets showed better accuracy and efficiency than methods. Frequency-domain dynamics offer a natural fit for the strongly periodic data that fills forecasting practice.
arxiv-2510-04533:
Hyunmin Cho and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on fixing a flaw in diffusion image models. Such models lead the field in image generation, yet their samples often break the prompt or the scene logic. Existing fixes lean on outside signals or change the model design, and both routes add cost. The team proposed a guidance method that works only on the sampling path itself.

The method takes an intermediate sample as a base point along the path. It then splits the score signal into parts parallel and tangential to that base. Boosting the tangential part steers the sample toward regions the model rates as more likely. A first order expansion in the paper proves that this push raises sample density. The module plugs into existing models with no change to their design. Added compute stays minimal. The result is fewer mixed up objects and broken body plans.
arxiv-2510-04633:
Lukas Gienapp and three coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on judging search results without huge human effort. Test collections for search engines rely on pooled judgments, which leave most documents unjudged. New systems then get scored against holes in the record. Many teams now ask a language model to judge, but the same model may also be a contestant. The team instead trains a classifier for each topic.

Their classifier fine tunes a ranking model on the judgments of one assessor for one topic. An adaptation method aligns it with that assessor sense of relevance for the topic. Rankings scored by the classifier matched the rankings with near perfect correlation. As few as 128 human judgments already improved comparability across systems. The approach proved more reliable than language model judges in their tests. Human judgments stay the gold standard, since the classifier learns from them. Code, models, and data were released.
arxiv-2510-04733:
Kollatschny and five coauthors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on a quasar that nearly vanishes in X rays. The quasar PG 0043+039 is the weakest X ray emitter of its kind and shows absorption in ultraviolet light. The team observed it in 2022 with space telescopes in X rays and ultraviolet, plus a ground telescope in visible light. All three views were taken, so changes could be compared fairly across bands.

The quasar stayed faint in X rays, as in 2005, though it had flared several fold in 2013. Its visible and ultraviolet glow dipped slightly over the span. Some ultraviolet emission lines swung, changing strength by factors of eight or more. Other lines barely moved, and the visible lines stayed nearly calm. Methods gave black hole masses of a few hundred million suns. Absorption troughs shifted back and forth in speed as one. The pattern points to outflows that vary together across the system.
arxiv-2510-04933:
Amir Hameed Mir's 2025 arXiv paper tackles a stubborn problem in artificial intelligence: large language models often state falsehoods with full confidence. Mir calls this failure hallucination. His paper, The Geometry of Truth, looks for a way to catch those false statements from inside the model itself, without checking outside sources.

Mir tracks how the meaning of a reply shifts across the model's layers as it forms. True answers settle into a steady path, while false ones drift away. His method, Layer-wise Semantic Dynamics, scores that drift in a single pass. On the TruthfulQA test set it reached an F1 score of 0.92 and beat sampling-based checkers while running far faster. The work gives builders a cheap, real-time warning sign for unreliable answers.
arxiv-2510-05133:
Du and four colleagues map the safe limits of training AI on its own output in this 2025 arXiv paper. Synthetic data from language models now feeds many training pipelines. Nobody knew exactly how much synthetic data a model can absorb before it degrades. The team ran about 300 controlled training runs to find out.

They trained Pythia models from 410 million to 12 billion parameters on five tasks. Performance stayed stable with up to 20 percent synthetic data. Beyond 30 percent, degradation accelerated sharply, reaching 8 to 15 percent. Larger models tolerated roughly twice the synthetic share of smaller ones. Calibration slipped before accuracy did, giving an early warning signal. Reasoning tasks degraded faster than retrieval tasks.
arxiv-2510-05333:
Michelle Bucher and Alessio Savini sharpen how group cohomology can be represented on boundaries in this 2025 arXiv paper. For a semisimple Lie group, Monod showed every continuous cohomology class has a measurable representative on the Furstenberg boundary. The authors ask how regular that representative can be made.

They prove the representing cocycle can be chosen continuous on an explicit set of generic tuples. An analogous result holds for bounded cohomology. They then apply the characterization to the comparison map between bounded and ordinary cohomology. The map is injective in degree three for complex hyperbolic isometry groups. It is also injective in degree four for real hyperbolic groups of dimension at least two.
arxiv-2510-05933:
Stephens and colleagues map magnetic fields across ten Milky Way bones. Bones are massive filamentary clouds, the Galaxy's largest coherent star-forming structures. Their magnetic fields' role in collapse and star formation was largely unconstrained. The 2025 FIELDMAPS program observed them with the SOFIA airborne observatory.

The fields vary from bone to bone with no single preferred alignment. At higher column densities, spines more often run perpendicular to the field. Alignment shows no strong correlation with young stellar object locations. Field strengths measure roughly thirty to one hundred fifty microgauss. The fields are strong against gravity, leaving most bones magnetically subcritical. Without the fields, low virial parameters imply much of the bones would collapse. Fields may also slow and guide gas flow during dissipation. Recent star formation likely happens in dense pockets at smaller scales. Some low-density stretches appear gravitationally unbound despite the fields.
arxiv-2510-06033:
Dai, Wu, and Zhang work on scheduling servers in uncertain service systems in a 2025 operations research paper. Such stochastic processing networks appear in hospitals, transport systems, and communication networks. Managers must assign servers to jobs in batches, and the number of joint assignments explodes as systems grow.

The authors break each joint assignment into a sequence of single-server choices, which they call atomic actions. They study two policy types, one that may change its rule at each step and one that repeats a single rule. Both types provably reach the same best long-run average reward as the original joint policies. The policy size stays fixed no matter how many servers the system has. The theorem explains why an atomic version of a popular learning algorithm already performed well in hospital, switch, and ride-hailing tests.
arxiv-2510-06133:
Wang and seven co-authors speed up diffusion language models by trusting early hunches in a 2025 paper. Diffusion models write text through repeated denoising, confirming only high-confidence tokens per step and remasking the rest. Studying traces, the team noticed models often settle on the correct token steps before its confidence crosses the threshold.

That lag forces needless remasking of already-correct tokens. Trace Credit instead accumulates a token's past scores to estimate its potential. CreditDecoding fuses that credit with current logits, which lifts correct but hesitant tokens over the threshold sooner. It needs no retraining and runs alongside standard inference optimizations. Across eight benchmarks it delivered speedups up to about 5.5 times on LLaDA-8B with a small accuracy gain, and it scaled cleanly to long contexts. Diffusion models could thus serve text far faster with no new training.
arxiv-2510-06533:
Akitoshi Kawamura and Yusuke Kobayashi work on a scheduling puzzle called the pinwheel problem. In their 2025 paper, a daily task must be given to one of several agents. Each agent can do the task at most once within a set number of days. The question is which sets of agents can cover every day without breaking their limits.

The pair determines the exact best constant for the covering version of the problem. That constant is about 1.264, and any instance above it can always be scheduled. The result settles an open problem posed by Soejima and Kawamura in 2020. Their proof mixes new mathematics with an exhaustive computer search. It builds on earlier methods developed for the packing version of the problem. Computer-assisted proofs like this one show how careful searching can finish arguments that pure theory leaves open.
arxiv-2510-07133:
Zhang, Kantarci, and Siddique address the safety testing of self-driving cars in a 2025 paper. Real road tests cannot cover every risky scene a car might meet. Lab tests also face a basic puzzle. No one can always say what the correct response should be. The authors build a virtual copy of the car and its world to test it safely.

Inside the virtual world, the team varies weather, road shape, and surroundings. An image generator makes the new scenes while keeping the core sense of the old one. Three test rules, drawn from real traffic behavior, check whether the car responds in a sane way. Trials ran in a well-known driving simulator. The method widened test coverage and caught faults that simpler tests missed. Safer testing of this kind matters before cars drive themselves in public.
arxiv-2510-07433:
Pandey and Khan show how a heavy, shy neutrino could be the dark matter, born from a low-energy seesaw. Their 2025 paper extends the type-I seesaw, the standard account of tiny neutrino masses, with a second Higgs doublet that talks only to neutrinos. The lightest sterile neutrino barely interacts at all, earning the label FIMP. Earlier work missed its dominant birth channel: decays of W and Z bosons in the hot early universe. That channel alone fixes how much dark matter the model produces, the authors calculate.

A tiny vacuum value for the neutrino-loving doublet widens the workable mass range greatly. Candidate masses span from below a kiloelectronvolt up to a fifth of a gigaelectronvolt. Fresh forest observations of intergalactic hydrogen still allow both warm and cold versions of the candidate. One light neutrino comes out extremely light as a side prediction.
arxiv-2510-07733:
Nguyen and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on software that writes survey papers automatically. Researchers struggle to keep up with publication growth in fast fields. Language models can draft surveys, but simple summarizers ignore how papers relate. The result lacks a coherent map of the field. The authors build a multi-agent framework, SurveyG, that treats citation structure as first-class knowledge for the writing process.

SurveyG builds a hierarchical citation graph over the source papers. Its layers separate founding works, later developments, and the current frontier. Agents search across and down those layers to build layered summaries. Those summaries merge into a structured outline for the draft. A validation stage with several agents checks consistency, coverage, and factual accuracy. Human experts and model judges both rated SurveyG above rival frameworks. Its surveys covered more ground and matched each field's taxonomy more closely.
arxiv-2510-08133:
Miyajima, Takeuchi, and Akibue wrote this 2025 quantum information paper asking whether quantum metrology, like quantum computation, has universal resource states, and whether too much entanglement can hurt. Measurement-based computation runs on one special entangled state, while overly entangled states are useless for it. The authors ask the same questions for sensing. For a class of linear Hamiltonians, they prove universal resource states for metrology exist.

Highly entangled states are also useless as metrology resources for linear Hamiltonians, echoing the computation result. Random pure states, carrying near-maximal entanglement, are basically useless for sensing even under more general Hamiltonians. The analysis covers a wider Hamiltonian class than earlier work. The moral tempers a common intuition: entanglement powers quantum advantage only in the right structure and dose. For sensor designers, the results narrow where to look for useful probe states.
arxiv-2510-08233:
Yuchen Zhu and co-authors present DMPO in a 2025 arXiv paper, a training method that sharpens reasoning in diffusion language models. These models write text by refining noise step by step, unlike standard models that predict one word at a time. They may answer faster, but they need good fine-tuning to reason well. Reinforcement learning helps, yet existing methods were built for the standard model type.

DMPO, short for Distribution Matching Policy Optimization, steers the model's output mix toward a reward-shaped target mix. It does this through cross-entropy training, which rewards outputs that match the target pattern. Small training batches caused problems, so the team added a weight baseline trick to steady learning. On reasoning benchmarks, DMPO raised accuracy by up to 42.9 percent over prior best baselines, and that gain came without any supervised fine-tuning stage.
arxiv-2510-08633:
Ann Marie Cody, Lynne Hillenbrand, Shreya Chandragiri, and Marvin Morgan chart the flickering of young intermediate-mass stars in a 2025 arXiv paper. They study one hundred eighty-eight Herbig Ae/Be stars, young stars heavier than the Sun, using the TESS satellite. Full-frame images covered each star for at least one twenty-seven-day sector over the mission's first 3.3 years. A custom pipeline produced light curves for detailed variability analysis.

About ninety-five percent of these stars vary on timescales from ten minutes to one month, the team finds. Stochastic, irregular variation is the most common light curve shape. Roughly fifteen percent show quasi-periodic patterns instead. Compared with low-mass T Tauri stars, Herbig stars show far fewer dipper fading events and periodic modulations. The authors conclude magnetic starspots are rare on these stars. Their inner dust rims sit at much larger radii than around low-mass stars.
arxiv-2510-08833:
Loch-Temzelides, the corresponding author, and collaborators model why partnerships between species arise and later fall apart, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their running example is the bond between land plants and mycorrhizal fungi, which trade nutrients through roots. Fossil and genetic records show plants have gained, partly dropped, and regained this partnership many times. The puzzle is why a bond that pays off overall ever gets abandoned.

The team frames the choice as a coordination game, where a strategy pays only once enough players adopt it, as in a market that needs scale. The game yields three stable outcomes that match the states seen in plant family trees. Using tools for rare random shifts, the authors characterize how evolution drifts among the outcomes over long spans. Partnerships mostly persist, but cheaper-looking exits grow likelier when the benefit-to-cost balance sours, and shifts usually pass through half-committed states.
arxiv-2510-09033:
Cheang and co-authors challenge a hopeful claim about language models: that their inner activity reveals whether an answer is true, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Several studies had found factuality signals in hidden states, suggesting models know what they do not know. Yet the same training that rewards correct answers also produces confident fabrications. The team compared two kinds of false answers by how they arise.

When a hallucination grows out of what the model recalls about the subject, its internal processing follows the same path as a correct answer. The hidden-state patterns overlap so completely that no probe can separate them. Fabrications detached from subject knowledge look different inside and cluster apart, which makes them detectable. The authors conclude that the internals encode patterns of recall, not truth. A model can therefore sound, and internally feel, exactly as sure when it is wrong as when it is right.
arxiv-2510-09233:
Lion and co-authors map how the surface of gallium oxide rearranges itself, pairing quantum simulations with microscope images, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Gallium oxide is an ultrawide-bandgap semiconductor prized for next-generation power electronics. Its beta phase's (001) surface is where new crystal layers grow, and the atoms there settle into reconstructions, repeating patterns that shape the material's quality. Knowing which patterns form under which conditions guides growth.

Combining ab initio thermodynamics with replica-exchange molecular dynamics, the team charted stable reconstructions across oxygen and gallium conditions. A previously unreported pattern stood out: a doubled cell of paired gallium-oxygen tetrahedra, stable across wide growth conditions. In it, two gallium atoms share one oxygen bond, just over two and a half angstroms apart. Electron microscopy of grown layers matched the prediction. Indium substitution tests showed a cooperative uptake effect with its own stability regions.
arxiv-2510-09333:
Till Aczel, Lucas Theis, and Roger Wattenhofer tackle the scoring of human judgements in a 2025 arXiv paper. People often rate generative models by comparing two outputs side by side, since direct scores are noisy and costly. Pairwise comparisons are steadier, but turning them into one ranking must handle raters who differ in skill and care.

The authors propose BBQ, a Bayesian version of the classic Bradley-Terry ranking model. Their method models each rater's quality, downweights unreliable raters, and can drop them entirely. An expectation-maximisation algorithm, which alternates between estimating scores and rater quality, is guaranteed to improve the fit step by step. Tests show faster inference, well-calibrated uncertainty, and rankings that hold up better than baseline models, even with noisy crowdsourced raters.
arxiv-2510-09433:
Raffaele Cristodaro, Benjamin Kraner, and Claudio Tessone test the privacy of a cryptocurrency mixer in a 2025 arXiv paper. Tornado Cash is a decentralised service that uses cryptography to break the visible trail between a deposit and a withdrawal on a blockchain. In practice, careless user behaviour can quietly rebuild that trail.

The authors run the first cross-chain study of Tornado Cash, covering Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, and Polygon. They apply three clustering heuristics: address reuse, transactional linkage, and a new first-in-first-out rule that matches deposits to withdrawals by timing. Simple reuse and linkage alone already traced between about five and thirteen percent of withdrawals. The timing rule added fifteen to twenty-two percentage points more, and the matches were far too consistent to be chance. In total the heuristics linked over two point three billion dollars of withdrawals to deposits.
arxiv-2510-09633:
Bernhard Mueller, the sole author, introduces Hound in a 2025 arXiv paper, a tool for auditing complex code for security flaws. Auditing interrelated systems is hard because a vulnerability often spans several components. Hound builds relation-first knowledge graphs, where the connections between code parts carry analyst-defined views such as money flows, authentication roles, call graphs, and protocol rules.

For any question, the engine retrieves exactly the code that matters, often across components, letting the analyst zoom from system structure down to decisive lines. A persistent belief system keeps long-lived vulnerability hypotheses alive and updates their confidence as evidence accrues. Planning balances coverage against intuition, and a final checking stage confirms or rejects each hypothesis. On five projects from the ScaBench suite, Hound roughly quadrupled recall over a baseline language model analyser and raised its quality score, at a modest cost in precision.
arxiv-2510-09733:
Yubo Sun and seven co-authors reduce visual hallucinations in image-based question answering in a 2025 arXiv paper. Visual retrieval-augmented generation supplies vision-language models with external images as evidence. With several images in play, models still hallucinate and often fail to pick out the evidence the question actually needs.

Their framework, EVisRAG, first observes each retrieved image and records the question-relevant visual evidence it contains. Reasoning and answer generation then run on the aggregated evidence rather than on the raw pile of images. A training method, RS-GRPO, ties reward signals to the token spans of each stage, improving stability and jointly optimising evidence localisation and reasoning. Across multiple visual question answering benchmarks, the framework beat its backbone model by about nineteen percent on average. Visual hallucinations dropped substantially, which the authors credit to explicit evidence collection and stage-scoped rewards.
arxiv-2510-10033:
Gant and Ben Williams determine motivic homotopy groups of spheres in this 2025 arXiv paper in algebraic topology. Motivic homotopy theory imports the tools of topology into algebraic geometry. Its sphere spectrum plays the role the ordinary sphere plays in classical theory, and its groups are a central computation.

Over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, the authors show these groups are fixed by two simpler inputs. One is the p-completed sphere spectra, studied one prime at a time. The other is the motivic cohomology of the ground field. Only the groups in degrees zero and minus one may escape that determination. The result reduces a hard global computation to local and cohomological data.
arxiv-2510-10233:
He, Zakk Heile, Jayson Tran, Alice Wang, and Shrikant Chand build a rigid-invariant sliced Wasserstein distance in this 2025 arXiv paper on geometric data analysis. Comparing two distributions is hard when their supports differ by an unknown rotation, reflection, or shift. Shape matching faces this constantly.

Classical optimal transport distances react to such rigid moves, while Gromov-Wasserstein distances ignore them but cost too much on large data. The authors use independent embeddings to make a sliced Wasserstein variant that is invariant to rigid transformations yet stays fast. Slicing projects the data to lines and compares those cheap summaries. The result aims at Gromov-like invariance at sliced-Wasserstein prices.
arxiv-2510-11033:
Leandro Aurichi, Fortunato Maesano, and Lyubomyr Zdomskyy introduce a density version of a classic covering property, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Scheepers property comes from topology. It is a selection principle about open covers of a space. From each cover in a sequence, one picks finitely many sets. The picked sets must still cover the space in a strong eventual sense. Such principles organize many covering notions into one framework.

The authors define the density counterpart of the property. The covering demand is replaced by a density style condition. They then study how the new property relates to known density properties. Their main theorem gives an equivalence. The density Scheepers property matches M-separability, another selection style property. The match holds under a principle of Blass and Weiss, the Near Coherence of Filters. Results like this map the logical geography of topology, showing when two differently motivated properties coincide.
arxiv-2510-11133:
Models often fail on new data because they lean on features that correlate with the answer without causing it. Yingnan Liu, Rui Qiao, Mong Li Lee, and Wynne Hsu attack that weakness in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Their method, Test-time Adaptation by Causal Trimming, adapts a trained model to unlabeled target data at test time by removing the non-causal parts of its internal representations.

TACT creates augmented copies of the data that keep causal features fixed while varying the rest, then uses principal component analysis to find the directions of highest variance tied to non-causal features. It trims each representation by deleting its projection onto those directions and predicts from what remains, refining the directions during adaptation. The authors support the approach with theory and tests on real-world out-of-distribution benchmarks, where TACT beat state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin.
arxiv-2510-11233:
Detecting depression risk from social media text could help reach people earlier, but Chinese-language resources for that research are scarce and usually limited to a yes-or-no label. Jinyuan Xu and co-authors release a richer resource in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their dataset CNSocialDepress collects Chinese social media posts for depression risk detection and structured psychological analysis, going beyond binary classification.

The dataset contains 44,178 texts from 233 users, within which psychological experts annotated 10,306 depression-related segments. Alongside binary labels it adds structured psychological attributes, enabling fine-grained analysis of depressive signals, not one opaque score. They show its use for structured psychological profiling and for fine-tuning large language models. Their tests highlight its value for depression risk identification in Chinese-speaking populations. The resource is released publicly for other research groups.
arxiv-2510-11333:
A superconducting spin valve is a layered device whose superconductivity switches depending on whether two magnetic layers point the same way or opposite ways. A. A. Kamashev and co-authors study a device built from iron, silicon nitride, and lead layers in this 2025 arXiv condensed matter paper. The silicon nitride is an insulating spacer whose thickness tunes how strongly the magnetic and superconducting layers interact.

The team varied the thicknesses of the superconducting and insulating layers to optimize the size of the effect. With the best geometry, flipping the magnetizations from antiparallel to parallel switched the structure completely between its normal and superconducting states. The largest effect was 0.36 kelvin, reached in a magnetic field of one kilo-oersted, a modest applied field. The authors argue that insulating interlayers give a tuning knob for these valves, with uses in superconducting spintronic devices.
arxiv-2510-11833:
Suraj Maurya and three colleagues test how fast black holes grow complex inside. In holographic theories, a black hole's internal complexity, roughly the shortest recipe for building its quantum state, is dual to a geometric volume or action. Leonard Susskind conjectured that the growth rate equals the product of the hole's horizon temperature and entropy. Their 2025 arXiv paper checks this across four black hole families.

Using both the complexity-volume and complexity-action dualities, they study BTZ, Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordström, and Kerr black holes. In each case the growth rate indeed tracks the temperature-entropy product. They then ask how the growth rate changes under physical processes. Extracting energy by the Penrose process or superradiance always speeds the growth. Dropping in a particle can speed it, stall it, or reverse it, depending on the particle's spin direction. For reversing cases, an honest accounting must include the horizon's own dynamics.
arxiv-2510-12133:
Han Zhu and ten colleagues stress-test multimodal AI safety across whole conversations, not single prompts. Real misuse unfolds over turns, each message innocent enough alone. Existing benchmarks barely cover that. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces SafeMT, ten thousand multi-turn dialogues grown from harmful queries paired with images, spanning seventeen scenarios and four jailbreak methods.

A new Safety Index scores a model's general safety through conversations. Assessing seventeen models, the team finds attack success climbs as harmful dialogues lengthen: safety mechanisms fail to recognize hazards accumulating across turns. Their remedy is a dialogue safety moderator that sniffs concealed malicious intent in the conversation and hands the model the relevant safety policies. On several open-source models, this moderator cut multi-turn attack success more than existing guard models. The warning label on the paper is honest: it contains harmful examples by necessity.
arxiv-2510-12433:
Godinho and Murphy show that triangulated categories with a linear generator are far more rigid than expected, in a 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Triangulated categories organize objects and triangles that play the role of exact sequences in much of modern algebra and geometry. The authors introduce the notion of a linear generator, a single object with special control over the category.

Their main result is an equivalence between a completed cluster category of one Dynkin type and the perfect derived category of a given differential graded algebra. The equivalence respects the suspension functor and keeps triangles with at least two indecomposable terms. More broadly, a linear generator lets them describe every indecomposable object. It also lets them determine the key triangles and bound the Rouquier dimension by one. Every triangulated category with a linear generator is equivalent to a thick subcategory of the cluster category in their main theorem.
arxiv-2510-12933:
Hunter, Kwan, Sauermann, and Sawhney bound a failure probability for random sign matrices in this 2025 arXiv paper. Take a square matrix filled with independent random plus and minus ones. Its corank measures how many dimensions short of full rank it falls. Mathematicians have long studied how likely a large shortfall is, since near-singular random matrices test deep ideas in probability.

The authors prove that the probability of the rank dropping by at least a given amount decays exponentially in the product of the matrix size and that amount. The decay carries a fixed positive constant. Earlier results reached this only when the shortfall grew slowly, or through separate geometric arguments covering part of the range. Their bound holds across the whole range, and they note the proof ideas may extend to broader entry distributions using known techniques.
arxiv-2510-13233:
Mukherjee, Hazra, and Vats build Bayesian methods for mixed-type spatial data in this 2025 arXiv statistics paper. Modern spatial datasets often record several response types at each location: a binary indicator here, a count there, a continuous measurement elsewhere. Popular spatial mixed-effects methods handle only single response types, and joint models are rare.

Their approach places latent multivariate Gaussian processes beneath the observations, yielding a Bayesian model class that works for any combination of exponential family responses. To escape the computational bottleneck of Gaussian processes at many locations, they use a Vecchia approximation enabling fast posterior inference and prediction. They establish identifiability and covariance structure theoretically. Inference runs through Markov chain Monte Carlo with elliptical slice sampling inside a blocked Gibbs scheme. Simulations and a joint model of United States wildfire counts and burnt areas demonstrate the method.
arxiv-2510-13333:
Pacaud and co-authors solve security-constrained power flow on GPUs in this 2025 arXiv paper. Grid operators must choose generator dispatch that stays feasible not only normally but under hundreds of contingency failures. That is a huge nonlinear optimization called security-constrained AC optimal power flow. Standard solvers can take hours on realistic corrective versions with complementarity constraints modeling operator actions.

Their algorithm builds on an augmented Lagrangian method for nonlinear constraints whose subproblems are solved by an interior-point method. The augmented Lagrangian term steadies the Newton systems inside that solver. This enables a pivoting-free factorization that parallelizes on GPUs. The method tolerates infeasible or complementarity-laden models. Their code, MadNCL, solved a five hundred bus case with two hundred fifty-six contingencies fully on the GPU in under three minutes. A leading commercial solver needed over three hours.
arxiv-2510-13433:
Elumalai and co-authors build a pipeline that probes what visual neurons respond to, directly in three dimensions. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses a flaw in standard methods, which search over flat pixel images. Pixel searches mix shape, pose, and lighting together, so single factors stay hidden. The brain, by contrast, reads the world as three-dimensional scenes.

Their method renders deformable meshes and adjusts them to excite a chosen neuron most strongly. Mesh changes are shaped by radial basis functions, which keep the forms smooth and regular. The result is a most exciting input defined in 3D, not in pixels. Applied to models of monkey area V4, the pipeline probes tuning for pose and lighting. V4 is a visual brain area known for shape and material sensitivity. The work links inverse graphics with systems neuroscience in one tool.
arxiv-2510-13533:
Guo and co-authors measure how often fast X-ray transients occur and how bright they get. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses the latest catalogue from the Einstein Probe telescope, launched in 2024. The probe has caught hundreds of these brief, intense X-ray flashes. Their physical origins remain unclear, so rates and brightness patterns are key clues.

The team applies a model-free, non-parametric method to the catalogue data. They find strong brightness evolution across cosmic time, rising steeply with redshift. After correcting for that trend, the local brightness distribution follows a broken power law. The local formation rate comes out near twenty-eight events per cubic gigaparsec per year, with wide error bars around that value in the authors' estimate. That rate resembles the rate of low-luminosity long gamma-ray bursts. The match supports a link, with most transients tied to collapsing massive stars.
arxiv-2510-13733:
Asselah, Silvestri, and Taggi drive a classic cluster growth model with branching random walks and find a sharp change with dimension. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies internal diffusion limited aggregation, where particles spawn at a centre and settle at a cluster's edge. In the classical version the growing aggregate settles into a spherical shape. Replacing plain walks with branching ones changes the growth mechanism entirely.

Here each particle can split into offspring as it wanders, since the branching is critical, balanced between dying out and exploding. The authors prove a spherical shape theorem holds in dimension three and above. In dimensions one and two, no such spherical limit exists, they show. Worst-case deviations from the sphere are bounded by polynomial terms in both regimes. That polynomial behaviour, they expect, is a genuine feature of the branching model. The paper pins down exactly where the geometry flips.
arxiv-2510-13933:
Tianxiang Yang and co-authors present a method for recovering facial animation controls from images, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Animators drive digital faces with rigs, sets of controls based on the Facial Action Coding System, which catalogues facial muscle movements. Rig inversion works backwards, estimating which control settings produced a given face, a task usually done by hand.

Their framework reads two kinds of input at once: ordinary color images and normal maps, which encode surface direction as color. Separate transformer networks process each input type, and the combined features predict 102 rig parameters. Tested on synthetic faces and on scanned real faces, the method carried over to the scanned data. It produced faithful reconstructions. The dual input seems to help the system generalize beyond its training images.
arxiv-2510-14033:
Iryna Dubovets'ka and Mykhailo Moklyachuk study optimal estimation for periodically correlated stochastic processes observed through additive noise, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A periodically correlated process has statistical patterns that repeat on a fixed cycle, like daily or seasonal rhythms. Estimating its unknown values from noisy observations is a recurring problem in signal processing and time-series analysis.

The authors target linear functionals, weighted combinations of the process's unknown values. They give formulas for the mean-square error and the spectral characteristic of the optimal linear estimate. Two situations are covered: when the spectral densities are known exactly, and when they are unknown but confined to a given class of allowed densities. For the second case, they derive the least favorable densities, the worst in the class, and the minimax spectral characteristics. Together these define a robust estimate. It guards against the least cooperative spectrum allowed.
arxiv-2510-14533:
Sharma and Lau, writing on arXiv in 2025, study how quantum learning methods can grow beyond toy problems. Their test case is the traveling salesman problem, which asks for the shortest route through a set of cities. Training a quantum policy on large versions is usually out of reach. So methods trained on small versions often fail when the problem gets bigger.

The authors use equivariant quantum circuits, circuits that respect the symmetry of reordering the cities. That symmetry lets settings trained on a small city count transfer directly to larger problems with no retraining. They also derive new generalization bounds for this transfer setting. The bounds include a term for how different the small and large problem structures are, which caps the expected loss in performance. In experiments, policies trained on small problems kept strong performance on larger ones, and improved further with a little fine-tuning.
arxiv-2510-14733:
Cheshire, Armstrong, and Tan report, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a spectroscopic census of young star clusters that tests how such clusters come apart. They took spectra of more than six hundred candidate baby stars in the clusters NGC 2264 North and South, Collinder 95, and Collinder 359, using an instrument on the MMT telescope. Emission and lithium absorption marked the true young stars, and satellite data supplied their motions and positions.

The team confirmed 354 young stars in the NGC 2264 pair, 130 in Collinder 95, and only 7 in Collinder 359. Comparing two clocks, traceback ages from the stars' motions versus ages from stellar models, gave opposite lessons. In NGC 2264 the motion ages run younger, suggesting the clusters stayed bound for a few million years before expanding. In Collinder 95 the motion ages run much older, implying many of its stars were never part of one compact group.
arxiv-2510-15233:
Amitesh Badkul and Lei Xie work on making AI predictions say honestly how uncertain they are, a need that sharpens in drug discovery. Their 2025 arXiv paper focuses on predicting how strongly a drug candidate binds to a protein, where lab noise varies and new chemicals differ from training examples. Most uncertainty tools either miss their promised coverage, give intervals too wide to act on, or fail to grow when errors grow.

Their method, TESSERA, routes each case through a mixture of expert models and then calibrates the spread with conformal prediction, a technique that guarantees coverage under stated assumptions. In tests with both ordinary and deliberately shifted data splits, TESSERA hit close to its promised coverage while keeping intervals tight. It also posted the best balance between coverage and width among strong rivals. The authors pitch it for choosing which drug candidates deserve costly follow-up testing.
arxiv-2510-16133:
Daniel Sainati, Joseph W Cutler, Benjamin C Pierce, and Stephanie Weirich tackle strictness. Strictness is a trait of code that decides which inputs a function must have before it can run. Knowing strictness lets lazy languages, which delay work until it is needed, run fast instead of slow. Yet strictness at the source level is hard to pin down and easy to misjudge.

The authors give a sharper sense of strictness that tracks how each input gets used, not just whether it is used. They build type systems around it for two styles of running code, and they prove the types match real run-time use. A bridge also moves code safely from one style to the other, keeping its strictness notes intact. All proofs were checked by machine in the Rocq proof tool, so the claims rest on more than hand-waving.
arxiv-2510-16333:
Junha Song and four co-authors challenge a lazy assumption about multimodal language models: that their skill comes from the words side alone. These models pair a text brain with a vision encoder, the part that actually sees. The team asks how the last training phase, plain fine-tuning versus reinforcement learning, reshapes that seeing part.

On strongly visual question tests, reinforcement learning pulls clearly ahead of fine-tuning. Probes from image sorting to segmentation show why: learning by reward builds stronger, sharply placed visual features inside the encoder. The authors distill this into a recipe, PIVOT, for training vision encoders by preference signals. A PIVOT encoder beats bigger, costlier rivals inside full models while using under one percent of the usual training compute. The result points to cheap, targeted training as the way to sharpen machine sight.
arxiv-2510-16433:
Tatsuya Shirai leads five co-authors in a 2025 study of fuzzing, a way to hunt bugs by feeding odd inputs to code. Many teams now fuzz in short bursts each time code changes. The group asks what this steady fuzzing truly finds. They pull logs from OSS-Fuzz, a free fuzzing service run by Google.

The logs cover about 1.12 million runs across 878 projects in total. Many bugs sat in the code before steady fuzzing even began. Reach into new code kept growing as runs went on, and new reach led to new bugs. The findings give teams a clear view of what non-stop fuzzing buys them.
arxiv-2510-16533:
Eilene Tomkins-Flanagan, Connor Hanley, and Mary A. Kelly present a new coding tongue in a 2025 paper. Their tongue, Doug, makes each typed program halt in polynomial time. Polynomial time means run time grows in a tame, power-like way. Doug's types and terms are coded as points in a learned space. That space comes from vector-symbolic codes, which pack facts into long number lists.

Doug reworks a known light linear tongue with strict use rules. Its slot-value code lets near points hold near types in sense. Types can thus be learned by a neural net, not just set by hand. The team links skill gains to program search in this tongue. Fast skill gains, at a human pace, are the long goal.
arxiv-2510-16733:
M. Q. Dong, working with five co-authors, proposes a new kind of material in a 2025 physics study. The material joins two orders that usually fight each other inside one substance. One order is electric, meaning charges can line up and stay put. The other order is magnetic, meaning electron spins follow a set pattern.

The authors couple a fractional form of the electric order with a newer magnetic pattern. Flipping the electric order then flips the spin pattern in a linked way. Computer models point to real candidate materials, including manganese telluride. That material keeps its magnetic order near room temperature. The team also designs a memory junction switched by voltage alone. Such control could cut the power used by future spin-based electronics.
arxiv-2510-16933:
Matyáš Brabec, Jiří Klepl, Michal Töpfer, and Martin Kruliš test AI coding help in a 2025 paper. CUDA is the language used to program graphics processors. Fast CUDA code needs expert knowledge of parallel patterns. The team asked whether top reasoning models can write it well.

Models produced code for well-known tasks, then received graded hints. Automatic checks measured correctness and speed gains. Human reviews added a closer look at code quality. An interactive mode let models fix their own earlier mistakes. The models proved to be skilled coders overall. Still, only with tutoring did they match expert-written speed. The study maps which optimizations models find alone and which need guidance.
arxiv-2510-17033:
Leixu Huang, Zedian Shao, and Teodora Baluta expose a tension in federated learning in a 2025 paper. Federated learning trains one model across many separate data owners. Watermarks hidden in training text can later prove data came from someone. Such marks are called radioactive when they survive training detectably.

The authors confirm the marks do survive joint fine-tuning strongly. Even a small watermarked share left a confidently detectable signal. Trouble comes when the central server turns hostile. Watermarked updates look like outliers beside ordinary updates. A server filtering outliers for robustness erases the watermark too. Every tested radioactive watermark failed against that filtering server. Provenance, robustness, and usefulness now look fundamentally in tension.
arxiv-2510-17433:
Astronomers have always reasoned from incomplete data, but the tools for that reasoning have changed beyond recognition. Rafael S de Souza, Emille E O Ishida, and Alberto Krone-Martins trace that history in a short invited review. Rather than listing every advance, they pick out the milestones that reshaped how astronomers draw conclusions from observations, from early fitting methods to the present day.

The story moves from classical optimisation to Bayesian inference, which weighs prior knowledge against new data, and then to gradient based methods powered by deep learning. De Souza and his co-authors close with adaptive models that now shape which data get gathered in the first place. They argue that grasping this shift is essential for reading modern astronomy and judging where the field is heading.
arxiv-2510-17633:
Models that listen as well as read face a safety gap: harmful requests spoken aloud slip past defences tuned on text. Weilin Lin, Jianze Li, Hui Xiong, and Li Liu present SARSteer, a defence for large audio language models that works at inference time, without retraining. Text based steering methods fail on audio because the model inner activations for sound sit far from those for text, while prompt based defences refuse too many harmless spoken requests.

SARSteer steers the model toward refusal using signals derived from text, leaving the audio input untouched, and carves away part of the safe response space to curb over-refusal. Lin and his co-authors report that the method raised refusal of harmful spoken queries while preserving answers to benign ones. They release their code and data sets with the paper.
arxiv-2510-17733:
Tong Chen and four co-authors work on a common flaw in language models. Models often state false claims that their training data never supported. The authors call this extrinsic hallucination, meaning invented facts beyond the source. Past fixes often weakened writing quality or other skills.

Their method rewards a model only when its whole answer is correct. A retrieval step checks the answer against outside sources first. On open-ended writing, false claims fell by about thirty-nine percent. On short questions, the model learned to say it did not know. Math, code, and instruction tasks kept their earlier quality levels.
arxiv-2510-17833:
Ángela López-Cardona and four co-authors review whether brains and language models represent the world alike. The team examined twenty-five brain imaging studies from recent years. All used functional MRI, which tracks blood flow during tasks. Two guiding hypotheses shaped the review's questions.

One hypothesis says improving models converge toward one shared world representation. The other says middle layers of a model hold the richest features. Evidence across the studies supported both ideas. Brain and model patterns seemed to share abstract structure. The authors argue the findings justify deeper work on brain-model alignment.
arxiv-2510-18033:
Matthew Thoms, Hao Sun, and Laurent Karim Béland grade thirty-four computer models of nickel against a broad test suite. Nickel is a workhorse metal, and the models that mimic its atoms vary in style and age. Their automated suite checks forty-seven measures, from basic crystal traits to defects, grain boundaries, and step edges.

Most models nailed lattice size, stiffness, and surface energy. Accuracy fell for migration barriers and for atoms squeezed very close together. A pattern analysis grouped the measures that move together. Materials teams get a clear shopping guide for picking a nickel model that suits the job at hand.
arxiv-2510-18433:
Yuanhe Guo and his seven co-authors release ImageGem, a data set built from real use of a generative image platform. The data cover about fifty-seven thousand users who together built roughly two hundred forty-two thousand customized model add-ons, wrote three million text prompts, and created five million images. Such detailed records of what individual users actually like have been missing, and that gap has slowed work on models tuned to personal taste.

With these preference records, the team trained better models for predicting what a user will favor. They also tested personalized image search and model recommendation for single users. Finally, they built a full framework that edits a customized image model inside its internal weight space so its output matches one person's preferences, opening a new path for personal image generation.
arxiv-2510-18633:
Roxana Petcu and her six co-authors improve evidence gathering for hard questions. Their target is retrieval-augmented generation systems. Such systems split a request into sub-questions. They fetch documents for each one. They then merge the results into an answer. Fetch too broadly, and noise and cost pile up. Fetch too narrowly, and key material is missed. The authors frame that tension as a balance. One side explores new sub-questions. The other exploits ones already proving useful.

Framed so, the task becomes a bandit learning problem. Each fetched document updates a belief about a sub-question's value. That belief guides the next choice. Several bandit methods were tested. Judging relevance from rank data and human judgments worked best. Document-level precision rose by about thirty-five percent. A ranking quality measure rose by about fifteen percent. Long-form answers downstream improved as well.
arxiv-2510-18733:
Ruolin Liu, with Jerome Quintin and Niayesh Afshordi, shows how a quantum theory of gravity could produce the inflationary early universe and then hand control back to Einstein's theory. Their setting is quadratic gravity, a theory that stays well behaved at very high energies. Quantum corrections make its couplings drift with energy scale, and that drift, they find, can drive a slow-roll inflation phase as the universe cools toward lower energies.

When enough matter fields feed into the running, the predicted pattern of primordial fluctuations can match current cosmological observations, in a regime where the older Starobinsky model has fallen out of favor. As inflation ends, the theory nears strong coupling, so general relativity must emerge as the effective description for reheating. Avoiding that strong coupling regime sets a floor on the predicted gravitational wave signal, a testable consequence.
arxiv-2510-18833:
Hassan Manshouri and Moslem Zarei study decoherence from Bremsstrahlung. That is the radiation a charged particle emits when deflected. Decoherence limits quantum sensors and interferometers. Its mechanisms deserve exact treatment. The authors use quantum field theory tools. They build on the quantum Boltzmann equation. The model covers fermions and photons in a Stern-Gerlach interferometer. That device splits atomic beams by spin.

From the model they extract the dephasing factor. It says how much coherence the radiation carries away. A check against classical Bremsstrahlung confirms the method's accuracy. The framework is offered as an advance in decoherence studies. Quantum sensing could apply it directly. Atomic interferometry could apply it too. In both fields, uncontrolled dephasing is the main enemy of precision.
arxiv-2510-19033:
Andrew Anderson and four co-authors report a field study of over-the-hood inclusivity bugs in user-facing artificial intelligence products. Beyond hidden bias in data or algorithms, the visible design of a product can shut out users whose problem-solving style differs from what designers assumed.

Three product teams applied an existing inclusive design method, not built for artificial intelligence, to hunt for such barriers. They found six kinds of inclusivity bugs unique to these products and fixed them. The study shows teams a practical way to spot who a product quietly excludes before release.
arxiv-2510-19133:
Geonhee Han, Andrew Gelman, and Aki Vehtari speed up scenario analysis for real-time Bayesian election forecasting. Forecasters blend polls with economic and political indicators, as in a collaboration with a major magazine, but testing what-if changes normally means refitting the whole model. This is too slow on election night.

Their meta-modeling strategy walks through a family of posterior meta-models with a sequential sampling scheme, so tweaks to priors, data, or settings can be explored without full refits. Analysts can trace how sensitive a forecast is to each input while the race is still unfolding, and explain those dependencies to readers.
arxiv-2510-19233:
Haonan Wang, Ying-li Zhang, and Teruaki Suyama propose that collapsing bubbles in the early universe made primordial black holes with nearly one single mass, possibly forming all of the dark matter. Their two-field model couples the inflaton to a second field so that the energy gap between false and true vacuum peaks during inflation, when most bubbles form.

After inflation the gap reverses and the bubbles collapse into black holes. Tuning the model yields a sharply peaked mass distribution. This could describe dark matter black holes, lighter sub-solar ones, or supermassive ones, all without extra power enhancements that other models require.
arxiv-2510-19433:
Nika Mlinarič Hribar, Matjaž Depolli, and Gregor Kosec study how wind averaging distorts estimates of how much current a transmission line can safely carry. Dynamic thermal rating promises extra capacity when wind cools a line, but utilities average wind readings over minutes, and the way that average is taken can bias the cooling estimate.

Using one-second wind data from a Slovenian line, they compare vector and hybrid averaging against the high-resolution truth. Averaging shifts both the heat transfer measure and the allowed current significantly, with the error depending strongly on the angle between wind and line. Grid operators should treat averaging as a modeling choice, not a detail.
arxiv-2510-19533:
