Clio Johnson and three co-authors use quantum Monte Carlo calculations to map the energies of two-dimensional Fermi fluids made of dipolar atoms. Fermionic cold atoms in optical traps can simulate correlation effects in electronic systems. The atoms here interact through a repulsive dipolar force that softens at short range.

The team fits formulas to fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo data for both one-component and two-component fluids, expressing the energy as a function of density. Within the ranges studied, itinerant ferromagnetism proves unstable whether or not the interaction is softened. The fitted formulas are meant to support density functional studies of real, non-uniform cold atom experiments.
arxiv-2510-19733:
M. H. I. Abdalla and four co-authors present Zhyper, an efficient way to steer a large language model toward a stated culture, political outlook, or other text-specified conditioning. Prompting alone cannot guarantee the model behaves as asked, because pretraining biases push back. Earlier fixes fine-tuned LoRA adapter weights directly for each conditioning, at a large parameter cost.

Zhyper instead uses a factorized hypernetwork that generates context-aware LoRA adapters from a written description of the desired conditioning. On multiple benchmarks it matched leading baselines while using up to twenty-six times fewer parameters. Extended to cultural alignment, it generalized better to settings outside its training domain and captured finer-grained contextual values.
arxiv-2510-19833:
Shiva Meucci revisits Fresnel's 1818 derivation of the drag coefficient for light moving through moving transparent matter, a result interferometry later confirmed exactly. Fresnel built his argument on a mechanical picture that Meucci argues was workable but mislabeled: where Fresnel said density, the mechanics, in his reading, says compliance. A single constitutive calculation then yields the full first-order coefficient.

The coefficient, Meucci shows, contains two laws that history fused together: Fresnel's non-dispersive share law and the resonance law Lorentz derived and Zeeman confirmed. He argues the resonance law is universal mechanics, appearing even in sound in bubbly liquids, while the share law depends on the medium carrying its own response. A documentary history traces how the two laws were conflated from Fresnel to Zeeman.
arxiv-2510-19933:
Egor Shulgin and three co-authors supply the missing theory for the Muon optimizer as it is actually used in training large neural networks. Muon's update depends on orthogonalizing a matrix, which practical implementations approximate quickly, for instance with a few Newton-Schulz steps; all earlier theory assumed the exact, intractable version. The authors analyze the inexact update inside a general oracle-based optimization framework.

Their error model gives explicit bounds on how performance degrades as the orthogonalization gets sloppier. A practical coupling emerges: lower precision demands a smaller step size but larger momentum, so the approximation budget must be tuned together with the learning schedule. Experiments training a small GPT model confirm the predicted shifts in optimal learning rate.
arxiv-2510-20033:
David Dukić wrote this doctoral thesis on adapting pre-trained neural language models for sequence labeling. Sequence labeling gives each token in a text a label. The work focuses on transfer learning, which reuses knowledge from prior training for new tasks. Its test cases include event trigger detection, spotting words that signal an event.

Dukić offers three linked improvements. One adds a signal from a separate, domain free text system inside a shared multi-task model. A second changes the model layout so information can flow both ways across layers. That change targets autoregressive models, which normally read in one direction. A third uses guided learning in context plus response based tuning. Together, the results argue that careful adaptation brings out the best labeling results.
arxiv-2510-20233:
Sven Buder and five co-authors ask whether the Milky Way Splash population was heated by the galaxy last major merger or was already born on hot orbits. Splash stars have disc-like chemistry but halo-like motion, often read as proof of violent heating of an early disc. Using a high-resolution simulation of a Milky Way analogue, they trace birth positions, ages, and present-day orbits of the stars.

The protodisc stars in the simulation were already born moving on dynamically hot orbits, with only limited extra splashing despite a major merger. A subset near the solar neighborhood shows merger-driven redistribution of angular momentum, but the overall pattern changes little. The authors suggest the Splash mainly reflects a turbulent early disc.
arxiv-2510-20633:
Satoshi Nishimoto studies clusters of linked spins called multi-magnon bound states in a one dimensional chain where two kinds of exchange pull in opposite ways. Working alone, he uses a large matrix method to map how stable these clusters are across magnetic field strength and the balance between the two exchanges.

Nishimoto measures binding energy for clusters of growing size and compares the near saturation results with known two magnon formulas. He finds a clear order in which cluster sizes win out, a quick drop in stability near a key balance point, and stronger binding below full saturation in some cases. The map gives labs a guide for tests on thin magnetic chains.
arxiv-2510-20933:
Moin Safdar leads six co-authors on a network for medical image segmentation that joins focal modulation with two way feature fusion. Precise outlines of organs and lesions guide diagnosis and treatment plans, so border accuracy has direct clinical weight.

Convolutional networks read only local patches and struggle with global context, while transformers capture wide links at higher cost. The proposed design aims to keep both strengths, sharpening focus on relevant regions while fusing features in both directions across scales. The goal is cleaner borders on structures of varied size and shape, tested on medical segmentation tasks where small errors change care decisions.
arxiv-2510-21133:
Divyanshu Kumar leads four co-authors on quantifying chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear risk in ten leading commercial language models. A new two hundred prompt risk set and a subset of the FORTRESS benchmark are attacked with a three tier methodology.

Deep inception style attacks succeed far more often than direct requests, exposing shallow filtering, and safety performance varies dramatically between models, from near total refusal to wide exposure in the reported figures. The first comprehensive comparison of its kind gives regulators and labs a shared scale for dual use risk in frontier systems.
arxiv-2510-21733:
Jia-Huei Ju and three co-authors enrich a public data set of hard research questions with finer-grained relevance labels. The Researchy Questions collection holds about one hundred thousand real queries. Their answers sprawl across several aspects of a topic. Each query is already split into sub-questions by a language model. Yet nothing records which documents answer which sub-question.

The team uses a seventy-billion-parameter open model as judge. It labels every sub-question against the documents users actually clicked. That manufactures the missing associations at scale. The augmented data set is training ground for retrieval systems that serve complex needs aspect by aspect. Such supervision could teach search engines to cover all parts of a research question. They would no longer settle for its easiest facet.
arxiv-2510-21833:
Ngoc-Bao-Quang Nguyen, Tuan-Minh Do, Cong-Tam Phan, and Thi-Thu-Hong Phan compare ways to sort waste from photographs. Automated recycling systems depend on that step. Rather than testing one method, they benchmark three families side by side. The families are classic machine learning on hand-built features, deep networks, and a hybrid of the two.

The tests used three public datasets. In one of them, the team corrected forty-three wrong labels. The hybrid won consistently across all three. Deep networks pulled out the image features. Classic classifiers such as support vector machines made the final call. Scores were near perfect on two sets. Trimming the feature list by over ninety-five percent kept accuracy intact. It also sped up training and use, a useful trait for cheap sorting hardware.
arxiv-2510-22033:
Tianxiang Wang, Yingtong Ke, Dhananjay Bhaskar, Smita Krishnaswamy, and Alexander Cloninger adapt a transport-based embedding to single-cell data. Each patient is a cloud of thousands of cells, not a tidy row of numbers. Comparing such clouds across patients is the heart of the problem. Accurate black-box tools hide the biology doctors want to read.

Linear Optimal Transport flattens each cloud into a fixed-length vector. The distributional shape is kept. Any two patients' cells are also lined up against each other. Within that space, the team reports classification of COVID-19 patient states. The classification is accurate and interpretable. The classifier's weights point back to meaningful cell populations. The framework aims to keep the geometry of the data without surrendering readability.
arxiv-2510-22833:
Skilled humans get faster and use less effort with practice. AI agents rarely do the same. Adrian Orenstein leads a team with four co-authors. In 2025 they test agents that reason about their own compute. Agents see compute cost. They can choose when to spend it.

Tests run in the Arcade Learning Environment. That suite holds classic video games. With the same training budget, such agents did better. They won on three quarters of games. They also used three times less compute on average. Per game analysis shows where savings arise. The work hints at more energy efficient agents.
arxiv-2510-22933:
Inyoung Cheong, Patty Liu, Dominik Stammbach, and Peter Henderson ask where AI could truly help public defenders in the United States. Defenders carry heavy caseloads with few resources, yet AI research rarely starts from their daily work. The team spoke at length with 17 defense professionals across the country.

From those talks they map defense work into five parts, from digging into evidence to planning strategy. Interviewees pointed to tasks where AI could lift routine load, and to ethical limits it must not cross. The study gives builders and courts a grounded view of help that respects clients and counsel.
arxiv-2510-23433:
Anti Maria Aader, Viktor Abramov, and Olga Liivapuu extend Lie algebras to ternary structures built on cube roots of unity. They define a ternary Lie algebra at cube roots of unity, using omega-symmetry where omega is a primitive cube root. A method for constructing ternary associative algebras is developed alongside.

For ternary algebras they introduce the ternary omega-associator and omega-commutator. If a ternary algebra has associativity of the first or second kind, its commutator structure yields the new Lie-type algebra. The work opens a branch of algebra where operations take three inputs at once, with possible links to physics symmetries.
arxiv-2510-23533:
Joel Johansson and thirty-three co-authors report the discovery of SN 2025wny, an exploding star seen through a gravitational lens. A foreground galaxy bent the light of a distant background galaxy, and follow-up imaging resolved four separate images of the supernova. Spectra from the brightest image place the event at a redshift just above two, deep in the early universe.

The team classifies the event as the first gravitationally lensed Type I superluminous supernova ever found. Comparing its brightness with similar unlensed events gives a magnification between twenty and fifty for the brightest image. The find shows that ground-based telescopes can catch lensed supernovae much farther away than once assumed. Such events also open a window on dwarf galaxies and offer a route to measuring cosmic expansion through time delays.
arxiv-2510-23633:
Xun Su and a co-author present a new way to solve linear inverse problems — recovering a clean signal from blurred or partial measurements — using pretrained diffusion models. These models can fill in missing content, but steering them with the measurements is a balancing act. Push the data in too hard and the generation breaks; push too softly and the answer ignores the measurements.

Their method, Noise Combination Sampling, builds the best noise vector from a whole noise subspace, chosen to mimic the measurement score. That crafted noise replaces the usual noise term in the diffusion process, so the conditions enter naturally, with no step-by-step tuning knobs. The method plugs into many existing solvers, even image compression, and shines when few generation steps are allowed. Tests show better results with almost no extra computing cost, plus improved stability.
arxiv-2510-23933:
Cheongho Han and fifty-nine co-authors hunt for pairs of brown dwarfs using gravitational microlensing, the brightening of a background star when a foreground object passes before it. From the 2023 and 2024 seasons, they select events with sharply resolved caustics and short timescales under nine days. Tiny angular Einstein radii complete the fingerprint of a low-mass binary lens.

Six candidate events survive the cuts. Modeling gives precise values for the event timescale and Einstein radius, and a Bayesian analysis turns those into mass estimates for both components. In four events, both components most likely sit in the brown dwarf range. In the other two, the lighter partner is probably a brown dwarf while the heavier is likely a low-mass M dwarf star. The verdict can be sealed later with high-resolution images taken once lens and source have drifted apart.
arxiv-2510-24333:
The BESIII Collaboration, a team of 708 authors, tests CP symmetry in the neutral decays of the lambda baryon using data from the BESIII detector. They analyze about ten billion J/psi events through a full angular study of a decay chain ending in neutral pions. CP symmetry predicts that a particle and its antiparticle decay in mirror fashion.

They measure the decay parameters for lambda and antilambda neutral decays with the best precision yet for this channel. The combined CP asymmetry comes out near zero, consistent with symmetry, within small statistical and systematic errors. Ratios to the charged decay parameters are also reported, tightening tests of fundamental symmetry in baryon decays.
arxiv-2510-24633:
Mingyue Liu and Andrew Cropper study logic based machine learning, where a rule set is learned from facts. Most such tools train once and keep just the last rule set. Their twist is to save the rule sets made along the way, not throw them out.

They then join those saved rule sets, weighting each by how short and neat it is. Tests on game play and image thought tasks raised right calls by four points on average. The extra cost was less than one point of added run time. So one training run can give a group gain that once took many runs.
arxiv-2510-24733:
Richard Csaky, the sole author, wrote a thesis on reading brain waves logged from outside the skull. The work uses two such log types, from scalp wires and from magnet fields near the head. It asks what the brain does when a person sees a sight or thinks words in silence.

One part of the thesis builds new deep learn ways to read such logs. It starts with plain line models for one person, then moves to group reads that face wide gaps between people. Spread of the logs, within and across people, is a core theme in both parts. The last part tests the new reads on real tasks.
arxiv-2510-25333:
Yilong Lai led six co-authors on CRMWeaver. Yipin Yang, Ting Liang, and Jialong Wu helped. Zhenglin Wang, Jianguo Lin, and Keping Yang followed. Their 2025 paper builds a business agent using language models. Business agents answer user needs through tool calls. They query databases and internal knowledge bases. Tasks range from statistics to knowledge questions.

CRMWeaver trains agents with synthetic data and reinforcement learning. That helps the model handle complex data relationships. Varied and mixed tasks become easier to manage. At inference time, the agent uses shared memories. It learns from guidelines in similar past problems. That improves performance on unseen scenarios as well. Tests used the CRMArena-Pro data set. Their lightweight model reached competitive results there. Scenarios covered both business-to-business and business-to-consumer work. The authors stress practical value for real applications.
arxiv-2510-25533:
Bastian Castorene led four co-authors on critical engines. Martin HvE Groves, Francisco J Pena, and Eugenio E Vogel helped. Patricio Vargas closes the five-author team. Their 2025 physics paper presents an analytical approach. It covers critical two-isothermal engines from quantum Stirling cycles. Ground-state level crossings shape those cycles at low temperature.

Reversible heat exchange is governed by structural entropy change. Internal energy remains constant during that exchange. A Primarch Formula gives an exact quasistatic expression. It links extracted work and efficiency to degeneracies. Engines reach Carnot efficiency without a classic regenerator. Thermal excitations reduce ideal work and efficiency. Exact numeric runs validate the approach overall. A one-dimensional antiferromagnetic Ising model is applied. Profound connections to number theory appear there. Fibonacci-Lucas degeneracies govern the engine work scaling. Three distinct work-scaling regimes are identified. Carnot efficiency is attained in all regimes.
arxiv-2510-25733:
Livia Ferro, Ross Glew, Tomasz Lukowski, and Jonah Stalknecht study ABJM loop geometry. Their 2025 physics paper investigates BCFW geometry for loop integrands. ABJM theory loop-level geometry uses lightcone geometries. Dual space lightcone geometry admits a natural fibration. One loop variable lives in a fiber over lower loops. Varying lower geometry leads to half-chamber definitions.

L-loop half-chambers keep half the next fiber unchanged. A full classification and surprising bijection are provided. N-point L-loop half-chambers correspond to Feynman diagrams. Those diagrams belong to a cubic scalar theory. The scalar theory has half as many particles. Summing half-chambers computes the ABJM amplitude directly. That sum corresponds to scalar amplitude diagram sums. Loop fibers realize those Feynman diagrams geometrically. Half-chamber expansion equals loop-level BCFW recursion, they argue. Chambers emerge as intersections of two half-chambers. Concrete examples illustrate the construction.
arxiv-2510-25833:
Charlotte L. Jackson leads six co-authors in a study of about one hundred thousand quasars, the bright centers of young galaxies fed by black holes. They ask how disc winds, outflows from the feeding disc, relate to radio jets, black hole mass, and feeding rate. Their data combine Sloan survey spectra with low frequency radio measures from the LOFAR Two Metre Sky Survey.

Jackson and the team split quasars into radio loud and radio quiet groups and match them by mass and feeding rate. Jets form most readily for very heavy black holes or fast feeders. Wind signs and jets tend to oppose each other, a link they tie to differences in the light each quasar emits.
arxiv-2510-25933:
Nissan Yaron, Dan Bystritsky, and Ben-Etzion Yaron present a small language model that they report matches a much larger model on factual grounding. Their model, named Humains-Junior in the record, has three point eight billion parameters and is tested on the FACTS Grounding public set, which checks whether answers stay tied to given sources. They compare it with GPT-4o under the same judges on five hundred questions.

Scores for the two models differ by less than one percentage point, and a formal equivalence test passes at a five point margin. Their method adds directed reasoning scaffolds, called exoskeleton reasoning, plus fine tuning that teaches protocol discipline rather than facts. The two parts together gave a large gain and lower variance.
arxiv-2510-26133:
Yuanhao Yan and Li He study when averaged Taylor sums converge in higher order weighted Dirichlet spaces. These are spaces of analytic functions where size is measured with derivatives and a weight. Fejer theorem guarantees that Cesaro means, averages of partial sums, converge in the Hardy space, but that comfort generally fails in Dirichlet type spaces, especially at higher order.

Yan and He show that plain Taylor partial sums are not uniformly bounded in these spaces and may diverge in norm. They restore convergence with modified polynomials whose coefficients are adjusted by a weight array, under mild conditions. A coefficient correspondence principle and a local Douglas formula carry the proof, and explicit formulas follow when the weight is a finite sum of point masses.
arxiv-2510-26533:
Adrien Weihs, Andrea L Bertozzi, and Matthew Thorpe extend a learning method built for hypergraphs. A hypergraph links items in groups, not just in pairs, which suits data where ties come in bunches. Their method, higher-order hypergraph learning, enforces smoothness at several scales using powers of the hypergraph's Laplacian, a matrix that encodes its links.

Weihs and his two co-authors prove that a trimmed version of the method stays consistent, meaning it settles toward the right answer as data grows. They also give explicit rates for that settling when it is used in fully supervised learning. Tests in active learning, where the method picks which items to label, went well. So did tests on data with no underlying geometric shape, which the authors take as a sign of range and robustness.
arxiv-2510-26633:
Colin Doumont, Victor Picheny, Viacheslav Borovitskiy, and Henry Moss unify the tools used to search structured spaces. Bayesian optimization picks the next test point in a search by modelling the unknown function, and it needs kernels, similarity measures suited to the space. For combinatorial spaces, such as molecule designs or program layouts, several kernels exist with unclear relations.

Doumont and his three co-authors build a unifying frame from heat kernels, derived in a systematic way with simple closed forms. They prove many known combinatorial kernels are heat kernels in disguise, or close kin, and their experiments back that claim. Heat kernels also avoid a known weakness: some rivals fade when the best point lacks a certain structure. A fast pipeline built on them matched or beat slower, complex rivals.
arxiv-2510-27033:
Simindokht Jahangard, Mehrzad Mohammadi, Abhinav Dhall, and Hamid Rezatofighi address spatial reasoning for robots that must find objects by description. Vision-language models perceive scenes well but often miss fine spatial relations, since they reason from correlations in images alone. The team's neuro-symbolic framework pairs neural perception with explicit symbolic reasoning to model those relations directly.

One module detects entities and their attributes from both wide images and three-dimensional point clouds. A second module builds a structured scene graph that supports precise, readable queries. On the JRDB-Reasoning dataset, the approach proves more accurate and reliable in crowded, human-built spaces. Its light design suits robots and embodied systems that must act on what they find.
arxiv-2510-27233:
Victor Miguel Banda Guzmán, Rubén Flores Mendieta, and Johann Hernández ask how often a basic crash makes particles quantum-linked, in a 2025 study. The crash is pion-pion scattering, where two pions, light particles made of quarks, bounce off each other. The link is entanglement, a tie where each particle's state mirrors the other's. They study the tie after fixing the outgoing paths.

Using a standard low-energy theory of strong forces, with one round of corrections, they build a way to score the link. Most starting states end up linked, acting like the two- or three-level units used in quantum computing. The link is strongest just above the energy threshold and near a right-angle bounce. One channel of the strong force drives most states toward strong links.
arxiv-2511-00233:
Rayehe Karimi Mahabadi, Jianfeng Lu, and Hossein Salahshoor tackle a math problem that appears in materials science and game theory. Some hard problems become easier when each point is replaced by a spread of possible values, an object called a Young measure. The catch is computing that spread well, and the authors turn to deep neural networks for the task.

Their trick rewrites the spread as the push-forward of a simple bell-shaped distribution. A network then learns the map that does the pushing, guided by a loss built from the original problem. Worked examples show the method in action. The authors hope it opens a practical route for the many fields that use Young measures.
arxiv-2511-00433:
Sachin Ballal and Tushar Halder study orderings of special subgroups inside finite groups. A subgroup is automorphic when some symmetry of the whole group maps the group onto it in a matching way; collecting one representative per class gives a set that can be ordered. Tarnauceanu had earlier studied the parallel poset of isomorphic subgroup classes and posed open questions, one of which this work takes up.

The authors define a partial order on the automorphic classes and prove structural results for two families. For dihedral groups and for generalized quaternion groups, the resulting poset is a distributive lattice, a well-behaved grid-like order. They also characterize every class of finite groups for which the poset collapses into a simple chain. The work extends a tidy corner of subgroup lattice theory.
arxiv-2511-00533:
Yi Jiang, Chenglin Wang, Yibin Xiao, Jian Zhang, and Shihui Zhu return to the Hartree equation with a harmonic potential. The model has particles interacting through a smoothed, averaged field while sitting in a trap. They focus on normalized ground states, the lowest-energy states at a fixed total mass, and ask the dynamic questions: do such states always exist, are they unique, and are they stable?

A mass-energy constrained variational approach confirms a ground state exists for every prescribed mass. Strict convexity of the energy functional then gives uniqueness, ruling out rival ground states of the same mass. Finally, the Cazenave and Lions argument proves orbital stability: nudge the ground state slightly and it stays nearby, orbiting rather than flying apart. The trio of results completes the basic theory for this trapped Hartree model.
arxiv-2511-01033:
Tiberiu Musat and colleagues investigate induction heads, a circuit pattern inside transformer models that helps them learn from context. Induction heads copy and complete patterns seen earlier in the input, and they are thought to be a key mechanism behind in context learning.

Working with a minimal task and a modified two layer transformer, the team finds the weight matrices that implement an induction head have a simple, interpretable structure. They prove training dynamics stay inside a nineteen dimensional subspace of the parameter space, and in practice only three dimensions account for the head's emergence. Inside that small subspace, the time until the head appears grows quadratically with context length, a tight bound they establish.
arxiv-2511-01333:
Muhammad Ahmed Mohsin and colleagues estimate wireless channel state information for fast changing channels, where user motion, Doppler spread, and multipath reflections keep rewriting the channel's statistics. Accurate channel knowledge is needed for next generation systems. But pilot based estimation is costly. Deep learning methods also degrade when pilot patterns shift.

Their pilot aided framework uses a flash attention transformer. It joins model driven pilot acquisition with data driven reconstruction, attending over patches. Training uses a physics aware loss. That loss enforces phase alignment, correlation consistency, and smoothness in time and frequency. Under a standard 3GPP setup it beat classical and recurrent baselines by a wide margin in error, with lower bit error rates, while cutting pilot overhead sixteen fold.
arxiv-2511-01433:
Seunghun Yu, Youngjoon Lee, Jinu Gong, and Joonhyuk Kang shrink what federated Kolmogorov-Arnold networks must communicate. Federated learning trains across devices without centralizing data, and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, which learn spline functions on their edges, are attractive there for their interpretability. Extending their grids to model complex functions, though, inflates the messages devices must exchange.

Their compressed grid variant sparsifies the extended grid and transmits only the essential coefficients, staying inside a communication budget. In communication constrained settings it reached up to about thirteen point six percent lower prediction error than a fixed grid version. The authors also derive a theoretical upper bound on the method's approximation error.
arxiv-2511-01733:
Jiaxuan Li, Jenny Greene, Shany Danieli, Scott Carlsten, and Marla Geha count the satellite galaxies of a dwarf galaxy, DDO 161, and find far too many. Satellite counts test the standard cosmology and galaxy formation physics at small scales, but dwarfs' own satellites were largely unexplored, since they are faint and hard to confirm.

DDO 161 is an isolated dwarf about 6 million parsecs away. The team's systematic search found eight satellite candidates inside its projected virial radius, and surface brightness fluctuation distances from deep Magellan imaging confirmed three new ones. With a previously known companion, DDO 161 hosts four confirmed satellites above the stated mass threshold, the richest system known around a dwarf. Compared with the TNG50 simulation and standard galaxy-halo models, its abundance far exceeds all current expectations.
arxiv-2511-01833:
Ming Li and eight colleagues benchmark a new skill in artificial intelligence: thinking with images. Here a model actively creates and manipulates pictures as part of its reasoning. It crops, transforms, and inspects them with tools mid-thought, as OpenAI's o3 does. Older benchmarks barely test this; the common Visual Search test asks only for localization and cropping.

TIR-Bench spans 13 diverse tasks, each demanding novel tool use for image processing inside the reasoning chain. The authors evaluated 22 multimodal language models, open and proprietary, including some with explicit tool-use training. Every model found the benchmark hard, and the results indicate that strong scores require genuine thinking-with-images ability rather than static visual skill. A pilot study comparing direct fine-tuning with agentic fine-tuning rounds out the report.
arxiv-2511-01933:
Iryna Golichenko, Oleksandr Masyutka, and Mykhailo Moklyachuk solve an estimation problem for random fields that vary over time and across a sphere. Their field is periodically correlated in time and isotropic in space. It is spread evenly over a unit sphere. It is observed only in the past. Worse, it is seen only through a second, uncorrelated noisy field added on top.

The task is optimal linear estimation, extrapolation, of functionals of the field's unknown values. When the fields' spectral densities are known exactly, the authors derive formulas for the mean square error and the spectral characteristics of the best estimate. When the densities are not known, only a class of admissible ones, the picture changes. The authors identify the least favorable densities. They also find the minimax, robust spectral characteristics. The estimate is thus protected against the worst case the class allows.
arxiv-2511-02033:
Andrei Zaitsev, a mathematician working in probability, sharpens a classic question about sums of many random quantities. The central limit theorem says such sums behave nearly like a normal distribution, and earlier work bounded that closeness using the Wasserstein transport distance. Zaitsev studies bounded random vectors with zero mean and asks how the bound depends on the bounding value.

His main result is a stronger and more precise estimate, using a transport cost that grows exponentially with distance between the two distributions. He also extends the result to distributions whose cumulants grow slowly, a class he introduced in earlier work. A final section discusses whether the same approach can work in several dimensions.
arxiv-2511-02133:
Suyang Li, Fernando Fajardo-Rojas, Diego Gomez-Gualdron, Remco Chang, and Mingwei Li built a visual tool for metallurgists searching vast spaces of possible alloys. Designing an alloy with several functions means juggling composition, structure, and properties at once, but existing software shows only flat projections and gives little help with trade-offs or sensitivity. Their system, AlloyLens, combines several coordinated views in one interface.

A scatterplot matrix, dynamic sliders, gradient-based sensitivity curves, and nearest-neighbour recommendations work together to expose hidden structure in simulation data. Users can see how a small composition change shifts properties locally, and what compromises appear when no exact match exists. Case studies developed with domain experts cover structural, thermal, and electrical alloy design, and the tool received an honourable mention in a visualisation contest.
arxiv-2511-02233:
Songyang Liu, Yunpeng Tan, and Shuai Li build a training system that restores the depth perception laparoscopic surgery takes away. Operating through a flat, monocular camera view, trainees often misjudge where their instruments are, which can lead to ineffective or unsafe movements. Dry-lab models and recorded videos give few depth cues, so the team built their framework inside the NVIDIA Isaac Sim simulator.

Trainees keep working from the standard two-dimensional clinical view, preserving the real operative perspective. In the background, validated AI modules locate the instruments and detect contact with tissue, and when a spatial misjudgement is detected, synchronised three-dimensional feedback appears through a mixed-reality interface. The training covers navigation, manipulation, transfer, cutting, and suturing, and cases that look identical in flat view become distinguishable once the added depth context is shown.
arxiv-2511-02433:
Stefan Mihai, Florin Stoican, Martin Monnigmann, and Bogdan Ciubotaru speed up a control technique that works out its decisions offline. In explicit model predictive control, the controller's response is worked out in advance for every region of the state space. Enumerating those critical regions, though, grows exponentially with system size and prediction horizon. When constraints have the shape of boxes or zonotopes, the feasible set has a compact description as a constrained zonotope, and that structure can be used.

The team reformulates the multi-parametric problem in the lifted generator space of that representation and solves it through second-order optimality conditions. Low-rank matrix updates cut the computing time, and listing the candidate active constraint sets produces the explicit solution as a tree. The geometric reformulation, rather than brute force, is what makes larger explicit controllers workable.
arxiv-2511-02533:
Hortence Nana, Andreas Athanasopoulos, and Christos Dimitrakakis rethink college admissions as a fairness problem. In many-to-one matching, each college admits many students, and the twist here is that colleges judge sets of students through nonlinear utility functions that reward diversity within the admitted class. Under that twist, the authors show, the classical stable matchings that anchor matching theory may simply not exist.

Their alternative follows the philosopher John Rawls: judge an outcome by its worst-off participant, and maximise the minimum utility across colleges. Deterministic and stochastic algorithms iteratively improve the lot of whichever college is currently worst off, offering a practical route to fair allocation when stability cannot be guaranteed. The paper positions Rawlsian objectives as the right design principle for matching markets where institutions care about the composition of the whole class, not just individual rankings.
arxiv-2511-02733:
Jeremy Booher, Steven Groen, and Joe Kramer-Miller classify a subtle invariant of certain algebraic curves in characteristic two. They study Galois covers where one curve wraps another twice, and ask what Ekedahl-Oort type the upper curve can have. That type encodes how the curve's cohomology splits into pieces.

When the base curve is ordinary, the answer is clean: the type is fully fixed by the genus of the base and the ramification of the cover. For a general base, they prove bounds driven by the base curve's own type and the ramification. Along the way they build a theory of enhanced differentials of the second kind. That tool lets them work with de Rham cohomology directly through differentials, in any characteristic.
arxiv-2511-02833:
Abhishek Panigrahi, Bingbin Liu, Sadhika Malladi, Sham Kakade, and Surbhi Goel tackle teacher choice in knowledge distillation, where a big model generates data to train a smaller one. Picking the best teacher for a given student and task usually means costly trial and error. Their 2025 paper proposes GRACE, a light score of how well a teacher will suit a student.

GRACE reads properties of the student's gradients and needs no verifier, teacher internals, or test data. It ties, through information theory, to the stability of gradient methods, which governs how well students generalize. On GSM8K and MATH, GRACE matched later student scores with up to 86 percent rank correlation. Students trained on the GRACE-picked teacher gained up to 7.4 percent over those given the strongest teacher by default.
arxiv-2511-02933:
Andy Dimnaku, Abdullah Yusuf Kavranoglu, and Yaser Abu-Mostafa propose a training method that teaches vision models known invariances directly. Standard data augmentation shows a model altered copies of images, but the lesson stays indirect. Their 2025 method, generative hints, uses a generative model to make fresh unlabeled images that follow the training data's pattern.

On those virtual examples, extra objectives force the model's answers to obey known rules, such as staying the same when an image shifts. Training mixes normal labeled learning with these hint losses in a semi-supervised way. Across data sets, network types, and invariance kinds, the method beat standard augmentation. Gains reached 2.10 percent on fine-grained photo tasks and averaged 1.29 percent on the CheXpert medical images.
arxiv-2511-03333:
Y Alipour Fakhri extends a geometric model of direction-dependent superconductors by adding an outside control field. The base model blends Finsler geometry, where length depends on direction, with the Ginzburg-Landau picture of superconductivity. The control field shifts the geometry inside its tangent space, deforming the core energy rule in a controlled way.

Fakhri proves the new energy keeps the traits that make the math workable, including convexity and growth control. Controlled best states are shown to exist through variational arguments over allowed setups. Limiting cases as a small parameter fades are also treated. The setting gives theorists a rigorous way to ask how outside control might steer anisotropic superconducting behavior.
arxiv-2511-03433:
Arvid Siqveland rebuilds the notion of a scheme, the basic space of modern algebraic geometry, from pure category language. Earlier books by the author built schemes for associative algebras from formal moduli of simple modules. For ordinary commutative rings, local behavior at maximal ideals can play that moduli role instead.

The categorical definition reached this way matches Hartshorne's classic one exactly. Building sheaves from presheaves through projective limits sits at the heart of the construction. The author argues that core results of scheme theory then flow more naturally. A cleaner foundation can help learners and may ease moving scheme ideas into wider algebraic settings.
arxiv-2511-03733:
Pratham Gandhi's thesis presents HACI, a glove-plus-web tool that lets visually impaired students feel and hear their code. Introductory programming leans heavily on visual layout, leaving blind learners without cues sighted peers take for granted. HACI pairs a light web editor for JavaScript with an Arduino-driven glove carrying six small vibration motors.

Touch signals mark navigation, structure, and errors while audio carries detail, aiming to keep mental load low. Design principles, build details, and an early evaluation with learners fill the thesis. Tasks covered span reading, summarizing, editing, and debugging code without sight. Tools like HACI press computer science education toward equity by design rather than by afterthought accommodation.
arxiv-2511-03833:
Christian Kuehn and Giacomo Landi compare two continuum accounts of Kuramoto-type interacting particle systems. The continuum limit tracks particles pointwise, while the mean-field limit follows a typical particle, and the two equations differ in structure despite both assuming infinitely many particles.

Solutions of one equation can be generated from solutions of the other, the authors first show. Their main result then proves that the unstable manifold of the homogeneous steady state in the continuum limit is the direct analogue of the famous Ott-Antonsen manifold in the mean-field limit. That direct link clarifies a long-standing puzzle about how the two reduced accounts relate in time.
arxiv-2511-03933:
Joshua Renner and eight colleagues present Back-Propagation Counting, a new way to count electrons for direct electron detectors in electron microscopy. Single-electron counting improves signal quality, but at high fluence several electrons can strike one pixel and standard counting breaks down.

The method borrows machine learning tools built for large tensor operations yet needs no large training dataset. On synthetic data it counted multiple strikes per pixel and stayed robust as occupancy rose. On real data it reconstructed diffraction peaks from single nanoparticles with higher relative intensity and produced images with better contrast than a standard method. High-flux movies and diffraction work stand to benefit most.
arxiv-2511-04233:
Yaara Jahn and Orit E Raz improve the Elekes-Ronyai bound for how large the image of finite grid sets under a multivariate polynomial must be. The bound holds unless the polynomial has a special degenerate form. Earlier results handled two and three variables, and a general bound gave growth with exponent three halves for set size.

A new notion, the rank of the polynomial, sharpens the estimate. When rank is at least three, the image grows with a higher exponent that depends on rank, improving the prior bound for those polynomials. An application lower-bounds the number of distinct volumes spanned by point configurations. Expansion phenomena of this kind sit beneath many incidence geometry arguments.
arxiv-2511-04333:
Federico Pirola, Fabio Stella, and Marco Grzegorczyk propose full Bayesian learning of dynamic Bayesian networks from incomplete intensive care data. Such networks model how patient variables evolve together while staying readable for clinicians, but missing-data methods borrowed from static networks ignore time, weakening uncertainty estimates where they matter most.

Each missing value becomes an unknown parameter with a Gaussian spread inside a Gibbs sampling scheme. Unobserved values are drawn from their full conditional spreads at every pass, giving principled filling-in and uncertainty in one pass. Simulated and real-world tests check the method. Trust in intensive care models depends on honest temporal spread, which this framework is built to supply.
arxiv-2511-04433:
F. Tavecchio, writing alone, asks where the TeV gamma rays from quasar 3C273 come from. The VERITAS telescopes recently detected very-high-energy emission from this famous bright quasar. Its timing and spectrum do not match the beamed glow of the inner jet seen before.

Tavecchio proposes that the rays form far out, along the kiloparsec-scale jet. There, electrons boosted by shear in the flow scatter light up to extreme energies. The same electrons could explain the puzzling X-ray knots that Chandra saw in large jets. If right, the model links two long-standing puzzles of quasar jets in one picture.
arxiv-2511-04733:
M. Tristram leads ten authors combining three cosmic microwave background datasets in one analysis. Data come from the Planck satellite, the Atacama Cosmology Telescope, and the South Pole Telescope. A unified likelihood models the sky signal, foregrounds, and instrument effects together.

Galactic and far-off foregrounds are fit jointly rather than assumed away. The team also averages over foreground template choices to cut hidden bias. Core cosmic parameters stay remarkably stable under those changes. Extension parameters prove more sensitive, with larger error bars, a useful honesty check for claims beyond the standard model.
arxiv-2511-04933:
Sarif Khan, Jinsu Kim, and Pyungwon Ko join two topics in one frame: cosmic inflation driven by a dark Higgs field, and dark matter made of dark photons. Both parts rest on a dark force added to the known model of particles.

The team studies a case with low reheating, where much dark matter forms as the hot early cosmos reheats and its share is then diluted. They scan both weakly and feebly linked cases against lab, collider, and sky data. Dilution lets feeble cases use stronger links, which may soon be in reach of tests.
arxiv-2511-05133:
Urslla Uchechi Izuazu and co-authors propose a secured form of intent-based networking, where users state what they want and the net sets itself up. That trust is a weak spot: a man-in-the-middle can alter an intent before it runs and force bad settings.

Their system adds a data-driven guard that spots tampered intents, with time-aware checks. It aims to tell true user aims from hostile edits before the net acts on them. The work names a blind spot in self-driving nets and offers a shield for the path from user words to network acts.
arxiv-2511-06033:
Zihui Zhao and co-authors fill in missing depth in camera depth images by teaching spatial and frequency views to correct each other. Depth cameras using time-of-flight or structured light leave holes where reflections are weak or shadows fall. Most completion methods work only in the image domain and ignore the physics of raw depth data.

Missing regions change the image's frequency pattern, the authors note. Their framework treats amplitude and phase spectra with a dedicated fusion module. Spatial and spectral features are compared in one shared space, and each refines the other step by step. On two standard indoor data sets the method beat the previous best by a clear margin in accuracy.
arxiv-2511-06833:
Zhenjie Liu and four co-authors present ConsistTalk, a system that animates a still portrait so it appears to speak given audio. Video diffusion models have improved such talking-head creation, but results still flicker, drift away from the person's identity, and fall out of sync with the voice. ConsistTalk attacks all three problems together.

An optical-flow module separates motion from static appearance to cut flicker. A distilled audio-to-intensity model converts sound and facial speed into a frame-by-frame intensity sequence, giving fine control over how strongly the face moves while staying matched. Finally, a noise search at creation time enforces background coherence and motion continuity. Tests show clearer identity preservation and steadier, higher-quality video than earlier methods.
arxiv-2511-06933:
Christof Schötz studies how to compute a trustworthy average for data that live in curved metric spaces rather than on a number line. Transformed Fréchet means generalize the classic Fréchet mean, which minimizes squared distances, by applying a transformation to the distance first. Choosing the transformation interpolates between the median and the plain mean, and includes power means and the Huber mean.

Schötz proves finite-sample error bounds in expectation under minimal assumptions, reaching the parametric convergence rate with fewer than two finite moments. A subclass of these estimators has a breakdown point of one half, the strongest robustness possible, meaning half the data can be corrupted before the estimate fails. The results hold in general Hadamard spaces, including infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and nonpositively curved geometries, and yield new insights even in plain Euclidean settings.
arxiv-2511-07533:
Andrew Boyle, Luke Bouma, and Andrew Mann hunt for lost sisters of the Pleiades. Star clusters slowly dissolve, scattering siblings across hundreds of light years. After a hundred million years, linking scattered stars back to their birth cluster grows hard because ages blur.

Rotation rates from the TESS telescope plus motions from Gaia feed a Bayesian method that reunites diffuse cluster remnants. Applied to the Pleiades region, the method reveals a dissolving complex of related groups. Spin periods act as clocks that confirm shared birth. The census rewrites how one famous cluster was born and how its family spread through the Galaxy.
arxiv-2511-07633:
Arya Bangun and colleagues sharpen microscope images that reveal electric fields inside materials. Four-dimensional scanning transmission microscopy records diffraction at every probe point, and the transport of intensity equation can turn intensity changes into phase. Thick samples scatter dynamically and break simple assumptions.

FlowTIE blends that physics equation with a learned flow representation of the phase gradient. Physics priors steady the neural network where data alone would drift. Simulations of crystals show better accuracy than classical and optimization methods, with faster runs. Reliable phase maps help materials scientists read charge, strain, and fields in thick real-world specimens.
arxiv-2511-07733:
Kosuga, Matsui, and Diamond ask when heat bursts inside a fusion plasma escape into its edge. Experiments hint that avalanches of heat cross the separatrix into the scrape-off layer, widening the heat load that walls must bear. A reduced model turns that hint into a testable threshold.

Avalanches penetrate when their temperature gradient at the separatrix beats a critical value set by the parallel heat flow time. Strong avalanches steepen until they shock at the boundary, then spill through. The drive for steepening correlates with penetration as predicted. Fusion designers need that criterion because edge heat spreading decides wall survival in reactors.
arxiv-2511-07833:
Chanakya Ekbote, Vijay Lingam, and Sujay Sanghavi extend group-based reinforcement learning to code that improves over several rounds. Standard GRPO learns from one prompt and one answer, but real coding agents read error feedback and revise. Single-turn training wastes that loop.

MURPHY builds rollout trees where failed attempts branch into feedback-conditioned retries. Retrospective credit assignment then decides which earlier choices deserve blame or praise for later success. Self-correcting generation becomes the training target itself. Code assistants that debug their own work need exactly this multi-turn credit logic, since final success often redeems a flawed first draft.
arxiv-2511-08333:
Gary Greaves and Huu An Phan count congruence classes of characteristic polynomials for matrices whose entries are plus or minus one, taken modulo a power of two. The matrices are symmetric or skew symmetric with constant diagonal, and the exponent is at least three with size large enough. Their symmetric count resolves a conjecture posed by Greaves and Yatsyna in 2019, with the answer depending on whether the matrix size is even or odd.

Matching formulas are proved for the skew symmetric case as well. The main new tool is the lift graph or lift tournament, built for this problem. A walk polynomial for graphs supports the construction, showing the needed lift tournaments actually exist for the required sizes.
arxiv-2511-08533:
Sergey Matveenko and Nikita Rastegaev study a one-dimensional model of enhanced oil recovery, where a slug of water carrying dissolved chemicals pushes oil through rock. Their focus is the polymer flood case and a known gap that appears in solution curves near the chemical shock front.

Earlier work built partial solutions by switching to Lagrange coordinates and solving a simpler conservation law by the method of characteristics. The Jouguet principle was suggested to close the gap, but it had stayed a heuristic without proof. The authors pin down when the gap appears and justify the principle using a uniqueness theorem for conservation laws. They also add a second splitting step that makes the analysis easier.
arxiv-2511-08733:
Carlos Taveras, Santiago Segarra, and César Uribe shrink large graphs while respecting the geometry of optimal transport. Graph coarsening merges nodes to make huge networks manageable, and their approach measures the damage of each merge with a new distortion formula inside Gromov-Wasserstein geometry.

Two algorithms come out of the formula. Greedy Pair Coarsening merges the locally least damaging pair again and again until the target size is reached. Its sibling first clusters nodes by pairwise distortion and merges whole clusters at once. The authors state conditions under which the coarsening is provably optimal. Across six large datasets and a downstream clustering task, both methods beat existing approaches over wide ranges of settings.
arxiv-2511-08933:
Minjin Kim, Suyeon Son, and Luis Ho measure how quasar light flickers across years, using repeated spectra of about ninety thousand active galactic nuclei from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Pairing observations across epochs yields roughly two million comparisons, enough to build a statistical structure function for how much brightness changes over time.

Splitting the sample by black hole mass, luminosity, and Eddington ratio shows the flicker depends chiefly on luminosity and rest-frame wavelength once each factor is isolated. The variability timescale grows with both, close to what the standard accretion disk model predicts. At short wavelengths, though, the wavelength exponent drops well below the prediction, a three to four sigma tension. The authors read that as a sign the disk's radial temperature profile may be steeper than the standard model assumes.
arxiv-2511-09133:
Ritsu Sakabe and three co-authors test whether language models get Japanese humor, using Oogiri, the improvisational comedy game of answering absurd prompts with wit. Earlier humor benchmarks graded jokes on a single funny-or-not scale, which flattens everything interesting about why a line lands.

The team expands existing Oogiri collections with new sources and model-generated replies, then annotates everything by hand on five-point scales. The six dimensions are novelty, clarity, relevance, intelligence, empathy, and overall funniness. Models generate at a level between low and mid-tier humans but show a marked empathy deficit. Their judging also diverges from human judging in kind: models reward novelty first, humans reward empathy. The authors release the corpus to push conversational systems toward emotional intelligence, not just cleverness.
arxiv-2511-09233:
Jia-Bin You, Jian Feng Kong, and Jun Ye borrow tensor networks from quantum physics to forecast chaotic systems. Chaotic dynamics, like weather-like flows, resist long prediction because small errors grow quickly. Their tensor network model packs correlations across time and scales into layered bundles that stay readable.

Tested on the Lorenz and Rössler systems, the model rebuilds short-term paths and truly captures each attractor's shape. It forecasts well beyond several Lyapunov times, a useful horizon under chaos. Uneven parametrization of the weight tensors improves convergence, and accuracy levels off at modest bond sizes, matching the attractors' low intrinsic dimension. The authors position tensor networks as a general tool for data-driven modeling of complex dynamics.
arxiv-2511-09333:
Roland Becker and five co-authors present a practical route to goal-oriented error control in biomechanical simulations. Instead of refining a mesh everywhere, the dual weighted residual method gauges error in one user-chosen quantity. The mesh then refines only where that quantity needs it.

The chapter shows the method fits current engineering practice for biomechanics. The setting is general on purpose, covering complex shapes, nonlinear tissue models such as hyperelasticity, and fluid-structure coupling. Multi-goal versions, targeting several outputs at once, are also covered. Numeric tests back the work. Adaptive refinement sharpens relevant predictions without wasting effort on regions that barely affect the answer.
arxiv-2511-09433:
Brian Rogers and five co-authors introduce a method for finding what a generative model has failed to capture in its internal representations. Learned representations bury useful factors of variation, and analysts need them exposed for annotation, discovery, and filtering. Their approach, called What We Don't C, works by deliberate removal.

Built on latent flow matching, the method disentangles latent subspaces by explicitly deleting information already present in the conditional guidance. What remains is a residual representation where uncaptured factors become easier to access. The authors show guidance along the flow path necessarily represses the guiding variables' own information. They frame the technique as a simple tool for analyzing, controlling, and repurposing representations in data-rich sciences.
arxiv-2511-09633:
Madhumita Sarkar and four co-authors report the first lab observation of dynamical freezing in programmable Rydberg atom arrays. Freezing should keep a driven quantum system from absorbing energy, preserving engineered states for long times. Real arrays, though, contain extra interactions that open heating channels and shrink the freezing regime.

The team worked with arrays of up to one hundred atoms in one and two dimensions. Single-frequency driving produced strong freezing, but only in a narrow window. A perturbative Floquet analysis pinpointed the microscopic heating processes at fault. Modulating both detuning and Rabi frequency together cancels those absorption pathways, they show. The dual control greatly broadens the freezing regime across varied array geometries.
arxiv-2511-09833:
Lequan Lin and nine co-authors propose ACT, a data annotation pipeline in which language models label data and also judge labels with critical thinking. Human labeling is costly, while model-only labels still trail human quality. In ACT, model annotators and model judges flag the most suspicious cases, and human effort goes only to reviewing those.

The pipeline works across language, vision, and multimodal tasks using multimodal models. From empirical studies the authors derive seven insights, turn them into practical guidelines. Analyze how to adjust the training loss so models trained on ACT data perform like models trained on full human labels. Tests cut the performance gap below two percent on most benchmarks while saving up to ninety percent of human cost.
arxiv-2511-10233:
Jianghan Zhu and seven co-authors help neural routing solvers cross from tidy synthetic maps to messy real delivery problems. Neural combinatorial optimization shines on uniform random instances but degrades on real vehicle routing benchmarks. Their system, EvoReal, uses an evolutionary module guided by large language models to synthesize training instances whose structural statistics mimic genuine real-world cases.

Pre-trained solvers are then adapted in stages: first aligned to the enriched synthetic distributions, then fine-tuned directly on benchmark instances from TSPLib and CVRPLib. The staged adaptation markedly improved generalization across problem scales. Remaining gaps to optimal solutions shrank to about one percent on TSPLib and under three percent on CVRPLib, showing that realistic instance generation can substitute for scarce real training data.
arxiv-2511-10433:
S. M. Tschopp, H. Vahid, and J. M. Brader compare routes for computing how a fluid's density varies near surfaces and in external fields. Classical density functional theory gets profiles from a free energy functional. A rival force-based route uses a different equation, tied to the virial route of thermodynamics. The two routes can disagree, a tension known as structural inconsistency.

The authors build a third scheme from the Lovett-Mou-Buff-Wertheim equation and show it stays consistent with the compressibility route, like standard theory. Both their scheme and the force route can share one closure relation for pair correlations. That shared form opens the door to optimizing approximations so the disagreement between routes shrinks. Numerical tests cover two-dimensional particles with hard cores and repulsive or attractive tails.
arxiv-2511-10533:
Yuval Frid and Liron Barak work on a practical problem for particle detectors: telling real photons apart from neutral pions when their energy showers overlap inside a calorimeter. The overlap gets worse at high-luminosity colliders, where traditional shower-shape methods start to fail.

Using full detector simulations with finely segmented calorimeter cells, they benchmark three approaches: boosted decision trees and dense neural networks on shower-shape features. The third is a ResNet convolutional network that reads the raw cell energies. The ResNet clearly outperformed both baselines, and it improved further when given a soft scoring output and an auxiliary task of predicting the angular separation. The authors conclude that residual convolutional designs with physics-informed losses can substantially sharpen photon identification.
arxiv-2511-10733:
Arsenii Titov shares a set of model files that particle theorists need to simulate a leading extension of the Standard Model. The framework, called nuSMEFT, adds right-handed neutrinos to the effective field theory of known particles, and testing it at colliders requires machine-readable versions of its interactions.

The release provides FeynRules and UFO model files covering operators up to dimension six that involve the right-handed neutrinos. A highlight is a UFO version of four-fermion operators with Majorana neutrinos that works with the MadGraph5_aMC@NLO event generator, built by adding auxiliary fields that do not propagate. All files are public in a GitHub repository, ready for phenomenology studies.
arxiv-2511-10833:
Sanchit Kabra, Shobhnik Kriplani, Parshin Shojaee, and Chandan K. Reddy introduce SURFACEBENCH, a benchmark for finding equations by machine, aimed at a gap in current tests. Existing benchmarks for symbolic regression mostly fit simple curves and grade answers by string matching or regression error. They cannot tell whether a discovered formula describes the same surface.

The benchmark holds 183 hand-built, science-inspired surface equations across fifteen groups, in explicit, implicit, and parametric forms. Each task names its symbols and gives sampled three-dimensional data. Grading combines symbolic sameness checks with distances between surfaces and error scores. Testing evolutionary, neural, and language-model-driven methods, the authors find none performs consistently across representation types. Language models show strong instincts for structure but shaky parameter calibration and multi-equation reasoning.
arxiv-2511-11233:
Huajian Zhang, Mingyue Cheng, and their colleagues present STaR, a slow-thinking model for reasoning over tables with large language models. Table reasoning matters for systems that have to read and analyze tabular data, but current methods reason shallowly and wobble from run to run. Shallow, implicit steps miss multi-step logic, and model uncertainty makes answers unstable.

Training runs in two stages: supervised fine-tuning on a self-verified data set, then reinforced fine-tuning with a difficulty-aware reward. A trajectory-level uncertainty score fuses token confidence with answer consistency to pick better reasoning paths. Wide experiments back the gains in depth and stability.
arxiv-2511-11933:
Karthikeyan K and three co-authors argue that language model agents should never touch sensitive data directly. The usual pattern, an agent writing and running code against a database, is a security incident waiting for a prompt. Their alternative forces all contact through a fixed set of secure, verified tools.

To test whether models can still do real analysis under that restriction, they introduce InData, a dataset of multi-step, tool-based analysis questions that demand composing tools, not just picking one. Existing benchmarks mostly check tool selection and single executions. Secure-by-design analysis will only be adopted if agents prove they can reason in steps while locked out of the raw data.
arxiv-2511-12133:
Qingyu Zhang and nine co-authors build AI-Salesman, a system for telemarketing dialogue driven by a large language model. Persuasive, goal-driven calls need planning over many turns and strict faithfulness to facts. Direct use of a language model tends to be brittle in strategy and prone to making things up.

The team first releases TeleSalesCorpus, a dataset grounded in real sales dialogue. Their framework then learns sales strategies from noisy calls with a Bayesian-guided reinforcement method, and at run time uses a dynamic outline agent that draws on a script library turn by turn. In automatic and human tests it beats baseline models.
arxiv-2511-12233:
Dongdong Zhao, Qiben Xu, Ranxin Fang and Baogang Song warn that deep hashing models can leak their training data. Deep hashing turns items into compact binary codes for fast search, but an attacker who can rebuild original data from those codes could forge biometric records or breach privacy. Attacks aimed at hashing models had not been studied.

Their framework, DHMI, is the first diffusion-based inversion attack made for deep hashing. It clusters extra data to build surrogate hash centers, then guides a denoising search with a score that mixes class consistency and closeness to target codes. Several surrogate models refine the candidates, aiming at high-fidelity reconstructions with clear semantic content.
arxiv-2511-12333:
Wei Jin and four co-authors build a Bayesian method for discovering causal structure from observational data when the graph may contain cycles and hidden confounders. Most causal discovery tools assume no hidden confounding and no feedback loops, yet real systems often break both rules. That mismatch can produce wrong causal stories.

Their framework, BayCausal, leans on identifiability results from independent component analysis with noise and on recent factor analysis advances to show the causal structure can be pinned down under mild conditions. A fully Bayesian learner then estimates it. Simulations show gains over leading alternatives, and an application to a women's HIV study gives interpretable, clinically meaningful findings.
arxiv-2511-12433:
Taekyun Kim and Dae San Kim work on degenerate versions of Bell polynomials, a family tied to counting set partitions with a deformation parameter. A recent Spivey-type recurrence for the fully degenerate case involved two-variable Fubini polynomials in a way the authors call unnatural. Their aim is a cleaner family with recurrences that fit its structure.

They introduce a new family under the same name, together with two-variable counterparts, and derive natural Spivey-type recurrences by operator methods. The results extend to r-counterparts, the fully degenerate r-Bell polynomials. For all the new families they give finite-sum formulas in the style of Dobiński, plus operator expressions.
arxiv-2511-12633:
Xunzhi Xiang and seven co-authors present a denoising variational autoencoder for images that fixes a hidden problem in high-dimensional latent spaces. A larger latent space rebuilds images more faithfully but can harm generation, and recent fixes lean on external foundation models. The authors first show that redundant high-frequency parts in such latents slow diffusion model training and degrade output quality.

Their spectral self-regularization suppresses that high-frequency noise while keeping reconstruction quality, with no external model needed. The resulting autoencoder uses a vision transformer backbone and produces cleaner latents, leading to better generation and faster convergence. A further spectral alignment step is introduced to strengthen the link between latent structure and generation.
arxiv-2511-12733:
Ahmed Hussain and four co-authors improve near-field beamforming, a technique that focuses radio energy at a specific distance as well as direction. Beams formed this way have sidelobes, stray energy lobes along both the range and angle axes, which invite interference and weaken detection. Taper methods borrowed from far-field design cannot suppress both kinds at once. The authors propose an amplitude taper based on the Slepian window, chosen to concentrate energy in the main lobe.

In simulations, their taper cut peak sidelobes by about twenty-four decibels sideways and ten decibels along the range axis, compared with a plain uniform window. Those are large margins in antenna engineering. The work is a short letter aimed at near-field communications and sensing, where focusing close to the array is the point. Better tapering means cleaner targets and fewer false echoes from sidelobe leakage.
arxiv-2511-12933:
D. B. Karki studies tunneling in quantum Hall circuits with several sites. At high transparency, one- and two-site circuits are well described by the simplest backscattering processes, which map them onto the boundary sine-Gordon model. Karki shows that picture fails for circuits with four or more sites: higher-order backscattering becomes important and changes the low-energy physics qualitatively, while three-site circuits sit exactly at the boundary case. Focusing on four sites, the paper builds an effective low-energy theory for the new regime.

Near the quantum-critical points that emerge, conductance and scaling take universal forms, and the associated non-Fermi liquid behavior is robust. Karki also treats multichannel circuits, showing the sine-Gordon description can be restored by looping selected edge channels. Heating effects are analyzed as well.
arxiv-2511-13233:
Jun Sashihara and 4 co-authors build a simulation of data marketplaces where buyers and sellers are language model agents. Real marketplaces trade datasets from third parties, yet how buyers, sellers, data, and rules shape each other is still poorly mapped. Each agent in the system holds clear goals and acts on its own.

Agents plan, search, buy, set prices, and update data while also guessing future demand. Tests compare purchase counts per dataset, per buyer, and repeat buys with patterns from real marketplaces. The language model system matched real trading patterns more closely than rule-based models and showed market trends forming over time.
arxiv-2511-13433:
Emmanuel Flachaire and Bertille Picard rebuild the Kitagawa-Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition of group gaps with machine learning tools. The classic method splits a mean gap between two groups into a part explained by observed traits and a part left unexplained. Results hinge on the reference outcome chosen, plus overlap and model errors.

Their version uses potential outcomes and extends a weighted reference approach with a doubly robust estimator. Neyman orthogonality and double machine learning let the method avoid trimming and guessing beyond the data. Two real examples show the gains in flexibility, though the authors warn that adding useless explanatory variables can still distort results under this reference choice.
arxiv-2511-13533:
Jeffrey Wen, Rizwan Ahmad, and Philip Schniter propose a minimax method for multi-target conformal prediction in imaging problems. Conformal prediction wraps a point estimate in an interval with a coverage promise, but most imaging work covers only one target at a time. Real tasks often need several targets covered jointly.

Their asymptotically minimax approach gives tight intervals while keeping the joint coverage promise across targets. They show how it fits blind image quality scoring with several metrics, multi-task uncertainty work, and staged measurement plans. Tests on synthetic and magnetic resonance imaging data beat existing multi-target methods, and code is public for reuse.
arxiv-2511-13933:
Alireza Fadakar and Andreas F. Molisch design a wireless front end that senses and communicates at once while sharing spectrum politely. Their framework merges cognitive radio with integrated sensing and communication, using a stacked intelligent metasurface mounted at a secondary base station. The surface learns beam patterns that locate a secondary user while keeping interference at primary users low.

An alternating optimization algorithm tunes the surface across all OFDM subcarriers, and a learning method modeled on neural network training refines it further with gradient steps. Numerical tests evaluate the full system. The goal is a programmable 6G front end that protects licensed users, losing them only a few percent of spectral efficiency.
arxiv-2511-14033:
Sun Han Neo, Sachith Seneviratne, and four co-authors speed up flood mapping with latent diffusion models. Detailed flood maps guide emergency planning, but physics-based simulators need fine grids and heavy computing, too slow for real-time use at large scale. Neural networks are faster yet often fail on regions they never trained on.

Their system, Flood-LDM, sharpens coarse flood maps into fine ones using a diffusion model, with physics-informed inputs added to guide it. Tests show fine-grid accuracy with far less inference time, plus stronger generalization to new locations than convolutional approaches. Transfer learning adapts the model to fresh regions quickly, suiting it for live flood risk management.
arxiv-2511-14133:
Jessy Xinyi Han and Devavrat Shah estimate how an intervention would change the timing of an event, not just whether it happens. Such when-if questions arise when treatments start at different times across units and records are censored. Their method, Synthetic Survival Control, builds a unit's counterfactual hazard path as a weighted blend of other units' observed paths.

To justify the method they set up a panel framework with low-rank structure, which classic parametric survival models naturally produce. Within it they prove identification and finite-sample guarantees for the estimator. A multi-country cancer treatment data set, where new therapies arrived in staggered fashion, serves as a quasi-experimental validation.
arxiv-2511-14233:
Wei Xiang, Ziyue Lei, Jie Wang, and five co-authors build a co-driver that warns about risks drivers have not noticed. Standard systems flag likely collisions but miss risky behavior in situations where nothing has crashed yet. Visionary Co-Driver combines video analysis with a large language model to spot potentially dangerous road users, and it watches the driver's own eye movements to judge what was actually seen.

Warnings appear on an adaptive head-up display, directing attention dynamically toward the missed hazard. A study with forty-one drivers confirmed the system improved risk perception and helped drivers recognize roadside dangers. The design treats attention, not just detection, as the bottleneck in road safety.
arxiv-2511-14433:
Diana C. Benjumea, Marie Farrell, and Louise A. Dennis present Safe-ROS, a plan that splits a robot's brain from its safety guard. One part runs smart control for the day-to-day work. A second part, the safety system, holds set safety tasks that can be checked with formal proofs. It watches for slips the first part might miss, much as guards work in other strict trades.

The team shows the plan on an AgileX Scout Mini robot at work in a nuclear site mock-up. One rule, keep clear of blocks in the path, was made into a safety task run by a thinking agent that halts the robot when it comes too close. The agent and its fit into the whole were both checked, and the set-up was tried in sims and in the lab.
arxiv-2511-14733:
Prakruti Sudarshan, Mario Flock, and three co-authors test whether starlight alone can carve ring patterns into planet-forming disks. Young disks often show bright and dark rings, and planets are only one possible cause. A flared disk lit by its star can turn unstable: lit regions puff up and throw shadows behind them, building a staircase shape.

The team runs detailed radiation hydrodynamics simulations with careful light transport to find when this thermal wave effect holds up. Starlight-driven shadows prove strongest under set conditions that the simulations map out. Knowing those limits helps observers judge whether a ringed disk truly needs a young planet to explain it.
arxiv-2511-15333:
Nayoung Oh and four co-authors present C2F-Space, a coarse to fine framework for grounding spatial instructions with vision language models. Grounding means locating regions described in natural language. Language models reason well about distance and relations, yet output coarse regions. Classic methods lack that complex reasoning altogether.

The framework first asks the model for a spatially consistent approximate region. A grid based prompt with a propose and validate strategy yields a valid ellipse region. Superpixel refinement then adapts that region to the local environment. The two stages combine semantic strength with fine spatial fit. Tests target instructions involving geometry and inter object relationships that defeat single stage methods.
arxiv-2511-15833:
Chengxi Zeng, Yuxuan Jiang, and Aaron Zhang distill a large video concept segmentation model into efficient on device students. The teacher unifies a vision backbone, a detector, and a dense memory tracker, which is too heavy for devices. Their progressive hierarchical distillation transfers capability in three stages. Stage design matches the teacher architecture piece by piece.

First the image encoder aligns features with prompt in the loop training. Next a compact Perceiver module replaces dense temporal memory. Finally the full pipeline fine tunes on official concept segmentation data. Student variants use three lightweight backbones for different budgets. The family aims to preserve concept level performance while enabling local video understanding.
arxiv-2511-15933:
Jiahe Wang computes Jordan constants for groups of volume-preserving Cremona maps. A Cremona group holds birational maps of projective space, maps that are rational in both directions. The Jordan property says every finite subgroup has a large abelian normal subgroup. The Jordan constant bounds the index needed, measuring how far the group is from abelian in finite pieces.

For the volume-preserving plane group, Wang shows the constant is exactly twelve. For the three-dimensional volume-preserving group he gives a bound of one hundred forty-four. He also gives a weaker geometric bound for the full plane Cremona group with no volume condition.
arxiv-2511-16133:
