LLRC learns mask weights that select singular values directly, in a fine-tuning-free setting. Training on a calibration set cuts more and more values while keeping internal activations close to the source model. At 20% compression on Llama-2-13B, it beat the STRS method on MMLU by 12%, BoolQ by 3.5%, and OpenbookQA by 4.4%. It also beat fine-tuning-free variants of SVD-LLM and LLM-Pruner across rates.
arxiv-2512-14433:
Alexandre Parriaux and five coauthors report a free running ring quantum cascade laser with a very narrow linewidth in a 2025 paper. The laser emits a single frequency mode near 7.7 micrometers, in the mid infrared, with no external stabilization.

Using a gas cell filled with nitrous oxide as a frequency to voltage converter, they measured the frequency noise spectrum and extracted the linewidth. The full width at half maximum sits close to 50 kHz at one second integration time. That is at least a sixfold improvement over state of the art quantum cascade lasers above 7 micrometers. They also show the laser works well for frequency modulation spectroscopy, opening high resolution metrology and spectroscopy uses.
arxiv-2512-14833:
Pallabi Dey, Debasish Banerjee, and Emilie Huffman map where a stubborn computing problem does and does not bite. The fermion sign problem blocks Monte Carlo methods, a main tool for lattice gauge theories with matter. They study a quantum link model, where gauge fields act like tiny spins tied to one flavor of fermions.

Gauss law splits the system into sectors, and only some sectors suffer from the sign problem. The authors find, for any number of space dimensions, which sectors can be simulated cleanly. The ground state sector is clean and matches a quantum dimer model with moving monomers. The usual zero charge sector is not clean, and matches a fully packed loop model instead. They also show how magnetic energy moves the system between sectors.
arxiv-2512-14933:
Caitlin Smith and three coauthors improve a way to film fluids moving beneath a solid layer. Their test setup layers clear plastic over water, a stand in for tasks like watching blood flow through bone or skull. Sound and light based imaging both struggle there, because waves bend sharply when they cross into the fast layer.

Their method, RC-DAS, corrects for that bending by enforcing Snell's law when it computes travel times. On bench phantoms with layers of different shapes, it tracked a slow drift of carbon microspheres at about 4 millimeters per second. Speed errors fell by 0.41 to 0.63 millimeters per second, and direction errors narrowed by up to 17 degrees. The work shows refraction correction is essential for honest flow measures in layered media.
arxiv-2512-15033:
Xidan Song and three coauthors argue that chess scores alone cannot show whether a language model truly reasons about the board. A model may match a strong engine like Stockfish on standard positions by memorizing common layouts. Their Geometric Stability Framework instead checks whether judgments stay consistent when the board is transformed.

The transforms include rotation, mirroring, color inversion, and format changes, applied to about 3,000 positions across six leading models. A paradox appeared: the top scoring model on plain accuracy, GPT-5.1, scored near the best, yet its errors surged by over 600 percent under rotation. Claude Sonnet and Kimi K2 stayed consistent across all transforms. Gemini Flash led at rejecting illegal positions, at 96 percent. The authors conclude stability is a separate, essential yardstick that exposes memorization dressed as reasoning.
arxiv-2512-15233:
Yi Zhang and four coauthors refine LoRA, the popular low cost way to fine tune big models, by confining its updates to empty space in the model's weights. Pretrained models have non trivial null spaces, directions their weights never use. Adapting inside a subspace can work as well as adapting everywhere, the authors note.

Their method, Null-LoRA, freezes parts of the low rank matrices to cut redundancy and raise effective rank. It then constrains the whole update to lie in the null space, so every added parameter serves the new task. Across image text retrieval and visual question answering tests, Null-LoRA beat the state of the art while using fewer parameters. The study shows that where an update lives can matter as much as how big it is.
arxiv-2512-15533:
Lorin Werthen-Brabants and Pieter Simoens turn a sampling based control method into an Ising machine problem in a 2025 paper. Model predictive control plans actions over a short horizon, and the path integral version samples many candidate action sequences. Probabilistic computers built on Ising models may run such sampling well.

The authors rewrite the control problem as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problem, which maps onto an energy landscape for Gibbs sampling from an Ising model. That framing lets the machine explore near optimal control paths efficiently. In tests, the Ising version tracks reference trajectories as accurately as a standard implementation. The work points to real time control uses in robotics and autonomous systems.
arxiv-2512-15633:
P. P. Avelino, A. R. Gomes, and D. A. Tamayo examine bulk viscosity as an alternative to dark energy in a 2025 paper. Bulk viscosity is a fluid's resistance to volume change, and it has been proposed to drive the speed up of cosmic expansion, both early and late. The authors test two physical origins for the effect.

One origin is nonminimal interaction between two fluids, the other is elastic collisions in an ideal gas. In the first case, getting the standard viscous tensor costs violation of all classical energy conditions. In the second, pressure stays non negative, too weak to drive acceleration. The results expose physical hurdles for viscous dark energy models.
arxiv-2512-15733:
Soufian Ben Amor, Alain Bui, and Guillaume Guerard model the smart grid as a complex system in a 2014 conference paper, later posted to arXiv. A smart grid must optimize power production, transmission, and use, yet its sheer complexity blocks any single global optimization. Modeling and simulation offer results that real world trials cannot afford.

Their context free model combines game theoretic and classical methods at different levels of the system. That mix keeps the optimization flexible and scalable while preserving generality. The approach suits grids that evolve in size, elements, and strategy over time, since the fundamental goals stay fixed. The work appeared at the DS-RT 2014 distributed simulation conference.
arxiv-2512-15933:
Dwip Dalal and co authors test whether multimodal language models can navigate real cities from visual input in a 2025 paper. Current benchmarks for embodied agents lean on language tasks or simulators, missing the knowledge heavy reasoning of real navigation. Their new task, sparsely grounded visual navigation, targets that gap.

The CityNav benchmark spans four global cities and over 50 decision points per route, with no annotations or special architecture allowed. Agents must localize from city cues and landmarks, reason spatially, and plan routes on their own. Leading models and reasoning techniques underperform badly. The authors' Verbalization of Path method, which probes the model's cognitive map of landmarks and directions, substantially improves success.
arxiv-2512-16033:
Qihao Wang and five co-authors study online shopping recommendations in an arXiv paper released in 2025. Most recommenders suggest single items, but stores also want to guess which product categories a shopper might enjoy next. Category-level hints can spark new interests, help shoppers with little history, and guide later item picks.

The team argues that simply reusing item-level models misses key differences between items and categories. They propose CCRec, a cascading model that uses a variational autoencoder to compress item-level signals before predicting categories. In experiments, CCRec beat methods built for item recommendation at the category task. The work shows that treating category choice as its own problem, rather than a side effect, gives better results.
arxiv-2512-16133:
Ren Nakagawa and six co-authors teach computers to spot cattle behavior in work posted to arXiv in 2025, accepted to WACV 2026. Knowing when grazing cattle interact matters for farm management, for example to detect when a cow is in heat. Interactions are rare, though, so there is little labeled data showing two animals acting together.

Their method, CattleAct, breaks each interaction into the separate actions of the two animals. It first learns an action space from a large data set of single-animal behavior, then fine-tunes that space with a few interaction examples so actions and interactions share one map. A working system combines video and GPS inputs. On a commercial-scale pasture, CattleAct detected interactions more accurately than baseline methods, and the code is publicly available.
arxiv-2512-16333:
Rawan Hoteit and four co-authors improve 3D printing control in an arXiv paper uploaded in 2025. Material extrusion printers lay down melted filament, and defects in that flow ruin parts and waste material. Feedback control can catch defects mid-print, but only if it tracks the target filament width accurately.

The team built a linear quadratic regulator that uses force feedback to track width precisely. On top of it, they optimize the reference force itself, accounting for how the controller behaves and for machine limits, so the closed loop gets the best possible target. Simulations showed faster, more accurate tracking. On a real fused filament printer, root mean square error improved by 39.57 percent versus the unmodified reference, and settling time shrank by 83.7 percent. The two-layer design squeezes more quality from the same hardware.
arxiv-2512-16433:
Maeve Madigan and five co-authors probe group AI for bias in their arXiv paper from 2025. Teams of AI agents deciding together can beat single models on prediction tasks. In high-stakes fields like consumer finance, though, biased group decisions mean regulatory breaches and real losses, and few methods exist to measure that risk.

Running large simulations across many multi-agent setups, with different ways for agents to communicate and collaborate, the team measured fairness on financial tabular tasks like credit scoring and income estimation. Bias emerged at the group level that could not be traced to any single agent's parts, evidence of genuinely collective behavior. The authors argue fairness risk in such systems is a real component of model risk. Multi-agent systems, they conclude, must be audited as whole entities, not piece by piece.
arxiv-2512-16533:
Julien Hermant and coauthors work on faster methods for minimizing rough, non-convex cost functions, a core task in machine learning. In smooth convex settings, flow-like views of momentum methods give sharp insight, but for non-convex costs the flow view and the step-by-step view often disagree.

The team uses a mixed frame that blends flow and steps, first built by Even and coauthors. They widen it to cover non-smooth energy tools, then sharpen its path-by-path promises for fast linear rates. Applied to strongly quasar convex functions, a broad non-convex class, the frame improves the known rate by a fixed factor and softens the terms on the set of lowest points.
arxiv-2512-16633:
Mauro Sanchiz writes a short note on Nakano sequence spaces, which are lists of numbers judged by a norm whose exponent changes from place to place. He studies when the plain inclusion map from one such space into another is strictly singular, a strong form of not being reversible.

Sanchiz gives a clean test: the inclusion is strictly singular exactly when the gap between the two exponent lists stays away from zero far out. He also notes that no such inclusion is compact, nor weakly compact in two standard senses, and gives an easy test for weak compactness. The same test was found by Lang and Nekvinda with a different proof.
arxiv-2512-16933:
Juri Dimaschko studies the motion of a degenerate wormhole in empty space, with no matter present. He proposes widening the equivalence principle, the rule that gravity and acceleration act alike, to cover matter-free objects that themselves source gravity.

Using the Klinkhamer metric as the case in point, he shows a degenerate wormhole is just such an object. The widened rule then shrinks its radial motion to that of a test particle falling in a Schwarzschild field. From that, any bound state of the traversable form must in time collapse into a nontraversable Einstein-Rosen bridge, though the traversable state can be long-lived.
arxiv-2512-17033:
Joseph Guzman and coauthors measure age gaps in three very young star clusters, NGC 2004, NGC 7419, and NGC 2100, using a statistical tool called Stellar Ages on their color-magnitude diagrams. Recent work hinted that ages for clusters under 50 million years clash by tracer.

Two gaps stand out. Red supergiant ages run older than bright blue star ages by 0.60 dex, a factor of about four. And low-mass main-sequence stars fall short of counts expected from a standard initial mass function, given the red supergiant and blue star tallies. The team reads both gaps as population-level clashes with single-star evolution models, unique to massive star life cycles.
arxiv-2512-17533:
Christina Goldschmidt and Liam Hill rebuild a random family tree of the continuum world by snapping sticks. The alpha-stable tree is a random branching shape that describes how big family trees look when offspring numbers have heavy tails. Aldous built the gentler Brownian tree by breaking a line at random points and grafting the pieces on. Goldschmidt and Hill copy that recipe with a twist.

The breaking rate is itself random, driven by a stable jumping process, and new segments attach at spots weighted by jump size. With that one change, the stable tree's full statistics fall out directly. As a bonus, their discrete version of the construction yields a fresh proof of Duquesne's theorem linking finite branching trees to the stable limit.
arxiv-2512-17933:
Xavier Raynaud leads a nine author team presenting BattMo, a MATLAB toolbox for simulating battery cells. Battery makers test new chemistries on computers before building them, and they need models that are quick to set up. BattMo covers many chemistries and even full 3D shapes like round and block cells.

Settings come in through structured text files that follow a shared battery vocabulary, which keeps data clear and reusable. The core model tracks heat as well as charge, and can add wear effects like surface layer growth. Because the solver can compute exact slopes, users can fit model numbers to lab data with standard search tools.
arxiv-2512-18533:
S Mahmudul Hasan, Shaily Roy, and Akib Jawad Nafis test how far text alone can go in spotting political fake news. Automated fact-checking struggles with subtle, well-written disinformation. Their study, posted to arXiv in December 2025, runs nine machine learning algorithms on the LIAR benchmark, comparing word-count features, TF-IDF, and GloVe embeddings.

They find a hard performance ceiling: fine-grained classification never passes a weighted F1 score of 0.32. A simple linear SVM, at 0.624 accuracy, matches the RoBERTa transformer at 0.620, so model size is not the bottleneck. Tree ensembles memorize the training words, topping 99 percent in training but collapsing to about 25 percent on test data. Adding synthetic data through SMOTE changes nothing. The limit, they conclude, is semantic: without outside knowledge, the words themselves stay ambiguous.
arxiv-2512-19333:
Clara Bertinelli Salucci, Hedvig Borgen Reiersrud, A. L. Read, and Anders Kvellestad warn that hunt-the-peak statistics in particle physics can be badly misread. Likelihood ratio tests usually borrow a chi-squared law from Wilks' theorem. That law fails when key parameters sit on a boundary, such as a signal strength that cannot go below zero.

For counting experiments with two signal peaks, the authors show the true law is a chi-squared mixture whose weights come from the Fisher information matrix. Using Wilks or the one-parameter Chernoff limit instead can misstate significance by a lot. Their fix is a boundary-aware calibration for discovery claims.
arxiv-2512-19633:
William Cvetko, Melissa Joseph, and Gustavo Marques-Tavares retest two ideas meant to ease the Hubble tension. That tension is the clash between early- and late-universe measures of how fast space expands. Both ideas add dark radiation that interacts with other dark matter. One drops in a step as the dark sector cools. The other stays coupled to part of the dark matter for a long time.

Old fits to Planck data let both ideas ease the clash. New data from the Atacama Cosmology Telescope change the picture. That telescope reads the microwave sky far deeper into its fine detail. With its data in, the room for extra radiation shrinks a lot. Most of the space that once let expansion run faster is now closed. A mixed model with both free and self-interacting radiation lands in line with those tighter bounds.
arxiv-2512-19733:
Federico Ottomano, Yingzhen Li, and Alex Ganose introduce NMIRacle, a generative system that works backward from spectra to molecular structure. Chemists normally read infrared and nuclear magnetic resonance spectra by expert interpretation, a slow craft skill. NMIRacle splits the problem into two stages, first learning how molecules assemble from fragments, then learning to read spectra.

Stage one trains a generator to rebuild structures from count-aware fragment descriptions, recording both which fragments appear and how often. Stage two adds a spectral encoder that maps infrared, proton NMR, and carbon-13 NMR inputs into the same latent space, fine-tuning the generator for direct spectra-to-molecule prediction. In tests it beat existing baselines at structure elucidation and held up as molecules grew more complex.
arxiv-2512-20333:
Junren Li and Luhua Lai attack a familiar frustration in computer-aided drug design. Generative models propose many novel molecules, but a large share could never actually be synthesized in a lab. Filters and templates fix that by force, often destroying the very features that made a molecule interesting.

Their approach, SynCraft, reframes the fix as structural editing. A large language model predicts a sequence of atom-level edits that nudge a molecule across the synthesis cliff, the point where small changes yield large feasibility gains. Benchmarks show better synthesizable analogues with higher fidelity than leading benchmarks. With interaction-aware prompting, the system even mimics expert drug chemistry judgement on known inhibitor families.
arxiv-2512-20433:
Felipe Atenas strengthens the theory of a workhorse optimization method. Nonconvex problems are usually only guaranteed to reach stationary points, which may be saddle points rather than genuine minima. Atenas analyzes the Davis-Yin three-operator splitting method on structured weakly convex, semialgebraic problems.

His key move is to follow the method's shadow sequence instead of the traditional fixed-point sequence. From that perspective, he proves convergence to local minimizers, almost surely, escaping the saddle-point trap that weak guarantees allow. Numerical experiments add a practical point: Davis-Yin tolerates parameter choices more robustly than the forward-backward method. That holds even in settings where forward-backward looks like the obvious tool for the job.
arxiv-2512-20533:
Kyriakos Stylianopoulos, Paolo Di Lorenzo, and George C Alexandropoulos turn the wireless channel itself into a neural network. Goal-oriented links skip rebuilding the data at the far end. The two ends instead work together to pull out just the features a prediction task needs. Tunable metasurfaces, surfaces that steer radio waves on command, make the channel itself programmable enough to compute with.

With stacked metasurfaces of this kind, the whole chain of sender, channel, and receiver trains end to end as one network. The result matches fully digital neural networks on several data sets. Doing part of the math inside the air saves energy twice: fewer sums at the devices, and less power spent sending. The chapter maps a path where edge prediction rides on the physics of the waves.
arxiv-2512-20833:
Vidit Agrawal and fifteen co-authors release CHAMMI-75, a dataset meant to free cell-image models from one microscope style. Models that measure cell shape are usually trained on a single imaging type. A new study with a different number of image channels then cannot reuse them, wasting the training.

CHAMMI-75 gathers multi-channel microscopy images from seventy-five diverse biological studies, all openly available and curated from public sources. Models trained on it can adapt to whatever channels a study provides. Experiments showed better performance on multi-channel tasks, credited mainly to the dataset's wide variety of imaging methods. The resource points toward one reusable generation of cell morphology models.
arxiv-2512-20933:
Juan Sebastian Hernandez, Cesar Nieto, Juan Manuel Pedraza, and Abhyudai Singh work out how precisely a cell can tell time. Many cellular events fire when a regulatory protein crosses a threshold, and real timers usually chain genes that switch each other on in sequence. Using a hybrid stochastic model of bursty production and dilution, the team derives when adding another gene to the chain sharpens timing and when it blurs it.

For two-gene cascades they find three regimes set by the noise levels and dilution rate. For cascades of identical genes, timing noise falls as the chain lengthens, provided the mean firing time grows too. The conditions define the intrinsic limits of biological timekeeping and give synthetic biologists a rule for how long a timer cascade should be.
arxiv-2512-21533:
Yuya Maeda, Takashi Yamamoto, and a team of co-authors demonstrate a photonic interface connecting an array of neutral atoms to an array of optical waveguides. Networking separate quantum processors through light is a leading route to larger quantum computers and quantum networks. The interface must catch photons from many atoms at once, a capability called multiplexing.

The device is a glass-based photonic integrated circuit holding a thirty-two-channel waveguide array with a twenty-five micrometer pitch. Ten channels couple to photons from ten sites of the atom array, whose spacing is set by Rydberg gates. The team verifies the link by measuring correlations between the atoms' states and the photons' polarization, finding a visibility of zero point eight seven. That correlation is the resource from which atom-photon entanglement is built. The authors argue the design can scale toward large multiplexed entanglement generation for networked quantum processors.
arxiv-2512-21933:
Large language models split text by a fixed vocabulary, so ordinary words often break into fragments, as when one tokenizer splits martial into mart and ial. Sachin Pawar and colleagues hypothesize that such fragmentation of natural words measurably hurts model performance across natural language processing tasks.

To test the idea, they define penalty functions that score how badly a given text is tokenized for a specific model. Across multiple tasks and several different language models, the penalty correlates with performance loss strongly enough to establish statistical significance. The study turns a widely suspected nuisance of subword tokenization into a quantified effect, giving practitioners a diagnostic for when vocabulary choices are likely to cost accuracy.
arxiv-2512-22933:
Danni Xu, Shaojing Fan, Harry Cheng, and Mohan Kankanhalli introduce RW-Post, a benchmark for checking social media posts that mix text with images. Multimodal misinformation often works by pairing misleading words with repurposed or manipulated pictures, and fact-checkers need tests grounded in real posts rather than synthetic ones. RW-Post links each original post to reasoning traces and to specific evidence items drawn from human fact-checking articles.

The annotations were extracted and audited with help from a language model, keeping every claim tied to checkable evidence. Systems can be tested in three regimes: from memory alone, with only the supplied evidence, or with open web access. A reference agent called AgentFact sets the baseline. Experiments with strong open vision-language models show substantial headroom, since models often fail to ground verdicts in the evidence, while evidence-bounded testing improves both accuracy and faithfulness.
arxiv-2512-23033:
Fuyad Hasan Bhoyan and co-authors built diagnostic software that classifies gallbladder disease from ultrasound images and explains its answers. Gallbladder ultrasound is hard to read, and early accurate detection matters for treatment. Their hybrid deep learning model, MobResTaNet, sorts images into ten categories: nine disease types plus normal. A small model size, just over two million parameters, keeps the system light enough for everyday devices.

The platform wraps the model in web and mobile applications built with standard tools including Flutter. It shows explainable AI visualizations in real time, so clinicians can see which image regions drove a prediction. Reported accuracy reaches up to about ninety-nine point nine percent on their evaluation. The authors position the software as accessible, trustworthy point-of-care support, designed to make an AI diagnosis transparent rather than a black box that clinicians must accept on faith.
arxiv-2512-23533:
Alexia Nix and Evangelos Tsolakidis study stress-tensor deformations of quantum field theories, a family of modifications built from the theory's own energy-momentum tensor, known as T-bar-T deformations and their relatives. Their tool is the massive gravity approach, which rewrites these deformations in a gravitational language. The paper matches the published version.

Several results follow. Adding a trace term to the deformation can be recovered in perturbation theory. The authors construct the deformed action for an interacting non-abelian spin-1 model together with a spin-1/2 seed, which yields new algebraic identities for hypergeometric functions. They sharpen the link between the trace-flow equation and the local renormalization group in any dimension, recover Fierz-Pauli massive gravity in higher dimensions. Extend the framework to powers of the trace deformation and nonlinear electrodynamics.
arxiv-2512-23633:
A large team from the LearnLM project and the tutoring platform Eedi report a randomized trial of AI tutoring in British classrooms. One-to-one tutoring works well but is too expensive to offer every student. In five UK secondary schools, one hundred sixty-five students received chat-based mathematics tutoring in which a pedagogy-tuned model, LearnLM, drafted replies that expert human tutors supervised and could edit before sending.

The supervision was light: tutors approved about seventy-six percent of the draft messages with zero or minimal edits. Students supported this way learned at least as well as peers chatting with human tutors alone, and they were somewhat more likely to solve novel problems on later topics. Interviewed tutors praised the model's Socratic questioning and some reported learning new teaching moves from it. The authors present the study as exploratory evidence that supervised AI tutoring can scale safely.
arxiv-2512-23933:
Zhao Li, Shaoqi Hou, and Wen Zhao compute, rigorously, how a black hole bends and distorts gravitational waves passing near it. Gravitational-wave lensing matters for future detectors, but the usual asymptotic expansions used for scattering diverge and turn unreliable near the optical axis, exactly where interesting effects live. Working within black hole perturbation theory for a Schwarzschild black hole, the authors change the setup: the observer sits at finite distance. No such expansion of the radial waves is made.

The partial-wave series then converges cleanly with no regularization tricks, and the rebuilt waveforms show the Poisson spot and strong wavefront distortions directly. Older methods matched only roughly at wide angles and failed in forward scattering. Frequency-domain transmission factors also diverge by a lot from Kirchhoff diffraction estimates, because that shortcut ignores long-range gravity and polarization evolution. The framework gives lensing modelers firmer ground.
arxiv-2512-24133:
Yifei Zhu, Jiahui Zhang, Binni Huang, and Zhenggang Lan automate a chore in computational chemistry. The chore is reading nonadiabatic dynamics simulations. These trajectories show how molecules behave after absorbing light. Experts have traditionally read them by eye. The process leans on intuition and pattern sense. Such skill is hard to formalize as rules.

Their framework, VisU, staffs the job with two large language models. The models form a virtual research team. A Mentor supplies physical intuition through visual reasoning. An Engineer builds and adapts analysis scripts. A Student runs the pipeline and manages the data. Four stages organize the work. Reaction channels and key nuclear motions come out of it. Professional reports are generated at the end.
arxiv-2512-24233:
Sang-Shin Baak and Hyun-Yong Lee study sound waves in analogue gravity. A flowing quantum fluid can mimic a curved spacetime. Sound in the fluid plays the role of light in the analogue. The authors include backreaction in this picture. The fluid's motion reshapes the effective spacetime it creates.

They adopt a number-conserving approach. Even with backreaction, the analogue metric keeps its usual form. Sound speed, fluid density, and fluid velocity pick up small corrections. Those corrections carry the backreaction effects. The modified fluid equations also introduce a mass. That mass depends on spacetime position. A linearized Bogoliubov-de Gennes equation is written with number conservation. It can be solved numerically. In a finite Bose gas example, backreaction strengthens correlations. The gain is about ten percent in the bulk and more near the edges.
arxiv-2512-24333:
R García-Delgado studies quadratic Lie algebras built around the Heisenberg algebra. A quadratic Lie algebra carries an inner product that its own operations preserve. The Heisenberg algebra sits inside as an ideal. The paper gives a construction for all such algebras. Every example with the Heisenberg ideal arises from that construction.

Two decision questions receive exact tests. The first asks when a basic example is just the Heisenberg algebra extended by a derivation. Sharp conditions settle it. The second asks when the quotient by the ideal admits a preserved metric. Conditions settle that as well. A special case gets its own treatment. There the nilradical of the whole algebra equals the Heisenberg ideal. The results serve readers who classify Lie algebras with metric structure.
arxiv-2512-24533:
Hatem Barghathi and Adrian Del Maestro find a change in how entanglement scales, driven by which entropy you measure. Entanglement growth with subsystem size reveals phases and critical points. The von Neumann entropy is the standard measure but costly to obtain. Experiments prefer the second Rényi entropy, assuming it tracks the same scaling. Earlier work on constrained spin models showed that assumption can fail.

The authors build a number-conserving many-body state for interacting fermions. Its leading entanglement scaling changes with the Rényi index. Power-law and logarithmic behaviors both appear, depending on the index chosen. That generalizes the spin-model warning. A practical diagnostic follows. A symmetry-aware lower bound on the von Neumann entropy is built from charge-resolved Rényi entropies. Experimentalists can test for anomalous scaling with accessible data alone.
arxiv-2512-25033:
Sotiris Kanellopoulos, Edouard Nemery, and Christos Pergaminelis initiate the study of perfectly envy-free orientations of graphs as allocations. Vertices are agents and edges are goods contested only by neighbors; orienting an edge gives the good to one endpoint. Envy-free up to any good orientations were studied before, but exact envy-free orientations were not.

Parameterized complexity is their main lens, asking which structural parameters make the problem tractable. Fair division readers get a new problem with clean graph form. Neighbor-only contention models shared resources such as parking spots or border facilities, where fairness must hold exactly, not approximately.
arxiv-2601-00133:
Qinyang Li leads eight coauthors in building a foundation model that predicts material traits from small datasets. Their 2026 system learns in context. It takes examples inside the prompt instead of long retraining. The model joins composition data with structure aware inputs. A pretrained transformer is paired with graph network embeddings. New descriptors add bond ionicity and charge transfer data.

Tests use the MatBench suite and a separate heat conduction dataset. The system matches or beats leading models at far lower training cost. With no training at all, it won five of six composition tasks. One phonon task improved by about ten percent. On heat conduction, it captured phonon scattering and mass contrast effects. The authors also show its inner space smooths raw feature clusters. That smoothing helps prediction between known points.
arxiv-2601-00433:
Fredrik Jansson contributed a chapter on formal modelling to a forthcoming Cambridge University Press volume on cultural evolution, edited by Johan Lind and Anna Jon-And. The chapter explains what models are and why researchers use them. Models give scholars a shared, precise language, turning fuzzy assumptions into clear claims that can be compared and tested.

Four families of models are surveyed, from single optimizing agents up to whole populations and agent-based systems. Approaches covered include Bayesian reasoning, game theory, reinforcement learning, compartmental models, and social networks. Jansson then offers a general template that links system states, mental processes, behavior, and large-scale outcomes in loops connecting people, groups, institutions, and their surroundings.
arxiv-2601-00533:
Wenrui Li and colleagues extend all-in-one video restoration, where a single model cleans up footage damaged by unknown problems, to a harder and more realistic setting. Rain, snow, blur, and low light rarely stay fixed during a clip; they strengthen, fade, and blend into each other smoothly over time. Earlier methods mostly treated each frame's damage separately.

The authors name this the smoothly evolving unknown degradations scenario and build a synthesis pipeline that creates test videos with single, compound, and gradually changing damage. Their model, built around recurrent processing with adaptive prompts, is designed to track those slow changes instead of restarting at each frame. The work pushes restoration toward the messy conditions of real outdoor and driving footage.
arxiv-2601-00733:
Saak Gabriyelyan and two co-authors study, in 2026, a space of tame functions on a general space. The functions are the Baire-one kind, built as limits of plain continuous ones. They are read with the pointwise view, where closeness is checked point by point. The authors ask when this space has strong forms of completeness. Completeness means that sequences which look settled do in fact settle inside the space.

They prove that five claims about the space all stand or fall together. The space is complete in the strong senses exactly when it holds every function at all. That holds exactly for one named class of base spaces. They also sort out weaker forms, such as stepwise completeness. For a compact base space, one weak form holds exactly when the space is scattered. The separable, distance-based case gets a full study of its own.
arxiv-2601-01133:
Xuanlong Ma, Samir Zahirović, and Katarina Žigerović study a graph built from a finite group. They start from the enhanced power graph, which links elements when one is a power of a shared element, then remove the links of the plain power graph. What remains is the difference graph, with isolated points dropped. Their focus is on special sets, called dominating sets, that reach every point of this graph.

The main result caps how far apart two points in such a graph can be. For nilpotent groups, where the group splits neatly into prime-power parts, the diameter is at most four steps. The team then sorts all nilpotent groups by the exact diameter of their graph, from one to four, refining an earlier result by other authors. The work ties group structure to graph shape in a complete way for this class.
arxiv-2601-01633:
Andrey Sladkov proposes a hybrid model for simulating how laser light interacts with plasma in three dimensions. Full particle tracking is accurate but costly, while pure fluid models miss key detail. Sladkov treats ions as tracked particles and electrons as a fluid carrying ten moments, which captures pressure differences by direction and nonstandard particle spreads efficiently.

A laser envelope model adds energy and pressure heating without resolving each light wave cycle. Collision and ionization steps keep energy and charge states consistent as the plasma evolves. Built into the AKAM code, the framework scales for high-energy-density and laboratory plasma work, bridging the two older approaches.
arxiv-2601-01733:
Junsheng Fang, Chunlan Jiang, Liguang Wang, and Yanli Wang work on a question in operator algebra. Take a well-behaved map from a C-star algebra into a von Neumann algebra. Can it be adjusted, by a change of basis, into a true representation? A true representation preserves the algebra's star operation.

They prove the adjustment is always possible when the target algebra has a property called QWEP, the quotient weak expectation property. The result connects to famous work by Pisier. He showed that such adjustments for all targets would force the source algebra to be nuclear. It also connects to Kirchberg. He tied QWEP for every von Neumann algebra to the Connes Embedding Problem. That long-standing question was answered negatively. The paper thus sharpens exactly where the boundary of the adjustment property lies.
arxiv-2601-03033:
Eojin Kim and Brian F. Farrell study the turbulent Ekman layer, the boundary layer that forms where wind or currents drag across a surface under Earth's rotation. Roll and streak structures appear in this layer, as they do in oceans, the atmosphere, and laboratory shear flows, but the mechanism that sustains them has been debated. The authors apply a statistical state dynamics approach, previously used on wall-bounded turbulence.

Extending that framework's stability analysis to the Ekman layer, they show the same mechanism operates there. A Reynolds-stress-driven instability works together with inflectional instability to create and maintain the rolls and streaks. The results link geophysical boundary-layer turbulence to the better-understood turbulence of engineering shear flows, giving both fields a shared mechanistic picture.
arxiv-2601-03233:
Yoav HaCohen and twenty-eight co-authors introduce LTX-2, an open-source foundation model that generates video and its soundtrack together. Text-to-video diffusion models can produce striking footage but stay silent. That misses the cues that audio provides. LTX-2 uses an asymmetric dual-stream transformer. One stream, with fourteen billion parameters, handles video. A smaller stream, with five billion, handles audio.

Cross-attention layers link the two streams in both directions, with temporal position data, so sound and picture stay in sync. Shared timestep conditioning keeps the two in step. A multilingual text encoder broadens prompt understanding. A modality-aware guidance method improves alignment and control. Beyond speech, the model produces rich audio tracks that follow the characters, the setting, and the action on screen.
arxiv-2601-03333:
Mrinal Kanti Roychowdhury builds a geometric theory of optimal quantization on the surface of a sphere. Quantization here means choosing a small set of representative points that best approximate a probability distribution. He studies finite uniform distributions spread over the whole spherical surface, rather than along circles or arcs. He establishes that optimal sets of representatives exist and characterizes them through centroidal spherical Voronoi tessellations.

Three structural results follow. A cluster purity theorem shows that well-separated parts of the support each keep their own Voronoi regions. A ring allocation theorem, a discrete water-filling rule, says exactly how representatives distribute across latitude rings, with closed-form distortion. A stability theorem bounds how much the optimum moves when the support is perturbed slightly. A spherical version of Lloyd's algorithm rounds out the theory.
arxiv-2601-03533:
Vladimir Braverman and four co-authors study the experts problem under a sliding window, where only recent days should count. Each day a learner may ask a few experts for predictions and wants regret, the gap versus the best expert, to stay low over any recent window. Such setups fit traffic monitoring, epidemic tracking, and automated trading, where old data loses value.

The team shows one query per day cannot reach the near-optimal regret target, but two queries can, using very little memory. Their algorithms also hit the same quality over every interval of days, not just the latest window. That is a large memory improvement over earlier interval methods. The result draws a sharp line: a second daily query changes what is possible.
arxiv-2601-03733:
Xiaoxian Shen and seven co-authors introduce RadDiff, a system that describes in plain language how two sets of radiology images differ. Comparing image sets drives clinical insight and helps doctors audit what medical AI systems respond to. RadDiff reasons in a radiologist-like comparative style and builds on an earlier proposer-ranker design from a system called VisDiff.

Four additions mirror real diagnostic workflow. Domain-adapted vision-language models inject medical knowledge, and reports are reasoned over alongside images. Hypotheses are refined across rounds, and a targeted visual search zooms into salient regions for subtle findings. The team built RadDiffBench, fifty-seven expert-validated study pairs with reference descriptions, where RadDiff reached forty-seven percent accuracy. Even partial success matters, because describing cohort differences is how imaging studies become clinical knowledge.
arxiv-2601-04133:
David Vizgan and twenty-two co-authors take a census of gas and star-formation tracers in two distant, dusty galaxies magnified by lensing. Both galaxies come from a South Pole Telescope survey and are seen as they were when the universe was young. New and archival ALMA data cover several emission lines and the dust glow beneath them.

Pixel-by-pixel study finds broad agreement among tracers for the link between gas surface density and star formation. Dust emission is more compact than line emission, and one carbon line spreads widest, which warns that it may not always trace gas or star formation well. The team also develops a line flux ratio as a quick proxy for gas depletion time. That proxy could be applied to large samples without full multi-wavelength modelling.
arxiv-2601-04233:
Zhiyuan Zhao and five co-authors release LEMAS, a very large open speech data set with word-level timestamps across ten major languages. The corpus runs well past one hundred thousand hours and is built by an efficient pipeline that checks quality and annotation as it goes. Fine timestamps are rare at this scale and unlock precise training signals.

Two benchmark models test the corpus under different generative styles. LEMAS-TTS uses a flow-matching design for zero-shot synthesis in many languages, with accent-adversarial training and a CTC loss to curb cross-language accent drift. LEMAS-Edit uses a decoder-only design that treats editing as filling masked tokens, guided by the word alignments. Both reach high-quality synthesis and editing, which the team reads as proof of the data set's quality for prompt-based speech work.
arxiv-2601-04733:
Nicholas S. Yama and three co-authors put diamond's best quantum defects into a manufacturable photonic platform, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Silicon-vacancy centres in diamond have superb optical and spin coherence, but diamond itself resists scale-up: its suspended device geometry and weak nonlinearity force a second processing chip into any real network. The team instead fabricates gallium phosphide nanophotonic cavities directly on diamond, hybrid-integrating more than six hundred of them above near-surface silicon-vacancy centres.

In a device holding two strongly coupled centres, they confirm above-unity cooperativity by several independent measurements — the regime where light and spin interact deterministically. A permanent magnet resolves the spin transitions optically; the measured spin relaxation time exceeds four tenths of a millisecond at four kelvin. the coupling enables spin-dependent transmission switching plus single-shot readout of quantum jumps. Gallium phosphide's strong nonlinearity completes the pitch.
arxiv-2601-05133: Nikolaj Glazunov's 2026 paper looks at picked parts of non-Archimedean quantum math and non-Archimedean quantum computing. The non-Archimedean world uses number sets, such as the p-adic numbers, where the old rule that a size can be topped by piling up copies no longer holds. Glazunov sets out how quantum math and quantum computing can be built in that world.
arxiv-2601-05333:
Floor van Donkelaar and 4 co-authors probe star clumps born in the wild fringe of young galaxies in a 2026 paper. The Webb scope has shown tight, huge clumps of new stars in galaxies from the dawn of time, their light bent by the pull of mass in front. The team trace how such clumps form in the gas halo round rich young galaxies. They use a fine-grained run of a toy cosmos that tracks gas, stars, and dark stuff at once.

They find a host of clumps that are made most of plain stuff, not dark stuff. The clumps form clear of the discs, in the halo gas. Lone, tight clumps of that kind have been dubbed cosmic wallflowers. To place their birth helps folks read the Webb finds, which may be the seeds of the old star balls that ring our own galaxy now.
arxiv-2601-05433:
Rachid El Aitouni and Ahmed Bouhlal surveyed more than 250 physics and chemistry teachers in Morocco for a 2026 study on school experiments. The question was practical: do real bench experiments or digital simulations help middle and high school students learn and pay attention better?

Most teachers favored simulations, except for simple work such as electrical circuits. Material shortages, large classes, and safety rules drove that choice. Teachers also said simulations let them repeat or slow an experiment for clarity, but they wanted specific training in the tools. The strongest strategy was hybrid: simulations for abstract ideas, real experiments for hands-on skill and critical thinking.
arxiv-2601-05833:
Liu Zai and Iraklis Klampanos introduce Peek2 in 2026, a faster pretokenizer for byte-level byte-pair encoding on edge devices. Pretokenization is the sequential first pass that splits text before token encoding, and it had received little optimization attention for on-device inference. Their replacement targets the pretokenizers used by several major model families.

After analyzing the original logic, the authors designed a method with linear time and tiny constant memory that avoids regular expressions entirely. It produces results identical to the regex baseline. Microbenchmarks reportedly ran up to about two and a half times faster, and end-to-end encoding throughput raised by about fourteen percent depending on dataset. For phones and other edge hardware, such front-end savings compound across every generated response.
arxiv-2601-05933:
Brandon B Le and 2 co-authors map in 2026 the space of ground states of the kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet as a network. This frustrated magnet cannot satisfy all its interactions at once, leaving a huge manifold of coplanar ground states. The authors turn that manifold into a graph whose nodes are states and whose edges are loop rotations that move between them.

Each state maps to a three-coloring problem on a dual honeycomb lattice, where loops of two alternating colors define the moves. Comparing networks with all loops against networks restricted to short six-spin loops revealed sharply peaked connectivity, different spectral shapes, and distinct fractal geometry. Energetic constraints thus shape the global structure of the magnet's configuration space.
arxiv-2601-06033:
Generative AI helps both attackers and defenders online, report Patrick Gage Kelley and 4 co-authors in a 2026 study. Their work covers Trust and Safety, the field that fights harmful content and abuse on platforms. Misuse worries are growing, while defensive uses remain less studied.

The team interviewed 43 experts across child safety, election integrity, hate and harassment, scams, and violent extremism. Attackers gain scale and speed, with lower barriers to propaganda and deepfakes. Defenders imagine using the same tools to detect harm at scale, run investigations, answer with counternarratives, support moderators, and help users. The paper offers a strategic framework for using generative AI responsibly to make online spaces safer.
arxiv-2601-06533:
Grid chiefs must call the next hours of power use with care. Call low, and plants strain. Call high, and fuel is waste. Qi Dong and 5 co-authors bring a fresh tool to that call in a 2026 paper. Their base is the spread-out style of AI that made waves in art tools.

First, the load line is split by pitch, from slow swells to fast ticks, and the parts are joined anew. Noise is then laid on the joined form in a planned way, which thins the noise in the raw data. A clean-up net, with both loop and focus parts, strips the noise back off. The last call is drawn from the taught net. On grid data from two lands, the tool beat each past tool it faced. The pitch split seems to be the key that lets this style work on load lines.
arxiv-2601-06633:
Zhangqi Duan, Nigel Fernandez, and Andrew Lan present KASER in 2026. KASER simulates student errors on open-ended coding tasks for education. Such tasks give detailed insights into student knowledge, they note.

Training language models to simulate student errors is challenging, though. Models often suffer mode collapse when generating plausible wrong answers. They also miss diversity in syntax, style, and solution approach. Student responses vary widely on all three of those axes. KASER is knowledge-aligned, aiming to match errors to student understanding. Better simulators could help teachers anticipate mistakes before grading piles arrive. Computing education readers get a tool for generating realistic wrong answers. That supports practice, feedback, and test design at scale.
arxiv-2601-06733:
Tamara Alshammari and Mehdi Bennis plan sense-based talk for agent teams in a 2026 paper. New 6G nets speed up self-rule, smarts, and links between machines. Big teams of agents thus gain quick, supple ways to act.

That same gain lifts the risk from shocks that can hit such teams. Shifts in the world, faults, and false tales all pose threats to them. Hostile acts by some agents add one more threat to the list. Sense-based talk, led by logic, aims to keep teams in tune through stress. To share sense, not just bits, could screen noise and lies far more. Tough teams need just that screen when the world turns rough round them. The work links talk theory with team strength in one frame for 6G.
arxiv-2601-06933: A 2026 arXiv preprint appeared in 2026. It covers application of analytic functionals to mean field theory and wilson- fisher fixed point. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors consider application of the analytic functional approach to the conformal field theories associated with mean field theory and Wilson-Fisher fixed point. The authors study the constraints imposed by the crossing symmetry on the coefficients of the operator product expansion. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07333: Research by Tessa Pulli and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with OSCAR. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. 6D object pose estimation plays a crucial role in scene understanding for applications such as robotics and augmented reality. To support the needs of ever-changing object sets in such context. Modern zero-shot object pose estimators were developed to not require object-specific training but only rely on CAD models. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07433:
A 2026 preprint on arXiv deals with design of optimal controls in acausal LQG problems. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. In control theory, a system which has output depending only on. The present and past values of the input is said to be causal (or nonanticipative).

Respectively, a system is acausal (or non-causal) if its output depends on future inputs as well. Overall majority of literature in stochastic control theory discusses causal systems. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07533:
Julian Schelb and colleagues present Loci Similes, a benchmark for finding echoes between Latin texts. Intertextuality research traces how one writer quotes, copies, or alludes to another. Such links help scholars rebuild the library an author drew on. The connections range from exact quotations to faint paraphrases. Their 2026 preprint supplies test data for that task.

Latin makes the search hard, because word forms change with grammar. A copied phrase may look quite different on the surface. Automated tools need a fair benchmark to show whether they truly find these links. Loci Similes gives the field shared material for comparing methods. Digital humanities scholars working on historical texts are the intended readers.
arxiv-2601-07633:
Guang Yang and a collaborator compare detector designs for tracking fine particle patterns, in a 2026 preprint. Fine-grained scintillator detectors serve precision work in nuclear and particle physics. They reconstruct interaction vertices and the directions of secondary particles. That accuracy separates signal events from background. The design choice under study is the fiber readout geometry.

Traditional two-view systems use crossing X and Y fibers. Three-view designs add a third layer of fibers at another angle. The extra view gives unambiguous three-dimensional voxel identification, the authors note. Benchmarks for both layouts show what the third view buys in practice. Detector builders weighing cost against resolution are the readers. The paper supplies performance numbers for that design decision.
arxiv-2601-07733:
Joseph L. Shomberg runs a reaction-diffusion equation backward using a physics-informed generative network. His 2026 preprint reconstructs the starting state of the Chafee-Infante equation on two-dimensional domains. The final state comes after one hundred explicit forward steps and sits near equilibrium. Boundary values are fixed by Dirichlet conditions. Reconstructing the start from such a smoothed end state is an inverse problem.

His tool is a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty, guided by the physics of the equation. Generative networks can propose plausible starting states that fit the observed end. Physics information keeps those proposals honest. Inverse problems like this arise in heat flow, chemistry, and pattern formation. The paper speaks to scholars who blend neural networks with known equations rather than treating data alone.
arxiv-2601-07933:
Yeuk Hay Joshua Lam and Daniel Litt link a curvature test to cohomology in algebraic geometry. They study a smooth projective family of shapes over a base. Katz proved the Grothendieck-Katz p-curvature claim for the Gauss-Manin connection on cohomology in their case. The claim links p-curvature that fades at a vast range of primes to monodromy that factors through a smaller group. Their 2026 preprint works on p-curvature and non-abelian cohomology at once.

The Gauss-Manin connection tracks how the field shifts as the shape moves in its family. p-curvature measures its behavior in characteristic p. The non-abelian side extends these tools past the linear case. Progress here feeds the arithmetic of differential equations. The paper serves those in algebraic geometry and number theory. It builds on a landmark proved case to push into richer coefficients.
arxiv-2601-08633:
Victoria Bollo and co-authors present new results from the MUSE-ALMA Haloes survey. Their 2026 arXiv paper, the thirteenth in the series, studies galaxies tied to strong hydrogen absorption. The survey includes 79 galaxies associated with absorption at redshift near 0.5.

An ALMA Cycle 10 large program added observations of 39 systems. Combining MUSE optical data with ALMA radio data links galaxies to the gas around them. Absorbing gas traces the circumgalactic medium, the reservoir that feeds and receives galaxy gas. Readers in galaxy evolution get fresh evidence on how galaxies exchange matter with their surroundings at cosmic midday.
arxiv-2601-08933:
Denis Tramonte tests four forms for how push falls off with range in a galaxy cluster. A cluster is a vast swarm of galaxies held by pull. Hot gas in it pushes out, and that push shape tells us the heat state of the gas. One form is oft called the shared, or universal, form for all clusters.

He fits all four forms to new data from the ACT scope, which reads a faint shift in old space light. Forms span a curved fall, a plain power fall, and a heat based fall. A reader in cluster work gets a head to head fit test. It shows if one shared form can serve, or if each cluster needs its own shape.
arxiv-2601-09433:
David Reid and Ognjen Arandjelović ask whether transformers read ancient Roman coins better than convolutional networks. Their 2026 arXiv paper compares the two model families on coin motif recognition. Automated coin analysis could help researchers mine large collections and help collectors judge what they buy or sell.

Recent work has targeted the semantic elements shown on coins, the portraits, gods, and symbols, using convolutional neural networks. The authors test whether transformer models, now dominant in image tasks, do better on the same job. Reading motifs at scale would turn museum trays into searchable data. The comparison shows which architecture suits this niche of cultural heritage.
arxiv-2601-09633:
Sahil Mishra, Srinitish Srinivasan, Srikanta Bedathur, and Tanmoy Chakraborty grow sorted term lists without hand labor. Their 2026 arXiv paper, TaxoBell, places each term in a soft box in space and learns from the list itself. Such lists, called taxonomies, organize knowledge for catalogs, search, and medical work.

New concepts appear faster than curators can file them. A box inside a bigger box mirrors a child term under its parent term. Trained this way, TaxoBell proposes where new terms belong in the tree. Growing lists this way would keep large catalogs current without armies of editors doing the filing by hand.
arxiv-2601-09733:
Xin Gao and five co-authors treat training data as an engineering problem with a feedback loop. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses OpenDataArena to build better supervised fine-tuning datasets. Dataset construction is a critical but under-theorized stage of model post-training.

In practice, teams pile up data by heuristic rules, with little sense of what each sample adds. A data arena can score and compare samples by their effect on performance. Closing that loop means datasets get designed, not just gathered. Better data recipes would lift every model that is trained on them.
arxiv-2601-09833:
Xiaoxu Ma, Xiangbo Zhang, and Zhenyu Weng measure the personalities of language models from the inside. Their 2026 arXiv paper evaluates traits using internal activations rather than questionnaires. Trait scores from questionnaires swing with small changes in prompt wording or role-play setup.

That instability also gives little insight into why a model scores as it does. Reading activations promises steadier, more explainable measures. Knowing a model's traits helps compare systems and deploy them responsibly. An internal ruler could flag subtle shifts after fine-tuning that ordinary surveys would miss entirely in practice.
arxiv-2601-10033:
Wan Jou She and co authors built a data set of kind talk for care in Japanese. The set is named EmplifAI. It holds talks with patients who live with long term ills. Such patients feel a wide range of moods, from hope to despair.

Those moods shift as care goes on. A reply that fits one stage may miss at the next. The set tags talks with fine mood labels. It spans both bright and dark moods in its tags. Such a set can train tools that reply with care. It can also test how well a tool reads a patient's state.
arxiv-2601-10133:
Ruowei Li and Zhigang Yao fit a low dim sheet to high dim data with wild noise. Real data oft sit near a thin sheet in a large space. But noise can be large with no cap. Past fits may bend the sheet to chase noise.

The team use a curve driven fit. The sheet is smooth, with a set reach. Points are spread near flat on the sheet, then noise is added. The noise is Gauss in form but with no cap on its size. The paper asks when the true sheet can still be found. It gives terms for a sound fit in that hard case.
arxiv-2601-10333:
Florin Hemmann, Vincent Glauser, Ullrich Steiner, and Matthias Saba make random nets to order. Such nets model frames and links at many scales. Waves that cross them can shift phase, trap, spread, or block. Each act rests on the net's shape traits.

To test those acts, labs need nets with set traits on call. Hand made nets are slow to build. The team give fast code that grows nets with the traits asked. It can tune links, gaps, and spread. The tool lets labs sweep traits and watch acts change. That speeds the study of waves in such nets.
arxiv-2601-10633:
Hagen Gress and co-authors report the first tiny resonators made from a two-dimensional polyaramid. Polyaramids form sheets one molecule thick, held by strong hydrogen bonds, much like graphene's carbon sheets. The material here is called 2DPA-1. The team turned its films into vibrating membranes as thin as eight nanometers.

To build them, the team moved thin films onto chips etched with arrays of round microwells. The films span the wells and can ring like drumheads. Such resonators sense mass and force with great care. A strong, light new material for them could sharpen future sensors. The work opens a path for molecular-sheet devices in precision measurement.
arxiv-2601-10833:
Pratima Hebbar and Leonid Koralov study the front of a branching Brownian motion. Particles wander like Brownian motion and split into more particles as they go. In the supercritical case, the cloud expands with a clear front speed. Branching here is compactly supported: births happen only inside a bounded region's influence.

The authors track how particles spread near the front over long times. It is known that normalized counts in a window moving below the front speed settle down. Their work sharpens the picture of that edge zone. Front behavior governs invasions, epidemics, and reaction waves, so exact edge laws matter well beyond this model.
arxiv-2601-10933:
Yizhou Dang and co-authors tackle the long-tail problem in sequential recommendation. Sequential systems learn from each user's history of clicks and buys. Most users touch only a handful of items, while most items are rarely consumed. That imbalance starves the model of signal for both quiet users and niche items. Their fix is tail-aware data augmentation.

Augmentation creates extra training examples where data are thin. Tail-aware design adds them where the tail needs them most, not uniformly. The aim is recommendations that serve niche tastes, not just blockbuster items. The work serves platforms whose catalogs are vast but whose per-user histories are short and sparse.
arxiv-2601-11333:
Manuel Friedrich, Jose Matias, and Elvira Zappale widen a theory of deformations. Their 2026 preprint brings structured deformations to linearized elasticity. Structured deformations split motion into smooth and jump parts. Linearized elasticity is the small-strain theory of solids.

The team gives an integral form for the base energy. That form has both bulk and surface contributions. Bulk terms count strain through the body's volume. Surface terms count what happens at cracks and slips. They reach the form by two routes for safety. One is a direct global relaxation method in BD space. The other starts from nonlinear energies of nonsimple materials. Agreement of both routes strengthens the result.
arxiv-2601-11833: Anthony Joon Hur works on fast brain scan cuts for glioma, a type of brain tumour. Good cuts guide care and surgery. Deep learning gives the best cuts so far. Yet it needs big data sets or heavy machines, which many clinics lack. His method uses a Karhunen-Loève expansion to build a map of odd spots. That map flags parts that do not fit the norm. A light method could bring tumour cuts to small clinics.
arxiv-2601-12033:
Muhammad Alif Al Hakim, Alfan Farizki Wicaksono, and Fajri Koto guard fairness and safety when large models are shrunk. Shrinking, called quantization, cuts the cost of running a model. Its effect on bias and safety was not well mapped, most of all for dynamic forms and many tongues.

They test static and dynamic shrinking on bias and safety test sets. They also guard key weights that hold fair, safe acts. The aim is a small model that keeps its guardrails. Such care matters as shrunk models reach phones and cheap servers.
arxiv-2601-12133:
Dominik Śliwiński studies the spectrum of a new family of operators tied to the Riemann zeta function. The operators come from work by Connes, Consani, and Moscovici. Their eigenvalues are thought to near the zeros of zeta on the critical line as two terms grow large.

That link, if firm, would bear on the Riemann hypothesis, a core open problem. Sliwiński adds spectral analysis of these operators. Each firm step helps test if this route can reach the zeros. The work is pure maths with a famed target.
arxiv-2601-12533:
Md. Ahanaf Arif Khan and six co authors build a dataset for finding faces in overhead images. Faces seen from above look very different from faces seen head on. Their scale can vary wildly, and clutter in the scene adds to the challenge. Standard face detectors, trained mostly on front views, struggle in this top down setting.

Their dataset is called BirdsEye-RU. It holds 2,978 images with over eight thousand annotated faces. Each face is marked so detectors can be trained and graded on the set. Overhead views matter for drones, crowd monitoring, and search tasks. A shared dataset of this kind gives the field a common test bed. It also shows how large the overhead gap really is.
arxiv-2601-12833:
Monika E. Mycroft, Rostyslav O. Serha, Andrii V. Chumak, and Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero prepare quantum states of magnons. Magnons are spin waves in a ferromagnet, and the target mode is ferromagnetic resonance. The team propose to prepare and certify Gaussian quantum states of that mode. Their drive is longitudinal, acting along the magnetization.

Quantum optics strategies for such states rely on light based tools. This approach instead harnesses a purely magnonic feature: spin wave nonlinearity. That nonlinearity generates magnon squeezing, a quantum signature. Squeezed magnons could serve quantum sensing and information tasks in magnetic devices. The work opens a route to quantum magnonics without optical intermediaries.
arxiv-2601-12933:
Sharifa Sultana and six co authors study how Bangladeshi women perceive deepfakes. Deepfake technology grows more accessible each year, and concerns about misuse are escalating. The Global South faces added risk, since digital literacy and regulation are often limited. Prior research focused on detection and media manipulation in general terms.

A gap remains in understanding how individuals in these regions perceive and interact with deepfake media. Women may face distinct risks, from harassment to reputational harm. Hearing their views directly grounds policy in lived experience, not speculation. The study serves debates on platform duties and media education. It centers voices often missing from deepfake research.
arxiv-2601-13033:
Members of the ATLAS team report on hunts for odd signals from dark sectors of nature. ATLAS is a huge detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Many ideas past the Standard Model guess new long lived bits of matter. Such bits would fly some way from the crash point and then decay.

Those late decays are hard to rebuild from the raw hits. They also face odd and tough noise from known paths. The report sums up fresh results from hunts tuned to dark sector ideas. All hunts use proton crash data that ATLAS has stored. For readers, the piece gives a compact tour of how one big team chases faint, strange tracks that standard hunts would miss.
arxiv-2601-13133:
Mingshuang Luo and co-authors build a train path for vision tasks that centre on people. Such tasks span watch cams, health care, and how people use machines. Huge sets of unmarked photos of people now exist. The field needs one broad pre train model that can serve many such tasks.

Their path is self taught, so it needs no hand marks to start. It is led by CLIP, a model that links text and image. It can also adapt to fit each new task. The aim is a single base that lifts scores across many people centred tasks at once. Teams gain a start point that is both broad and cheap to tune.
arxiv-2601-13333:
Yuhan Liu and Yijian Zou bound how close two mixed quantum states are, in set time. That closeness, called Uhlmann fidelity, is a core score for mixed states. To sum it in full needs the roots of huge matrices. The size blows up with each added bit, so full sums fail for many body states.

The pair treat states held as matrix product density operators, a chain form that stores big states in small room. They give a polynomial time rule that yields sworn low and high bounds for the score. Sworn bounds let staff trust a read with no full sum. The work also bears on how mixed state classes are sorted.
arxiv-2601-13433:
Priyanka Mary Mammen, Emil Joswin, and Shankar Venkitachalam test if language models bow to claimed expertise. Past work shows a model's score on sense tasks can be swayed by hints and nods in the prompt. A nod from a famed source may weigh more than one from a lay source. That source effect was thinly probed.

The team varies who is said to back a hint while the hint stays the same. They then read if the model's pick shifts with the claimed rank of the source. They also try to steer that bias once seen. For teams that ship such models, a rank bias is a trust risk in law, care, and news uses.
arxiv-2601-13733:
Chisato Uno and Tetsuo Hyodo study bound states held by two kinds of force at once in 2026. One force is the Coulomb force, the pull between electric charges. The other is a short-range force that acts only up close. Together they can bind particles into states with set energies.

The pair analyze the binding energies and wave functions of these states. They show that Coulomb-driven shifts in energy track the spatial spread of the wave function. That link ties how deep a state binds to how wide it sits. Such links help read data on exotic atoms and nuclei.
arxiv-2601-13933:
Mingming Zhang and co-authors build an agent system to fix security flaws in code in 2026. As software grows in complexity, vulnerabilities grow more prevalent and costly. Fuzzers and other detection tools have advanced much of late. Effective resolution of a found flaw still often depends on human expertise.

Existing automated vulnerability repair leans on manual annotations. Their VulnResolver is a hybrid agent framework for LLM-based resolution. Agents can search, reason, and patch with less hand-holding. Faster, sound fixes would cut the window in which flaws can be exploited. Less hand work in the loop means fixes can start much soon. Small teams with no full-time security staff stand to gain most.
arxiv-2601-14033:
Xiaochen Zhu, Mayuri Sridhar, and Srinivas Devadas protect the answers of AI models served through APIs in 2026. Modern models are increasingly deployed behind such interfaces. Standard weight privatization, like DP-SGD, adds noise to the whole model. That can be unnecessarily noisy at the cost of utility.

Model responses to specific inputs are much lower dimensional and more stable. That fact motivates privacy guarantees directly on model outputs. Their PAC-Private responses handle adversarial composition, where many queries combine. Output-level privacy could keep useful detail while hiding training data. The work keeps the guard on each reply, not on the whole model at once. That focus can save much of the sharpness users value.
arxiv-2601-14133:
Yuzhuo Miao and co-authors protect a robot model's general knowledge while it learns body tasks in 2026. Vision-language-action models harness pre-trained vision-language models for embodied intelligence. Standard robotic fine-tuning inevitably disrupts the pre-trained feature space. That disruption causes catastrophic forgetting of general visual understanding.

Their TwinBrainVLA uses an asymmetric mixture-of-transformers design. Separate branches can guard old knowledge while new skills form. The goal is to unleash generalist models for embodied tasks without the usual loss. Robots that keep broad knowledge adapt better to new homes and jobs. The split design lets one branch guard broad sight while the rest learn touch and grip. That guard is the core bet of the work.
arxiv-2601-14533:
Oscar Bates and five co-authors work on transcranial ultrasound in this 2026 paper. Ultrasound through the skull could serve both imaging and therapy. The human skull is a significant barrier, though, and it distorts the waves. High-fidelity numerical simulations can compensate for skull-induced distortions. They require precise skull templates, typically derived from CT scans. They also need exact spatial alignment to the patient's anatomy.

The team's title names their advance: automatic skull-template alignment without a guidance image. Removing the guidance image simplifies the clinical workflow. The gain is time. A team can set up a run fast and skip a step that used to slow them down. Readers get a method that brings simulation-based correction closer to routine use in brain ultrasound.
arxiv-2601-14833:
E. Legnani, J. Elvin-Poole, and the Dark Energy Survey team report results from the survey's sixth year. Their 2026 arXiv paper looks at how gravity bends light from far galaxies. This bending, called lensing, can magnify galaxies and shift where they seem to sit.

If that shift is not modeled, it can bias maps of how galaxies cluster. The team tests the effect on galaxy clustering and on galaxy-galaxy lensing. They use the survey's main lens sample, called MagLim++. The work checks how much the bias matters for cosmology and for the survey's headline results.
arxiv-2601-14933:
Yogesh Darmwal and Ketan Rajawat tackle hard matrix equations that show up in control theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper seeks matrix answers that are symmetric and positive definite. Such equations also arise in dynamic programming and in stochastic filtering.

For a large matrix, standard methods cost far too much per step. The cheap methods lean on sparsity or on low-rank answers, or need too many steps. The authors propose a rank-one method that moves along curved matrix space. It works within a small subspace at each step to cut the cost.
arxiv-2601-15033:
Fernando De Terán and Froilán M. Dopico ask what the Jordan form of a typical real matrix looks like. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with real square matrices and their canonical forms. The Jordan form lays bare a matrix's structure, but most matrices share only a few generic shapes.

The authors find those generic real Jordan forms. They prove that all real matrices split into a small count of sets, called generic bundles. The count grows as half the matrix size, rounded down, plus one. Each bundle's closure covers its share of the whole space.
arxiv-2601-15133:
André Eberhard, Gerhard Neumann, and Pascal Friederich teach machines to read a graph out of a picture. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with visual graph recognition. Tasks such as image classification and object detection have leapt ahead, but pulling a relationship graph from an image lags behind.

The authors blame the lack of a canonical way to frame the task. Their approach turns recognition into subgraph prediction. The model predicts the pieces of the graph rather than the whole structure at once. That split gives the learner a cleaner target to aim at.
arxiv-2601-15233:
Jaeyun Moon asks how to describe the basic excitations of a very thin gas. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with dilute gases, the far end of the spectrum of matter. In solids, atomic vibrations are charted in reciprocal space as phonons, labeled by frequency and wavevector.

A gas is usually described quite differently. Its story is told through atoms or molecules that collide and fly in real space and time. Moon seeks elementary excitations for the gas itself. The work builds a bridge between the two pictures of how matter moves.
arxiv-2601-15533:
Zhikang Chen and Tingting Zhu argue that AI world models need firmer ties to physics in a 2026 arXiv paper. A world model simulates how a setting changes under actions. That lets an agent plan by imagining futures, not just reacting. Recent models have grown strong at making video. The authors say looks can mislead.

They name the flaw visual conflation. Sharp, pretty video does not prove a model grasps physical or causal rules. A model can render a falling cup yet miss how gravity works. The paper presses for physical grounding as an imperative, per its title. Grounded models could serve as actionable simulators for planning. Ungrounded ones risk confident plans built on false physics.
arxiv-2601-15833:
T. Haidamak and a large team study a magnetic crystal with sound waves in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their material is EuAl12O19. It is a quasi-two-dimensional anisotropic ferromagnet. Magnetoelastic coupling links its magnetism to its lattice. That coupling plays a crucial role in field-induced transitions in such magnets. Ultrasonic methods suit this physics well. Sound velocity reveals elastic constants with high sensitivity.

The team measures sound velocity in magnetic fields. The fields point perpendicular to the spontaneous magnetization. Changes in velocity mark how the lattice responds as the field drives transitions. Elastic constants are the basic numbers that summarize that response. For condensed matter physics, such data test models of coupled spin and lattice behavior.
arxiv-2601-16133:
