Matthias Heinz works on code schemes for a key step in nucleus maths. His 2026 preprint deals with the in medium similarity method. That method solves the core maths for nuclei by a smooth twist of the state maths. The twist is oft cut at a set low order. A key sum, the Magnus sum, builds that twist step by step.

Heinz sets out schemes to work that sum with care. Good schemes cut cost while they keep the result true. Nuclei with more parts need such care to stay in reach. The work aids teams who run large nucleus sums. It sits at the code and maths join of the field.
arxiv-2601-16933:
Jingran Zhang, Ning Li, Yuanhao Ban, Andrew Bai, and Justin Cui add reward checks to video bots. Most video bots build clips by views from both ends. Step-by-step bots can make clips live, frame by frame. Past step bots leaned on big teacher bots. That lean caps their skill when teachers are weak. Their 2026 preprint swaps the teacher lean for reward marks.

Clips gain marks as they grow, and low marks get cut. The bot learns to chase high-mark paths on its own. Live clip tools could gain skill with no big teacher. Such tools serve ads, games, and quick film drafts.
arxiv-2601-17133:
Inderjeet Singh, Eleonore Vissol-Gaudin, Andikan Otung, and Motoyoshi Sekiya join chatbots in a peer web with no hub. Fine-tune work needs rich data from many sites. Those sites can't share raw text, for law and trust. Hub-based crowd learn has one weak point at its core. That hub can fail, and its acts can be probed. Their 2026 preprint builds a peer-to-peer frame in its place.

Peers trade model steps with no boss node. An orchestrated plan keeps the trades in time. No raw text moves in the scheme at all. Banks and wards could train shared bots this way.
arxiv-2601-17333:
Lalit Pant and Shivang Nagar lay out a blueprint for search tools that take plain speech. Their field is Natural Language Query, or NLQ for short. NLQ lets users ask systems in human words, not code-like syntax. The blueprint is tuned for finance knowledge search. Finance data is vast, dense, and time-bound.

The design covers how such a system should be built today. It links user questions to stored knowledge they can trust. Good finance search saves analysts hours of digging. It also cuts errors from poor query syntax. The blueprint gives teams a plan to build from. It stresses fit for finance tasks, not generic chat.
arxiv-2601-17533:
Silong Chen and six co-authors show that training data can be rebuilt from federated language models. These models freeze the main network and train small adapters. Adapters cut compute, storage, and network costs. They seemed to limit gradient leaks too. Past inversion attacks looked blocked by that design. The authors test that belief.

They reconstruct training data from the adapter setup. A working attack proves privacy claims need care. Web-scale apps use federated adapters to guard user text. If text can be rebuilt, that guard is thin. The work warns builders and users alike. It sets a test that future private designs must pass.
arxiv-2601-17633:
Rakesh Nadig and co-authors present Conduit for near-data processing in solid-state drives. Near-data processing moves compute to where data sits. That cuts the data movement bottleneck. SSDs are a natural host. They store datasets too big for main memory. They also hold many kinds of compute units inside.

Conduit makes that power programmer-transparent. Coders need not hand-manage each unit in the drive. Hidden complexity has blocked NDP use for years. A transparent layer could spread it to daily workloads. Big data and AI tasks move vast bytes for small math. Processing in place attacks that waste at its source.
arxiv-2601-17833:
Xiaohui Hu and co-authors build an agent-based tool for auditing Ethereum smart contracts. Their 2026 preprint starts from a hard problem in blockchain safety. Smart contracts hold real money, and flaws in their business logic can be costly. Manual audits do not scale. Static tools raise many false alarms, and fuzzers get lost in deep logic paths.

The team's frame sets software agents on the audit task. Agents can plan steps, call tools, and follow logic across a whole contract. The authors stress cost as well as skill, since audits must run at scale. If the frame works as hoped, it could catch deep flaws that older tools miss, at a price teams can pay.
arxiv-2601-17933:
Laurent Caraffa frames machine learning as a system that must manage its own energy and decay. His 2026 preprint proposes a dissipative learning frame for adaptive systems. Models in the field must adapt for years, stay stable, and work with finite resources. Yet core flaws like forgetting, overfitting, and collapse of features lack a shared, principled account. Fixes like weight decay and dropout are used one by one, without a unifying theory.

A dissipative view treats learning like a physical process with flows and losses. That view may explain why the flaws arise and when fixes help. The goal is systems that stay viable over long runs. The paper aims at a theory base for long-lived learning machines.
arxiv-2601-18033:
Ahana Ghosh, Advait Sarkar, Siân Lindley, and Christian Poelitz test designs that make AI users think before they accept help. Their 2026 preprint studies cognitive forcing functions in AI-assisted writing. Generative tools speed up writing and coding, but they also invite overreliance and lazy thinking. Forcing functions are design moves that make a user engage with the task to proceed. The team runs an experiment on such moves built into execution plans.

They measure effects on trust, overreliance, and how useful people find the tool. The trade-offs are real: friction can guard thought but also annoy. The results guide designers who want AI help without dull users. Keeping human judgment awake is a core design problem of the AI era.
arxiv-2601-18133:
Yu Zhang, Xun Chen, and Miguel Angel Martin Contreras let a neural network draw the field that shapes heavy quark states. Their 2026 preprint builds a holographic model of heavy vector quarkonia. In the bottom-up AdS/QCD approach, a dilaton field sets the rules of the model. Most work picks a simple formula for that field by hand. The authors instead train a multilayer perceptron to learn the field's slope as a smooth function of the holographic coordinate.

A learned field can fit data without the bias of a guessed form. From it, the team computes the spectrum and decay constants of the states. The method joins machine learning with a theory of strong forces. It may sharpen predictions for particles that bind a heavy quark pair.
arxiv-2601-18233:
Daniel W. Boutros, Kolluru Venkata Kiran, John D. Gibbon, and Rahul Pandit study the long-run fate of active turbulence. Their 2026 preprint deals with the Toner-Tu-Swift-Hohenberg equations. These equations model turbulence in active matter, above all the swarming of bacteria in suspension. They blend traits of the Navier-Stokes, Toner-Tu, and Swift-Hohenberg equations. The authors study the global attractor of the system: the set toward which all solutions are drawn as time runs on.

They also work out the attractor's properties. An attractor tells which patterns a swirling bacterial bath can settle into. That knowledge guides both theory and lab work on active fluids. The study anchors a model that is becoming basic to the field.
arxiv-2601-18633:
Tong Shi and four colleagues build talk-ing heads that move in true three dims from a lone still shot and a voice track. Past tools cheat the move with flat warps of the face. Those warps can look fine from the front but break from the side. They also tend to give a poor build of the head's true form, so the whole clip feels off.

Their tool builds the head from soft blobs of light in space, a form that holds up from all sides. The blobs move with the speech, so lips and jaw track the voice. A true build could give clips that work in free-view calls and games. It could also cut the need for a full shoot for each new line. The team aim for heads that look real from each view a user may take.
arxiv-2601-18933:
Kaustubh D. Dhole builds a test set for tiny language models trained like young children learn. Most tests of reasoning in such models assume adult skills: wide world knowledge, hard steps, and grown up speech norms. Baby language models learn from child directed speech and simple tales, so those tests fit them poorly.

His bench, BabyReasoningBench, makes tasks drawn from how children grow and learn. The tasks check which reasoning skills show up when training stays close to what a child would hear. Fair tests of this kind can show what small models truly learn, not just where adult tests mislead.
arxiv-2601-19333:
Rahul Raychaudhury and three co-authors cluster data when exact distances are out of reach. Clustering groups like items together and powers much of unsupervised learning. Classic methods assume they can read exact pairwise distances, which many modern settings cannot supply.

Their setting gives only weak comparison oracles: answers that say which of two distances looks bigger, with noise and limits. Algorithms that cluster from comparisons alone could work where numbers are untrusted or private. The work tests how far ranking style information can carry a classic task that was built for exact numbers from the start.
arxiv-2601-19733:
Nicholas Biglin studies the long-term behaviour of a model for charged matter spreading under its own repulsion. The repulsive pressureless Euler-Poisson system describes a cloud of mass whose parts push each other outward. There is no pressure to resist the spread. The paper works in one dimension with distributional solutions, a weak notion that tolerates sharp concentrations.

Biglin analyses where the mass ends up as time grows large. Asymptotic results describe the final pattern of spreading. Such systems model plasmas and semiconductor flows in simplified form. Knowing the long-run behaviour checks that simulations settle correctly. The work adds rigor to a system whose solutions can form singularities.
arxiv-2601-19933:
Kei Saito studies a habit of language models: they commit to one meaning too early. Given an ambiguous input, a model tends to collapse several valid readings into a single answer. It does so before enough context has arrived to choose safely. That early commitment discards information later turns may need.

His system, NRR-Phi, maps text to a state that preserves ambiguity instead. Multiple interpretations stay alive in the representation until context resolves them. Dialogue systems, legal readers, and translation tools all meet ambiguity daily. A representation that refuses to guess early could cut costly misunderstandings. The work treats ambiguity as information to keep, not noise to remove.
arxiv-2601-20233:
Tài Huy Hà and Nguyen Cong Minh extend two classic formulas of monomial ideal theory. Hochster's and Takayama's formulas describe pieces of local cohomology modules through simplicial complexes, which are shapes built from points and faces. The authors develop a relative version for quotients of monomial ideals.

Their formula expresses the graded pieces for a quotient using relative homology of pairs of degree complexes. As an application, they obtain a relative Reisner criterion that tells when such quotients are Cohen-Macaulay. These results give algebraists sharper tools for a class of ideals that model discrete, combinatorial data.
arxiv-2601-20933:
Precision Jet Substructure of Boosted Boson Decays with Energy Correlators is studied by Anjie Gao, Kyle Lee, and Xiaoyuan Zhang in this 2026 paper. They initiate the precision study of boosted jet substructure using energy correlators. The test case is hadronic Higgs decays. When a Higgs boson moves fast, its decay products merge into one jet. Reading that jet's inner pattern is the challenge.

The authors show the two-body decay leaves a distinct mark. It appears as an angular peak in the correlator. The peak's position is set by the boson's Lorentz boost factor. Such a clean signature could sharpen Higgs studies at colliders. Energy correlators are prized for their calculability in theory. This work brings that precision to a flagship measurement. It may guide how future analyses tag boosted bosons.
arxiv-2601-21033:
Omer Rochman-Sharabi and Gilles Louppe teach diffusion models to obey hard rules. Their 2026 paper presents Predict-Project-Renoise, a sampling framework. Diffusion-based neural emulators show promise for scientific work. Vanilla models, though, cannot guarantee physical accuracy. Nor can they promise that constraints will hold. A generated weather field or flow must respect laws and observations. The framework enforces hard constraints at generation time.

The name sketches the loop. The model predicts a sample, projects it onto the constraint set, then renoises and repeats. Projection forces each draw to satisfy the rules exactly. Physical laws and observational consistency are the target constraints. That guarantee matters when outputs feed real decisions. The work serves scientists who need generative speed without lawless samples.
arxiv-2601-21433:
Katherine Elkins and Jon Chun audit how language models handle instructions that say what not to do. When a user states that someone should not act, a model should treat that as a ban. The audit finds that many models do the reverse and read the ban as approval.

The team tested many models across a set of ethical scenes. Open models endorsed banned acts at high rates, worse under layered wording. Paid models did better but still swung widely with phrasing. The results expose a basic reading failure with real safety stakes, since guardrails often rest on plain negations.
arxiv-2601-21533:
Youngjin Jin, Hanna Kim, Kwanwoo Kim, Chanhee Lee, and Seungwon Shin organize multi-expert AI debates into explicit argument maps. Systems that pool several expert models usually merge their views by simple voting or averaging. That hides which arguments actually drove the final call.

Their framework, ARGORA, builds graphs where arguments support or attack each other. Reasoning for decisions is then grounded in that visible structure. A reader can trace the winning claim back through the debate. Such traceability matters for decisions in law, medicine, and policy, where a bare answer with no visible reasons is hard to trust.
arxiv-2601-21633:
Pu Cao, Yiyang Ma, Feng Zhou, Xuedan Yin, Qing Song, and Lu Yang revisit a trade-off inside latent diffusion models. The autoencoder in these models must do two jobs: rebuild images faithfully and provide a space where generation works well. Recent large-scale studies tilt hard toward generation scores.

The authors note that rebuild quality is reported less and less. Selections based on ablations often crown the best generation score even when rebuild fidelity drops. Their tilted seesaw view argues the balance has swung too far. Restoring weight to fidelity matters for editing tools, where a model must first copy an image well before changing it.
arxiv-2601-21833:
Yuichi Harikane and co-authors report a puzzling galaxy from the early universe. The James Webb Space Telescope has found many bright galaxies at very early times, more than models expected. This 2026 preprint studies one luminous galaxy seen as it was when the universe was young, at redshift eleven.

What surprises the team is how weak its star formation activity looks for such a bright object. A galaxy can shine brightly yet form few new stars if its light comes from an earlier burst or another source. Cases like this test the story astronomers tell about how the first galaxies grew so fast. Each odd example forces the models of early galaxy formation to become more precise.
arxiv-2601-21933:
Rui Zhao and co-authors ask how much a deep visual feature can be distorted before the change becomes noticeable. Deep features, the internal representations of vision networks, now serve as the interface in many systems. Machines, not just eyes, consume images and features.

The just noticeable difference is the largest distortion that stays imperceptible, whether to human or machine vision. Modeling it for deep features, as this 2026 preprint does, lets engineers describe feature quality and control it. That control matters for compression and transmission: bits spent below the noticeable threshold are wasted. While damage above it degrades the systems that read the features downstream.
arxiv-2601-22033:
Ehsan Mirafzali and co-authors borrow an idea from quantum gravity to build generative models. The holographic principle says a volume of space can be described by a theory on its boundary. Its sharpest form is the anti-de Sitter and conformal field theory correspondence, a duality between gravity and field theory.

Their 2026 preprint builds holographic generative flows on that correspondence, combining it with deep learning and transport theory. In plain terms, samples are generated by flowing along a structure inspired by the duality. Crossovers like this are worth testing: the mathematics of holography is deep and highly structured. And generative modeling has repeatedly advanced by importing strong structure from physics.
arxiv-2601-22333:
Mihai Marciu reworks a bold twist on gravity that adds the square of matter's energy and push to the rules. His 2026 preprint takes care of a term past work left out: how the matter rule itself bends when the metric shifts. That term grows out of heat-and-flow grounds.

With it in place, he recasts the theory in a scalar-tensor form, which is easier to test. He then checks the new form for basic stability. The work keeps a fringe gravity idea honest and testable. It shows what the full math, done with care, demands.
arxiv-2601-22433:
Shahria Hoque and a team blend language models with a fuzzy decision method to rank job seekers. Their 2026 preprint notes that picking the right staff is key to a firm's success, and the race for talent is fierce. Their system reads and scores software engineer profiles on its own.

The method, Fuzzy-TOPSIS, ranks options that sit close to an ideal and far from a worst case, while allowing graded, fuzzy scores. Auto ranking can speed a first cut through many files. It must still be watched for bias and error. The work tests how far such a blend can go.
arxiv-2601-22833:
Emilio Santos re-examines the ground rules behind Bell tests, the classic checks of local realism in physics. Bell's conditions say what a local, realistic world must obey in optical experiments. Santos argues that Bell's picture of how detectors respond to signals was far too idealized.

With more physical detector conditions, he builds a local model of an optical setup that breaks the famous inequality. The claim does not end the debate, but it sharpens it. It asks experimenters to state their detector assumptions plainly when they test nature. The critique is aimed at optical experiments in particular, where detector behavior shapes what the data can honestly prove.
arxiv-2601-22933:
Fraser Birks and four co-authors trace how amorphous carbon deforms under stress. In glassy solids, deformation comes from tiny local shear events that group into avalanches. The authors model the carbon with a machine-learned potential, which mimics atomic forces at low cost.

By following the energy landscape with a method called arclength continuation, they resolve how avalanches form and organize. Seeing the steps behind sudden slips helps explain why hard carbon coatings wear or crack. The approach may guide tougher materials for tools and engines. Following the landscape step by step also reveals how separate shear events link into a single avalanche across the sample.
arxiv-2601-23233:
Nguyen Minh Duc and Viet Cuong Ta predict future links in networks that change over time. Temporal link prediction matters for social, financial, and transport systems. Standard temporal graph networks learn from past interactions, but they give single point guesses for future links.

Their sequence diffusion model adds an explicit way to capture uncertainty and the sequential shape of future interactions. Knowing the range of likely futures, not just one guess, supports safer decisions. Diffusion methods bring generative modeling to a classic network task. Uncertainty and sequential structure of future interactions are what discriminative point estimates leave out, and diffusion supplies.
arxiv-2602-00133: Avi Arora and Ritesh Malpani introduce PredictionMarketBench, a benchmark for testing trading agents on prediction markets. Such markets suit agent tests because contracts pay in binary form, prices read as probabilities, and success hinges on microstructure, fees, and settlement risk. The bench replays past limit order book and trade data in a deterministic, event driven way, with a realistic simulator for maker and taker rules and fees. Four Kalshi episodes span crypto, weather, and sports, and naive agents lose ground to transaction costs and settlement effects.
arxiv-2602-00233: Alexander Van Werde studies exact cospectrality probabilities for uniform random matrices under orthogonal conjugation. Given one fixed orthogonal matrix defined over an algebraic number field, he asks how likely its conjugate stays integral. The random matrix has entries uniform in the ring of integers. His main result gives an exact formula for that probability in terms of Smith ideals tied to the orthogonal matrix. Readers in number theory and random matrix theory will find the core argument here.
arxiv-2602-00333: Parmida Davarmanesh and team introduce an attention guided steering system for large language models. Steering means directly shifting internal activations toward specific concepts, promising insight into how concepts are stored and used. Existing methods are brittle: seemingly fixed concepts become fully steerable through subtle choices in feature extraction. The new framework tackles three challenges: picking token embeddings, varied concept features across activations, and finding key layers. Across a benchmark of 512 semantic concepts, it greatly improves steering results over prior methods.
arxiv-2602-00533: Core Francisco Park separates the world, the data process, and learned representations to study how their geometry forms and adapts. In a setup, 5,075 city points define the world and 7 shape tasks generate training data. Different tasks yield distinct world geometries, yet multi-task training aligns them, giving controlled evidence for the Multitask Scaling Hypothesis, part of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis. Training on all tasks then fine-tuning on new cities shows divergent tasks can harm new-entity uptake and generalisation, while multi-task training aligns outputs.
arxiv-2602-00733: Yinuo Zhang and colleagues propose EchoReview, a tool for learning peer review from citations, as growing papers strain traditional peer review. Existing fine-tuning on real review data is limited by one data source and by human bias and inconsistency. It mines implicit signals from citations and turns long-term judgements into structured review-style data. From this pipeline the authors build EchoReview-16K, a multi-year review data set, and train the reviewer. Experiments show gains on evidence support and breadth, validating citation context for peer review.
arxiv-2602-00833: Marco Cherubini and colleagues place the H3S Tc peak in a centrosymmetric zone of strong nuclear quantum fluctuations above a quantum critical point. They map the H3S phase diagram across temperature and pressure, including thermal and quantum effects. They use path integral molecular dynamics with a MACE potential trained on BLYP. The diagram turns on a displacive transition between Im-3m and polar R3m phases, rooted in a quantum critical point near 134 GPa. Finite-size scaling puts the transition in the 4D Ising universality class.
arxiv-2602-00933: Chaithanya Bandi and colleagues introduce MCP-Atlas, a benchmark for tool-use competency against production MCP servers. Existing evaluations miss realistic multi-step workflows, breadth across real servers rather than mocks, and structured claim-level scoring free of verbosity or style. MCP-Atlas holds 1,000 tasks by human experts spanning 36 real servers and 220 tools, with prompts specifying no servers, tools, or parameters. Agents must find relevant tools among plausible distractors and compose multi-step, cross-server workflows, scored against atomic claims from tool outputs. Answer-centric scoring credits valid alternative trajectories.
arxiv-2602-01133: Yanbin Huang and co-authors rethink spike nets for parallel training, dropping the reset step. Reset ties time steps in knots that block parallel runs, yet any swap must keep reset's jobs and keep serial runs cheap at test time. Their decay spike cell meets both bars. On 16k-long runs it trained 25.6x faster than the first parallel cell, and nets trained on 2k runs held firm to 30k. It held up across five job kinds, three net forms, and two spike modes, firing less than old cells.
arxiv-2602-01333: Haruka Fukihara and co-authors test ion-neutral drift speed as a new gauge of dust growth and magnetic push in star cradles. Sky reads put drift speeds near 100 meters per second in clouds and dense cores, and theory ties magnetic drag closely to dust size spread in ambipolar drift. Sims of dust growth by sticking and clumping show both dust growth and a 200 microgauss field are needed on core scales to match observed drift speeds. Core-scale drift reads may thus pin down dust size spread and field strength.
arxiv-2602-01433: Muhammad Hasan Ferdous and co-authors propose a decomposition-based causal framework for multivariate time series. Finance, climate, and healthcare series blend trends, seasonal patterns, and swings, muddying causal inference. The framework splits each series into trend, seasonal, and residual parts for analysis. Trends get stationarity tests, season parts get kernel dependence measures, and residuals get constraint-based discovery. Merged component graphs form a unified multi-scale structure separating long- and short-range effects. Synthetic benchmarks and real climate data show it recovering ground-truth structure better than baselines.
arxiv-2602-01733: Junxian Liu and colleagues tighten backward prediction, where a cap on set size replaces the coverage build. Conformal methods build coverage but leave set sizes open, while backward methods fix a size cap and give the coverage. Markov slack leaves a gap between claimed and real coverage, so the authors introduce a change of nonconformity scores, fitted to the data, to narrow that gap. They develop a change and prove it beats the baseline, and tests cut the gap from about four percent to about one percent.
arxiv-2602-02033: Shuo Lu and colleagues present One Size, Many Fits, aligning group click preferences. OSMF begins with product-aware grouping. Generation uses a Group-aware Multimodal Large Language Model, pre-trained to comprehend group features, and fine-tuned with Group-DPO, enhancing click rate. They also introduce the first Grouped Advertising Image Preference Dataset, with 600K groups. Experiments show state-of-the-art performance.
arxiv-2602-02233: Jonas Hummel and others present CHOMP, the first earphone-based system for steady finding of chewing-side preference, a risk factor for temporomandibular disorders. Using an open earable platform, the team collected multimodal data from twenty participants across foods, activities, and acoustic interference. The setup used motion, pulse, and pressure sensors, microphones, and a bone-conduction microphone. Paired-ear time traits feed modality-given recurrent networks with fusion and prototype classification, and microphones perform best alone while fusion performs best overall.
arxiv-2602-02733:
Prodromos Fotiadis and 3 co-authors simulate the cyclotron lines stamped on X-ray pulsar spectra to explain why those lines wander, in research posted to arXiv in 2026. Cyclotron resonant scattering features shift in energy and width as luminosity changes, most below the critical luminosity. Resonant scattering and Doppler shifts from plasma flowing in the accretion funnel are the prime suspects.

A relativistic Monte Carlo code performs radiative transfer through the funnel above the hotspot, using analytic density and speed profiles that include light pressure. Emergent spectra show a strong asymmetric line with a broad blue wing. The line sits redshifted from the classical cyclotron energy, less so at higher luminosity and larger viewing angles. Energy and width both rise with luminosity at every angle, while geometry drives strong pulse-phase swings. Applied to the pulsar GX 304-1, the model reproduces observed swings across nearly tenfold luminosity changes.
arxiv-2602-02833:
Afonso Rodrigues, writing alone in 2026, studies how firms choose the features of the products they sell. His paper builds a new version of linear demand, a simple model of how much buyers want. Product features affect both how much people value a good and how strongly goods compete.

Rodrigues shows what the model can reveal about design choices. Firms can use it to improve existing goods. They can also predict demand for products that do not exist yet. The setup handles many goods, firms, and features. It covers markets with different structures, including uneven firms and both quality and style differences.
arxiv-2602-02933:
Alexei Miasnikov and 1 co-author develop a nonstandard version of free groups in a 2026 mathematics paper. Free groups are basic objects in group theory, built from generators with no extra relations. Interpretation, a logic tool, lets one form be coded inside another to produce new, equivalent models.

Interpreting the free group inside the natural numbers yields what the authors call nonstandard free groups. They extend the idea to a wide class of groups. Ultrapowers of a group, a standard construction, can then be viewed as such nonstandard models. The paper also introduces nonstandard subgroups, normal subgroups, and presentations. The method helps answer a longstanding question raised by Malcev.
arxiv-2602-03033:
Programs that build and run other programs are given a safer language by Haoxuan Yin and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Such metaprogramming is powerful for optimization. With higher-order references for code, though, free variables can escape their binders, threatening type safety in ways ordinary languages do not face during compilation or execution.

Their language, Contextual MetaML, tracks free variables explicitly with contextual modal types. It is presented as the first such language supporting stored, runnable open code under strong type safety. The authors build a semantic model based on interaction traces from game semantics. That model captures contextual equivalence. They prove full abstraction, meaning semantic and program equivalence coincide, plus a new theorem about closing substitutions.
arxiv-2602-03333:
Hidden adversarial bumps on 3D point clouds are scrubbed by Haoran Li, leading 5 other authors, in a spectral defense called PWAVEP. Recent attacks achieve spatial imperceptibility with high success, taxing defenders. Earlier defenses often need invasive model changes, costly training, or extra data. Their analysis instead links imperceptible perturbations to high-frequency spectral parts, suggesting a plug-and-play purification route that leaves the target model untouched during deployment.

Each point receives a spectral graph wavelet saliency score and a local sparsity score. The most salient points, deemed hardly recoverable outliers, are removed. A broader set of moderately salient points undergoes spectral filtering that weakens high-frequency coefficients. Wide reviews showed superior score and strength over earlier methods. Code and datasets are publicly available.
arxiv-2602-03433:
Control engineers design systems that steer machines, while large language models now need steering of their own. Komeil Nosrati and 3 co-authors map this two-way relationship in a 2026 paper. Prompts can help design controllers, and control theory can in turn shape prompts and model behavior toward specific goals.

The authors first review how language models assist control directly, by drafting and tuning controllers, and indirectly, by speeding up research work. They then show how control ideas steer model trajectories through activation-level interventions, parameter editing, and input optimization. A final section treats the model itself as a dynamical system inside a control loop. The paper closes with open challenges for trustworthy, controllable models.
arxiv-2602-03533:
Models that both understand and generate content are routine in 2D, but 3D has resisted unification. Yongwei Chen and 6 co-authors present PnP-U3D in a 2026 paper, a plug-and-play framework joining 3D understanding with 3D generation. Forcing everything through one autoregressive model, they argue, degrades quality and costs too much training.

Instead, understanding uses autoregressive next-token prediction, while generation uses a continuous diffusion model. A lightweight transformer bridges the language model's features and the diffusion model's conditions, letting the two exchange information without erasing their pretrained strengths. Across benchmarks the framework reaches state-of-the-art results in 3D understanding and generation, and it also performs strongly on 3D editing tasks.
arxiv-2602-03733:
Wenfang Sun and 4 co-authors want vision-language models to reason about images in rounds, pointing at what they mean each time. Their 2026 paper presents a benchmark for multi-round visual reasoning and a system, RegionReasoner, trained for it. Existing systems mostly reason once, or only in text, so their reasoning cannot be refined round by round or checked.

The benchmark spans detection and segmentation tasks with training and test sets built for iterative scenarios. RegionReasoner enforces grounded reasoning: every reasoning trace must cite the reference boxes behind its claims. A global-local consistency reward aligns scene-level and region-level descriptions with the trace. Structured rewards that combine grounding fidelity with semantic alignment drive the reinforcement learning. The 7-billion-parameter model improves reasoning accuracy and grounding precision a lot.
arxiv-2602-04333:
Galaxy neighborhoods shut down star formation along two distinct paths. Ryo Albert Sutanto and colleagues map overdensities in twenty JWST survey fields in a 2026 paper, the fourth from the BEACON pure-parallel imaging program. A density method using full redshift probability distributions found over two hundred significant overdensities in the early universe.

Systems in more massive halos show higher quenched fractions and lower star formation rates. That trend weakens earlier on, consistent with cold gas streams feeding galaxies through hot halos. A second dependence ties quenching to local density separately. The data sketch how environment first feeds, then starves, young galaxies.
arxiv-2602-04433:
Chris J Mitchell and 1 co-author tighten the ceiling on how long a negative orientable sequence can run. These periodic sequences use alphabets of at least three symbols. Any block, or the negative of its reverse, appears at most once per period. They were introduced in 2024 to generate orientable sequences for position location.

Their new upper bounds on the period are significantly sharper than the previous one for block length above two. The proof examines nodes in a subgraph of the de Bruijn graph, using that in-degree must equal out-degree at every vertex. A gap to the best known constructions remains.
arxiv-2602-04733: A. Kushaeva and S. Nasyrov compare two ways of measuring distance inside a square in a 2026 mathematics paper. One is the hyperbolic metric, borrowed from non-Euclidean geometry. The other is the triangular ratio metric, which weighs the straight distance between two points against the shortest detour touching the square's boundary.
arxiv-2602-05033:
Causal representation learning tries to recover the hidden variables behind raw observations, along with the arrows between them. Jiaxu Ren and 2 co-authors extend that program to continuous time in this 2026 machine learning paper. Many real systems, from firing neurons to accumulating mutations, are point processes that evolve continuously, and earlier identifiable methods handled only snapshots or discrete steps.

The authors study when the hidden process can be identified at all, by studying the shape of the parameter space. They then build MUTATE, a variational autoencoder with a time-adaptive transition module that infers the hidden stochastic dynamics. In simulated and empirical studies, the system answered concrete scientific questions, including how mutations accumulate in genomics and what triggers neuron spikes under changing conditions.
arxiv-2602-05533:
Diffusion models can generate samples that fit a pattern, but forcing every sample to meet a hard constraint is a stricter demand. Zhengyi Guo, Wenpin Tang, and Renyuan Xu study conditional generation where outputs must satisfy a set event with certainty, as in safety-critical work and rare-event simulation. Soft guidance based on rewards cannot promise that, so they build on the probabilistic roots of diffusion models.

Their framework uses Doob's h-transform to add an explicit drift correction to a pretrained model, leaving the trained score network untouched. Two new learning algorithms estimate the needed correction from the model's own trajectories, using losses based on martingales and their covariation. The authors prove error bounds in total variation and Wasserstein distance that account for score and guidance errors. Numerical tests show the methods enforce hard constraints and produce rare-event samples well. Code for the experiments is shared online.
arxiv-2602-05633:
The same model answer can harm one student and help another, yet most safety tests score responses without asking who receives them. Rui Jia and 9 co-authors define student-tailored personalized safety and build CASTLE, a benchmark grounded in educational theory. It covers fifteen educational safety risks and fourteen student attributes, across a large bilingual set of scenarios in Chinese and English.

Three metrics score the models: risk sensitivity, for spotting dangers, emotional empathy, for reading a student's state, and student alignment, for matching a reply to that student's attributes. Eighteen leading language models were tested, and every one scored below the middle of the five-point safety scale on average. The authors read that as a substantial deficiency in personalized safety assurance. The benchmark is aimed at teams building AI tutors and school-facing assistants.
arxiv-2602-05733:
Errors in an exact formula can be a message rather than a nuisance, and Inês Aniceto, James Ratcliffe, and Itamar Yaakov read them that way for a supersymmetric gauge theory. They study the partition function of a superconformal Yang Mills theory on the four sphere, computed by supersymmetric localization. They ask what its analytic continuation to all coupling values means physically.

Their construction, built on the chiral algebra subsector of the theory, links two dimensional unstable instantons to the complex saddle points that appear as singularities in the localization integral. The picture also aligns with an alternative Higgs branch localization of the same quantity. The result gives a physical interpretation for a mathematical resurgence phenomenon: the error terms encode real saddle structures. It should interest readers who use localization to extract exact results from strongly coupled theories.
arxiv-2602-05833:
Synthetic data that mimics a private data set is valuable for training and testing, but generative models trained on the original can leak it. Laura Plein, Alexi Turcotte, Arina Hallemans, and Andreas Zeller reframe the task as search based testing rather than pure generation. Their system, SecretFan, pairs a discriminator with a fuzzer: the discriminator learns from the data, while a fuzzer, not a generator network, produces candidate samples.

Because the private data only guides the search indirectly, evolved samples can match the original statistical distributions while resisting membership inference and reconstruction attacks. The generate and discriminate loop echoes a GAN, with the fuzzer playing the generator role. Evaluation covers eight data sets used to judge leading techniques. The authors report synthetic data with utility close to the original data, without the direct exposure that model based generators carry. The work targets researchers who need shareable stand in data.
arxiv-2602-05933:
Policy mirror descent is a principled reinforcement learning frame used inside the training of advanced language models. Its ideal update, though, needs a partition function that is hard to estimate from few rollouts. Zhenghao Xu, Qin Lu, Changlong Yu, and Tuo Zhao study a practical variant, PMD-mean. It replaces the log partition term with the mean reward under the sampling policy, and regresses in log policy space.

They characterize the population solution of that approximation. It turns out to optimize mirror descent subproblems with an adaptive mixed regularizer, blending KL and chi square penalties. The extra penalty restrains large probability jumps, making updates more conservative when rewards are low and more robust to sampling error. Experiments on math reasoning tasks show better performance with improved stability and time efficiency over alternatives. The paper explains why a convenient approximation quietly helps.
arxiv-2602-06533:
Language models score well on logic benchmarks, yet it is unclear which core logical skills they actually command. Brian Rabern and 2 co-authors present LogicSkills, a benchmark that isolates three skills. First, translating premises into first-order logic. Second, building a finite countermodel to show an argument invalid. Third, judging whether a conclusion follows.

Items come from a two-variable fragment of first-order logic without identity, written in plain English and in a nonce-word language that blocks memorized answers. Every item was checked with an automated solver for correctness and non-triviality. Instruction-tuned models did well on validity judgment but poorly on symbolization and countermodels. Reasoning-tuned models performed strongly across all three, suggesting a more systematic skill profile.
arxiv-2602-07133:
Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 slowly loses charge as it reads out images, and that loss biases brightness measurements.  Benjamin Kuhn tracks this charge transfer efficiency problem across nearly fourteen years of observations, from October 2009 to February 2024.

The report measures how flux loss varies with source brightness and background level, and it supplies updated correction coefficients for both uncorrected and corrected image products.  One useful finding stands: a total background of about 20 to 25 electrons per pixel still best limits the damage.  Astronomers reducing Hubble data will use these numbers. Hubble image teams still use these fixes today.
arxiv-2602-07333:
Job platforms hold scattered text about each member: profiles, professional records, and search logs.  Rajat Arora and nine co-authors build a reinforcement learning method that distills those heterogeneous sources into one unified, concise, interpretable textual representation per member.

Implicit engagement signals such as clicks and applications supply the main reward, while rule-based rewards enforce formatting and length, which matters for latency-sensitive online serving.  Offline tests across several LinkedIn products show clear gains on key metrics.  Personalization builders get a useful recipe for turning messy member text into representations a language model can use.
arxiv-2602-07633:
Conformal prediction gives distribution-free uncertainty sets with exact finite-sample coverage, but in high dimensions those sets are hard to draw, sample from, or use downstream. Trevor Harris shows that any regular enough differentiable nonconformity score induces a deterministic flow whose paths converge to the edge of the conformal set.

That flow yields a training-free, fast method for sampling set boundaries in any size. Mixing across levels produces predictive spreads whose cutoff regions match the sample sets. An approximation bound decomposes error for the method. Teams in this field get a geometric tool that makes such sets usable for sampling and forecasting.
arxiv-2602-07733:
Numeric schemes for wave-like equations often add artificial viscosity, a smoothing term usually assumed to stay positive. Arun Govind Neelan lets a computer learn that viscosity field freely for the linear convection equation, using an unstable basic scheme plus auto differentiation to fit the exact answer.

Oddly, the learned viscosity turns locally negative near peaks and troughs, yet the answer stays stable and nearly exact. Old theory predicts a strictly positive real viscosity, so the author recasts viscosity as a space-time fix that compensates for unresolved errors while keeping entropy stability. The paper invites numeric analysts to rethink a textbook guess.
arxiv-2602-07933:
Parkinson's disease is hardest to catch early, when symptoms are subtle and biomedical signals interact in complex ways. Olamide Samuel Oseni and two co-authors compare attention-based deep learning models against traditional methods for early detection from tabular biomedical data, using voice measurements from patients and healthy controls.

Four models are tested, including a multilayer perceptron, gradient boosting, TabNet, and SAINT. SAINT leads on every metric, reaching weighted precision of 0.98, recall of 0.97, and an F1-score of 0.97, with a Matthews correlation coefficient near 0.999. The study suggests attention mechanisms can capture the feature interactions that simpler models miss, offering clinicians a promising screening aid.
arxiv-2602-08033:
Should people rate items one by one or compare them in pairs? Julien Fageot and four co-authors show that combining both kinds of judgment can beat either alone. Their SCoRa model learns scores from comparisons and ratings together in a unified probabilistic method.

Theory shows the maximum a posteriori estimator is well-behaved, satisfying monotonicity and robustness guarantees, and tests confirm accurate score recovery even when the model is misspecified. The advantage of combining signals is largest when correctly ordering the top items matters most. Preference-learning users gain a versatile foundation, since real systems usually collect both kinds of feedback anyway.
arxiv-2602-08333:
Training a neural network looks smooth from the outside, yet inside it the pattern of active units can shift in jumps. Cristian Pérez-Corral and five co-authors test whether learning runs on two clocks: an early stage where activation patterns churn, and a later stage where weights are refined inside mostly fixed patterns. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies ReLU networks, where each input picks a region in which the model behaves like a straight-line map.

Theory first shows that small weight changes usually leave a given input's pattern untouched. Experiments then track both quantities across several architectures and find that pattern changes fade about three times sooner than weight updates do. Readers get a simple, architecture-free gauge of training progress, plus a hint that late-stage optimization could be redesigned around stable patterns.
arxiv-2602-08433:
Projecting pictures onto curved surfaces warps them, and fixing the warp usually needs tedious calibration. Kejin Peng and two co-authors build CSPR-Net, a self-supervised network that corrects geometric distortion on its own. Their arXiv paper targets non-planar projection without ground-truth deformation fields.

Two coordinate-based networks learn the mapping between projector and camera in both directions, tied together by a cycle-consistency constraint. A gradient-based loss softens the effect of ambient light and captures fine geometric detail. Physical tests show a 20.7 percent gain in end-to-end fidelity over the baseline, plus smaller gains on forward and inverse mapping. Readers get a route to seamless projection without structured-light rigs.
arxiv-2602-08733:
Ordinary differential equations model much of science, but recovering their vector fields from noisy paths is hard and expertise-heavy. Maximilian Mauel and four co-authors propose FIM-ODE, a pretrained model for ODE inference that predicts the vector field in a single forward pass. Their arXiv paper targets low-dimensional ODE inference without system-specific priors.

Pretraining on low-degree polynomial vector fields with neural operators yields strong zero-shot performance, matching or beating a recent symbolic baseline across regimes. Fine-tuning from that start adapts fast and stably, outperforming modern neural and Gaussian-process baselines. Readers get a foundation-model shortcut for ODE inference that lowers the expertise barrier.
arxiv-2602-09033:
A century after Schrödinger's 1926 wave equation, W. David Wick argues its philosophy was left unfinished, and claims nonlinear math can now complete it. The wave equation rules atomic physics, he notes, yet the ideas beneath the wavefunction faded from view. Chaos theory and related work, in his account, allow a single nonlinear addition to the equation.

The author claims that change resolves both the measurement problem, why tests yield definite outcomes, and the randomness problem, where probabilities come from. If so, the wavefunction alone would explain many test results, with particles pushed to the shadows. Readers should note this is a programmatic argument, not a settled result.
arxiv-2602-09133:
Model predictive controllers that stop their solvers early can still stabilize a system, but mixing a fast, rough solver with a slow, accurate one needs care. Luke Fina and one co-author develop a hybrid controller that unites two mixed-integer quadratic MPC solvers, one with low iteration limits and one with high limits, for both branch-and-bound and quadratic-programming iterations. Asymptotic stability and robustness are proved for the combined feedback system.

An interpretable branch-and-bound algorithm and an implementable uniting controller are provided, then tested in simulation on spacecraft rendezvous problems, including switching-thruster and minimum-thrust scenarios. The work shows how to get the speed of early stopping without giving up the guarantees of thorough optimization.
arxiv-2602-09233:
Catching a room's sound usually means gauging its echo reply, but Jackie Lin and five co-authors make it instead. Gencho, a spread-transformer model, predicts complex-spectrogram echo replies from echoey speech alone. A structure-aware coder splits early from late echoes to build a tough guiding signal, while the spread decoder yields varied, true-to-ear echo replies.

The model plugs into standard speech pipes for sound matching and beats non-AI-made baselines on richness while holding strong scores on standard echo-reply marks. A text-guided mode extends the idea to steerable sound faking, letting users describe a room and hear it. Gencho offers bendy echo-reply making for AI-made audio.
arxiv-2602-09433:
As AI systems graduate from assistants to agents that act, the security frontier moves from model outputs to tool execution. Logs, perimeter guards, and after-the-fact reviews cannot guard actions that cannot be undone, run at machine speed, and may stem from compromised control layers. Herman Errico's single-author 2026 paper introduces Autonomous Action Runtime Management, an open plan for securing AI-driven actions while they run.

The plan defines a runtime system that catches actions before execution, gathers session context, checks policy and intent alignment, enforces go-ahead decisions, and records tamper-evident receipts for later replay. Its threat model covers prompt attacks, confused-deputy attacks, data exfiltration, and intent drift. Actions sort into forbidden, context-based deny, and context-based allow classes. Four build designs are proposed, and the plan stays model-, framework-, and vendor-neutral to head off a private split.
arxiv-2602-09533:
Direct preference optimization aligns language models with human preferences, but its standard form assumes the response-level Bradley-Terry model while treating models as autoregressive only afterward. Masanari Oi and four co-authors revisit those foundations in their 2026 paper, introducing the autoregressive assumption before applying the preference model. The resulting variant, Autoregressive DPO, keeps the theory intact while changing the loss's shape.

The derived loss elegantly moves the summation outside the log-sigmoid function, a small formal shift with real consequences. Theoretical analysis reveals two distinct length measures that designers must weigh: token length and feedback length. The authors claim to be the first to separate these measures explicitly and analyze their implications for preference optimization. The paper thus refines alignment theory at its foundations.
arxiv-2602-09633:
Farm machines have sought a fast successor to the slow CAN bus backbone of ISO 11783, known as ISOBUS, for over a decade, yet no protocol fix has reached standardization. Timo Oksanen's 2026 paper presents ISO FastLane as a short-term answer: modern planters, sprayers, and Virtual Terminals already strain against bus bandwidth. Ethernet, under FastLane, carries ISOBUS traffic bound for one destination, while broadcast messages remain on the CAN bus.

The gateway-less dual-stack design needs no new state machines, no middleware, and no application code changes: only a simple routing decision plus light peer discovery called Augmented Address Claim. Legacy devices keep working unmodified, unaware of FastLane traffic. Early tests show Virtual Terminal object pool uploads speeding eightfold and Task Controller message rates exceeding the current specification limit by over a hundredfold. Built on existing conventions, FastLane could be implemented by ISOBUS engineers within weeks.
arxiv-2602-09733:
Trusted study of quantum states is a core task in quantum info science. Yixuan Hu and two co-authors note that quantum state scanning, the standard frame for rebuilding states from measurement data, is often harmed by lab noise. Cutting such noise is thus vital for exact guessing in real settings. Their 2026 paper offers a scalable scanning method based on multi-layer net models that cut unknown noise through guided learning.

The approach is data-driven and thus rests on no explicit guesses about the noise model or measurement, making it readily usable for general quantum systems. Number tests ranging from special pure states to random mixed states show the method cutting noise well across a broad range of cases, against the case without cutting. Noise-robust scanning thus gains a scalable, guess-light tool.
arxiv-2602-10233:
AlphaEvolve-style LLM-guided evolution searches for novel mathematical constructions, but evolving one monolithic program that outputs a full solution strains the model. A 2026 paper led by Alexey Kravatskiy, with two co-authors, presents ImprovEvolve, which evolves three specialized operators instead: initialization, local improvement, and perturbation. Iterating local improvements with intensity-scheduled perturbations drives a basin-hopping search run by LLM-evolved routines.

In hexagon-in-hexagon packing, ImprovEvolve finds new state-of-the-art packings for eleven, twelve, fifteen, and sixteen hexagons, plus fourteen, seventeen, and twenty-three after minimal expert tuning. For the second autocorrelation inequality, the evolved program, scaled up by humans, slightly raises the lower bound. For spherical codes, it lowers the best-known maximum cosine for most of ninety diverse state-of-the-art codes, with relative gains up to about two and a half percent.
arxiv-2602-10433:
Spencer Dowdall and four co-authors prove new invariants for free-by-cyclic groups in a 2026 math paper. A free-by-cyclic group can split as a mapping torus in more than one way. That raises the question of which traits of the splitting are truly intrinsic to the group. The paper answers with the structure of attracting laminations.

The authors show that the poset of attracting lamination orbits of an automorphism is canonical: other splittings give isomorphic posets. From that poset they define lamination depth, the size of its largest chain, and prove it is a commensurability stable. The result gives group theorists a robust tool for distinguishing and classifying free-by-cyclic groups.
arxiv-2602-10733:
Paolo Palumbo transfers a quantum information protocol for evaporating black holes in a 2026 paper. A recent protocol by Verlinde and van der Heijden addressed information retrieval for evaporating black holes. Palumbo extends it to inclusions of type III von Neumann factors, the algebras that arise naturally in quantum field theory.

The resulting formula admits reading through the number size of superselection sectors. For black holes undergoing charge evaporation, the index-statistics theorem gives that reading a heat flavor. A constraint on index values yields a final remark on quantization of the charge emitted during evaporation. The paper bridges rule algebra, quantum information, and black hole thermodynamics in a single protocol.
arxiv-2602-10933:
Riccardo Barbano and four co-authors compose multiple spread models through team control in a 2026 paper. Steady-time creative models shine at image repair and making, but controlling the mixing of several ready models stays open. Today's plans combine chance spreads by algebra, through products or mixes of experts, if the aim spread is known plainly, which it almost never is.

The paper recasts mixing as a team random best-control problem. Ready spread models become linked players whose paths are as one guided toward a shared goal on their pooled output. Checks on guided hand-drawn-digit making and tests against spread-mixing marks show the control way composing models that algebra alone cannot line up.
arxiv-2602-11133:
Diffusion language models refine every token to the last step, wasting work. Zakhar Kohut and nine co-authors propose token-level early stopping that freezes each token once it has settled. Light signals from forecasts and local context decide, per position, when to stop.

No task-specific tuning is needed, and freezing adapts to each token rather than to the whole sequence. Across maths thinking, general question answering, and science tests, the method cuts total diffusion steps sharply while keeping output quality. The paper shows that much of the late refinement in diffusion text models is redundant, and that per-token timing is the cheap fix.
arxiv-2602-11233:
A rotating magnet field can steer spins with exact, closed-form control. Zhichen Liu and Richard A. Klemm derive exact nuclear- and electronic-spin wave functions for fields that combine a steady component with a rotating transverse component. Those solutions allow controlled transitions between entangled states.

An atom or molecule driven this way can thus act as a quantum computer. The same solutions enable precise magnet resonance measurements of nuclear moments. Examples cover nitrogen, lithium, and caesium isotopes. Because current caesium hyperfine data disagree, the proposed tests offer a route to measure all seven of its nuclear moments with high precision.
arxiv-2602-11833:
Space-based sharing of quantum entanglement will underpin global quantum networking, but designing orbiter systems needs realistic models. Jasminder Sidhu and three co-authors study entanglement-based quantum key distribution from low Earth orbit, where low matching count rates make finite-key effects especially severe compared with trusted-node links. Their high-fidelity model captures orbital dynamics, angle-dependent loss, background noise, and detector effects.

Joined to a rigorous finite-key security framework for the BBM92 protocol, the model tunes secret key length across overpass shapes, orbital heights, and ground station spacings. The results give quantitative bounds and design guidelines for near-term satellite quantum key missions. They enable informed trade-offs between orbiter payload complexity, ground gear, and secure key throughput possible.
arxiv-2602-11933:
Speech translation systems are mostly tested on clean, curated data, yet real speech bends words through inflection, dialect, and non-native accents. Abderrahmane Issam and three co-authors show that leading end-to-end speech translation models are highly vulnerable to a text-based adversarial attack on inflectional morphology, adapted here to speech. Building adversarial speech data to train against such attacks is costly and technically hard.

Their answer is Cross-Modal Robustness Transfer, a framework that moves adversarial robustness from text to speech, removing the need for adversarial speech data in training. Across four language pairs, the method improves adversarial robustness by more than three BLEU points on average. It sets a new baseline for robust speech translation without the overhead of generating adversarial speech.
arxiv-2602-12033:
Energy integrals with non-standard growth pose sharp regularity questions, especially at the limit where exponents meet. Eleuteri and three co-authors establish local Lipschitz smoothness for local minimizers of x-dependent integral functionals. There, the energy density obeys p-q growth in the gradient variable and belongs to a Sobolev class in the spatial variable. The result holds under a precise relation among the exponents and the spatial integrability.

The authors present a unified approach covering the limit case, where the ratio attains its maximal allowed value, and recover earlier results as special cases. For variational problems with x-dependent energies, that limit case is the sharp boundary: smoothness that holds inside the range must be shown to survive at its edge. The paper shows it does.
arxiv-2602-12233:
Generating categories, such as words, image tokens, or graph parts, in few steps is hard because choices are discrete. Daan Roos led this work with seven co-authors, presenting Categorical Flow Maps, a flow-matching method that speeds few-step generation through self-distillation. A flow map toward the simplex shifts probability mass toward a predicted endpoint, keeping predictions in bounds.

Because the paths are continuous, not discrete, the model can train with existing distillation tools and with a new endpoint-consistency goal. The same continuity unlocks test-time steering, reusing guidance and reweighting tricks from continuous models. Results lead the field for few-step image, molecular graph, and text generation, staying strong even in a single step.
arxiv-2602-12833:
Thinking over long hospital records strains language-model systems that keep re-reading whole past notes or passing free-form notes between agents. Zhan Qu and Michael Färber present Vital Trace, a multi-agent system bound by fixed rules for calling future care risk in ICU care. Instead of open-ended text past notes, it keeps a compact patient-state memory and splits thinking among four agents: a router, a thinker, an auditor, and a steward.

A hand-picked global rule set gives body change rules. A live state record tracks heart, lung, kidney, metabolic, and swelling trouble over time. On MIMIC-IV and eICU, the shaped approach raised time-based fit, steady talk, tuning, and clarity over free-form multi-agent plain rivals. It also kept strong forecast scores across long ICU stays.
arxiv-2602-12933:
Melanoma that spreads to the brain creates lesions that vary widely in place and appearance, complicating studies across patients and scanners. Nanna Wielenberg and eight co-authors propose a deep-learning registration framework that warps each pathological brain onto a common atlas while preserving tumour tissue, without needing lesion masks or preprocessing. A forward-model similarity metric handles missing correspondences, and a volume-preserving term keeps deformations plausible.

Applied to 209 patients from three centres, the method reached Dice scores of 0.89 to 0.92 with small surface errors, while preserving metastatic volumes. Mapping lesions onto anatomical, arterial, and perfusion atlases showed cortex and putamen hosting more lesions than expected, white matter fewer, and clustering near the grey-white junction. No arterial territory stood out after volume correction. The public implementation supports reproducible multi-centre work on brain tumours.
arxiv-2602-13433:
Pointing at distant or cluttered objects in augmented reality is error-prone, since the system must guess which target the user means. Uncertain Pointer explores feedforward visuals that show candidate targets before confirmation. Candidates get a distinct visual identity such as color, or varying intensity such as opacity to signal system uncertainty. The authors first built a pointer space of 25 designs from 30 years of literature on placement and visual signifiers.

Two online experiments with 60 and 40 participants measured preference, confidence, mental ease, visibility, and how easy targets are to tell apart, across distances and scene densities. From the results come design tips for choosing pointer styles by AR context and disambiguation technique. Ching-Yi Tsai leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13633:
Keyhole surgery rests on what the surgeon sees live, yet that seeing shifts across surgeons and cases. That spread makes steady judging, training, and trustworthy machine help hard, since most surgical tools are built for one narrow job and fail to carry across cases or hospitals. ZEN is a broad base model for video sense inside operations, trained on over four million frames from more than twenty one procedures with self supervised multi teacher distillation.

The team built a large varied set of cases and tested several learning plans in one shared test. Across twenty downstream tasks, in full tuning, frozen base, few shot, and zero shot tests, ZEN beat earlier surgical base models and held up across procedures. Those gains point to one shared picture of the surgical scene, with promise for live help and judging training. Kanggil Park leads the work with eleven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14233:
Yaxuan Kong and nine co-authors argue in a 2026 arXiv position paper that finance AI tests must name their biases. Language models now enter financial workflows, yet evaluation practice lags behind. Biases can inflate scores, contaminate backtests, and make results useless for deployment claims.

The paper names five recurring biases: look-ahead, survivorship, narrative, objective, and cost bias. A review of 164 papers from 2023 to 2025 found no single bias discussed in more than 28% of studies. The authors propose a Structural Validity Framework and a checklist with minimal bias-diagnosis requirements, to be enforced before any result supports a deployment claim.
arxiv-2602-14633:
Edited images often gain small errors, and current checks lump them all together. Joanna Wojciechowicz, with six co-authors, presents VIGIL, a benchmark and detector for image recontextualization errors. It splits errors into five kinds, from object detail to missing objects.

A multi-stage pipeline runs open-source models tuned to each error kind and explains each flag in words. The set holds 1,269 hand-labeled samples across five product areas. The split pipeline scores the best macro-F1 among open detectors. Both the data and the code are openly released for further work.
arxiv-2602-14833:
Hang Zou and colleagues introduce RF-GPT, a radio-frequency language model that teaches AI to see the wireless world. Large and multimodal models reason well over text and images, yet radio-frequency signals remain foreign to them, while conventional RF deep learning stays tied to single signal tasks. RF-GPT bridges that gap by feeding visual encoders of multimodal models with RF spectrograms.

Complex in-phase and quadrature waveforms map to time-frequency pictures the model can already read, joining RF perception to high-level reasoning. Telecom AI thus gains eyes for spectrum, not just words about it. Wireless signals become a language models can learn to perceive.
arxiv-2602-14933:
Mikhail Venchakov studies rook boards and coadjoint orbits for top unipotent groups in finite symplectic groups. By Kirillov's orbit path, such a group's orbits rule its complex trace maps, and nigh all key orbit and trace kinds known so far fit one rook-board tale through straight rook sets.

Venchakov builds a half-split form for those trace maps in the Mackey small-group spirit, and from it gives a plain form for the trace of a top-size orbit. Trace lore thus gains a rook-board road to unipotent group traces.
arxiv-2602-15133:
Alam solves the brachistochrone for a body moving underwater. Without friction, the fastest descent under gravity is a cycloid. Underwater, buoyancy, viscous drag, and added mass of entrained fluid change the problem fundamentally. The paper solves the underwater case, combining all three effects with a Reynolds-number-dependent drag coefficient.

The cycloid grows suboptimal as body density nears fluid density. Below a critical density ratio it never reaches the endpoint at all. Near the drag crisis Reynolds number, the best path turns acutely sensitive to density ratio and object size. Constant-drag approximations can mislead badly. Ignoring drag and added mass together predicts a transit time roughly half the true minimum. Omitting added mass alone underestimates it by about 20 percent. A three-point version through a waypoint reveals a finite reachable domain absent in the old problem. The method offers a planning tool for short-range buoyancy-driven vehicles.
arxiv-2602-15233:
Konicki and colleagues present a fast method for finding Perfect Bayesian Equilibria of two-player long games with imperfect information. Such outcomes refine Nash equilibria by forcing match between agents' plans and belief systems over pasts within information sets. The team adopts Bonanno's 2011 rule, using a match concept from belief theory.

Their method adapts what-if regret cutting to cut mean regret at each information set given beliefs, while keeping match criteria. The team proves it correct for two-player zero-sum games, with only modest slowdown relative to old CFR given extra polish work. Tests show solid solution quality and running time on medium-to-large non-zero-sum games. Finally, using Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium as a meta-strategy solver in a tree-exploiting Policy Space Response Oracles variant yields higher-quality test game models. It beats plain Nash-based solvers on games with complex hidden information.
arxiv-2602-15333:
Im offers a single view on selfish teamwork for spread-out air control. Spread-out air control needs teamwork among self-keen parties working under joint safe and room limits, where usual central or quietly team plans do not well hold this scene. The paper moves a single view in which results arise by shaping rewards and giving cues that bend own best rather than forcing team or force.

The setup moves along three paths: growing balance building via reduced-rank and doubt-aware linked balances, spread-out machine building for balance pick without force, and shaped selfish motion with meeting pledges. Beyond these, the paper covers core rules ruling reward-fitting teamwork in spread-out nets. Together, these results set a base for growing, robust teamwork in safety-critical air control systems.
arxiv-2602-15933:
Anand and colleagues study spin and energy transport in non-integrable, long-range Heisenberg models with tensor network methods. Isotropic integrable chains such as the Heisenberg model show superdiffusive spin transport in a class closely tied to Kardar, Parisi, and Zhang, or KPZ. The team tests whether that result extends to more generic one-dimensional models feasible in quantum simulators.

For power-law models with exponent between 2 and infinity, they find long-lived z equals 3/2 superdiffusive spin transport. Two-point correlators match KPZ scaling functions, up to times around 10 to the power 3 over J. They trace this transport to nearness of such models to the integrable Inozemtsev family, which also shows KPZ-like spin transport across all ranges. Anisotropic models realised in Rydberg atom arrays and ultracold polar molecules show a wide range of long-lived, non-diffusive transport in experimental settings.
arxiv-2602-16033:
Ruiwei Xiao leads a team of seven researchers testing how to teach university students to use generative AI as a tutor rather than an answer machine. Their semester-long randomized trial in a first computer science course involved nearly a thousand students across four teaching conditions of rising engagement, based on the ICAP framework. Each group took a pre-test, an immediate post-test, a delayed post-test, and surveys.

All four conditions improved prompting skill, with gains growing from the lightest to the most engaged condition. Students with similar starting scores who gained more on the immediate post-test also scored higher on the final exam, though no direct gap between groups showed up there. The authors present the approach as a scalable way to turn classroom AI policy into practical prompting instruction.
arxiv-2602-16233:
Prabhjot Singh and coauthors measure what circuit cutting really costs when training quantum neural networks. Circuit cutting splits a large quantum circuit into smaller pieces run independently, with expectation values recovered by combining piece outcomes classically. Prior work characterizes cutting overhead through subcircuit counts and sampling complexity, but its end-to-end impact on iterative training has been under-measured. Their pipeline, DistributedEstimator, treats cutting as a staged spread workload across four phases: partitioning, sub-test generation, parallel runs, and classic rebuild.

Using logged runtime traces and learning results on Iris and MNIST tasks, they quantify overheads, scaling limits, and sensitivity to injected stragglers. Rebuild dominates per-query time, taking over half the time at three cuts, which caps speedup under parallelism. Test accuracy is fully preserved on Iris and holds without systematic degradation on MNIST. Robustness under noise and adversarial perturbations is similarly kept.
arxiv-2602-16333:
Matija Bucić leads four coauthors on long cycles in vertex transitive digraphs. A famous conjecture, written down by Thomassen in 1978 after Lovász in 1969, says any large enough connected vertex transitive graph has a Hamilton cycle. The directed version goes back further, to Rankin in 1946, and Trotter and Erdős showed in 1978 that infinitely many connected vertex transitive digraphs are not Hamiltonian.

That left open how long a directed cycle can always be guaranteed. Alspach asked in 1981 whether the maximum perimeter gap, the gap between circumference and order, grows with the vertex count. The authors answer yes: it grows at least as fast as the natural log of that number. They also prove a directed cycle of length at least a constant times the cube root of the vertex count always exists. It is the first lower bound that grows with the count, and a directed analogue of Babai's 1979 result.
arxiv-2602-16833:
Zhicheng Zhang, Ziyan Wang, Yali Du, and Fei Fang propose Verbalized Action Masking for controlled exploration in reinforcement learning post-training, studied in chess. Exploration is a key snag when feedback is sparse and action spaces are large, risking collapse into repeat acts. Verbalized masking states an action mask in the prompt and forces the model to output an action from the masked set.

Iterative pruning extends it. If the target action is not sampled, sampled valid actions are cut from the mask and resampling proceeds under the smaller set, until the target appears or a budget runs out. Two training regimes are tested: engine play and a fixed set of positions with verifier scores. Across held-out puzzles and full games judged by average centipawn loss, verbalized masking lifts learning speed and final scores over strong baselines.
arxiv-2602-17133:
Linwei Zhai led an eight-author team rethinking vector quantization, a core piece of modern generative modeling. Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoders often train unstably and suffer codebook collapse, because representation learning and discrete codebook optimization are tangled together. The paper proposes VP-VAE, which drops the explicit codebook during training and treats quantization as structured perturbation in latent space.

In place of a rigid quantizer step, VP-VAE injects perturbations drawn via Metropolis-Hastings sampling, matched to the latent spread and scale. That gains stable training and robustness to inference-time quantization error. Under near-uniform latents, a light variant called FSP explains and improves fixed quantizers of the FSQ style. Tests on image and audio benchmarks showed better rebuild quality and far more balanced token use, without the shaky training that comes when codebook and learning are tied.
arxiv-2602-17433:
Francesco Ortu led an eight-author team auditing how language models handle contested history. Large language models increasingly serve as sources of historical information. That creates a need for scalable audits on contested events and politically charged narratives in real user chats. The team built HistoricalMisinfo: five hundred contested events from forty-five countries, each paired with a factual reference narrative and a documented revisionist one.

Each event appears in eleven prompt settings: questions, textbooks, social posts, and policy briefs. An LLM-as-a-judge protocol compares model outputs with the two references. Tests run under neutral prompts asking for accurate facts, and under robustness prompts where the user requests the revisionist version. Under neutral prompts models mostly track the factual reference, though scores signal reference alignment, not proof of revisionism. Under robustness prompts every model scored sharply higher on revisionism, showing limited resistance or self-correction.
arxiv-2602-17533:
Subotić led a four-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on the low-momentum Drell-Yan lepton pair spectrum. At small momentum, the spectrum probes intrinsic parton transverse motion and soft gluon radiation from the initial state. Modeling those effects well matters for precision physics. The team studies the spectrum with PythiaPB, a new Parton Branching implementation in Pythia that treats non-perturbative effects systematically.

A close look at primordial transverse momentum there, with an improved recoil treatment, pins down the width of the intrinsic distribution and its energy dependence. That dependence comes out steeper than in plain Parton Branching but much flatter than in standard Pythia, and the authors trace why the three treatments differ. They also test different handlings of the strong coupling at low scales against available data, finding the low momentum spectrum sensitive at the highest energy studied to the perturbative and non-perturbative boundary.
