arxiv-2602-17633:
Shayan Kiyani and team formalize a choice that shapes reasoning with language models: when to trust a cheap internal check, and when to ask a human to look. Cheap checks, such as self-consistency or proxy rewards, are fast and scalable but noisy. Human inspection is trustworthy but costly, so it cannot run on every output.

The authors frame weak-strong verification policies that decide when to accept, reject, or defer to strong checks. Over a population, optimal policies take a two-threshold form, and calibration and sharpness set the value of weak checkers. An online algorithm then provably controls acceptance and rejection errors, with no assumptions on the query stream, the model, or the weak checker. The result is a principled dial for trust versus cost.
arxiv-2602-17933:
Gikyu Yamamoto and Osamu Hirota compare how four secure communication schemes actually protect data: the mathematical cipher, the Wyner scheme, QKD, and the quantum stream cipher known as Y-00. New global comms technology demands ultra-high speeds, low cost and strong security. Yet practical security challenges differ by system setup, and scheme ideas keep spreading.

The schemes rest on very different security principles, which makes it hard for researchers in different fields to follow each other. This lecture note explains the Y-00 mechanism, presented as a third pillar in the optical quantum domain. It sits beside the principles of the other mechanisms. Its aim is modest and practical: comparative explanations that promote mutual understanding across fields, as a first trial toward shared language for physical-layer security from microwave wireless systems to quantum optical links.
arxiv-2602-18133:
Sihui Zhong and two co-authors look for a warning sign in the Sun's hot outer air before a flare erupts. Their 2026 paper tracks how the flicker of extreme ultraviolet light is spread across speeds of change in flare-prone active regions. In quiet regions the low-speed flicker index stays steady, but near a flare site it swings widely just before eruption.

Across fourteen flare events, the low-speed index crossed a set threshold right where the flare later broke out, shortly before it did. In some cases the gap between low- and high-speed indexes shifted thirty to ninety minutes ahead. The authors present this only as a test case: the pattern could one day help short-term flare warnings, but it still needs checking on a much larger set of flares.
arxiv-2602-18233:
Markus Diehl and one co-author measure how much two-loop corrections matter for double parton distributions. At small gaps between two partons, the pair usually comes from one parent parton splitting in two. That contribution can be computed from single-parton distributions and splitting kernels.

The paper shows two-loop corrections to those kernels shift predictions substantially and make double parton scattering forecasts steadier. It also treats heavy quark masses in the kernels in an approximate way. The result tightens a key input for predicting events where two hard scatterings happen in one proton-proton collision, giving later studies firmer numbers.
arxiv-2602-18333:
M. Reza Ebrahimi and three co-authors show state tracking troubles transformers even on familiar ground. Their 2026 paper shifts focus from out-of-distribution failures, like stretching to longer inputs, to data efficiency on familiar ground. Across many training setups, the team compares transformers with recurrent networks on state-tracking tasks.

Transformer data needs grow far faster as state spaces and sequences grow, compared with recurrent needs. Transformers also share almost nothing across lengths, learning one-off solutions for each length, sometimes to their detriment. Recurrent models share weights across lengths effectively, letting data at one length help others. Together the results mark state tracking as a fundamental transformer challenge, not just an extrapolation quirk.
arxiv-2602-18533:
Andrew Fraser shows word shapes steer image generators to identities. His 2026 paper shows morphological pressure creates gradients in the pipeline. Study 1 navigates identity basins in Stable Diffusion 1.5 with descriptors like platinum blonde, beauty mark, and 1950s glamour, without names.

A self-distillation loop making synthetic images from prompts and training a LoRA on them converges to an identity by ArcFace score. The trained LoRA creates a coordinate system for target and inverse. Maximal away-conditioning produces eldritch breakdown in base SD1.5 and uncanny outputs in the LoRA model. Study 2 extends this to prompts. From phonestheme theory, he generates two hundred nonsense words from clusters. Phonestheme-bearing candidates produce more coherent outputs. Three candidates achieve perfect consistency with zero training contamination, each with a distinct identity from sound. Together, the studies show morphological structure, in descriptors or prompt form, creates gradients in latent spaces.
arxiv-2602-18633:
Fangyuan Xu and fifteen co-authors generate synthetic text without private data. Their 2026 paper notes differentially private synthetic generation is key for building large models on private data, where owners cannot provide eyes-on access. Standard approaches trade off: DP finetuning trains a generator with formal privacy rules but still needs raw content, while methods avoiding exposure are bounded by an un-finetuned model often lacking fidelity.

The team introduces DP-RFT, an online reinforcement algorithm for text. It uses DP-protected neighbor votes from an eyes-off corpus as reward. The model learns to maximize votes via policy optimization. Evaluated on long-form generation such as news, transcripts, and abstracts, DP-RFT narrows the divide between private evolution and DP finetuning in fidelity and use.
arxiv-2602-18733:
When a language model repeats a passage from training, is it truly memorising that passage, or just producing a common phrase? Trishita Tiwari, with two co-authors, tackles that distinction in 2026 with Prior-Aware memorization, a lightweight test that needs no retraining and no trawl through training data.

The test asks whether a continuation is tied to its specific prefix. Whether it would also turn up often across many unrelated samples from the same distribution, which would mark it as statistical commonality. Checked against counterfactual memorization and on LLaMA and OPT corpora, it reclassifies most previously flagged sequences as common rather than memorised, sharpening how privacy and copyright risk should be measured.
arxiv-2602-18833:
Spotting plant disease from leaf photos is harder in a real field than in a lab. Subtle differences within leaf types can fool standard models. Asish Bera, with two co-authors, presents CLAP in 2026. It is a convolutional lightweight autoencoder for plant disease classification.

CLAP uses separable convolutional layers in its encoder and decoder blocks. A sigmoid gate sharpens the encoder's discriminative power, and the decoder improves it further. Encoder and decoder feature maps are then combined before classification. Tests on three public datasets cover cassava, tomato, maize, groundnut, grapes, and more. CLAP matches or beats rivals in accuracy while using only about five million parameters, with very fast training and inference per image.
arxiv-2602-19033:
Training datasets will increasingly contain AI-generated examples, so the output of one model will shape the training of another. Vibhas Kumar Vats, with two co-authors, shows in 2026 that a broad class of feedback runs converges to a low-dim fixed structure in latent space, a pattern called neural resonance.

Feedback is modelled as a Markov chain. Two conditions are needed for the pattern, ergodicity of the feedback process and directional contraction of the latent representation. Diffusion models on MNIST and ImageNet, plus CycleGAN and an audio feedback experiment, map how local and global manifold geometry evolves. An eight-pattern taxonomy of collapse behaviours is introduced. That pattern thus gives a unified explanation for long-term failing behaviour in generative models, and practical checks for identifying, mapping, and eventually easing collapse.
arxiv-2602-19533:
Grokking is the sudden jump from long memorization to generalization during neural network training. Pascal Tikeng Notsawo and two co-authors study it for learning multiplication in finite-dimensional algebras, moving beyond prior work focused mainly on group operations. More general structures are covered, including algebras that are non-associative, non-commutative, or non-unital.

Learning group operations turns out to be a special case of learning finite-dimensional algebra multiplication, which amounts to learning a bilinear product set by the algebra's structure tensor. For real algebras, the problem connects to matrix factorization with an implicit bias toward low rank. For finite-field algebras, grokking emerges as models learn discrete representations of algebraic elements.
arxiv-2602-19733:
Machine learning often differentiates through an iterative algorithm, a trick called unrolling, to tune hyperparameters or to meta-learn. A 2026 arXiv paper by Sheheryar Mehmood and two co-authors examines a known snag. The derivative iterates can at first drift away from the true Jacobian, a phenomenon called the curse of unrolling.

The authors give a non-asymptotic analysis that traces where this early drift comes from and which algorithmic factors control it. They show that dropping early derivative iterates eases the curse while also cutting memory use, and that warm-starting in bilevel optimization creates a similar truncation on its own. Numerical experiments back the theory. Readers get a practical remedy for a subtle failure mode in unrolled differentiation.
arxiv-2602-19833:
Planck stars are quantum-gravity-inspired black hole models with a finite core at Planck density, and their ringing patterns could carry subtle signatures of new physics. A 2026 arXiv paper by Davide Batic and two co-authors computes the quasinormal mode spectrum of such stars in scale-dependent gravity.

The setup fixes a running parameter by matching the effective Newtonian potential to a one-loop result. That yields a renormalisation-group-improved Schwarzschild metric rather than a true asymptotically safe realization. The authors use a spectral method prized for accuracy over older approximations. It resolves fundamental modes, large overtone families, and purely imaginary overdamped modes missed before. The oscillatory spectrum shows a robust Martini-glass shape, with nearly evenly spaced overdamped modes and isolated modes set far apart in the gravitational sector.
arxiv-2602-20133:
Program generation is moving from one-shot output to search at inference time. Language models serve as semantic mutation tools inside evolution loops. Those loops still run on fixed schedules. Fixed schedules ignore how search dynamics change over time. Compute gets wasted on stalled populations while promising frontiers go neglected. A 2026 arXiv paper by Mert Cemri and eleven co-authors introduces AdaEvolve. It recasts language-model-driven evolution as layered tuning that adjusts.

A running gain signal unifies decisions across three levels. Local adaptation tunes search level inside each population of solution entries. Global routing sends the overall resource budget across populations through bandit-based planning. Meta-guidance generates novel solution tactics from earlier solutions. Together the three levels let the search follow where gains actually build, rather than where a fixed schedule sends it.
arxiv-2602-20233:
Tuning a particle accelerator while beam runs is slow, fiddly work, and the machine's optics and steering interact. A 2026 arXiv paper by O. Hassan and five co-authors splits the job in two for the ISAC post-accelerator. Optics are set first with a digital copy of the machine; steering is then tuned by Bayesian optimization while beam is on.

The digital copy works out full tunes in seconds. It talks to the control system within limits on device settings, on how fast settings may change, and on beam loss. Three trials compare the split method with a baseline that tunes optics and steering together by Bayesian means, under the same conditions. The split method reaches high-transmission tunes in four to six times fewer steps, ending with mean transmissions in the mid-to-high nineties percent. Fewer knobs at once means faster, steadier convergence and simpler safety checks.
arxiv-2602-20433:
The geometry of Transformer weights, especially the unembedding matrix, has proven useful for interpreting language models, but its value for predicting downstream performance is unclear. Atharva Kulkarni and three co-authors test the link systematically across one hundred eight OLMo-style models trained under controlled variation, focusing on the effective rank of the unembedding matrix.

The best models often show high effective rank, but the trend is not universal across tasks and setups. Low effective rank does not cause late-stage degradation in small models, as prior work suggested; it merely co-occurs with it, and adversarial cases show low-rank models without saturation. Effective rank instead tracks pre-training choices such as batch size and weight decay, and no geometric metric reliably predicts performance. Geometry, the paper concludes, mainly reflects training choices rather than performance.
arxiv-2602-20533:
Spaces of non-plus bend can still hide wild large-scale shapes. Koichi Nagano proves a stiffness result for one class. Take an n-fold shortest-path complete CAT(0) space. If its Tits edge sits near enough to the standard unit sphere of one size lower, then it has the same shape as n-fold flat space. Gaps are stretched by at most a fixed factor in both ways. The theorem turns an edge nearness rule into a global shape result.

As a use, a shortest-path complete CAT(1) space of one size lower, near enough to the same standard sphere, has the same shape as it. The pair of results shows that near-round edges force near-flat shape. That gives a clean far-out order claim for these spaces.
arxiv-2602-20933:
Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting overfits when only a few views are available, and existing dropout methods fight it by randomly zeroing Gaussian opacities. Shuangkang Fang and seven co-authors show a flaw in that approach in this 2026 arXiv paper: neighbors compensate for dropped Gaussians, blunting the regularization. Their method, DropAnSH-GS, picks anchor Gaussians and removes their spatial neighbors too.

Dropping anchors with their neighborhoods breaks local redundancy and pushes the model toward robust, global representations. The method also drops high-degree spherical harmonic coefficients from color, concentrating appearance in lower degrees. That further curbs overfitting and allows post-training compression by truncating harmonics. Experiments show clear gains over existing dropout methods at negligible extra cost.
arxiv-2602-21033:
Medical image software must handle 3D data, varied file types, and niche training steps. Tianhao Fu and Yucheng Chen present MIP Candy in this 2026 arXiv paper, a free, modular, PyTorch-based setup for medical image handling. It spans data loading, training, running, and scoring, and users get a working chain by writing a single method for building the net.

A late setup tool allows run-time swaps of conv, norm, and activation layers with no extra class code. Built-in tools cover cross-checks, set look-over with auto region spotting, deep guidance, moving means, trial tracking across several frontends, training resume, and score forecasts. An open-ended bundle set adds pre-built models, and the code is open source under the Apache license.
arxiv-2602-21233:
Large-model shrinking spans bit trimming, guess-ahead reading, pruning, and boiling down, but tools rarely cover them at once. Rui Cen and twelve co-authors present AngelSlim in this 2026 arXiv paper, a full toolkit from the Tencent Hunyuan team that unifies shrinking into one chain toward factory use. State-of-the-art post-training bit trimming joins first-of-kind ultra-low-bit work, including the first factory-viable two-bit large model.

A training-matched guess-ahead reading setup nearly doubles throughput with no harm to rightness, and a training-free sparse focus setup cuts time-to-first-token in long contexts. Niche pruning handles vision and audio tokens for multi-sense models. By joining plays from low-level builds upward, the toolkit serves both method work and aided field use.
arxiv-2602-21833:
Large language models are increasingly used for auto code rework, yet quality may show gaps. Norman Peitek and two co-authors study LLM skills for code rework with a focus on improving code clarity. They ran a large-scale test using GPT 5 with 230 Java snippets, each varied and reworked for clarity across five rounds under three plans. Fine-grained changes were sorted into build, syntax, and comment shifts.

They then checked correctness and tested toughness with novel snippets. Results reveal three insights. Iterative rework shows an initial rebuild phase followed by settling, suggesting LLMs hold an inward grasp of an optimally readable version. Settling patterns prove fairly tough across code variants, and explicit prompting toward specific clarity factors slightly shifts rework dynamics. The insights ground assessment of LLM-assisted rework reliability and open paths for comparative checks across models and review of added software quality dimensions in LLM-reworked code.
arxiv-2602-22933:
Xueli Ke and two co-authors study blow-up and Liouville-type theorems for broad Camassa-Holm-Kadomtsev-Petviashvili systems with a mostly smooth non-straight term. Using the carry-on method, they set a blow-up test free of the initial data's smoothness score.

If the non-straight term's slope stays bounded throughout, they prove a blow-up theorem plus a weighted blow-up result via trail lines, a priori bounds, and the Riccati rule. The results extend to poly-controlled slopes, spanning typical non-straight forms including the standard CH-KP form. A Liouville-type single-solution theorem also holds when the non-straight term tops a squared lower bound for nonzero inputs.
arxiv-2602-23833:
Tuan Truong and three co-authors present a system for sorting DICOM medical image series by combining image content with acquisition metadata. The 2026 paper notes that series vary in length and slice content, and that metadata are often missing, incomplete, or inconsistent, which breaks simpler classifiers.

The framework encodes images and metadata with modality-aware modules and fuses them with two-way cross-modal attention. Metadata pass through a sparse encoder built on learnable feature dictionaries, which handles missing values without imputation. A two-and-a-half-dimensional visual encoder samples slices evenly to handle varied series lengths. Tests on a public liver MRI set and a large multi-site cohort beat image-only, metadata-only, and earlier multimodal baselines in-domain and out-of-domain, showing that explicit handling of sparse metadata improves robustness.
arxiv-2602-23933:
Preethi M and two co-authors show that internal activity reshapes dewetting and rupture in thin liquid films. The 2026 paper starts from the classical picture, where adhesion drives a spinodal instability and curvature-driven diffusion sets post-rupture coarsening, then asks what self-propulsion changes.

Using a minimal microscopic model of an active film on a solid substrate, the authors find a contest between active stresses and film-substrate adhesion. That contest yields two separately regulated length scales. The scales are vertical liquid buildup and lateral rupture spread. Activity turns transport from curvature-controlled diffusion into persistence-driven motion, raising the coarsening exponent well above the passive value. The rupture front likewise speeds from dissipative spreading toward ballistic propagation. Activity, the paper argues, creates a distinct nonequilibrium instability, not merely a rescaled passive one. In short, push from inside the film fights grip on the surface.
arxiv-2602-24033:
Sajal Naduvile Thadathil and sixteen co-authors study the Fermi surface of altermagnetic chromium antimonide. The 2026 paper combines electrical magnetotransport measurements at very high magnetic fields on microfabricated single crystals with first-principles calculations.

Chromium antimonide is a metallic, collinearly ordered altermagnet with particularly strong symmetry-induced spin splitting in its band structure. The team tracks how magnetic quantum oscillations in resistance vary with temperature and field direction, and finds that the observed frequency spectrum matches density-functional theory well. The results confirm the predicted band structure of altermagnetic chromium antimonide and underline how high fields are needed to map Fermi surfaces. In short, the team maps the shape of the Fermi surface. High fields bend the paths into Shubnikov-de Haas loops. The loops leave marks that read out the shape. That read-out is the point of the whole test. The marks match the team's earlier sums.
arxiv-2603-00033: Jiang's team presents a settling measure-based method for data-consistent inversion with multiple push-forward constraints. That problem sits at the heart of uncertainty maths: an input measure must map through a model onto several seen output measures at once. Their loop scheme repeats the inversion. It cuts total f-divergence and, under uniform start, gives the top-entropy answer. Strict settling analysis plus number cases, including a high-dim PDE-ruled case, show the loop dodges building high-dim joint seen patterns well.
arxiv-2603-00133: Zhao, Triantafillou and Triantafillou introduce GUARD, a framework that curbs memorization in text-to-image diffusion models by steering generation away from training images. It adjusts denoising so outputs stay distinct from training data yet aligned with the prompt, without harming image quality. Its steering target comes from cross-attention attenuation, using a statistical test that spots which prompt positions need dampening. The result is a surgical, per-prompt inference-time method that proves most robust across two architectures for both verbatim and template memorization.
arxiv-2603-00233: Jäger, Kiwit and Riofrío train quantum Wasserstein GANs on full MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, generating full-resolution images across ten classes with one quantum generator. Current quantum approaches usually shrink to toy examples or small datasets, resorting to reduction or multiple models for small patches. Building on classical image-loading methods, their system avoids such tricks and sets a new standard. It also extends to colour images on Street View House Numbers, and better noise inputs yield diverse images while preserving quality, even under shot noise.
arxiv-2603-00533: Wu and six colleagues launch Voices of Civilizations, the first multilingual question benchmark testing audio language models on full length music from many cultures. An automated pipeline with manual checks turns 380 tracks across 38 languages into 1,190 multiple choice questions on language, region, mood, and theme. Tests under four conditions find even leading models miss subtle cultural nuance without rich textual context and show systematic biases across traditions. The open data set aims to foster culturally inclusive music understanding.
arxiv-2603-00833: Liu reviews how X-ray observations reveal the accretion geometry of black hole X-ray binaries, ideal laboratories for accretion physics across a wide range of rates. X-ray studies indicate the disk reaches near the innermost stable circular orbit when the source is bright and hard. The review also covers X-ray techniques for measuring accretion geometry, current understanding, open questions, and hints of disk-corona-jet links.
arxiv-2603-00933: Qiu, Wang, and Yang prove gradient bounds for p-Laplace problems with cubic terms on complete Riemannian manifolds with lower Ricci curvature bounds. Where the function sits against three constants, they convert the problem with a log change or a tanh change. Joining a Sobolev bound with Moser steps yields Cheng-Yau type bounds, plus a Liouville theorem and a Harnack bound as uses.
arxiv-2603-01033: Smith re-examines net survival, usually read as survival if cancer were the only cause of death. He shows the standard Pohar Perme estimator misses that target. When cancer patients carry higher other-cause mortality from baseline health or treatment effects, the estimator returns cancer deaths plus both excess sources instead. Evidence puts other-cause relative risk from 1 for colorectal cancer to over 4 for head and neck cancers. So he urges reading net survival only as survival with general-population other-cause mortality removed.
arxiv-2603-01533:
K. K. Venkataratnam looks at brief walls between regions in the very early universe in this 2026 study. Such domain walls can form when a symmetry breaks, and they add energy for a short time. The question is whether that brief phase left any mark on the seeds of galaxies we see today.

Venkataratnam treats the walls as a short-lived shift in the expansion rate during inflation. Solving the changed expansion law gives a smooth rate that soon returns to the standard path. Fluctuations are then matched across the shift from the wall phase to normal inflation. Only waves that left the horizon near the shift change their path, so the seed spectrum shows narrow, scale-linked dips. Far from the shift, inflation keeps its usual success.
arxiv-2603-01833:
Ravshan Ashurov and Damir Shamuratov recover a hidden source term in a fractional diffusion equation. Their 2026 work uses Caputo derivatives, which let diffusion carry memory of its past states. The unknown is the spatial part of a source that splits into separate space and time factors.

Extra data at one interior time pins down that spatial part, a classic overdetermination trick. The spatial operator is a self-adjoint positive differential operator of order at least two. Solutions are written spectrally with a multinomial Mittag-Leffler function, the fractional cousin of the exponential. Sharp asymptotic expansions for that function yield a uniform lower bound on a key denominator. Those bounds give conditions for a classical solution to exist, and uniqueness holds under natural data assumptions, despite the problem being ill-posed.
arxiv-2603-02033:
Melis Yardimci, Samet Ok, and Belinda Kalomeni track brightness rhythms in three symbiotic binary stars over up to fourteen years. Their 2026 study merges ground and space monitoring in several wavelength bands. Symbiotic binaries pair a cool giant with a hot companion that feeds on its wind.

All three systems show coherent modulations apart from their orbital cycles, on scales of tens of days. One system dominant rhythm and its harmonic point to pulsations of the cool giant. The other two show stable mid-length rhythms that mix pulsation with disk or circumstellar effects. Space data add rapid signals down to tens of minutes in two systems. Those fast flickers suggest accretion or rotation activity layered over the slower giant pulsations, which constrains mass transfer models.
arxiv-2603-02333:
Xiaoyu Luo, Wenrui Yu, Qiongxiu Li, and Johannes Bjerva characterize memorization in diffusion language models in this 2026 paper. Standard language models sometimes repeat their training data word for word. That raises privacy and copyright risks for real users. Diffusion models generate text by unmasking, a very different process, and their memorization was unmapped.

Their framework covers both prefix-based and diffusion generation under any masking pattern. One theorem shows that finer sampling steps strictly raise the chance of exact data extraction. Standard generation appears as the extreme case of that scale. Experiments across model sizes and sampling styles confirm the theory. Under matched tests, diffusion models leaked far less personal data than standard models.
arxiv-2603-02633:
Mohammed Nowaz Rabbani Chowdhury, Hsinyu Tsai, Geoffrey Burr, and colleagues address a hardware problem for very large language models in 2026. Mixture-of-Experts models use only a few expert parts per input, yet still hold huge numbers of weights. Analog in-memory chips could run them with far less energy, but chip noise hurts accuracy.

Their fix splits the work instead of retraining the model. Experts shown to be noise-sensitive, plus attention layers, run on normal digital hardware. The rest run on the analog chips. Tests on two large expert models across several benchmarks kept accuracy steady despite analog flaws. The split makes low-energy hardware usable for models too big to retrain.
arxiv-2603-03133:
How a two-dimensional sheet stacks and what coats its surface decide whether aluminum ions can move in and out. This 2026 study uses density functional theory, a quantum simulation method, to test MXene materials as cathodes for aluminum-ion batteries. The candidates, two layered carbides, offer wide interlayer spacing and strong conductivity beyond lithium chemistry.

Four stacking arrangements and two ion sites were compared. Oxygen-coated layers in one stacking stayed remarkably stable, with the vanadium carbide barely swelling as aluminum entered, matching experiments. That stable stacking slowed ion motion compared with the alternative arrangement. Oxygen coatings also promised high storage capacity, while fluorine coatings destabilized badly after ion entry. The findings give battery designers concrete rules for tuning these sheets.
arxiv-2603-03233:
Zihang Zeng, Jiaquan Zhang, Pengze Li, and colleagues pit AI agents against each other to keep scientific code honest. Multi-agent systems can attack hard science problems, but language models hallucinate code and tests alike, and errors compound across agents. Their 2026 platform wraps the agents in a Bayesian adversarial framework, delivered as a low-code tool.

Three agents loop recursively, jointly improving the solution, the tests that judge it, and the prompts that drive generation. A Bayesian updating rule outside any language model tracks evaluation uncertainty, reducing dependence on one model's reliability. Domain experts state goals in plain language rather than engineering prompts. On a cross-disciplinary Earth science benchmark, the platform beat leading models, with a mid-size open model topping one far larger.
arxiv-2603-03333:
Jeongtae Lee and seven colleagues speed up language model generation with a new acceptance rule for speculative decoding. In that technique a small draft model proposes tokens and a large target model keeps only good ones. Their 2026 method, DropMatch, judges draft tokens by sampling: it applies dropout, a classic randomness trick, only to the model's final head and draws several decoding paths.

Those paths form an empirical picture of what the target model expects, and draft tokens are checked for consistency against it. The dropout rate adaptively controls path size without badly distorting the target distribution. Nothing needs training, extra data, calibration, or changes to the pretrained model, and the trick stacks with other accelerators. Benchmarks show longer accepted runs, kept task quality, and modest speed gains that grow when combined with an existing accelerator.
arxiv-2603-03433:
A large European collaboration, writing as the COSMIC WISPers network, surveys the hunt for some of the shyest particles ever proposed. Axions and other weakly interacting slim particles, all lighter than a billion electron volts, appear naturally in many extensions of the Standard Model. They could explain dark matter and several puzzling observations at once. This 2026 white paper reviews where the search stands.

Three fronts are covered: the theoretical motivation, indirect signatures hiding in astrophysical observations, and dedicated laboratory experiments. The document grows out of a European Union funded COST Action that coordinates WISP searches across Europe. It argues the current European program is rich, diverse, and cost-effective, with a real chance of a transformative discovery in the next decade. It also lays out a roadmap for keeping Europe in the lead.
arxiv-2603-03833:
Bogdan-Vasile Matioc and Christoph Walker prove linearized stability for equilibria that do not sit alone, in quasilinear parabolic problems, working in interpolation spaces. For lone equilibria, the spectrum of the linearized operator settles the question in the standard way, but such points often come in families rather than alone. The authors treat cases where an unbounded operator hinges on the solution itself, alongside a lower-order term, and their approach extends earlier results that relied on maximal regularity.

The method allows full freedom in choosing interpolation methods and needs only low regularity assumptions on the added lower-order term. Uses include the capillarity-driven Hele-Shaw problem and the fractional mean curvature flow, both free boundary problems of geometric interest. The work gives the field a broadly usable stability tool for parabolic problems whose equilibria form connected sets rather than lone points.
arxiv-2603-04333: Agrawalla and colleagues explain why flow matching aids temporal difference learning. The gain is not from modeling return distributions, which can even hurt results. Reading values by integration damps early errors at test time, unlike monolithic critics. Dense velocity supervision at many steps keeps features plastic for shifting targets. Flow critics thus beat monolithic critics by about twice on final results and five times on sample efficiency where plasticity fails.
arxiv-2603-05133: Teresa Stürzenhofäcker and team present an HDR imaging sensor based on spatially varying apertures, mixing two differently sized prototype pixels. Other light joining areas stretch dynamic range toward the lower end versus a standard high detail sensor. Non-regular pixel arrangement mitigates aliasing and overcomes detail loss from the larger prototype pixel's lifted joining area. Fourier-domain rebuild, where natural images are sparse, recovers the image with high detail. Runs suggest the layout acquires high dynamic range images free from aliasing artefacts.
arxiv-2603-05433: Hejian Sang and team present CRISP, teaching concise reasoning by self-distillation. Reasoning models make excess tokens. It needs no ground-truth answers. The reverse-KL objective compresses easy problems. The model is conditioned on a be-concise instruction for teacher logits, minimizing reverse KL gap. On Qwen3-14B, CRISP shortens MATH-500 reasoning by up to 56%, and AIME 2024 reasoning by 38%, raising MATH-500 accuracy by 3.3 points. Qwen3-8B compresses with accuracy preserved, while DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B raises accuracy across five benchmarks. General capabilities are preserved.
arxiv-2603-05633: Sheemar and team survey stacked smart metasurfaces, a design in which several tunable metasurface layers work together via wave travel. By using chained wave-matter meetings at front ends, stacked sheets widen the design space for tunable radio systems. The survey covers nature rules, model frames, hardware builds, and new designs. It looks at message jobs including speed tuning, wideband and near-field sending, learning-driven control, and joined sensing and message work. It names open problems spanning nature models, growth, co-design of hardware and code, and network joining.
arxiv-2603-05933: Zhu frames persona making with small models as style redo, splitting style from talk context. Data lack and splitting apart challenge models, while fine-tuning captures meaning but yields out-of-persona outputs. The Structured Style-Redo Framework breaks style into format, sentence, and use parts with chain-of-thought guidance. A Direct Choice Tuning stage aligns planning with doing, targeting output doing rather than thinking gaps. Across eight roles, a Qwen3 model hits a Valid Style Score of 0.632 with truth, placing on the Pareto frontier over baselines on hardware.
arxiv-2603-06233: Makri studies braid group theory and three dimensional topological dynamics, where classical braids aid surface homeomorphisms but no method covers such manifolds. She sets out loop braid groups, a 3D analogue of classical braid groups, for 3-ball homeomorphisms that keep a set of circles. Her theorem ties the generalized Lefschetz number to Burau matrices of loop braid elements, giving facts on fixed and periodic points and a periodic point estimate. The result gives a method that ties loop braid groups to Nielsen fixed point theory and 3D dynamics.
arxiv-2603-06333: Sahoo and his team set out SAHOO, a method watching and steering alignment drift during recursive self gain through three safeguards. The Goal Drift Index joins semantic, lexical, shape, and distributional signals to spot drift. Constraint checks enforce safety critical invariants, among them syntactic correctness and non-hallucination, and regression risk scores flag cycles undoing prior gains. Across 189 tasks spanning code generation, math reasoning, and truthfulness, SAHOO gains a lot, with code task gains of 18.3 percent. It keeps constraints in two domains and keeps truthfulness violations low.
arxiv-2603-06433: Laitinen and Dalla assess velocity dispersion analysis for finding injection times, using full-orbit proton simulations in a sun wind turbulence model. It combines transverse fluctuations, two-dimensional to the mean field, with a slab component. Readings for three strengths, read through a threshold, show inferred times and path lengths bending. Weak and moderate ones delay times by minutes and lengthen paths, while strong ones yield paths over 5 au. Background spectra shift times by minutes, so such times reflect it and background, not acceleration alone.
arxiv-2603-07233: Di Francesco, Rubbi, Jain and Liò build a plug-in that helps cell-response models borrow lessons from related gene experiments. Their PT-RAG module first picks candidate past perturbations by meaning, then selects among them from the cell state and the new query. Related genes can act differently across cell types, so relevance must be judged afresh. Tests on two model backbones show gains in matching true responses across cell types and perturbations.
arxiv-2603-07533: Zhang and colleagues rebuild odd-shaped slender continuum bodies, such as guidewires and catheters, from two views. Image-based methods often underuse camera math or lean on rigid rules that fail for highly soft shapes. Their ACCURATE framework joins a segmentation network with topology walks and dynamic planning under global biplanar match. It stays robust to blocks and epipolar ambiguity, reaching sub-millimeter mean errors on simulated and phantom data.
arxiv-2603-07933: Wang offers a new way to control encrypted digital assets, breaking with the rule that key possession equals control, blocking supervision, conditional delegation, and lawful transfer. Current fixes demand key exposure, on-chain state changes, or trusted intermediaries. Condition-Triggered Dormant Authorization Paths rest on destructible authorization factors in a root-derivable design. Control rights sit dormant as paths of credentials plus outside factors, dead until every factor is present, and revocation destroys factors, killing the path. Release follows triggers such as consent, inheritance, or timed events.
arxiv-2603-08033: Krinkin studies the gap between the smallest Boolean circuit and the smallest formula for the same function, over the And-Inverter Graph basis of AND and NOT with free inversions. He proves the gap is always 0 or 1, the Unit Gap Theorem. Sharing a gate between subcircuits demands at least as many essential variables as the optimum, and no sharing is needed when the optimum is 3 or less. When the gap equals 1, it comes from exactly one gate with fan-out 2, in dual-polarity or same-polarity form.
arxiv-2603-08133: Zhang and colleagues introduce FLED-GS, a fast framework for rebuilding 3D dark scenes from low-light, noisy, and motion-blurred imagery. Novel view synthesis under such combined flaws is valuable but hard. Current volume rendering methods struggle with combined flaws, and stepwise 2D prep work adds artifacts because the flaws interact. FLED-GS recasts 3D scene rebuild as a cycle of enhancement and rebuild, inserting brightness anchors that enable step-by-step recovery and keep noise blow-up from harming deblurring.
arxiv-2603-09033: David J Pascall builds a filter-based frame for when adding taxa improves phylodynamic study. Ordering tips for step-by-step Bayes analysis, he splits expected variance drop into learning, mismatch, and covariance bits and sorts targets by mismatch behavior. For absorbing targets, a seer knowing the hidden absorption state gains learning pledges the worker cannot reach, marking a hard limit of sequence data alone.
arxiv-2603-09133: Mikhail A. Ivanov and colleagues analyze possible new-physics effects in semileptonic decays of the Bs meson into Ds states with a tau and a neutrino. They extend the standard model with four-fermion operators beyond the usual V-A form and fit their Wilson coefficients to recent data. Form factors come from their covariant quark model with infrared confinement. The paper predicts the key observables for these decay channels, giving future experiments clear targets to test.
arxiv-2603-09433: Anna Matsui and colleagues automate critical pair analysis for string diagram rewriting, a handy check for confluence in rewriting systems. Bonchi and coauthors had shown this analysis valid for string diagrams in symmetric monoidal categories. The new algorithm lists every critical pair of a left-connected system, working by concrete moves on hypergraphs. They prove it correct and complete for such categories lacking a Frobenius structure.
arxiv-2603-09633: O. I. Kostyukova and T. V. Tchemisova sharpen bounds on how large maximal faces of the completely positive cone can be. Progress is slow because extreme exposed rays of the copositive cone lack a general characterization beyond small orders. For every odd dimension n, they prove the exact lower bound on maximal face dimensions equals n. For even dimensions from eight up, a new upper estimate places that lower bound between n and n plus three.
arxiv-2603-09933: Yash Kankanampati and colleagues give token pruning in late interaction search models a firm geometric basis. Models like ColBERT store one dense vector per document token, so indexes grow huge. Past pruning rules leaned on rough statistics and lacked formal support. Their frame treats each token's reach as a Voronoi cell in embedding space, pruning by cell size while keeping search quality and aiding interpretation.
arxiv-2603-10133: Priyadarshini Tamilselvan and coauthors propose an agentic control centre that improves data products on a continuous loop. Data products help users query their data through assets such as example question and SQL pairs, yet experts normally craft those by hand. Specialised agents surface questions, watch quality across many dimensions and refine the assets automatically. Human in the loop controls keep the automation trustworthy and observable throughout.
arxiv-2603-10233: Tasfia Seuti and Sagnik Ray Choudhury unify the grading of student work, from long essays to short factual answers, in one benchmark. Essay scoring and short answer grading have grown apart, with fragmented data sets and mismatched metrics. S-GRADES gathers many diverse grading data sets under a standard web interface with reproducible protocols. Testing three leading language models across it, with varied prompting and exemplar choices, exposes reliability and generalisation gaps.
arxiv-2603-10533: Siyu Lu and co-authors study word-scale graphics, tiny visual embellishments set at the size of type inside scientific papers. Such graphics can make text more expressive, yet how papers use them was unclear. The team pulled 909 examples from a huge corpus and built a framework around where they sit, what job they do, and how they look. Use is rare, icons dominate, and form tracks function, with quantitative mini-graphs used for data annotation. The authors discuss ways to spread the practice.
arxiv-2603-10633: Anusha Bhattacharya and Soma Maity prove a Cheng-type comparison theorem, for eigenvalues of the Hodge Laplacian on differential forms. They work with closed Riemannian manifolds whose Ricci curvature and injectivity radius are bounded below, and whose diameter is bounded above. On that class they bound those eigenvalues from above, in the spirit of Cheng's classic bound for functions. The result extends work of Dodziuk and Lott, which needed sectional curvature bounds as well. An application gives uniform estimates for the connection Laplacian on 1-forms.
arxiv-2603-10733: Julien Cassaigne and Raphaël Henry study smooth words over binary alphabets, the finite pieces of smooth sequences such as the Oldenburger-Kolakoski sequence. Their first result identifies the smooth words completely: they are exactly the factors of smooth sequences. Toward a conjectured growth rate for their complexity, they prove a lower bound valid over any alphabet and an upper bound over even alphabets. They also improve the known upper bound for odd and mixed alphabets, and link language, morphicity, and factor complexity in a dichotomy.
arxiv-2603-10833: Wai Ip Chu, Giacomo Tarroni, and Ling Li evaluate few-shot pill recognition under visual domain shift, from a deployment perspective. Automated pill recognition aims to cut adverse drug events, yet real scenes bring clutter, overlapping pills, and reflections. Their two-stage detector gets base training, then few-shot fine-tuning with one, five, or ten labeled examples per new class, and is tested on a separate cluttered dataset. Semantic recognition adapted fast, saturating with even a single example. Under overlap and occlusion, though, localization and recall fell sharply.
arxiv-2603-11033: Zoltán Király and coauthors simulate how laser light reshapes the breakup of the sodium hydride molecule. Light-induced conical intersections couple electronic, vibrational, and photonic motion. Their pump-probe calculations cover the first three singlet electronic states. They add several light-induced degeneracies and rotational motion. They add the coupling between electronic angular momentum and nuclear rotation. They compute dissociation probabilities. They compute kinetic energy release spectra. They compute angular distributions of the fragments. They do so within and above the linear regime.
arxiv-2603-11333: Haoting Zhang and coauthors build a language-model-augmented twin of a short-video platform. It is a closed-loop world where policy, creator rewards, and what users do co-evolve. Real counterfactual tests cannot be run there. Four twins, for users, content, interaction, and the platform, run on an event-driven layer. Policies sit as parts in the platform twin. Language models enter only as schema-constrained services, for personas and trends. One optimizer routes them, so the twin scales as AI use grows.
arxiv-2603-12033: Chen and Issa open a two-part study of vector spin glasses with a Mattis interaction term. Part one covers models whose spin glass part meets the usual convexity assumption. The authors find the limit free energy through a Parisi-type formula. They also prove a large-deviation result for the mean magnetization. The proof stays short, since the Mattis term is treated as a model parameter. A companion paper takes on the harder non-convex case at high temperature.
arxiv-2603-12133: Maniparambil and co-authors test language models on hard topology puzzles with TopoBench. Six puzzle families at three levels probe global traits like how regions connect and loops close. Even the strongest models clear less than a fourth of the hard cases. Two families stay nearly unsolved across all models tried. The team coded 750 reasoning traces to find where failures start. Early commitment and forgotten constraints hurt most, while repeated reasoning proved harmless. The bottleneck is pulling constraints from spatial layouts, not reasoning over them.
arxiv-2603-12333: Ephremidze, Kamionkowski, and Dvorkin speed up Fresnel integral work for gravitational-wave lensing with Fourier methods. Wave-optics effects appear when a wave's length nears the lens scale, as in subhalo lensing. Forecasts rest on a Fresnel integral that is tricky to compute across sky positions. The authors rewrite its lens-position dependence as a Fourier transform in two dimensions. FFT tools then evaluate all positions at once for general lenses, with derivatives at small extra cost. Their FIONA code runs far faster than current methods on dense grids.
arxiv-2603-12433: Mai and co-authors revisit model stitching for vision foundation models that differ in data, goals, and modality mix. Stitching joins early layers of one model to later layers of another through a light stitch layer. A systematic protocol varies stitch points, layer families, losses, and tasks. Plain feature matching or task loss training loses accuracy at shallow stitch points. Matching features at the target's penultimate layer instead makes mixed models stitch reliably. Deep stitches can beat both parent models, and a stitch tree shares early layers.
arxiv-2603-12533: Choi and co-authors tackle question answering about pointing gestures in egocentric video. Current multimodal models struggle here, lacking gesture-rich data and fine-grained pointing intent. The team builds EgoPointVQA, a benchmark of 4000 synthetic and 400 real videos across deictic reasoning tasks. Their HINT method encodes tokens from 3D hand keypoints and interleaves them with the model input. These Hand Intent Tokens give explicit spatial and temporal context for each gesture. HINT-14B reaches 68.1% average accuracy across six tasks, ahead of strong baselines.
arxiv-2603-12733: Francesco Maione and co-authors aim to catch catastrophic failures in marine diesel engines before they strike. Such failures are sudden, destroy the engine, and threaten crew safety. Past work focused on slow wear, not abrupt events. Their method watches how the gap between sensor readings and expected values changes over time. A random forest makes the predictions from real data of a failed engine. Warnings can come before alarms trip, so operators can shut down in time.
arxiv-2603-12833: Fangzhou Zhao and co-authors characterize when excitons stay weakly entangled and when strong correlation takes over. In the weak regime, Bethe-Salpeter methods describe excitons well. Under strong light in moiré materials, dense excitons may act fermion-like instead of boson-like. The team maps entanglement and binding across interaction profiles and electron-hole localization. Their checks confirm where perturbation theory still holds for excitons. The approach extends to multi-particle excitations in other many-body systems.
arxiv-2603-13333: Hongrui Zheng and co-authors introduce STL-SVPIO for robot task planning under formal rules. Signal Temporal Logic states complex spatiotemporal constraints, but turning them into long control paths is hard. Solver methods scale poorly, and sampling methods face sparse, long-horizon costs. STL-SVPIO treats STL as a differentiable reward-shaping signal that guides the whole search. Stein Variational Gradient Descent moves a swarm of control particles toward high robustness zones. The method beat rivals on classic tasks and solved multi-agent coordination jobs that broke baselines.
arxiv-2603-13633: Jesse T. Gonzalez and co-authors explore how people might interact with shape-changing architecture, where walls can move. Two studies ground the work. Design workshops with 20 people surfaced bold visions for such spaces. A Wizard-of-Oz study with 12 people then tested how users try to control them in set tasks. Desires clash in key ways: proactive automation versus user autonomy, and personalization versus public ownership. The authors call for a modality-agnostic model of evolving user intent, and give grounded design proposals.
arxiv-2603-13733: Grayson Lee and co-authors test Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation, or IMLE, as a planner for real-time model predictive control. Diffusion planners capture rich, multimodal behavior, but their iterative denoising is slow. Slow plans suit closed-loop control badly, since plans must refresh fast as the scene changes. IMLE keeps strong mode coverage and runs inference two orders of magnitude faster, the team shows. On offline reinforcement learning benchmarks it matched a diffusion planner, with much faster planning. A human navigation test ran in real time.
arxiv-2603-14133: Thorgeirsson, Weidmann, and Su ask which skills predict success at vibe coding, where programmers guide language models in plain words instead of editing code. Their preregistered study tests 100 tertiary-level students on CS achievement, general cognition, and writing skill. A custom environment mirrors commercial vibe coding tools under controlled conditions. Both writing skill and CS achievement predict vibe coding scores. CS achievement still matters after general cognitive skills are counted, which informs how such courses should be taught.
arxiv-2603-14233: Yuan and co-authors add uncertainty bounds to robust principal component analysis, which recovers low-rank structure from corrupted, gappy matrices. Most methods give one point estimate and no sense of error. Their CP-RPCA wraps recovery in conformal prediction, in split or full form. Weighted calibration handles uneven chances of seeing each entry. Theory promises finite-sample coverage. Simulations show sound intervals under heavy outliers and missing data, with speed close to plain recovery when the model fits.
arxiv-2603-14533: Kamali builds a Heisenberg-picture frame where quantum geometry comes from commutators. Time acts as a quantum observable here. A symmetry named gravitational conjugation supports that view. The core claim sets the position-momentum commutator equal to the metric itself. Algebra rules then force the metric to stay compatible. A worked expanding-universe case shows momentum generators that fail to commute. The mismatch scales with the Hubble rate. Bounds on metric spread and a toy early-structure case close the study.
arxiv-2603-14633: Erez and co-authors show that LLM red-team scanners wobble with their evaluator choice. Scanners report attack success rates to grade model risk. The judge that marks success is a hidden weak point. Swap the evaluator, hold attacks and outputs fixed, and reported rates shift a lot. Their two-phase frame first measures evaluator disagreement by attack type. A verifier then checks evaluators without heavy human labeling. On the Garak scanner, 22 of 25 attack classes prove unstable. Checked evaluators lift accuracy from 72% to 89%.
arxiv-2603-14733: Zhang and co-authors benchmark multi-video understanding and add a skill-based agent frame, SAMA. Models that ace single videos stumble when reasoning spans several clips. Naive joins of many videos cause training mismatch and frame loss. MVX-Bench turns 11 classic vision tasks into multi-video questions. The set holds 1,442 questions over 4,255 videos. SAMA wields visual tools plus task skills with a conflict-aware check loop. It beats strong open baselines and GPT on the bench, they report. Ablations credit both the skills and the conflict step.
arxiv-2603-14833: Peng and co-authors release an open multi-stream transformer and probe its streams by ablation and rescue. Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections split the residual path into parallel streams. How those streams share work stayed unexplored until now. Their 780M model anchors the study on Hugging Face. Stream ablation cuts one stream at a time during inference. Rescue steps then restore parts to test causal roles. Paired interventions split true redundancy from lopsided use. Stream value hides from similarity scores alone, they show.
arxiv-2603-14933: Enqvist-Pyk recasts Herbrand schemes as a functional interpretation of classical sequent calculus. Herbrand schemes pull Herbrand disjunctions straight from sequent proofs. No cut elimination step is needed for the extraction. A higher-order recursion grammar powers the scheme language. The note shows the core moves match a functional reading of the calculus. Gerhardy and Kohlenbach gave a kindred reading for classical logic. Game-based views of Herbrand's theorem sit nearby in spirit. Proof theory gains a computational lens on classical proofs.
arxiv-2603-15033: Laguna and co-authors argue that vision models should be built to forget, not patched after training. Their method, MUNKEY, stores instance-specific memory in keys kept apart from the model weights. Deleting a key erases that instance with no weight updates and no need for the original data. This design targets privacy rules, data errors, and harmful training images. Across natural, fine-grained, and medical image tests, MUNKEY beat all post-hoc baselines while keeping accuracy.
arxiv-2603-15733: Simidzija and co-authors extend a quantum method that finds hidden cuts in quantum states. A recent algorithm spots partitions into fully unentangled qubit groups. It turns each cut into a symmetry that a Shor-type method can detect. Real states are often only weakly entangled across such cuts. The team derives heuristics that hunt approximate symmetries instead. They prove a tight link between algorithm outputs and cut quality scores. Fewer state copies still yield samples that expose weak entanglement patterns.
arxiv-2603-16233: Hori and co-authors rebuild human motion from just four wearable devices. Their GRIP system pairs motion sensors with insole pressure sensors. That mix captures body motion plus ground contact forces. A digital twin in a physics simulator then shapes the motion. One network guesses poses and speeds from the sensors. A second network steers the twin to match. Their new PRISM dataset pairs both sensor types. GRIP beat prior methods on pose accuracy and physical realism.
arxiv-2603-16333: Adadurov and co-authors study auction formats for maximal extractable value on Ethereum. Their data cover 2.2 million transactions from three orderflow providers. Extracted values follow a log-normal shape with a heavy right tail. Searcher valuations are affiliated, which breaks revenue equivalence. The team models that link with a Gaussian common factor. They derive bidding and revenue for five auction formats. Open and second-price formats beat Dutch and first-price ones. The gap cost an estimated 10 to 18 million dollars.
arxiv-2603-16533: Sahlu and co-authors test a cosmos where dark energy and dark matter interact. The coexistence model yields an exact Hubble function formula. They fit its free parameters against late-time data. Cosmic chronometers, DESI acoustic data, gamma-ray bursts, and supernova sets all enter. The model fits these sets better than standard rivals. It also returns a smaller Hubble constant value. At high redshift it behaves much like the wCDM model.
arxiv-2603-16833: Li refines variance estimates for asymptotically linear estimators in semiparametric models. Standard practice trusts the influence-function variance and treats the second-order remainder as negligible. Li studies the case where the remainder still adds variance at order one over n. He splits the total variance into influence, remainder, and covariance parts. He shows the sandwich estimator works only when the scaled remainder variance fades. Near the boundary case, he proves the jackknife and pairs bootstrap stay valid. Simulations back the predicted coverage.
arxiv-2603-17233: Ni and co-authors present Draft-and-Prune, a method that makes auto formalization for logic problems more reliable. Auto formalization turns word problems into solver ready programs, but the programs may crash or encode the wrong meaning. Draft-and-Prune first drafts several natural language plans and conditions program generation on them. It then prunes programs that run yet contradict themselves or stay ambiguous. Surviving paths vote on the final answer. Across four benchmarks, the method beat strong baselines, reaching perfect scores on two sets.
arxiv-2603-17333: Sidhu and Hockenmaier build GSU, a text-only dataset for testing how well language models reason about space on grids. The tasks cover navigation, finding objects, and building structures from coordinate lists. Models handle basic grid ideas well, they report. They struggle with points of view tied to an embodied agent and with naming 3D shapes from coordinates. Fine-tuning a small model can match large frontier models, they find.
arxiv-2603-17533: De Nadai and co-authors introduce NEO, one language model for search, recommendation, and reasoning. Items become typed semantic IDs inside the same token stream as plain text. Prompts set the task, entity type, and output format. Constrained decoding keeps every generated ID inside the real catalog. Tests ran on a live catalog of over ten million items. NEO beat strong task-specific baselines and transferred across tasks, they report.
arxiv-2603-17833: Adnan, Gupta, Akshathala, and Vaidhyanathan launch ArchBench, a benchmark suite for software architecture tasks. Model tests have grown from code snippets to whole-repo fixes, yet design skill stays untested. ArchBench wraps tasks in one pipeline for data, inference, and scoring. Each task ships as a self-contained plugin that others can add to. A CLI and a public leaderboard keep results open and comparable. The aim is steady, shared growth in architecture testing.
arxiv-2603-18033: Santos sets out the Quantum Voronovskaya-Damasclin theorem for neural network approximations of quantum channels. It extends a classic scalar result to non-commutative operators in quantum information. New Sobolev and Hölder spaces are built with Fréchet tools and the diamond norm. The error splits into integer-order terms, fractional corrections, and effects from operator algebra. Uses include a quantum central limit theorem, a best interpolation method, and a Richardson-style speed-up step.
arxiv-2603-18133: Calderón-Infante and co-authors revisit end-of-the-world curvature singularities in dynamical cobordisms. These codimension-one singularities drive scalars to infinite field distance. They test them against Gubser and Maldacena-Nuñez criteria for acceptable singularities. Moduli flows pass the potential test but lack a near-extremal horizon version. They propose a new rule that bounds Ricci scalar growth along infinite-distance flows, admitting EFT strings and D7-branes.
arxiv-2603-18333: Cramer, Heiser, and Chang build trajectory landscapes for therapy design in agent-based tumor models. Multiplex imaging gives rich spatial data but few time points per patient. They perturb a tumor microenvironment model to build trajectory ensembles and a low-dimensional landscape. A Markov state model captures metastable states and transitions from spatial summary series. Patient snapshots map onto the landscape, and a decision process form supports treatment scheduling.
arxiv-2603-18933: Grunwald and co-authors study how light cavities can change the magnetism of strongly linked electrons. Such links have no single energy scale, so vacuum effects act off-resonance. They build a full cavity theory that keeps all light modes and screen effects. They apply it to the Hubbard model near half filling without weak-coupling shortcuts. Changes in magnetic exchange track a broad light-density factor. For a surface cavity, screening and dressing compete, yet the exchange grows overall in their results.
arxiv-2603-19033: Misuna builds an unfolded system for a free, massless hypermultiplet in supersymmetry theory. He shows that the standard harmonic superspace form of the model grows out of this system. The step turns unfolded one-forms tied to a symmetry into frame-like fields. The same system yields forms in harmonic, two-fold, and one-fold superspace. It also yields the plain component form in Minkowski space. He calls this trait background universality. He also notes a possible off-shell extension and how the harmonic part shows in the fiber.
arxiv-2603-19133: Zhang and co-authors present PicoSpec, a way to speed up large language models split between edge devices and the cloud. A small model on the device drafts text while the large cloud model checks it, and the two run at the same time. A sparse compression step cuts the cost of sending word scores back and forth. The method needs no new training. In tests, the team reports speed gains of up to 2.9 times over prior methods.
arxiv-2603-19333: Ping and co-authors tune chip design code for low power with help from language models. Their POET tool checks each rewrite against the source design as a golden oracle. Test benches come from fixed simulation, so no model invention enters the checks. An evolution loop then sorts designs by Pareto rank, with power first inside each tier. Survivors are picked in proportion, which steers the search toward low power. On 40 designs, all rewrites stay functionally correct. Each design also reaches the best power in the test.
arxiv-2603-19633: Takagi and Nitanda introduce a proximal sampler that needs only zeroth-order queries of the potential. Proximal sampling alternates forward and backward heat flow steps. The backward step once used rejection sampling, which they replace with direct simulation. The particle cloud is treated as a Gaussian mixture, giving a Monte Carlo score estimate. With controlled score error, the method keeps exponential convergence under isoperimetric conditions. It avoids rejection, allows flexible step sizes, and has fixed runtime. Tests show fast convergence to the target distribution.
arxiv-2603-19933: Ray and co-authors read a decade of airborne surveys over Lake Menindee in Australia. The lake's water level changed greatly between 2014 and 2024. Airborne electromagnetic surveys image shallow ground conductivity from fast-moving aircraft. That conductivity shifts with minerals, pores, and water content and chemistry. Even so, the team finds a steady picture of the regional geology across survey systems and years. The top ten metres vary most over time, which fits the changing lake storage above them.
arxiv-2603-20033: Burr and co-authors test if the red edge of vegetation can be read on Earth-like exoplanets. The red edge is a sharp rise in plant reflectance near 0.7 micrometres. Real planets have patchy clouds and mixed surfaces, unlike simple models. The team extends a retrieval frame to fit surface albedo that varies with wavelength. They test it on spectra from detailed 3D Earth models. Varied land views and cloud types are included. The method recovered an Earth-like planet in every case, with albedo steps detected despite clouds.
arxiv-2603-20133: Kartáč, Lango, and Dušek show that reasoning gets harder for language models inside a dialogue. Benchmarks test reasoning in isolation, but real task dialogue mixes reasoning with role and style rules. Their BOULDER benchmark covers eight travel tasks needing arithmetic, spatial, and temporal thought. Each problem appears in isolated and dialogue forms for a fair comparison. Eight models showed a large, consistent drop in the dialogue setting. Ablations blame the multi-turn format most, with role setup and tool demands adding strain. Dialogue-aware testing is clearly needed.
arxiv-2603-20433: Piao and co-authors probe in-context learning in large audio-language models. Such models follow instructions poorly at times, but example use was untested. Their pipeline removes textual guidance in three stages, step by step. Six models faced four audio tasks under two output constraint types. Demonstrations reliably improved format compliance across the models. They did not improve core task performance, though. Label shuffling and attention tests explain why this happens. Models use examples to learn output format, not input-output links.
arxiv-2603-20833: Johnson proposes governance aware vector subscriptions for multi agent knowledge systems. Agents subscribe to semantic regions of a shared knowledge base. Alerts should fire only for content the agent may legally use. His mechanism pairs similarity matching with policy checks on five dimensions. The checks rest on the EU DSM Directive and the EU AI Act. Tests inside the AIngram system used 1,000 chunks and 93 subscriptions. Governed mode enforced all policy rules while still sending allowed alerts. No single policy dimension alone gave full compliance.
arxiv-2603-20933: Sharma and Grossman present AC4A, an access control framework for language model agents. Agents today get full access to an API or page, or none at all. That forces users to trust agents with far more power than a task needs. AC4A lets users grant agents only the resources a task requires. It works for both API based and browser based agents. Apps lay out their resources as hierarchies and compute needed permissions at run time. Case studies show it working on real APIs and web pages.
arxiv-2603-21633: Guo and co-authors separate true collective flow from background effects in tiny particle collisions at the LHC. In proton-proton and proton-lead runs, momentum conservation creates links that mimic flow. Their Bayesian method joins momentum conservation math with ATLAS data on long-range azimuthal links. The cleaned elliptic and triangular flow values come out close in size. But backgrounds differ between the two systems, as does the flow-background interplay. Standard measures fit the proton-lead flow well yet understate the proton-proton flow, they find.
arxiv-2603-22233: The CMS Collaboration searches for Higgs bosons made at high transverse momentum that decay to two W bosons. The search uses proton-proton collision data at 13 TeV from 2016 to 2018. The sample holds 138 inverse femtobarns. Decay products are rebuilt as one large-radius jet, with one lepton or none. A transformer-based algorithm picks the Higgs candidate jets. They find no sign of a signal above background. The measured rate sits below the standard model value, with wide error bars.
arxiv-2603-22333: Shin and co-authors recast the Mamba2 sequence model as an adaptive filter bank. Mamba2 is a state-space model with parallel heads that run apart. That independence wastes structure the model could use. Their framework, HADES, reads Mamba2 as a filter bank on a line graph. Shared filters handle global low-pass behavior. Expert filters handle local high-pass detail, set by a structured bias on the step parameter. HADES matches Mamba2 scores across benchmarks. It does so with only about 59 percent of the parameters.
arxiv-2603-22433: Bennett and co-authors build a map between magnetic and electric quivers for three-dimensional gauge theories. The theories they study have moduli spaces tied to nilpotent orbits and related slices. Their map uses symmetric group actions such as wreathings, bouquets, and foldings. It induces a map on nilpotent orbits that partly resolves a known block to quiver dualities. The authors combine Coulomb and Higgs branch methods with localization formulas, and they present new quivers for exceptional cases.
arxiv-2603-22633: Mortezaagha and Rahgozar argue that biomedical search tools are judged too narrowly. Most tests reward finding the single best text chunk. But good answers often need facts spread across a paper's sections. The authors propose GraLC-RAG, which mixes late chunking with graph-aware structure. It detects section boundaries, adds UMLS knowledge graph data, and guides hybrid search. Tests use 2,359 PubMed Central articles and 2,033 cross-section questions. Plain similarity search scores best on rank but pulls from one section only. Structure-aware methods pull from far more sections.
arxiv-2603-22833: Lai and co-authors introduce RC-HEOM, a hybrid method for open quantum system dynamics. The HEOM method is exact but hides bath detail inside helper operators. Reaction-coordinate mapping shows the main bath mode clearly, yet treats the rest loosely. RC-HEOM joins both: the mapping for access, HEOM for the residual bath. It keeps exact memory effects and a view of the key mode. Applied to Anderson impurity models, it tracks the Kondo singlet as it forms. It also reveals a coherence revival driven by the reaction coordinate.
arxiv-2603-22933: Ajra and co-authors release an open dataset for studying brain activity across mental and motor tasks. Most open neuroimaging sets use one signal type and one task in a lab. This set mixes EEG, fNIRS, and ECG with behavior and self-report data. Thirty healthy people took part over three sessions. Seven tasks range from N-back and mental arithmetic to combined cognitive-motor work. The authors aim the raw data at new preprocessing methods. Uses include brain-computer interfaces and neurorehabilitation.
arxiv-2603-23333: Amiri and Janabi-Sharifi model and control a tendon-driven arm on a drone. Such aerial continuum manipulators mix drone agility with a soft arm's compliance. Past coupled models cost compute and skip the drone's underactuation. Their formulation joins a strain-based Cosserat rod model with the drone's rigid-body model in one frame. It avoids long symbolic derivations and runs as plain ODEs on SE(3). They add a dual-camera visual servoing scheme with wide coverage. Tests on a prototype show it works in real settings.
arxiv-2603-23433: Frey and Ethayarajh coin mecha-nudging: reshaping choice settings to sway AI agents, not people. Agents now shop and decide online in the same spaces as humans. The pair build a shared yardstick in bits from Bayesian persuasion and usable information. They apply it to over six million Etsy listings. After ChatGPT launched, listings held much more machine-usable signal about agent picks. The gain was 0.143 bits of a 0.355-bit ceiling. A human study found no such shift for people.
arxiv-2603-23533: Mangla asks what one language model call per text chunk buys a search pipeline. Many RAG setups pay that call to add titles, summaries, and questions at index time. His preregistered tests compare paid enrichment with free structure and stronger retrievers. The verdict: upgrade the retriever first and chunk at headers. Enrichment helps most under word search, and ties with contextual retrieval at far lower token cost. Under strong retrievers, a free section prefix matches or beats the paid route. Late chunking, by contrast, lowers recall.
arxiv-2603-23733: Dai and five co-authors study how older heart patients read their own health tracker data. Eight patients aged 64 to 82 kept diaries for a week, then sat for interviews. Six themes emerged, from tangled feelings to guarding their own health stories. Patients trust body feelings over charts and share data on their own terms. Most feel wary hope toward AI help. The team sketch language model aids that honor feelings, agency, and body sense. Human experts must stay in the loop for safety.
arxiv-2603-24033: Wang and co-authors present SRG, a generative method that helps solvers tackle mixed-integer linear programs. SRG learns a score model from a relaxation-guided stochastic differential equation. Feasibility and optimality signals shape the score, so samples favor good feasible regions. At use time, it samples varied candidates with no extra guidance module. Those candidates seed compact trust-region subproblems for standard solvers. On public benchmarks, SRG matches or beats top learning baselines. It also transfers zero-shot to new scales and problem types in several cases.
arxiv-2603-24133: Dirckx and co-authors speed up time-optimal motion planning for mobile robots with spline paths. Coupled methods put separating hyperplane variables inside one big control problem, which costs much compute. Their method decides the hyperplanes apart from the main problem, as a classification task solved by a linear system or quadratic program. That turns non-convex limits into linear ones and keeps continuous safety guarantees. In obstacle-rich tests, planning time falls by up to almost 60 percent versus fully coupled methods, they report.
arxiv-2603-24233: Capecchi and co-authors test whether hot industrial wastewater can raise the odds of waterspouts. The town of Rosignano Solvay in Italy has seen repeated waterspouts, and locals suspect a nearby plant's warm discharge. The authors model four intense events with a high-resolution weather model. Modeled precursor values fit strong waterspouts, though peak instability came two to three hours early. Warming the sea in tests changed key indices by at most 3 percent. They conclude large-scale weather governs these events, not the small warm plume.
arxiv-2603-24833: Agarwal and co-authors build a robust framework for matrix estimation with row and column side information. Earlier methods impose rigid structure, such as exact low-rank interaction terms. Their decomposition splits the matrix into four parts: a nonlinear interaction, a row-driven part, a column-driven part, and a residual low-rank part. Sieve projection with nuclear-norm penalties estimates each part separately before aggregation. Convergence rates show robustness across settings.
arxiv-2603-25633: Zhang, Fu, and Jin ask whether skill at solving math problems matches skill at grading them. They use the GSM8K and MATH parts of ProcessBench, which marks the earliest wrong step in a worked solution. Two tutor agents, built on GPT-4 and GPT-5, both solve problems and grade sample solutions. The authors find that grading is far more accurate on problems the same model solved correctly. Grading error-filled solutions stays harder than solving. They argue that step tracking and error location need separate skills.
arxiv-2603-25733: Han and co-authors present SlotVTG, an adapter that helps video models find the moment a text query describes. Fine-tuning for this task often teaches dataset shortcuts instead of real grounding. That hurts performance on new domains. SlotVTG adds a light slot adapter to a multimodal model. Slot attention splits visual tokens into object-like slots and rebuilds the sequence. Priors from a self-taught vision model keep slots meaningful. The authors report much better out-of-domain results, with in-domain scores kept and little added cost.
arxiv-2603-25833: Andrew and co-authors present a spatial filter that cleans radio interference from telescope data. Interference increasingly limits radio work, including fast radio burst surveys. Their filter builds on the Karhunen-Loeve Transform and adapts it for point-like pulses. They apply it to CHIME/FRB baseband data. On a sample of 100 bursts, the filter beats a spectral-kurtosis flagger on signal-to-noise. The authors report it should double the number of bursts localized by the CHIME/FRB Outriggers. The code is public and fits other interferometers.
arxiv-2603-25933: Wang and co-authors explore an AI tool that supports imaginal exposure therapy for social anxiety. In this therapy, clients picture feared scenes to reduce their anxiety. Homework is hard because clients must build and sustain vivid fear stories alone. The team co-designed ImaginalExpoBot with mental health professionals.
