On 82 questions with 181 steps, it reaches step F1 of 72.0, matching an LLM-only baseline while staying more decomposable. Every StepGap stage hurts F1 when removed, while most LLM-only removals help, a sign of competing errors masking each other. Used as a process reward, it lifts exact-match scores across three seeds.
arxiv-2605-25033: Bing Shao, Guangjie Zhang, Longwen Zhou, Jiangbin Gong, and Weiwei Zhu report localization transitions in a quasiperiodic ladder whose legs share one onsite potential but shift laterally. The lateral shift creates a magnetic flux in momentum space, a control knob for experimenters. Tuning it accesses flux-enhanced, flux-suppressed, and flux-induced transitions between localized, mixed, and extended phases. Band analysis with a commensurate approximation explains the mechanisms and phase boundaries, needing only small unit cells. The setup offers a tunable platform for localization physics and quantum switching.
arxiv-2605-25133: João Sedoc, Baotong Zhang, and Dean Foster introduce prover-verifier deliberation for selective language model prediction. The protocol produces an answer and a structured verdict. A prover backs an answer with checkable sub-claims as a verifier issues challenges, giving a verdict. The main experiment pairs Claude Sonnet as prover with Claude Haiku as verifier on GPQA Diamond. The high-confidence subset is questions accepted with no answer revision. That subset separates good answers from the rest, with a 30 point high-confidence precision gap.
arxiv-2605-25233: Andy Xu and Yu-Wing Tai build a system that turns plain task descriptions into checked multi-agent workflows. A planner first splits the job into a graph of agent roles with stated inputs, outputs, and checks, while search grounds each role. Code writes its prompts and tools. Failed artifacts trigger targeted rebuilding before execution, and a coordinator then gates each intermediate result. A three-level error analysis separates local, upstream, and structural faults, guiding retries or partial rework, and tests show steadier success than strong baselines.
arxiv-2605-25933: Ricka and five colleagues test whether body signals can grade posttraumatic stress disorder, a condition now judged largely by subjective clinical scales. They record heart rate and skin conductance from 21 people during an immersive simulation, then train a fear-response model on public spider-phobia data. Features drawn from the fitted fear curves separate cases from non-cases with 86 percent accuracy. Severity estimates miss by about 5.6 points on average, which the authors read as promise for low-effort screening and follow-up.
arxiv-2605-26033: Mao builds a theory of lattice point counting on connected, simply connected step-two nilpotent Lie groups. The groups carry a parabolic dilation and homogeneous norms fitted to it. Counting lattice points inside norm balls, Mao derives discrepancy estimates for all dimensions and all alpha above zero. The bounds are sharp when the group centre is one-dimensional and alpha equals two, in a certain rational sense. The work extends and sharpens earlier Heisenberg results of Garg, Nevo and Taylor, including a lower logarithmic exponent in dimension five.
arxiv-2605-26233: Sarbajit Mazumdar and six colleagues' 2026 study attacks superconductivity in the one-band Hubbard model with a spin-rotation-invariant slave-boson method. From live fluctuations around the mean-field saddle point, they build a pairing vertex. Solving the gap equation on the square lattice, they map where pairing sets in across doping, interaction, temperature, and gap structure, matching cuprate experiments in broad outline. The approach joins strong-correlation effects with clear pairing physics, giving a route that scales to multi-orbital pairing.
arxiv-2605-26433: Weixin Liu and five colleagues warn that vector traces of text can leak sensitive facts even when source documents stay locked down. They audit clinical discharge-summary generation, using recorded race as a test label. Two artifacts get checked: the last-token hidden state of the prompt, and the mean prompt representation. Shielding one artifact need not shield the other. Their SurfaceLoRA fine-tuning, built on a gradient-reversal discriminator, pushes race recovery from the targeted artifact toward chance while keeping summary quality. Yet pooled artifacts leak far more.
arxiv-2605-26733: Yang and six colleagues address looped language models, which reason by iterating a single layer but often peak and then collapse as iteration depth grows. Their STARS training framework steers latent states toward asymptotically stable fixed points by regularizing the Jacobian spectral radius, a measure of how errors amplify across steps. On arithmetic and mathematical reasoning tasks, STARS delivers reliable test-time scaling, curbs late-depth degradation, and lifts peak performance.
arxiv-2605-26833: Yadav and three colleagues introduce Periodic-TDL, a deep-learning framework for polymer design that captures chain periodicity and many-body interactions missed by single-unit graph models. It builds on periodic Vietoris-Rips complexes and a layered message-passing encoder that moves news from long-range links down to bonds. It beats top rivals on electronic, optical, physical, and thermal tasks. Tests back its predictions that ester-to-amide swaps and backbone methylation raise glass transition points.
arxiv-2605-27033: In their 2026 study, Kervadec and four co-authors present s-Trace, a method that estimates a small subgraph approximating a full language model's output. Computation organizes into two phases: a sparse early-layer core reconstructs the head of the output distribution, while added later-layer nodes, increasingly attention heads, refine it step by step. Needed computation per input tracks model uncertainty, and sparser subgraphs encode shallow statistics such as unigram frequency. The results suggest a consistent modular organization of effective model computation.
arxiv-2605-27233: Korsky proves that sums of roots can approximate any number with an error bound. For root degree and term count, integers in a range bring a sum of roots close to targets, with error shrinking with range size. The proof joins Schmidt's Subspace Theorem with an explicit transference argument. The exponent beats earlier higher-root and full-basis results, except where the term count plus one is a power of the root degree, at the cost of ineffectivity. For square roots, he gives constructions for two, three, and four terms.
arxiv-2605-27633: Bernardo Alonso reads four paradoxes built in the coq-paradoxes package: Burali-Forti, Diaconescu, Reynolds, and Hurkens. Each proves falsehood in a system near the Calculus of Inductive Constructions, showing where the Rocq kernel refuses to compile the proof. Together they set three boundary rules on the kernel: where impredicativity sits, how large elimination is curbed, and how universe rules bind.
arxiv-2605-27933: Somphong Jitman and Panthakan Boonsuriyatham extend the theory of good integers, divisors tied to sums of powers, to a new two-parameter subclass. They characterize these (T,k)-good integers at prime powers and for odd and even cases. They also give an explicit decision algorithm and apply the theory to Galois dualities in cyclic codes.
arxiv-2605-28033: Vanc and colleagues compare three ways to teach robots by demonstration: guiding the arm by hand, steering with a joystick, and using hand gestures. In a study with eight users across three tasks, hand guidance gave the shortest demos, lowest workload, and best success on orientation- and contact-heavy tasks. Joysticks won only simple peg picking; gestures beat expectations.
arxiv-2605-28133: Benjamin Heymann and Otmane Sakhi study bidding in repeated second-price auctions where a bidder's value shifts with time since their last win. With only total feedback at the horizon's end, the bidder must weigh winning now against its drag on future values. The pair derives regret bounds and shows a confidence-bound method learns the best policy at near-best speed.
arxiv-2605-28233: Lince and colleagues join fair regression for cases where group traits show or hide at decision time. They recast parity-constrained regression as moving mass, and work out best predictors under two penalties: one gives a smooth group-wide middle path, the other exact parity for some people. A plain, quick method matches or beats top rivals.
arxiv-2605-28333: Nikolai Maas lifts multi-constraint hypergraph splitting by fixing one step alone: rebalancing. His greedy local hunt restores balance with a score that always offers a balance-raising move, proven for two limits under capped weights. Plugged into the Mt-KaHyPar splitter, it cut link counts by over eleven percent on average against the next best rival.
arxiv-2605-28633: Christopher Harper and three colleagues show that lining up of odd-shaped grains in sheared granular flows follows from grain edge geometry. The nematic order value depends chiefly on grain shape ratio, barely on shear rate or grain-to-grain friction. Given even contact odds along a grain edge, they derive a transform linking edge curve to contact-normal spreads, limiting allowed grain angles. The model predicts lining-up strength across shape ratios for ellipsoids, rectangles, and cylinders, matching runs and lab tests on rice grains and glass rods.
arxiv-2605-29133: Emil Y. Sidky and colleagues build a two-stage reconstruction algorithm for wide-angle digital breast tomosynthesis with better depth resolution and in-plane contrast. The first stage, a low-resolution sparsity pass for quantitative accuracy, now also estimates a background image absorbing low-frequency artifacts behind image non-uniformity. Tests on three patient cases show the design goals met: sharper depth detail, stronger in-plane contrast, and fewer non-uniformity artifacts. The authors caution that more empirical results and task-based assessment are still needed.
arxiv-2605-29233: Xiaoyou Wu proposes BlockBatch, a new way to speed up diffusion language models. Small blocks keep local context but need many steps, while large blocks run in parallel but may commit too early. BlockBatch runs several block-size branches for the same request in one batched pass, merging tokens by confidence and refreshing the full sequence at intervals. In tests, it cut denoising steps by about one quarter and ran about one third faster than Fast-dLLM, with accuracy preserved.
arxiv-2605-29833: Wanhao Liu and twelve colleagues present OmniMatBench, a human-calibrated benchmark for multimodal reasoning in materials science. Older benchmarks stress property prediction, knowledge questions, or characterization, leaving the path from knowledge to application thin. The bench holds over three thousand expert questions and problems across nineteen subfields, from basic knowledge to engineering and applied work. Thirteen open and closed models were tested, and the best scored just over a third overall, exposing a wide gap. Scores swung by subfield, with fixed heuristics, patchy knowledge, and weak application when aided.
arxiv-2605-29933: Feng Xiao, Dazhi Fu, Chris Ding, and Jicong Fan build CLUBench, weighing twenty-four algorithms on one hundred thirty-one sets across tabular, text, and image data, in one hundred seventy-nine thousand runs. The study probes tuning, data-type effects, pretrained embeddings, language-model clustering, algorithm similarity, and low-rank score structure. Deep clustering methods show no clear edge over top conventional methods like KMeans on average scores. For image and text tasks, pretrained embeddings plus conventional clustering prove effective. Clustering stays hard, so the benchmark guides method choice.
arxiv-2605-30233: Zilu Tang and six co-authors ask whether language models track entities across state changes. Prior work studies entity binding without state changes, leaving realistic tracking unclear. They find models do not track world states step by step, but gather relevant information at the final token, processed in parallel once the query is clear. Probing single operations, they find REMOVE uses a fragile suppression tag, which predicts failure modes seen in behaviour. Removing that tag partly fixes the issue, and models solve a sequential task non-sequentially.
arxiv-2605-30333: David Busbib and Michael Werman introduce grounded future mathematical generation: generating a plausible future claim for an anchor paper from its citation graph and formal dependency graph. A plausible future claim must follow prior work and respect formal dependencies. They propose COMPOSE, conditioning a language model on citation context and formal theorem structure. They construct a dataset of 108,000 paired graph examples from arXiv and Mathlib, plus a benchmark of 47,000 future papers. Experiments show COMPOSE outperforms baselines on retrieval to real future papers, with the best performance under LLM-judge evaluation.
arxiv-2605-30433: Cian Roche and 11 co-authors present a simulation method to make strong lensing images from particle data, drawing lens, source, and middle objects from one structure. Their method pairs a remap of the volume into a lensing shape with ray tracing, letting plain boxes resolve cluster lenses and source galaxies. They find stray structure can shift lensed image spots by several arcseconds. It adds about six percent scatter to a cluster's curve area, and shifts total critical area near the cluster core by about 16 percent.
arxiv-2605-30533: J. W. Zhou and A. A. Han map voids in NGC 628 from the JWST MIRI F770W image using BlendMask, refining them by intensity contrast. Cross-matching with archival star cluster and association catalogs shows only up to about 18 percent of voids link to such stellar populations. Voids linked to star clusters show lower intensity contrast and larger sizes. These results back an evolutionary scenario: some voids start within molecular clouds, expand under stellar feedback, and gradually detach from parent clouds.
arxiv-2605-30733: Ting and colleagues resolve the weak-CN puzzle in red supergiants, where CN absorption was detected in stars across three galaxies. These stars sit in a regime, cool for CN to appear yet warm for titanium oxide to stay unsaturated. Comparing weak-CN and carbon-star coadds with atmospheres, they find supergiant models reproduce the weak-CN coadds. The observable is carbon-plus-nitrogen abundance rather than each offset alone, since CN forms from carbon and nitrogen. Weak CN is the signature of supergiants, not a carbon-star intermediate.
arxiv-2605-30833: Liu and colleagues spot a block in on-policy distillation, where a student trains on its own trajectories. They name it Supervision Fidelity Decay. As student prefixes lengthen, the teacher's distribution becomes less confident and less discriminative, weakening the signal. To mitigate this decay, they introduce Lookahead Group Reward, evaluating top-K tokens by teacher confidence at the next step. Across six math and code benchmarks, Lookahead Group Reward improves mean-at-8 by about two and a half points. Gains increase in generations, reaching nearly five points on AIME-26.
arxiv-2605-31233: Nakagawa and Sasa study, through global thermodynamics, liquid-gas coexistence under gravity and heat flow. They build a trial free energy function, split in two. The first part matches the balance free energy for weak gravity, using effective gravity instead. It decides the layout switch between two liquid-gas setups. The second is an extra excess-latent-heat part that vanishes without heat conduction. Though it does not pick the favoured setup, it serves the basic lab relation and averaged pressure. It reshapes barrier shape and surface quirks.
arxiv-2605-31433: Kwan and colleagues introduce SCOPE, a self-play framework for open-ended tasks. A Challenger generates tasks for a Solver answering through multi-turn retrieval. A frozen initial model self-judges, writing rubrics and grading Solver responses. Across three 7-8B models, SCOPE gains up to 10.4 points on eight open-ended benchmarks, matching GRPO trained on about 9K curated prompts. It also improves held-out short-form QA, surpassing GRPO on all three models. Co-evolving the Challenger keeps tasks near the Solver frontier, and rubric quality bottlenecks judging.
arxiv-2605-31533: Precioso and team present BERS, a two-stage system for maritime weather routing with just-in-time arrival. Routes are drawn as Bézier curves. Global evolutionary search pairs with local variational refinement. On synthetic benchmarks stressing seven operational criteria, BERS matches or beats published baselines under hard flow fields and land shapes. On real ocean data covering 366 days of departures in 2024 across two trans-oceanic corridors, route optimization alone cuts mean propulsive energy by 23 to 59 percent.
arxiv-2606-00033:
Lan and co-authors call for making mechanistic interpretability research auditable in this 2026 arXiv paper. Mechanistic interpretability studies how neural networks work inside, circuit by circuit. The field has yielded striking insights, yet it lacks standard ways to verify experiments. The authors cite a concrete failure: two studies explained the same model behavior differently, and a third showed both were partly right but hard to compare because their methods differed. Such ambiguity blocks use in medicine and autonomous systems, where correctness must be certified.

Their proposal adds continuous shared reviewing alongside ordinary peer review. A shared platform would organize critiques, reruns, negative results, and partial follow-ups that never fit inside papers. Good practices emerging there would become expert-verified guidelines and auditing rules. A source-based system would track which claims each argument depends on. The paper offers early examples and invites debate on designing the framework.
arxiv-2606-00133:
Zidan and co-authors survey world models, a fast-growing branch of AI. A world model learns how a place works and how acts change it. Agents use such models to plan, test moves, and weigh choices. Work spans robots, self-driving cars, and video tools, with no shared map.

The survey sorts the field by four axes. These cover form, method, thought style, and use. It traces roots in mind science to big names like PlaNet, MuZero, Sora, and Genie. It also weighs test norms and known flaws. Faults include drift over long runs and weak shifts from sims to real life. The close maps paths toward broad, safe world models.
arxiv-2606-01333:
Gold shows a worst case for the ReCom redistricting algorithm. ReCom samples balanced graph partitions for map drawing. At each step it merges two adjacent districts. It then tries to re-split the joined region. The transition step is fast in practice. But no polynomial time guarantee was known for it. Gold builds an explicit family of counterexamples. They are 3-partitions on planar square grid graphs.

From these starts, ReCom needs exponentially many steps in expectation. That holds even if near-balanced splits are allowed. So ReCom does not run in polynomial time in the worst case. It is also not rapidly mixing in the technical sense. Adversarial starts can trap it far from the stationary spread.
arxiv-2606-01433:
Köhler and Rheinbach push a multigrid coarse solver to four levels. Complex geometries can make the coarse problem too large. A direct solver then fails to handle it at all. Domain decomposition attacks that coarse problem here. Overlapping Schwarz methods split the domain into pieces. A GDSW coarse space boosts their scalability. Past work built monolithic versions up to three levels. Theirs applies the construction recursively three times.

Only the smallest fourth-level problem meets a direct solver. Tests use a 3D incompressible Stokes problem. The fluid is non-Newtonian, with a Carreau-type viscosity model. The geometry is an extrusion die with complex shape. Runs scale to 4,000 MPI ranks. Four-level results compare against two- and three-level versions.
arxiv-2606-01533:
Koh, Salakhutdinov, and Fried argue for multi-agent computer use systems. Today's computer use agents run as single serial agents. Complex long tasks suffer under that setup. Such tasks gain from decomposition, parallel work, and re-planning. Their MACU design centers on a manager model. The manager splits tasks into a directed acyclic graph. Nodes encode dependencies and goals for subagents. At each step, parallel subagents work the ready frontier.

The manager revises the graph as findings arrive. Nodes get added, canceled, or rewritten on the fly. Facts that later agents cannot re-observe pass through the manager. MACU beats strong single-agent baselines by 3 point 4 to 25 point 5 percent. Tests span desktop and web navigation benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-01633:
Campbell proves a conjecture on a generalized Euler totient function. Büyükaşik and others defined phi_k(n) in 2024. It sums a to the k over all a up to n coprime to n. At k equals 0, it gives Euler's classic totient. For each s, a set D_s collects all k at least s such that phi_s(n) divides phi_k(n) for every n. That set was proved finite for each s.

The conjecture said D_1 equals the set with 1, 3, and 15. Computations supported it but no proof existed. Campbell now proves the conjecture in full. His argument grew out of extensive interactions with GPT-5 point 5 Pro. The note is short and aimed at number theorists.
arxiv-2606-01833:
Cheng and co-authors speed up fake protein motion from learned models. Generative emulators mimic protein dynamics at low cost. But they inherit the spread of their training data. They tend to revisit known shapes, not rare ones. Long runs make that bias worse.

Their method adds a history-aware bias in the model's space. The bias pushes sampling away from past shapes. A support term keeps new shapes in valid zones. A repair step projects stray samples back to real shapes. Tests use the DynamicPDB-80 data set. The authors report diversity up by 35 percent. On 12 fast-folding proteins, coverage comes far faster. Gains reach up to 37 times with the repair step.
arxiv-2606-02033:
Allahverdizadeh and Achouri tackle a hard modeling problem for metasurfaces. Scientists often split their response into many multipole moments. Using many moments makes the math complex and hard to apply. The authors seek a simpler route that keeps results accurate.

Their method uses the fact that multipole moments depend on the choice of origin. They show that the best origins depend on the parity of the response. By splitting the sheet conditions into even and odd parts, they can judge effects at distinct places. This lets them drop higher order terms and rebuild scattering results from dipoles alone. They test the method on two numerical examples. One uses dielectric cones on a substrate. The other has broken symmetry and a double resonance. In both cases, the authors report close agreement with full simulations.
arxiv-2606-02133:
Zhang and co-authors learn the order in which to insert tokens during generation. Insertion-based models free generation from left-to-right order. Masked diffusion models are one popular example. Tokens can appear in non-fixed, prescribed orders there. Most such models stay order-agnostic in practice though. Fixed-length grids limit variable-length output as well.

A probabilistic framework for learning insertion order is proposed. Insertion trajectories correspond bijectively to permutations. That link reparameterizes the data likelihood exactly. It becomes a sum over permutations. Their Insertion Process model learns jointly from that form. What to insert and where are learned together. Adaptive insertion order supports variable-length generation. The work gives insertion models a firmer probabilistic base.
arxiv-2606-02433:
Wang and co-authors open a new task in table question answering. Past systems answer questions about fixed tables. Few can predict future values from past data. The new task joins forecasting with reasoning over tables. It uses real estate data as its test bed.

Their dataset is called ODTQA-FoRe. It is the first to cover forecasting and forecast-based reasoning together. The work must fetch exact past rows, run a forecast, and shape a clean answer. The team builds TimeFore, an agent with three roles. A Retriever writes SQL to fetch data. A Forecaster calls outside time-series models. An Analyzer joins the parts into one answer. Tests show the design works well across the new task.
arxiv-2606-02533:
Yu and Joseph design experiments that must both screen factors and fill space well. Computer experiments often use space-filling designs. Such designs spread points evenly over the input space. They fail at factor screening, though. When only a few inputs truly matter, that failure wastes effort. Newer screening designs find key factors but fill space poorly. Surrogate modeling then suffers.

The authors propose a new class of one-factor-at-a-time designs. The designs keep screening power while filling space better. Several numerical examples show the gains. The new designs beat existing options on both fronts at once. Researchers can now screen and model with one design. The work closes a trade-off that forced a choice between two design goals.
arxiv-2606-02633:
Bruda counts representations of integers as sums of polygonal numbers. Generalized polygonal numbers generalize square and triangular numbers. The count function tracks how many ways a number N splits into n such parts. A parallel count uses sums of n squares. Bruda modifies the Heath-Brown circle method for this setting.

A closed-form asymptotic relation links the two counts. It holds for polygonal index at least 3 and summand count at least 4. Consequences follow for sums of four polygonal numbers. Mean-square asymptotics are determined. A result of Bringmann, Jang, Kane, and Tse extends the relation to ordinary polygonal numbers. A 2-adic result supplements work of Meng and Sun. When 4 divides the polygonal index, bounded subsequences converge 2-adically. When it does not, no such bounded increasing subsequence exists.
arxiv-2606-02833:
Kundu and co-authors build a framework for mediation analysis with many ordered mediators. It uncovers how an exposure shapes an outcome through middle paths. Single-mediator tools are well established. Settings with several mediators in sequence lack rigorous treatment. Long-term cohort studies face exactly that setting. Effects act through chains of mediators over time.

The framework pins down path-specific effects. The total effect splits formally into its component paths. Estimation covers continuous and grouped outcomes. A new testing strategy supports the tests. It pairs a studentized statistic with data-splitting. Valid Type I error control holds under the composite null. Simulations span diverse data-generating setups. Two large-scale real-data studies apply the method. Reliable results and valid tests are demonstrated. Power to discover novel mediation pathways improves. The work gives applied researchers a rigorous chain toolkit.
arxiv-2606-02933:
Yong, Estey, and Nacenta compare three kinds of help for students in a second-year algorithms course. The supports are generative AI, algorithm visualization, and live human tutoring. Past work on AI help has focused on first programming courses. Drawbacks such as overreliance are known, but the mechanisms are not.

Twelve students took part in three 90-minute sessions on sorting, tree, and graph algorithms. The team recorded gaze and interaction data. Each session ended with a test of conceptual understanding. Generative AI raised self-efficacy more than live tutoring did. Yet it was linked to clearly lower learning outcomes. Students also used the visualizations poorly, and they hit barriers when using AI on advanced topics. Live tutoring gave the highest learning outcomes of the three. The study probes how help is sought during problem solving. It asks when students turn to each support, not just whether scores rise.
arxiv-2606-03033:
Daeijavad and Asoodeh build a contraction-based framework for proving how fast MCMC algorithms mix. Markov chain Monte Carlo methods sample from complex distributions. Mixing bounds tell users how long a chain needs to run. Their framework uses global and local contraction coefficients of Markov kernels under a family of divergences.

For projected Langevin Monte Carlo on a compact convex domain, Gaussian smoothing gives an explicit global contraction coefficient. That yields a direct proof of exponential convergence for smooth, possibly non-convex potentials. For independent Metropolis-Hastings, global coefficients are often trivial when importance weights are unbounded. The authors therefore define a local coefficient on a core region where weights stay bounded. It controls the rejection profile and gives warm-start bounds. The bounds recover sharp known rates when moments exist, and still work in heavy-tailed regimes where they do not.
arxiv-2606-03333:
Sharma and Upadhyay classify tetraquarks made only of light quarks. A tetraquark binds four quarks into one state. Fully light ones use just the up, down, and strange quarks. They form a key test bed for the dynamics of low-energy quantum chromodynamics. The team works inside SU(3) flavor symmetry.

Under that symmetry, the states sort into multiplets. The sorting yields a rich spectrum of forms. Some carry no strangeness. Some are singly or doubly strange. Some hide their strangeness inside. The classification gives a map of what states the symmetry allows and how they relate. Such maps guide searches for new exotic hadrons at colliders. They also test how well flavor symmetry holds in the four-quark sector. The authors frame the work as groundwork for the dynamics of light hadrons. Each predicted multiplet is a target that experiments can hunt or rule out.
arxiv-2606-03433: Obradovic and Tuneski estimate the first-order Schwartian derivative at zero for several classes of univalent functions. The Schwartian derivative of a function f combines its first and second derivatives in one fixed expression. The functions here are univalent on the open unit disc. The result gives a size estimate for the derivative of that expression at the origin. Such bounds help sort and compare classes of univalent functions in complex analysis.
arxiv-2606-03633:
Chanfray, Hansen, and Pradhan follow the nucleon into nuclear matter in the chiral confining model. This is the second part of their study. Part one set out the formal tools. Trial states for bound nucleons come from the von Laue stability condition. The question is how a composite nucleon changes inside dense matter.

The nucleon response to the scalar field takes center stage. Confinement and chiral symmetry breaking each play distinct roles in the mass shift. That shift governs the repulsive three-body forces behind nuclear saturation. Energy density and pressure profiles inside the bound nucleon also change. The authors map those changes in detail. Perspectives connect bound nucleon traits to the equation of state of dense matter. That equation rules the deep interior of neutron stars. Nuclear theorists get a bridge from single-nucleon physics to star-scale behavior.
arxiv-2606-03933:
Rodriguez and co-authors present a physics-led method for finding damage in thin structures. Guided waves are sent through a part by a bonded sensor. The waves scatter from edges and from flaws. That scatter can reveal harm, but many wave modes start at once. Mixed modes make the signal hard to read.

Their method, PISACMP, breaks the signal into single wave atoms. Physics rules are built into that split, not learned from data alone. The split yields wave numbers and travel distances. Those distances link the sensor, the flaw, and the receiver. Standard ellipse methods can then place the damage. The team frames the result as a clear, low-cost route to locating harm.
arxiv-2606-04033:
Savage, Burnett, and Price design new nuclear critical experiments by gradient methods. Advanced reactors and fuels need tests that closely match their target tech. Similarity is scored by a correlation value, c_k. A score of at least 0.9 marks a strong match. Past design work leaned on parametric searches over set options.

A physics-informed neural network predicts sensitivity for grid-based experiment layouts. Its smooth form lets gradients guide the search for better layouts. Material mixes inside the grid can then be tuned as one whole. They apply the method to a transport cask case with HALEU fuel. Three layouts scored 0.978 and 0.933, with the third just above eight tenths. Existing coverage for that cask was limited, the abstract notes.
arxiv-2606-04333:
Weiyan Kang and colleagues show in 2026 a detector that lifts telecom-band photons up to visible light. Ordinary silicon sensors can then count them. The lift uses two fiber lasers locked together passively, with no electronics to sync them.

The converter reached an efficiency above seventy percent. The full detector hit about thirty percent overall detection efficiency, with very low noise. The build uses polarization-maintaining fiber throughout. That makes it compact and rugged next to older bulk-optics versions. Over ten hours of running, count rates drifted by barely a quarter of a percent. The team targets uses that need robust handling of pulsed light.
arxiv-2606-04433:
Wang and colleagues give vision-language models a visual memory, in a 2026 arXiv paper about how these systems compare images. In today's models the vision encoder is stateless: it encodes each image alone, with no knowledge of images seen before. Small but crucial changes between images can fade before the language model ever compares them. The authors' stateful visual encoder instead conditions each new image's representation on the visual features that came before it.

After supervised fine-tuning, models with stateful encoders improved consistently on controlled tasks: combining spatial information across images, spotting differences among objects, and copying behavior from visual trajectories. The gains held across resolutions, model sizes, and model families. On real-world tasks, including radiology follow-up, fine-grained image comparison, and remote sensing, stateful models improved generalist baselines and matched or beat specialized models in selected domains.
arxiv-2606-04633:
Ruiz-Casternado extends a classical tool of functional analysis from linear maps to Lipschitz functions, in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. Lipschitz functions cannot stretch distances by more than a fixed factor. The tool he extends is sequence classes. He uses it to define classes of summing Lipschitz functions relative to two sequence classes.

He then introduces Lipschitz stable sequence classes. Under that property, the summing class with its natural quasi-norm forms a Banach Lipschitz ideal. This is a well-behaved family of maps closed under composition. As applications, he develops Rademacher type and cotype for Lipschitz functions. These are classical probabilistic measures of a space's geometry. He identifies them with summing spaces for concrete sequence classes. The type case forms such an ideal. The cotype case does not. This is a genuine difference created by the lack of linearity. He also analyzes composition and maximality for the type ideals.
arxiv-2606-04733:
Presberger and colleagues teach a model to recognize which Internet scanners are related, without any labeled examples, in a 2026 arXiv security paper. The authors train a transformer with contrastive learning to embed minimally preprocessed sequences of network flow records, so that related sequences land near each other in the embedding space.

Similarities from the model define a correlation clustering problem, which they solve locally. Experimentally, learned similarities are higher on average for sequences from the same source than from different sources, and this generalizes to unseen sequences from unseen sources. Correlation clustering then yields clusters consistent with scanner labels, even though no labels or pretraining were used. The result is a self-supervised route to mapping scanner campaigns from raw flow data.
arxiv-2606-05033:
Jan Kaspari and colleagues study how quantum dot spins are controlled with light in the Faraday geometry in this 2026 arXiv paper. Stimulated Raman transitions in this setup allow single-shot qubit readout and control at the same time, driving an unbalanced three-level system through an extra excited state. Because both transitions are driven together with unequal detuning, the time-dependent Stark shift creates extra resonance conditions beyond the standard picture.

The team finds a regime where repeated passages through avoided crossings produce step-like population inversion, arising from Landau-Zener-Stückelberg interference between those passages. By changing the detuning beatnote, meaning the frequency difference between the drives, they show a controlled crossover from Rabi-like oscillations to adiabatic switching. The results establish the oscillating Stark shift as a tool for engineering spin dynamics in this geometry.
arxiv-2606-05233:
Nicholas Saban tests whether frontier computer-using agents are as safe as red-teaming headlines suggest, in this 2026 arXiv paper, and finds their safety is conditioned on the domain. Prompt-injection attack success rates of 42 to 98 percent cluster on retired models and on the weakest model in each panel. Saban instead reproduces the attacks as crafted templates against current agents.

He releases CUA-HandCrafted, a benchmark of 793 episodes spanning 24 web tasks, 56 attack templates, eight attack families, and four system-prompt configurations. Against Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 the templates scored zero successes in 140 attacks, and an ablation showed the resistance lives in the model weights. Yet on a coding-agent benchmark the same weights fell to injection at rates up to 100 percent. Saban argues the high success rates reflect reinforcement-learned injection text rather than the attack categories. Browser-domain safety should not be extrapolated to agent modalities.
arxiv-2606-05533:
Rohan Bhatt and colleagues argue that robots should judge objects by use, not by looks, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Most robot planners sort objects by how they appear in an image. A planner, though, needs to know what an object lets the robot do. A cart matters because it can be moved. The team builds a shared space that groups objects by such uses, called affordances.

Their system, A4D, maps each image into that space and reads off likely uses. When no known use fits well, the system can propose a new one. In tests it named known uses with ninety-four percent accuracy, beating earlier methods by over fifteen points. For new uses it lifted accuracy from about seventy percent to over ninety percent, while training on less than a tenth of the data. It also ran about one hundred times faster than the older approach.
arxiv-2606-05633:
Yuejie Li and colleagues audit why rewritten evidence boosts question answering in a 2026 arXiv paper. Search-based systems often pass retrieved passages through a language model rewriter first. Scores then jump by tens of points, usually credited to cleaner evidence. The team asks a sharper question: does the gain come from the gold answer string sitting inside the rewrite?

They reran the reader after controlled edits to each rewrite. Deleting the answer span cut scores by twenty-eight to sixty-four points beyond a placebo edit. Adding the answer to rewrites that lacked it raised scores in ten of twelve setups. A side audit showed a common leakage probe is fragile: its verdict flipped under four of five sentinel choices. The authors release their audit tools so other rewriting claims can face the same test.
arxiv-2606-05733:
Murjani links financial news across companies in a streaming system built for speed in a 2026 arXiv paper. Single-stock forecasters miss contagion: trouble at one firm reaches its partners before its own price moves. His architecture maps attention between companies as a live graph driven by news text. A Rust front end parses records without copying data. A neural point process then spreads influence along the graph over time.

Parsing takes about one hundred nanoseconds per record, and a full stock scan about a microsecond. End to end, each news item clears in roughly thirteen milliseconds on one ordinary processor. On a month of held-out financial news, precision beat random picks by a factor of about one point seven. Against a same-sector baseline the lift was over threefold. Removing the graph collapsed precision to zero. Cross-company links, not stock features, carried the whole signal.
arxiv-2606-06133:
Eric Spencer and colleagues present TLA-Prover in this 2026 arXiv paper on automated formal verification. TLA+ is a language for writing precise specifications of distributed systems so a model checker can hunt for design errors. Language models often write specifications that parse yet fail the TLC checker on meaning. The team trains a twenty-billion-parameter model to write specifications that survive that checking process.

Training mixes supervised fine-tuning on verified examples with repair-based reinforcement learning, where the model learns to fix its own rejected drafts. A four-tier scale runs from Bronze, which merely parses, to Diamond, where a deliberately weakened property must be caught by the checker. TLA-Prover reached thirty percent at both Gold and Diamond on a held-out set of thirty problems, about three and a half times the best baseline rate the authors measured across twenty-five models.
arxiv-2606-06233:
Benedikt Seiter, Anya Fries, Julius von Kügelgen, and Jonas Peters adapt a classic data tool for many domains at once in this 2026 arXiv paper. Principal component analysis, or PCA, compresses data by finding the directions where it varies most. When data comes from several related domains, pooling everything can spotlight directions that vary wildly in just one domain. Those directions then fail on new, similar domains.

Their Anchor PCA instead favors directions of variation that the domains share. It balances total explained variance against agreement between the shared embedding and each domain's own embedding. The method reduces to ordinary PCA on a modified target matrix, so it stays fast. Theory shows it recovers a maximal invariant subspace, the part of the data untouched by domain shifts. On gas sensor data with drift over time, its embeddings explained more variance on unseen domains than pooling did.
arxiv-2606-06333:
Seyed Arshan Dalili and Mehrdad Mahdavi fix a structural flaw in a popular interpretability tool in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sparse autoencoders decode a language model's internal features into readable directions, one direction per feature. That design assumes each feature is a single line. Real features, the authors argue, often span whole planes or subspaces, and forcing them onto lines has a cost.

They prove the mismatch causes feature splitting in two ways. Geometrically, matching a feature of dimension two or more with single direction atoms needs exponentially many of them. Worse, the training objective itself prefers the split solution, so trained dictionaries drift there on their own. Their remedy, SASA, gives each feature a subspace instead of a direction. In a Mistral model, one learned subspace organized geographical concepts into clean clusters for cities, countries, and continents. A sports subspace likewise separated combat terms, titles, and general context.
arxiv-2606-06433:
M Derouich and S Qutub compute how collisions scramble light polarization in the Sun's atmosphere in this 2026 arXiv paper. Several helium spectral lines serve as diagnostic tools for solar magnetic fields, read through spectropolarimetry, the measurement of polarized light. Collisions with neutral hydrogen atoms knock helium atoms out of their aligned states, erasing part of that polarization signal. Modelers need the exact rates to interpret what telescopes see, and those rates were poorly known.

Working in the frozen core approximation, where the inner electron is held fixed and the outer one is treated as active, the authors compute full rate sets. They cover depolarization, polarization transfer, and population transfer, in both multi level and multi term forms. Results are tabulated at five thousand kelvin with scaling laws for hotter regions. The rates feed directly into the statistical equilibrium equations behind the main diagnostic lines, including the 10830 angstrom line.
arxiv-2606-06533:
Stella Biderman and co-authors argue that AI research studies the wrong end of a model's life in this 2026 arXiv position paper. Most analysis treats a trained model as a fixed artifact. It patches behaviors afterward: the fix it in post mentality of their title. But models are snapshots of a training process, shaped by data, objectives, and optimization. A real science of AI, they argue, must explain behavior through those training dynamics.

The paper sets a ladder of understanding. First predict outcomes from early training signals. Then intervene when trajectories go wrong. Finally design training that reliably yields wanted properties. Scaling laws already do this for loss. The challenge is extending prediction to capabilities, bias, robustness, and safety. The authors review progress in interpretability, fairness, memorization, and simplicity bias, and list open problems. Post hoc fixes, they conclude, cannot substitute for causal understanding.
arxiv-2606-06833:
Speech recognition that runs live must guess words before the sentence ends. Xie, Cullen, Montague, and Rubinstein exploit that weakness in this 2026 arXiv paper. They study adversarial attacks, crafted sounds that corrupt what a recognizer hears. Real time attacks were long held back by one limit: the attacker cannot hear the future.

Their Semantic Gambit attack borrows a language model as a fortune teller. The model predicts likely upcoming words from context. The attacker shapes its noise around those predictions in real time. Corpus word error rates jumped to about thirty six percent. That is roughly three times the best earlier result. The finding has a defensive edge. Common low latency language model tools are now easy to obtain. Anyone can use them to attack live transcription pipelines in a systematic way.
arxiv-2606-07233:
Does adding appearance cues help track many objects in 3D video? Borges and co-authors test that question in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is online multi-object tracking for multiplayer games, where players vanish behind obstacles and later reappear. Re-identification, matching a returning object to its earlier identity from images, is the proposed remedy. The study separates motion cues from appearance cues so each part can be measured alone.

The team benchmarked several image encoders as the appearance part, finding a clear speed-accuracy trade-off. One network with no transformer blocks reached about 79 percent mean average precision on a standard person dataset while running above 150 frames per second. A smaller network was fastest, passing 360 frames per second at lower accuracy. In the full pipeline, geometry handled most matching, while appearance mainly rescued identities after long occlusions.
arxiv-2606-07433:
Meng and a team organize the field of video understanding by multimodal language models around three abilities in this 2026 arXiv survey. Watching covers how models perceive detail across senses and long footage cheaply. Remembering covers how they store context, after the fact and while streaming. Reasoning covers drawing grounded conclusions, whether in text alone or while inspecting the video. The survey formalizes systems through their perceptual representations, memory states, reasoning traces, and predictions.

That structure exposes challenges across benchmarks: spatio-temporal perception, affordable long-video processing, memory modeling, streaming use, and faithful inference. Methods are catalogued by their role within a system rather than by task leaderboard. Application domains from egocentric and sports video to medical and narrative content get their own sections, alongside training datasets and evaluation benchmarks. The authors close with open problems for scalable, memory-aware, evidence-grounded video intelligence and maintain a repository tracking new work.
arxiv-2606-07733:
Richter-Addo and colleagues simulate the glowing filaments near the centre of our galaxy in this 2026 arXiv paper. These structures stretch for tens of parsecs. They shine by synchrotron light, given off by fast particles circling in magnetic fields. Nobody knows what supplies the particles. Pulsar jets would deliver mostly electrons, while interstellar shocks would deliver mostly protons.

Using the Athena++ simulation code, extended with energy losses from radiation and collisions, the team tracked both kinds of cosmic rays through varied magnetic fields, densities, and diffusion rates. Surprisingly, the electron-rich and proton-rich cases produced few visible differences. Heating, plasma flow, and emitted light all looked much the same. Because neither rival mechanism can be confirmed from these signatures, the authors argue a third idea deserves attention. The filaments may arise from patchy structures inside turbulent gas at the galactic centre.
arxiv-2606-07933:
Adeel Mahmood, Harish Viswanathan, and Jinfeng Du of Nokia Bell Labs ask how well compression-plus-transmission works when the channel is not the one the code was designed for. This 2026 arXiv paper takes the mismatch head-on. Joint source-channel coding squeezes a source and protects it against noise in one design, usually tuned to a known channel. Their setting is finite blocklength, short packets, over unknown channels, with lossy reconstruction allowed.

The team proves achievability results for mismatched designs, codes built for one channel law but deployed on another. A clean special case stands out. For block erasure channels, where packets are delivered or lost whole, channel mismatch costs nothing at all. They then build a universal code family covering the whole erasure-channel class with second-order guarantees. Short-packet systems that cannot know their channel in advance are the target.
arxiv-2606-08033:
Mattia Forlesi and co-authors ask how much synthetic data a crack-detection network can drink before it stops helping, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Cracks are an early warning of building damage, and convolutional networks can spot them in photos, but they hunger for large, varied training sets. Real masonry crack images are slow to collect, and public sets do not match complex masonry surfaces.

The team collected real crack images from buildings in Bologna and its surroundings. They built a synthetic companion set with a tool that overlays cracks onto background images at controlled positions. Screening several architectures on real data identified InceptionV4 as strongest. Six training scenarios then swept the ratio of real to synthetic images, finding where synthetic data stops complementing and starts diluting. The study is a practical recipe for inspection work: when real examples are scarce, generate them, but measure the mixture.
arxiv-2606-08133:
Cuong Le and co-authors estimate the forces between a moving human body and the ground using gravity as the guide, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ground contact forces matter for biomechanics and sports science, but measuring them needs force plates or pressure mats, confining studies to laboratories. Earlier estimates from motion capture used only the body's vertical distance to the ground, missing how pressure spreads across contact points.

Their model, GraCE, reasons from the body's centre of gravity. Contact points are inferred from the centre's position relative to the body, using a realistic mass distribution. The force at each contact is the predicted contact probability times the total external force from the centre-of-mass trajectory. On GroundLink, GraCE beat related work at estimating ground reaction forces, and on MOYO at predicting detailed contact pressure. The physics prior does the heavy lifting: where the mass is, the forces must answer.
arxiv-2606-08433:
Andronchik and Lokhmakov compare the security of sandboxes that run untrusted artificial intelligence code, in this 2026 arXiv paper, the first of two parts. A sandbox isolates guest code from the host kernel, the core of the operating system, and products differ sharply in how they isolate. The study reads six engine-level measurements together: host attack surface, information leakage, defense-in-depth stackability, vulnerability history, patch cadence, and fuzzing posture.

Three findings stand out. Engine classes, namely micro-virtual-machines, userspace kernels, and ordinary containers, separate cleanly on every architectural axis, but products within a class do not. The dominant variable is product pin policy, how long a shipped product lags behind upstream fixes. Engine-side patch latency aggregates to roughly zero days for coordinated disclosures, while downstream lag spans to well over a year. Fuzzing investment, systematic testing with random inputs, splits into distinct tiers.
arxiv-2606-08533:
Lixuan Jin and a large team teach a drone to pick up and deliver objects it has never handled, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Unmanned aerial vehicles are increasingly deployed in logistics, creating demand for autonomous payload acquisition and delivery. Existing approaches typically assume pre-attached payloads or rely on specialized grippers. Different payloads induce variable flight dynamics. A single policy must adapt online without manual calibration for each new load.

Their setting equips a quadrotor with a lightweight hook. It picks up, transports, and delivers diverse handle-equipped objects between randomized locations. The learning method is contextual contrastive meta reinforcement learning. The policy infers a context describing the payload's dynamics from recent flight experience, and adapts its control accordingly. The aim is a drone that copes with new loads on its own, flight after flight, with no pause.
arxiv-2606-08833:
Galinska, Pogodzinski, and Lenssen tune image generation to match how human eyes actually see detail, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Flow matching models build pictures gradually, removing noise step by step. Because real images concentrate their signal at low spatial frequencies, coarse content stabilizes early and fine detail arrives late. Human vision is unevenly sensitive too: the contrast sensitivity function says extreme frequencies need much stronger contrast before we notice them.

Their method, CSFlow, first estimates which frequencies each generation step produces. It then weights the steps so capacity flows toward the frequencies viewers are most sensitive to. The weights can be applied at inference time alone, or with a short fine-tuning run. Across experiments, CSFlow lowered the FID quality score by 4.7 percent, raised the Inception Score by 2.2 percent, and lifted GenEval scores by 2.5 percent. The images also look more realistic and less cartoonish.
arxiv-2606-09033:
Huang and colleagues show that editing a reasoning model's facts can look perfect on standard tests while its thinking rejects the edit, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Knowledge editing updates facts in a model. Reasoning models write chain-of-thought traces. The authors found three failure modes: edits that collapse the reasoning format, reasoning arguing against the injected fact from visual evidence, and shallow edits failing on rephrased questions. Teacher-forced accuracy read 100 percent while grounded success, judged on real reasoning, fell to zero.

Their benchmark, ReasonEdit-Bench, stratifies conflicts across hops. Their fix, CRANE, avoids rewriting weights per edit. It retrieves edits from a dual library, and training teaches arbitration between visual priors and injected facts. CRANE reached 96.9 percent grounded success on conflict scenarios and 96.9 percent intermediate-entity use in multi-hop chains. On an out-of-distribution test it scored 87 percent under gold retrieval, beyond weight-editing baselines.
arxiv-2606-09533:
Sleman Mouammar, Ítalo Brasileiro, and André Drummond study whether fibre-optic sensing can let metropolitan networks reroute traffic before a cable fails in this 2026 arXiv paper. Distributed fibre sensing listens to backscattered light in the fibre itself, detecting digging, vibration, and strain minutes before a cut. Just-in-time restoration uses those warnings to find new paths proactively, instead of reacting after services drop.

The authors simulated all-optical metropolitan networks without amplifiers, varying the sensing devices' prediction capability and scoring affected circuits, suspended circuits, bandwidth blocking, and downtime. With a prediction time capability of fifteen milliseconds, just-in-time restoration cut circuit disruptions by more than ninety percent compared with restoration that had no sensing information. Service continuity matched that of heavyweight protection schemes, which pre-reserve duplicate capacity, while using only a fraction of the spectral resources.
arxiv-2606-09933:
Luca Cirfeta fixes a blind spot in his own glitch hunter for gravitational-wave data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Glitches are brief noise bursts that can drown real cosmic signals in the LIGO detectors. His past tool read whole spectrograms, time-frequency maps of the strain, through one pooled token of the DINOv2 image model. Short bursts fill under five percent of the grid, so pooling washed them out.

The fix scores each patch of the map on its own. Patch scores are matched against a vector-quantized index, a codebook of cluster centers for nineteen known glitch shapes. On LIGO O4a data, wide burst shapes split cleanly from calm noise, with a KS gap of zero point nine six three. Ultra-short blips still slipped past the patch grid's time grain. The tool, Cirfeta notes, works best as a spotter, not a judge.
arxiv-2606-10033:
Chiem proves positivity results for amounts that measure chaos in quantum and wave systems, in a 2026 arXiv paper on mathematical physics. Lyapunov exponents measure how quickly nearby paths separate, and positivity signals chaos at work. He studies Schrödinger operators, the equations governing quantum particles, whose potentials are generated by hyperbolic dynamics and are anti-Hölder, a roughness condition running opposite to the usual smoothness assumption.

He proves an anti-Lipschitz estimate for functions tied to the orbit of a standard basis vector under that cocycle. Applying the estimate to subshifts of finite type and to maps with one expanding direction on tori of any dimension gives evenly positive Lyapunov exponents when coupling constants are large enough. Uniform positivity is stronger than pointwise positivity and matters for spectral theory of disordered systems. The work extends earlier results that required smoother potentials or special dynamical setups.
arxiv-2606-10133:
Infeld proves that a classic privacy design is mathematically optimal for hiding users in matching data, in a 2026 arXiv paper on combinatorics and privacy. In a bipartite graph linking users to behaviors, the number of perfect matchings measures anonymity: more matchings mean an attacker faces greater uncertainty about who did what. The question is which graph structure maximizes that count for a fixed number of edges, the infrastructure cost.

Using Brègman's theorem, Infeld shows partitioning users into equal-sized groups, each forming a complete bipartite component, achieves the theoretical upper bound on perfect matchings. Where edge counts prevent an exact partition, a constructed family of graphs attains the bound asymptotically as group size grows. The optimality is also robust: after an attacker de-anonymizes one user by the most damaging choice, the remaining graph is still a partition graph and remains optimal.
arxiv-2606-10933:
Sharma, Thorat, and Chopra test coding agents on languages they barely know in this 2026 arXiv paper. Six current agents face four esoteric languages, Brainfuck and Befunge-98 among them, in a setup with file editing, local runs, and hidden tests. The strange languages expose gaps that mainstream benchmarks compress into narrow bands.

The strongest agents, Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 xhigh, often dodge the target language: they write Python programs that generate the target code, then debug the generators. Banning that metaprogramming causes large score drops. Written advice alone does not lift weaker agents, but working helper code sharply improves mid-tier ones, while the weakest stays low.
arxiv-2606-11133:
Saavedra, Armas Padilla, and Muñoz-Darias separate two blended X-ray sources near the Galactic Center in a 2026 arXiv paper. SLX 1744-299 and SLX 1744-300 are low-mass X-ray binaries, neutron stars feeding from small companions, just 2.7 arcminutes apart. An archival NuSTAR observation resolves them spatially above ten kiloelectronvolts for the first time.

SLX 1744-300 proves slightly brighter. Its flux ratio is near 1.15 in the hard band, rising to about 1.3 at softer energies. Both sources sat in the hard spectral state, with variability near twenty-one to twenty-three percent. Their behavior diverged. SLX 1744-299 faded steadily as its accretion rate fell. SLX 1744-300 held steady and fired two short Type-I bursts from mixed hydrogen-helium burning. Combining luminosities with distance limits, the authors favor an orbital period under ninety minutes for SLX 1744-299, a compelling ultracompact candidate. Its neighbor's period falls under roughly one hundred five to one hundred fifty-five minutes.
arxiv-2606-11533:
Fujimoto and Benz argue AI researchers must help lead arms control in a 2026 arXiv position paper. Defense firms are investing in AI and partnering with AI companies, while researchers often focus on long-term superintelligence risks. The near-term concern is military AI: frontier models in defense applications could shake global security before governance catches up.

Arms control has reduced grave risks before, and lessons from nuclear deterrence can guide AI safety research toward verification and diplomacy tools. But technical solutions for trustworthiness, checks, and openness are lacking, so researchers must lead the work defining and easing instability in military settings. The authors propose venues fostering dialogue across disciplines, citing the Pugwash Conferences as a model of scientists reducing nuclear arms. They advise AI experts to learn how arms control specialists view agreements, stability, verification, and deterrence, and suggest new governance bodies may be needed.
arxiv-2606-12033:
Min Yang, Mi Zhou and Limin Wang bring brain-inspired spiking networks to video action detection in this 2026 arXiv paper, published in Pattern Recognition. Temporal action detection finds when actions start and end in long untrimmed videos. Conventional models are large and power-hungry, a problem for mobile deployment, while spiking neural networks promise low energy on neuromorphic chips. Their SpikeTAD is the first end-to-end spiking architecture for this task.

Spiking networks communicate in discrete spikes like real neurons, but converting trained conventional networks into them usually costs long time steps and accuracy. The authors use different conversion strategies for the backbone and the detection head, preserving pretrained weights. The result keeps extremely low power consumption while reaching an average detection score of about sixty-seven percent on THUMOS14 and about thirty-seven percent on ActivityNet. Those numbers demonstrate that low-power action detection is feasible today.
arxiv-2606-12233:
Hashemi and co-authors measure, for the first time, a set of numbers describing light with three modes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Partially coherent light is neither fully orderly nor fully random, and two-mode fields are summed up by three Stokes numbers. Three-mode fields need a three-by-three coherence matrix instead. Its expansion uses Gell-Mann matrices, borrowed from particle physics, giving eight Stokes-Gell-Mann parameters. Theory described them long ago, but nobody had measured them directly.

The team measures all eight on a photonic chip, a hexagonal mesh of Mach-Zehnder interferometers that split and recombine light. Seven measurement configurations suffice to extract every parameter. From them, the coherence matrix is rebuilt. That maps which three-mode fields convert into each other by unitary operations, and which share entropy yet cannot. Uses in communication, sensing, and information processing follow.
arxiv-2606-12633:
Kong and colleagues tackle continual learning for image-to-text models in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is open-ended image-to-text generation, where a vision-language model writes captions or answers questions about pictures. When new kinds of images arrive over time, retraining can cause catastrophic forgetting, meaning older skills fade badly. Earlier studies split tasks by separate object classes or backgrounds, which the authors call unrealistic.

Instead, they group tasks by main topic, the most prominent subject in each image, and update only the alignment module connecting vision with language. Their method, called ECA, mixes task-specific query tokens, expands the model using a Fisher information measure of importance, and replays stored embeddings rather than old images. Across four new benchmarks built for this setting, ECA records the best final average scores on the text-based suites while using far fewer trainable parameters than rival methods.
arxiv-2606-12733:
Agrawal and colleagues improve one-run privacy auditing for differentially private machine learning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Privacy auditing tests whether an implementation leaks as little information as its differential privacy guarantee claims. The efficient approach audits a single training run of DP-SGD, the standard private training algorithm, by planting canaries, training examples whose detectability measures leakage. Earlier one-run methods reduced each canary to a binary membership guess, discarding information.

Working in the white-box setting, where the auditor can inspect training internals, the authors show that canary-aligned signals form a sequence of random variables whose normalised sum is Gaussian for large samples. Building an audit on that distribution yields tighter privacy lower bounds from just 1 training run than the binary approach. The result makes verification of private training cheaper and sharper, helping catch coding errors or mis-set parameters that weaken a claimed guarantee.
arxiv-2606-12833:
Leung develops a quaternion and Lie-algebra framework for proving the local accuracy of SIDER, a recursive high-order interpolation method for data on the unit sphere, in this 2026 arXiv paper. SIDER builds interpolants from repeated spherical linear interpolation, or SLERP, between points on the sphere.

Points are represented as pure unit quaternions, and errors are measured in fixed-base quaternion logarithmic coordinates. In that setting each SLERP step has an exact Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff representation, turning the geometric problem into algebra. SLERP is affine to leading order, has no quadratic correction, and its first nonlinear correction is cubic and commutator-valued. Using this structure, Leung proves SIDER-2 has a 3rd-order divided-error form matching ordinary quadratic interpolation. Each recursive step raises the order by one, giving error of order h to the n plus 1 for every fixed order n at least 2.
arxiv-2606-12933:
Yi and colleagues build a micromagnetic model with bidirectional magneto-thermal coupling for spin caloritronics, the field linking spin transport with heat flow, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard models couple the 2 only one way: thermal fluctuations drive magnetisation dynamics, but the feedback of magnetic dissipation onto the thermal reservoir is missed. That shortcut misses energy flowing back from the magnet into its own heat bath.

The new framework joins the stochastic Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation, the standard model of magnetisation dynamics, with a generalised heat transfer equation, treating local temperature as a dynamic variable. Damping-induced dissipation and stochastic work feed back into the thermal bath as localised heat sources, closing the loop. Using Ito stochastic calculus, the authors prove exactly that the coupled system strictly obeys the first law of thermodynamics and recovers on its own the correct Boltzmann statistics at equilibrium.
arxiv-2606-13033:
Holmberg proposes selective mask propagation, a multi-object tracking algorithm that calls a video object segmentation model only on the frames where a cheap base tracker is uncertain, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Segmentation models preserve identity through hard frames but cost far more compute and memory if run everywhere.

The method dispatches from the base tracker to the segmentation model only on windows where an assignment-uncertainty signal fires. The base tracker's output is modified only when the segmentation model makes a confident prediction contradicting the base assignment; weak or inconclusive predictions preserve the base output. The approach is training-free and treats both components as black boxes, so a better segmentation model can be swapped in later. On SportsMOT, where identity preservation drives sports analytics, the SAM 3 variant with track association achieves state-of-the-art performance on the benchmark with a HOTA score of 86.8.
arxiv-2606-13133:
Baba and colleagues develop a learning-augmented approximation algorithm for makespan minimisation on unrelated machines, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In this scheduling problem, each job has a distinct processing time on each machine, and the goal is to assign jobs to minimise the maximum machine load. The classical polynomial-time guarantee is a 2-approximation, and beating a factor of 3 halves is NP-hard.

Using predictions of the placements of heavy jobs, the core guess a classical algorithm would need to search over, the authors achieve a polynomial-time approximation with factor 1 plus epsilon. That holds when predictions are accurate. The guarantee weakens smoothly as prediction error grows, falling back to the worst-case 2-approximation rather than crashing. The design targets the 3 learning-augmented desiderata: consistency when predictions are right, smoothness as they worsen, and robustness in the worst case.
arxiv-2606-13533:
Xuxin Zhang and colleagues present OneRetrieval in this 2026 arXiv paper, a proposal to unify search retrieval. Platforms serve hundreds of millions of items through retrieval branches: sparse keyword matching, dense semantic search, and collaborative filtering from user behaviour. Each branch has weaknesses, and merging their results is hand-tuned with little optimisation. Generative retrieval raises the prospect of replacing the stage with one editable model. The authors argue unification is blocked by more than accuracy: the inverted-index branch converts poorly yet survives because it is nearly the only channel for injecting listed items.

An editable generative model absorbs that function, so items can be inserted without retraining. The paper analyses what each branch contributes and what a unified model must preserve. The stakes are high: retrieval decides which fraction of the catalogue a ranking model sees, so its weaknesses cap the quality of the search experience.
arxiv-2606-14033:
Lu, Shan, and Wang characterize a basic class of algebraic objects by an ordering test. Monomial ideals are sets of monomial multiples in a ring of polynomials; projective dimension measures the length of their simplest resolution. Their 2026 arXiv paper proves an ideal has projective dimension one exactly when its minimal generators can be ordered so each successive colon ideal is principal, generated by one element. The test equals the monomial Hilbert-Burch lemma.

A colon ideal collects everything that multiplies a new generator back into the earlier ones, so principality is a strong simplicity condition. The proof leans on a known fact: such resolutions are supported on tree graphs. The authors then turn to powers. Any squarefree ideal of projective dimension one with a linear resolution has all its powers admitting linear quotients, a well-behaved ordering. A partial grouping follows.
arxiv-2606-14133:
Grebenkov studies a population breeding only on a sphere's surface, whose members wander away and may never return. Particles diffuse outside the sphere and replicate on it at a set catalytic rate. In three dimensions and up, diffusion is transient: particles escape for good, pitting breeding against loss. His 2026 arXiv paper exploits rotational symmetry and the explicit single-particle propagator to compute the full statistics of population size, not just its mean.

Three regimes emerge, set by the rate against a critical value of one over the sphere's radius. Below it, the population settles to explicit steady-state limits. At criticality, moments grow as power laws in time. Above it, growth is exponential, its rate the diffusion constant times the squared excess over threshold. In every regime the size probabilities approach steady limits; he obtains the limiting distribution explicitly. Higher moments follow recursively from the first.
arxiv-2606-14233:
Ferrari and colleagues test whether language models can spot disguised Android code by reading it, no handcrafted rules required. Developers disguise code to hinder reverse engineering, but the same tricks blunt static analysis and safety scanners. Existing detectors rely on engineered features or task-specific training that may not generalize. Their 2026 arXiv paper is a large-scale study of off-the-shelf language models detecting such disguise by semantic reasoning over Smali, Android's assembly-like code.

Evaluation spans a controlled benchmark, one app obfuscated with multiple techniques, and real-world Google Play apps, varying prompt design, model choice, and thresholds across open-weight and proprietary models. The models effectively detected disguised apps and identified the techniques used, with no dedicated training or signatures. Closed models performed strongest, beating traditional SAST-based detectors. The authors plan to study such disguise in malware, and whether models can also undo it.
arxiv-2606-14433:
Pałucki and colleagues release Kine2Go in a 2026 arXiv paper for robot learning research. Their subject is the Unitree Go2, a popular four-legged robot used in locomotion, navigation, and control studies. Learning methods such as imitation and reinforcement learning need demonstration data recording body motion plus the exact motor commands applied.

Collecting that data is slow and needs complex pipelines, so the team built one and shared the result. Their pipeline converts motion from other four-legged robots into Go2 format, trains control policies by reinforcement learning to follow each motion, then records robust, slightly perturbed movement data from those policies. The dataset holds eight hundred gait trajectories drawn from forty distinct policies, giving researchers ready-made training material for new Go2 controllers.
arxiv-2606-14533:
Tembine warns that a standard data reduction method can hide catastrophic risks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Principal component analysis compresses data by keeping the directions of greatest variance. Tembine proves a risk shadow exists: the method can preserve over ninety-nine point nine nine nine nine percent of total variance while completely erasing every signal about rare, high-impact failures.

When that happens, even the best possible classifier built on the compressed data degenerates into a constant predictor that never raises an alarm. The root cause is a mismatch between maximizing variance and staying aware of tail risk. He proposes two fixes, Expectile PCA and Tail-Preserving PCA, which reweight the covariance toward high-impact events. Theory shows the first strictly beats standard PCA at retaining rare-event information, and tests on synthetic data and credit card fraud detection support the claims.
arxiv-2606-14633:
Toll, Ghosh, and Srivastav speed up an event generator in a 2026 arXiv paper. The tool is Sartre. It mocks up rare collisions for two planned colliders. In these events a proton or nucleus stays whole instead of breaking apart. Sartre first works out interaction strengths and stores them in lookup tables. Fast event runs then read from those tables.

Making the tables was the slow step. It took a few CPU-years for each process pairing. Rapid swings in the math also caused glitches in the numbers. The new method speeds table making by three to four orders of magnitude. Any process's tables can now be built in a few hours. The glitches are gone as well. The team gives fresh forecasts for both planned colliders. They cover electron-proton and electron-nucleus runs.
arxiv-2606-14733:
Csipes and Vaško compute new data for a boundary conformal field theory in a 2026 arXiv paper. The O(N) model with a boundary, a BCFT, describes critical systems with an edge, like magnets at a surface. They work in the large N expansion across bulk dimensions between two and four, focusing on ordinary boundary conditions while noting the methods generalize.

They study three bulk two-point functions, expanding them in conformal partial waves whose coefficient functions encode the theory's data. The authors prove conjectures about boundary spectral functions from earlier work and reproduce a known bulk expansion as a check. Their expansion of the field-field correlator's partner function is new and yields the leading large N value of a previously unknown operator product coefficient, plus a mixing coefficient matching a nineteen-nineties result. Infinitely many further constraints appear but resist disentangling because operator mixing grows with degeneracy.
arxiv-2606-14933:
Jones and co-authors test starting points for a quantum chemistry algorithm in a 2026 arXiv paper. The algorithm is sample-based quantum diagonalization, run inside a quantum-centric supercomputing workflow. Its circuit uses the local unitary cluster Jastrow ansatz. An ansatz is a parameterized trial wavefunction. How its parameters are initialized could plausibly matter a lot.

Six initialization strategies were compared, from physics-based CCSD and MP2 starts to data-driven, zeroes, and random starts. Twelve molecular systems and three basis sets were tested. Amplitude errors against the CCSD start spanned many orders of magnitude. Yet final energies were largely insensitive to that spread. Most starts landed within chemical accuracy, about one point six milli-Hartree, of the reference. Random starts matched CCSD across all basis sets. Zeroes starts, though closest to CCSD, gave the worst energies. Configuration recovery, not initialization, drives accuracy.
arxiv-2606-15333:
Pang and coauthors speed up reinforcement learning based unlearning for language models in a 2026 machine learning paper.
