Unlearning teaches a model to refuse questions about content it should forget. The RL approach RULE samples rollouts from forget, retain, and boundary prompts. Easy prompts converge fast and then waste computation with gradients. Hard boundary prompts keep failing, yet their rollouts get discarded after one use. The authors' ReRULE stores those hard cases in a replay buffer for reuse.

Importance-sampled off-policy updates then train on the hard cases alongside ones. Theory gives ReRULE a tighter convergence bound on hard cases than on-policy training. On the MUSE-Books benchmark, retain quality rose from about forty-six to fifty-six. The training time stayed between five and eleven percent across benchmarks. Gains shrank on the TOFU benchmark, as the theory predicts. Replay helps most when hard and easy cases differ.
arxiv-2606-15633:
Loveland and colleagues diagnose in 2026 why language models stumble on graph reasoning, tracing the problem to how graphs are fed in as text. A text-attributed graph must be linearized into a sequence, and graph neighbours can land far apart in it. The team shows rotary position embeddings then impose bandwidth-dependent decay, suppressing attention between such neighbours.

That mechanism reframes the fix: not better prompts or bigger models, but correcting the attention misalignment itself. Their remedy, GaLA, is a lightweight inference-time tweak that biases the model toward graph-adjacent nodes while keeping the model's habits intact. Across benchmarks, GaLA improves node classification with negligible overhead, on semi-synthetic and real-world data alike. No retraining or architectural change is needed. Distortion from linearization turns out to be a correctable bottleneck with a geometric cause.
arxiv-2606-15833:
Kang and colleagues challenge a working assumption of knowledge-graph question answering in 2026: that a completed fact can be checked against text. Systems over incomplete graphs fill in missing edges, then verify them against retrieved passages. Using the gold deleted triples from the standard protocol, the team measures whether verifiability tracks correctness.

It largely does not. Between seventy-six and ninety-six percent of gold-correct edges have no supporting passage, even under exhaustive retrieval, since most graph facts never appear as head-tail co-mentions in text. Textual faithfulness measures provenance, not correctness. Most completed edges are also causally redundant: nearly all correct answers depend on no unsupported edge. TGComplete therefore admits edges only with provenance, abstaining otherwise. It reaches higher faithfulness and better edge precision than the baseline, with no detectable accuracy loss, at the cost of recall. For auditable systems, that trade is the point.
arxiv-2606-16433:
Özdem computes in 2026, for the first time directly, the tensor form factors of the nucleon-to-Delta transition using QCD light-cone sum rules. The transition, from the spin one-half nucleon to the spin three-half Delta, is a basic probe of hadron structure. Its tensor current matrix element decomposes into four form factors. Symmetry constraints from Lorentz covariance, Hermiticity, parity, and time reversal, plus the Rarita-Schwinger conditions, fix that parametrization.

The channel's natural parity and spin content force a trailing gamma-5 factor, as in the gravitational case. Using nucleon distribution amplitudes of several twists, Özdem evaluates the four form factors in the spacelike range from 1 to 10 GeV squared, for two sets of input parameters. Multipole fits extrapolate them to the static limit. A flavor decomposition into up- and down-quark parts shows three qualitatively distinct patterns across the four factors, including down-quark dominance in some.
arxiv-2606-16833:
Harju leads an international team measuring oxygen in a protostellar clump in a 2026 astronomy paper. In dense interstellar gas, oxygen hides mainly in atomic oxygen, hydroxide, water and carbon monoxide. Their far-infrared lines cool the shock-heated gas around newborn stars, but the split of oxygen among the carriers was poorly known.

Observations target OMC-2 FIR4, a clump in Orion holding several young stellar objects. Airborne and ground-based telescopes, plus archival satellite spectra, capture lines from all four carriers and their rare variants. An expanding spherical shell model reproduces the line shapes well, separating broad, medium and narrow velocity parts. In the broad, shocked part, atomic oxygen dominates: it outweighs water by a factor of hundreds and hydroxide by a similar margin. The pattern fits gas behind dissociative shocks that flood their surroundings with ultraviolet light, a concrete check on shock chemistry models.
arxiv-2606-16933:
Wibowo and colleagues build a taxonomy of distributional shift in reinforcement learning in a 2026 paper. Agents degrade when the world they meet differs from the world they trained in. The literature describes that mismatch in scattered ways, as train-test gaps or as non-stationarity, without a shared account of where shifts come from.

The authors move the dataset-shift idea from supervised learning into the agent-environment loop. Casting the setting as a partially observable decision process, they split the interaction into parts: state distribution, observation process, policy, reward, transition dynamics and the boundary where time regimes change. A shift is then classified by which part's generating mechanism changed. That causal-origin view unifies shifts seen in generalization tests with shifts unfolding inside non-stationary deployments. The taxonomy aims to tell researchers what kind of shift they face before choosing a remedy.
arxiv-2606-17233:
Lu and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper, published in Engineering Structures, on quantifying uncertainty in engineering models. A single costly simulation often yields several outputs at once under the same input settings. Surrogate models can cheapen that cost, but one fixed sample design may serve some outputs badly, since outputs differ in which inputs they respond to most.

The authors extend an adaptive sampling method for polynomial chaos surrogates to many outputs at once. New samples are picked from a pool by their local share of output variance, balanced against exploring untested parts of the input space. A normalised variance rule joins information across all outputs rather than sampling each output alone. On several engineering test problems, the method beat fixed Latin Hypercube designs in both accuracy and stability of the estimates.
arxiv-2606-18033:
Philippy and colleagues test whether English is really the best language to teach from when a model learns by example, in a 2026 paper. In cross-lingual in-context learning, a model sees a few worked examples in one language and answers in another. Folks often assume the lessons of supervised fine-tuning, where data volume and language similarity rule, carry straight over, and English is picked by default.

The team ran a broad study across seven tasks, six models, and a typologically varied language set, and also probed language confusion, where the model answers in the wrong tongue. Fine-tuning expectations often failed in the few-shot regime. Some lower-resource languages made surprisingly strong teachers, and the authors offer fresh heuristics for picking source languages. They caution the findings should guide prompt choice, not justify shrinking any language's presence in pretraining data.
arxiv-2606-18333:
Van Weeren and colleagues lay out how to calibrate the sharpest low-frequency radio images ever attempted in polarized light, in a 2026 astronomy paper. Low-frequency polarimetry probes magnetic fields in distant sources and in the medium between, plus magnetospheric emission from pulsars, active stars, brown dwarfs, and planets. The LOFAR array's baselines stretch up to two thousand kilometers, enough for sub-arcsecond resolution, yet polarized work has so far stalled near six arcseconds because beam depolarization grows at fine scales.

Their strategy applies full-Jones corrections to the international stations using an unpolarized calibrator inside the field itself, tracking leakage terms that drift with time and frequency. A bright polarized in-field source then aligns separate epochs in Faraday depth, letting corrections land on the visibility data before imaging. The payoff is deeper images and cleaner deconvolution than the older habit of stacking epoch images after the fact.
arxiv-2606-18433:
Elhachemy studies a class of reflected mean-field stochastic differential equations driven by both Brownian motion and sudden jumps from an independent Poisson process, in a 2026 probability paper. Such equations model random processes whose evolution depends on their own overall distribution and which are pushed back when they reach a boundary.

He proves that solutions exist and are unique, and derives estimates for their moments. As an application, the results yield a Feynman-Kac formula, a probabilistic representation, for the solution of an integral partial differential equation with Neumann boundary conditions. Those conditions prescribe behavior at the edge of the domain. The work extends mean-field theory, used widely in finance, games, and control, to reflected equations with jumps. It gives later researchers a firm existence result to build models on, rather than an equation merely written down and assumed to behave.
arxiv-2606-18533:
Day and Mutchnik ask what it really means for a property of mathematical theories to count as a patterning property, in a 2026 mathematical logic paper. Properties like the order property and the tree property, defined by patterns a formula can or cannot realize, are the backbone of classification theory's map of tame and wild theories.

The authors compare proposals from the literature for making the notion precise. These include definability by patterns of consistency and inconsistency, definability by interpreting partial orders, and a higher-arity strengthening they introduce. Their first main result settles open questions by showing the strict order properties are definable in both senses for all levels from four upward, completing the classification of the classical properties. Their second result uses classical theorems to show that, in countably categorical theories, implications between the positively definable properties must already appear at a simple quantifier level.
arxiv-2606-18733:
Zhao and the team propose building coding-agent training tasks by looking ahead to what real software projects will need next, not replaying their past, in a 2026 software engineering paper. Benchmarks assembled from GitHub issues and pull requests risk contaminating judging, since the same material flows through pretraining and model selection. Fully synthetic tasks, meanwhile, drift away from what repositories require.

Their method SWE-Future freezes a repository at a snapshot date. It uses only prior evidence to forecast families of future work: feature implementations, bugfixes, and refactors. It then checks those forecasts against later pull requests used for scoring. In an eighty-repository retrospective study, the forecaster's predicted families matched future work at above fifty-eight percent, under the semantic metric. Those families then conditioned the synthesis of a two-hundred-task dataset across sixty-one repositories, grounded in snapshots, not the validating pull requests.
arxiv-2606-18933:
Perets and colleagues present a 2026 method for choosing which features to measure next when labels are scarce. Active feature acquisition picks tests or traits one by one until a class call can be made. Classic methods need large labeled sets to learn what to pick. Large language models hold broad domain knowledge, but they are poor step-by-step planners, so the team splits the two jobs apart.

The model is asked only for facts it can give well, namely single-feature shifts and pairwise links that define a Markov random field. A maximum-entropy step then fills a gap, since the model tends to report what sets classes apart rather than each class alone. Tests use a real cohort of patients with inflammatory bowel disease, where diagnosis is hard and patients vary a lot. The method beats the language model alone, with the largest gains on the hardest patients.
arxiv-2606-19133:
Petersen and colleagues show in 2026 that equivariant graph neural networks improve optical spectra prediction for materials screening. Fast spectra prediction helps screen materials for solar cells and other optoelectronic uses. Surrogate models are often trained on lower-level theory, or use rotation-invariant scalar features that limit geometric expressiveness. Equivariant networks respect rotations by construction, so they can carry richer shape information into the prediction than scalar features allow a model to use.

The team adapts the GotenNet architecture to spectra prediction and tests it on several datasets. One key set holds more than ten thousand structures with spectra computed at the random phase approximation level, a high standard. The model beats the current state of the art overall. Gains are largest in the low-energy range most relevant to thin-film optics, and on the static permittivity. Better surrogates mean cheaper screening of candidates.
arxiv-2606-19333:
Paliwal and colleagues present Do as I Do in 2026, an algorithm that turns everyday human videos into dexterous robot handling data. How to generate such data at scale, especially for multi-fingered hands, is a core robotics bottleneck. Learning from human videos is a likely answer, since such videos are abundant. Estimating hand-object contact from single-camera RGB video and crossing the human-to-robot body gap have blocked that path until now.

The algorithm reconstructs hand-object interactions from egocentric and exocentric in-the-wild videos. It then retargets those estimates into action sequences a dexterous robot hand can execute. Experiments on ground-truth datasets and on online video clips show the method beats prior state of the art at estimating contacts and extracting paths. The authors distill a practical playbook for teams collecting human data, covering which videos yield usable robot training signal.
arxiv-2606-20233:
Tianyi Xiang, Mingming He, Li Ma, and Jing Liao composite green-screen characters into new video scenes with the physical and lighting realism film work demands. Their 2026 paper names two coupled effects earlier methods miss. Character-to-environment interaction covers how a person and props affect the scene. Environment-to-character harmonization covers how the scene's light should fall on the person. Props the character touches make both effects harder.

Their end-to-end video diffusion framework models both directions jointly. A tri-mask-guided design with RGB-D joint denoising keeps character, props, and scene consistent. A prior-driven data pipeline builds high-quality relighting pairs without expensive rendering. A reference-conditioned mechanism adds control over the new scene and allows precise prop replacement. In experiments, the framework beat existing methods at cinematic-quality dynamic compositing.
arxiv-2606-20333:
Xijia Tao and eight colleagues compress written agent skills into a handful of learned vectors. Their 2026 paper starts from how agent skills are usually deployed: as natural-language Markdown files encoding answer policies, evidence habits, and procedures. Those files are readable and portable, but a frozen model must reinterpret the whole text for every task instance. SoftSkill instead turns a skill into a compact continuous context object, refined by a trainable soft delta while the base model stays frozen, and deploys it as a latent behavioral prior.

Trained by next-token prediction, a length-32 SoftSkill prefix on Qwen3.5-4B beat no-skill prompting by 8.3 points on SearchQA, 42.1 on LiveMath, and 1.3 on DocVQA. Against SkillOpt, it gained 5.2 points on SearchQA and 12.5 on LiveMath, while replacing thousands of Markdown tokens with a few virtual ones. Agentic execution proved a harder boundary case, where trajectory imitation gave useful but incomplete signal.
arxiv-2606-20533:
Jun Zhan, Xianxin Wu, and Jiangping Hu map the magnetic order of high-Tc multilayer nickelates. Their 2026 paper investigates bilayer and trilayer systems inside a multi-orbital itinerant framework. These nickelates superconduct at high temperature, and their magnetism is a prime suspect in the mechanism.

For the bilayer, Hartree-Fock calculations slightly favor double-stripe order, but the single-stripe state's excitation spectrum matches recent RIXS and neutron scattering experiments well. Its spectrum shows an anisotropic low-energy cone and isotropic high-energy excitations. The authors also identify mirror-even optical interlayer modes whose energies match the mirror-odd modes. For the trilayer, both mode families appear as well. Magnetic excitations give experiment a fingerprint to test pairing theories against.
arxiv-2606-20633:
Yongchao Wang and three colleagues present a framework in 2026 for factoring the polynomial X to the power n minus one over integer residue rings. Those rings, written Z with a prime power modulus, matter in coding and cryptography, but older methods scale badly. Polynomial Hensel lifting updates global cofactors, while direct Newton methods need Jacobian inverses that grow costly because zero divisors appear, elements that multiply to zero without being zero.

Wang and colleagues offer three fixes. An ideal derivation principle finds coefficients as roots of a Dickson ideal. A cofactor-free lift raises one seed factor using a cached inverse. A dual-track step rebuilds the rest. Complete factorization supports cyclic codes and related algebra.
arxiv-2606-21033:
Jiancheng Zhao and four colleagues propose MoECodec in 2026, an image compression system built for both human viewing and machine tasks. Compression for machines should serve many downstream vision tasks in one codec. Task-specific designs raise cost and deployment burden. Transfer-based fixes stay external and ad hoc. Both lines share a flaw: static computation, where similar transforms are applied to all tokens regardless of content.

Image regions differ in semantic importance and complexity. MoECodec replaces feed-forward layers with token-wise mixture-of-experts layers. Computation then adapts per token, conditioned on content and task goal. A stable routing strategy joins expert-choice routing with spatial smoothness regularization. Experts specialize while neighboring regions stay coherent. Dynamic compute could cut bitrate and model size for machine vision pipelines, where most image content is never seen by a human eye.
arxiv-2606-21333:
Hugo Attali and Rachid El Jouhri introduce Ramanujan Propagation in 2026, a rewiring strategy that helps graph neural networks pass messages over long distances. Such networks learn by exchanging information along edges, but narrow bottlenecks cause over-squashing, where signals from huge neighborhoods are crushed into fixed-size vectors and lost. Ramanujan graphs, highly connected yet sparse, offer a structural fix.

The authors first prove that well-chosen Ramanujan graphs guarantee non-negative resistance curvature, a property tied to smooth information flow. Their algorithm then builds a rewired graph that adds these expander links while keeping the original local connectivity. In experiments the method outperforms nine leading rewiring techniques. The work casts such graphs as a principled prior for scalable message passing on graph data of many kinds.
arxiv-2606-21533:
Pedro Poblete and six colleagues simulate in 2026 what happens when a mature planet-forming disk, already hosting planets, is disturbed by its environment. Disks grow up in crowded stellar neighborhoods, so passing stars and infalling gas are common intrusions. The team ran three-dimensional Phantom simulations of a disk with two planets locked in a 2:1 resonance, adding dust species that push back on the gas. They then subjected it to a cloudlet infall and a stellar flyby.

Infall added mass and angular momentum and stirred the dust into eccentric, multi-ring patterns. The flyby clipped the disk's edge, compacted the dust, and drove episodic inward drift of grains. Both events excited eccentricity and rerouted how solids reach the planets, changing their growth and composition. Environmental scars, the authors conclude, can persist into later stages.
arxiv-2606-21733:
L. Naudin, C. Paillard, L. Bellaiche, L. Calmels, and R. Arras use first-principles calculations in 2026 to ask how point defects interact with domain walls in wurtzite aluminium nitride. Alloyed AlN is a rising ferroelectric: huge remanent polarization, wide band gap, silicon-compatible growth. Its switching mechanism is still debated, and its coercive fields are uncomfortably large. Vertical inversion domain walls are where switching happens, so what defects do there matters.

Every defect studied turns out energetically happier at or near the wall than in the bulk. Depending on the defect, the effect on wall motion cuts both ways: some should ease the wall's displacement during switching, others hinder it. The authors close by weighing which defects are plausible culprits for leakage currents and degraded ferroelectric behavior, a practical guide for cleaning up a promising memory material.
arxiv-2606-22033:
Villia and colleagues propose, in 2026, a framework for explaining graph neural network predictions through counterfactuals: the smallest changes to a graph that would flip the model's answer. Good counterfactuals for graphs may need edges both removed and added, and generic, efficient methods for producing them have been lacking. Their completion-aware approach attacks the missing-edge side of the problem directly.

The pipeline joins progress in factual explainability, which finds the subgraph behind a prediction, with missing-edge prediction models borrowed from link prediction research. That combination aims at explanations that are higher quality, more robust, and easier to read than earlier attempts. The authors test the framework on real-world and synthetic graph classification benchmarks, covering both binary and multi-label tasks. Across diverse metrics, the analysis shows advances over state-of-the-art baselines, supporting completion-aware search as a practical route to counterfactual explanations for graph models.
arxiv-2606-22133:
Hayami studies, in 2026, field-tunable quadruple-Q magnetic states driven by frustration in momentum space. Multiple-Q states superpose several ordering wave vectors, producing complex spin crystals and tilted textures even in magnets with inversion symmetry. The model is a minimal spin model on a square lattice with four symmetry-related wave vectors, bilinear and biquadratic couplings, and an out-of-plane field.

Using simulated annealing, Hayami maps the field-dependent phase diagram. It shows successive transitions among single-Q, double-Q, and several distinct quadruple-Q states as the field varies. States sharing the same wave vectors still differ in phase locking, amplitude distribution, and tilt. Those differences produce distinct real-space textures and scalar spin chirality patterns. The results identify momentum-space frustration plus biquadratic coupling as an efficient route to diverse higher-order spin textures.
arxiv-2606-22233:
Riva and colleagues present, in 2026, their open-quantum-system account of how electrons and phonons move together out of equilibrium when the dynamics are non-Markovian. Electron-phonon coupling drives polaron formation and sets the lifetimes of driven excitations, but memory effects make the motion hard to model. Their approach rests on four equations of motion, coupled to each other and closed as a set.

Those four govern, in turn, the electronic one-body density matrix, a density matrix for phonons, the coherent phonon, and correlations linking electrons with phonons. Memory emerges naturally from the coupling between the electron and correlation equations, beyond the Markovian limit. In the right limits the theory recovers known Fan-Migdal, random-phase, Ehrenfest, Lindblad, and Boltzmann results without storing two-time correlators. Benchmarked against the exact Holstein dimer solution under a strong drive, the dynamics capture spectral broadening from dissipation, plus energy conservation.
arxiv-2606-22533:
Alexander Gnedin studies symmetry notions for random partitions in this 2026 probability paper. A partition splits a set into blocks, and random ones model clustering in data. The strongest symmetry is exchangeability, which says relabelling the elements changes nothing. Weaker notions relax that demand in different ways.

Recent results show that on the natural numbers some relaxed symmetries still force the strongest one. Gnedin revises the hierarchy for finite sets, framing the question through the shape of all distributions obeying each symmetry. Single-orbit exchangeable partitions stay extreme among both spreadable and partly exchangeable stationary laws. The first split appears at five elements, where non-exchangeable extreme cases occur and the shapes stop being simplices. Representation theorems in the style of De Finetti link the finite structures to their infinite limits.
arxiv-2606-22633:
Weihong Qi and Kristina Lerman study how language models handle being contradicted in this 2026 paper. Models often face inputs that clash with their prior outputs, through user pushback, retrieved documents, or search results. The authors frame the response as cognitive dissonance resolution, borrowed from psychology.

They test persuasion attempts that differ on two fronts, source authority and evidence quality, across twelve health-science claims of differing epistemic status. A model can be persuaded, backfire away from the evidence, or stay immune. Their Trust Elasticity measure captures how readily a model yields to conflicting evidence. Across four models the measure varied substantially, yet clearly false claims drew near-zero elasticity everywhere. On two open-weight models, the variation tracked internal uncertainty signals, confidence miscalibration in one and uncertainty change in the other. The authors suggest future interventions should target that internal uncertainty directly.
arxiv-2606-22733:
Ivan Romualdo de Oliveira, Vinícius N. A. Lula-Rocha, and Moises Rojas test a nanoscale heat machine in this 2026 physics paper. The working substance is a single electron confined in a double quantum dot, in a magnetic field with Rashba spin-orbit coupling. It runs a quasistatic Otto cycle.

The controls are the Zeeman splitting, interdot tunneling, and the Rashba coupling, which induces spin flips. They compute heat exchanged, work extracted, and efficiency across parameters and reservoir temperatures. The Rashba interaction acts as a switch among four regimes: heat engine, refrigerator, heater, and accelerator. A numerical scan finds the best operating points. Top efficiencies occur near the largest temperature gradient explored and approach the Carnot bound. Peak work sits in a different parameter region. A clear trade-off results between efficiency and work, governed by how the controls deform the spectrum.
arxiv-2606-23233:
Sheng Lu, Lizhen Qu, and Iryna Gurevych set out a human-guided way to draft peer reviews in a 2026 paper. Tools that write whole reviews on their own could speed up science. But full automation sits badly where someone must answer for the verdict. Their mode keeps the human in charge. The reviewer gives a claim about the work's worth. The system then expands that claim into draft review comments. The work runs in a loop of draft, check, and refine. A user study records how reviewers use such a tool.

Lu and colleagues face two practical problems: how to score the process at scale, and how to trim the set of draft comments. They build ways to simulate the loop for large-scale scoring. A wrapper from statistics, which gives coverage guarantees, proved well suited to balancing set size against target coverage.
arxiv-2606-23533:
Power outage reports in the United States must follow strict machine-readable formats, and Phan and colleagues address that constraint in a 2026 language technology paper. Utilities need reports that software can read reliably, in formats such as JSON or XML, while also meeting energy regulators' rules for content and structure. General language models write fluent text easily, yet they often break such exact formatting demands.

The authors fine-tune an open seven-billion-parameter model with a new training loss that rewards both wording similarity and matching structure tags. Their system, POTracker, beats five other fine-tuning methods and one rule-based converter on one thousand outage reports, raising overall accuracy by up to fifty-one percent and reaching about eighty-six percent structural accuracy. Human experts also rate the reference reports used for training at just over four on a five-point quality scale.
arxiv-2606-23833:
Arzoumanidis, Johannsen, Middendorf, Eicker, and Dehbi reconstruct eight decades of Earth's water storage over South America using a graph neural network, in a 2026 paper on satellite geodesy and machine learning. Terrestrial water storage sums snow, soil moisture, surface water, and groundwater. The GRACE satellites measure it directly, but only since 2002, too short a record for many climate questions. Earlier reconstructions worked cell by cell.

The team adapts a graph neural network built for traffic forecasting, letting grid cells exchange information through links that mix geographic closeness with lagged climate correlations. Trained on weather data back to 1940, the model reproduces the satellite record with a basin mean correlation of about zero point nine four and almost no bias. It recovers the fingerprints of major El Niño and La Niña events. Against established methods it stays competitive while using far fewer inputs.
arxiv-2606-23933:
Naghdi and Baheri rescue old data for decision algorithms operating in environments that drift, instead of throwing the data away, in a 2026 paper on machine learning. Contextual bandits choose among options, learning from rewards while balancing exploration against exploitation. When markets drift, historical rewards become biased, and standard fixes discard them. Flow-Corrected Thompson Sampling instead transports past rewards to the present through an explicit drift model, weighting each by how trustworthy the transport is.

One template covers steady drift, periodic cycles, and recurring regime switches, reusing phase matched or regime matched data with closed form updates. Across five controlled studies and a portfolio benchmark with overlapping drifts, the method beats forgetting based baselines, most where the drift has recurring structure.
arxiv-2606-25033:
Mathieu Gross, Stephen Henrich, and Fotis Koutroulis generalise ultrarelativistic freeze out, a dark matter mechanism, to general reheating histories. Standard WIMP dark matter only dilutes after it freezes out. Ultrarelativistic freeze out is stranger: after the freeze out, the particles can pass through freeze in phases, driven by how the temperature evolves as the universe reheats. The authors rewrite it for a temperature profile, making the ultraviolet and infrared regimes explicit.

A scenario follows. Gravitational particle production at the start of reheating seeds an early radiation bath. That bath reshapes the freeze out parameter space, an effect named GUFO. For a quadratic interaction, matter like reheating accommodates dark matter masses up to ten million GeV, since thermalisation demands become less stringent. Radiation like reheating also stays compatible with the mechanism. The early universe's thermal history decides which masses and couplings can yield the observed dark matter.
arxiv-2606-25133:
The initial state of the inflationary universe need not be the standard vacuum. Ali Nayeri builds an explicit model of superoscillatory initial states. Interference inside a band limited wavefunctional creates a localised excitation with a rapidly winding phase. The construction starts from a simple boundary term on the initial time surface.

The construction yields the excitation coefficients and a primordial spectrum with an oscillatory feature fixed by the model's own parameters, not pasted in by hand. Projected onto the cosmic microwave background, the feature is strongly smeared by transfer functions; full calculations show a simple Gaussian estimate overshoots the peak by roughly a factor of three. Planck data give an indicative bound on the feature strength near the first acoustic peak. Galaxy clustering, Nayeri argues, is the sharper probe, since it keeps the full oscillatory structure the microwave background washes out.
arxiv-2606-25233:
Quantum entanglement is usually tracked through spin, but the Higgs boson carries another quantum label, weak isospin, that can play the role of a qubit. Hyun Min Lee and Rojalin Padhan work out in 2026 how entanglement shows up when Higgs bosons scatter. Their setting is effective field theory, the framework that packages unknown heavy physics into extra interaction terms. They treat the outgoing state as split between momentum and isospin, and compute entropy and concurrence measures from the scattering amplitudes.

Entanglement entropy grows with energy faster than in the plain Standard Model. Interference between terms cancels part of that growth at medium energies. The effect is strongest when the new physics comes from a massive graviton. Under stated assumptions the pair finds exact conditions where entanglement vanishes, and links that suppression to known positivity bounds on the theory's coefficients.
arxiv-2606-25433:
Positronium is an atom made of an electron and its antimatter twin; add a second electron and it becomes the positronium ion, a three body system held together by electric force. Nishat Ul Sani computes a rare weak decay of that ion in 2026, where it sheds an electron plus a neutrino and antineutrino pair. The calculation swaps the photon of a known radiative decay for a virtual Z boson, then works through every spin arrangement of the particles involved explicitly.

Handling the process as an effective two body transition gave a decay rate matching the standard spin summation machinery of quantum field theory, a useful cross check. The resulting branching ratio lands near that of a comparable weak decay of ortho positronium. Weak processes in this light exotic atom had drawn little attention beside its bright annihilation channels.
arxiv-2606-25633:
Some operators on spaces of analytic functions mix three actions at once: moving the input, multiplying by a fixed function, and taking a derivative. Aakriti Sharma studies this product type family in 2026 on the weighted Bergman space of the unit disk. There, functions are measured with a weight that grows near the rim. The question is which of these operators are complex symmetric, meaning they mirror themselves under a chosen conjugation, a kind of generalised flip.

The flip here is built from a weighted composition operator. Sharma finds exact conditions on the symbols that define the operator for this symmetry to hold. Two stricter classes are then pinned down on their own terms: the self adjoint operators and the normal ones. The results extend what was known for plain composition and multiplication operators to the harder case where a derivative joins in.
arxiv-2606-25833:
The highest energy photons in the universe would betray the accelerators that forge cosmic rays, but they are vanishingly rare. A team including Takashi Sako examines in 2026 whether hybrid radio detectors could catch them. Air showers from inclined particles spray radio emission. Antennas pick it up for photon and cosmic ray arrivals alike. Cosmic ray showers are rich in muons, though. Scintillator panels fire on them, and stay quiet for photons. Two combined observables, the radio signal's strength and the scintillators' total energy deposit, separate the two families.

The case study dresses the idea in real hardware: a layout matching GRANDProto300, the prototype of a giant planned radio array, with Telescope Array style scintillators added. Such a hybrid could set competitive upper limits on the photon flux, between roughly zero point three and three exaelectronvolts.
arxiv-2606-26033:
Peio Ardaiz Galé, Marcos Escartín Ferrer, and Conchita Martínez Pérez study Sigma invariants of groups through group actions. Sigma invariants measure finiteness properties of a group in each direction of its character sphere. Geometric group theory often reads such properties off an action on a contractible space. The team assumes a strong extra feature: a contractible strong fundamental domain for the action, plus well-behaved cell stabilizers.

Dichotomy is the theorem. Under those assumptions, the homological Sigma invariants, in the character sphere, are either empty or dense. Nothing in between can occur. The result was known for right-angled Artin groups and for pure symmetric automorphisms of free groups. New applications extend it further. The pure symmetric automorphism groups of right-angled Artin groups now fall under the same rule. The strong fundamental domain condition emerges as the engine behind a pattern seen across many group families.
arxiv-2606-26133:
Heinrich Hartmann reframes a classic calculus formula as a statement about composing Taylor polynomials. The Faà di Bruno formulas give higher derivatives of a composite function. Their classical forms drown in sums over partitions and indices. Hartmann works between Banach spaces with truncated Taylor polynomials, the reduced kind with the constant term removed. One identity carries the whole theory: the Taylor polynomial of a composite is the truncated composite of the two Taylor polynomials.

Proof needs no combinatorics at all. A plain estimate of the Peano remainder does the work. Expanding the identity hands back the classical formulas for free. Polarization yields the partition version, and coefficient extraction yields the multi-index version. The functorial heart of Taylor approximation is thus split cleanly from bookkeeping. A general higher-order product rule falls out as an application. The note offers a cleaner route into a famously messy formula.
arxiv-2606-26233:
Gabriel Gouraud, Miha Srdinšek, and Xavier Waintal propose grading a quantum annealer on its process, not just its answers. Annealers inch a system toward the ground state of a hard problem. Scorekeeping usually counts solved problems against classical rivals, a brittle yardstick. Their metric mirrors the fidelity-per-gate of circuit machines. It is a single accuracy number for the annealer's equation of state: how faithfully the device follows its intended physics.

Simulated annealing calculations set the benchmark values. One variational Monte Carlo variant reaches accuracies where annealer and thermal twin become indistinguishable. It scales to a hundred million atoms on one processor. A Green function Monte Carlo variant runs tighter still, on a hundred thousand atoms. Both outrun today's Rydberg atom annealing platforms in precision and size by wide margins. Future hardware must beat those classical marks to claim a working quantum process.
arxiv-2606-26333:
Behnam Gheshlaghi, Bahador Rashidi, and Shahin Atakishiyev carve a learning environment into a mesh so value can travel faster. Reinforcement learning in big, sparse-reward worlds suffers slow credit assignment. A reward found far away trickles back one step at a time. Mesh-RL borrows domain decomposition from finite element computing. The environment splits into overlapping subgrids, and temporal-difference updates are kept consistent across the shared borders.

Local learning and global coherence coexist under that rule. Rewards, the Bellman operator, and the reward function itself stay untouched; no planner is added. Hazard-filled grid worlds of varying shapes test the idea across Q-learning, SARSA, and Dyna-Q. Convergence speed, total reward, and stability all improve. Finer meshes keep exploration alive and rush value to distant states. Even Dyna-Q, which already plans internally, gains extra ground from the structured split.
arxiv-2606-26533:
Thoshitha Gamage and Lasanthi Gamage present OSC2Runner, a simulation framework for testing self-driving vehicles. Scenario-based testing replays scripted traffic situations in a simulator. The field still relies on an older scenario language, OpenSCENARIO 1.x. The newer 2.x version has a richer language but no native execution support. Adapting old interpreters introduces timing drift and unnatural motion jumps.

OSC2Runner instead compiles 2.x scenarios directly for the CARLA simulator. A translator working in several passes turns scenarios into behaviour trees, structured plans of actions. Those trees map onto CARLA's basic commands without static trajectory playback. Validation used highly concurrent adversarial cases. The framework showed tick-by-tick repeat runs with identical results. Trigger points were checked exactly, and actors stayed in step within a tenth of a second. The authors aim at rigorous testing back ends for co-simulation and hardware-in-the-loop work.
arxiv-2606-26833:
Aneesa Ahmad and four colleagues compute how tightly methanol and its relatives stick to interstellar ice. Complex organic molecules form and survive on icy dust grains in cold space clouds. Methanol is a key example, made on the ice and later released into gas. How long it stays depends on its binding energy to the ice surface. The team calculated those energies with quantum chemistry methods.

Their platform evaluates binding on clusters of amorphous water ice, the disordered ice coating real grains. Molecules that form hydrogen bonds stuck hard, with wide spreads of binding energies reflecting the ice's uneven surface. Water, methanol, and formic acid behaved this way. Weakly interacting gases such as carbon monoxide and methane stuck far more loosely. The values feed models of when molecules leave grains for the gas.
arxiv-2606-26933:
Corban Villa, Sohee Kim, Austin Chu, Alon Shakevsky, and Raluca Ada Popa present Chai, an AI system that hunts cryptographic misuse bugs. Misusing a crypto library, such as checking certificates wrongly, is a dangerous and common flaw class. Unlike memory bugs, it has no instrument that flags violations automatically. Chai instead mines natural signals: disagreements between implementations of the same standard.

Differential testing compares libraries against each other. Chai uses AI to judge which discrepancies are real security issues. It then catalogues each flaw once, at library level, and traces it through a dependency graph to the applications downstream. One audit thus covers many codebases. Across certificate, token, and login libraries, Chai found a previously unknown critical flaw in an SSL library used on billions of devices, plus bugs behind a major browser.
arxiv-2606-27033:
Karimov, Izmailov, and Nandi test a rival theory of gravity using a subtle timing effect on Earth. The theory, scalar-tensor-vector gravity, adds extra fields to gravity so galaxies can be explained without unseen dark matter. Its strength is set by a single adjustable number. Earlier work allowed that number a fairly wide range depending on the mass of the central object. The Sagnac effect, a timing gap for light beams circling in opposite ways around a spinning body, offers a sharp local test.

Using updated timing wobble limits from satellite navigation signals, the authors bound how large the gravity correction to that timing gap could be. If the wobble stays below the predicted correction, the adjustable number must be extremely tiny. Their bound shrinks the allowed range far below earlier estimates drawn from galaxy and cluster studies.
arxiv-2606-27333:
Guan and colleagues argue that the IKKT matrix model's renormalisation flow is secretly type IIB string theory in disguise. For D-instantons, pointlike branes with no space or time of their own, that map looked out of reach. Two tools are combined: heavy strings are integrated out in a Coulomb branch vacuum, alongside the matrix flow of Brézin and Zinn-Justin. In 2026, their letter works toward holography in zero dimensions.

The leading correction to the IKKT action ties to the string coupling. Its dependence on Coulomb branch position matches between matrix theory and supergravity. Applying the matrix flow to the partition function makes the coupling run with matrix rank. That running reproduces how the axio-dilaton field varies in the supergravity picture. Zero-dimensional holography thus gains a concrete computational foothold. Matrix models and string backgrounds tell the same running story.
arxiv-2606-27433:
van de Venn and colleagues ask how spacetime torsion and nonmetricity, features general relativity sets to zero, would tug on neighbouring free-falling probes. In metric-affine gravity the connection is independent of the metric, so both features can exist. The team derives a projected deviation equation extending the standard one to this geometry. Applied to nearby paths in the weak-field, slow-motion limit, the tidal acceleration splits cleanly. In 2026, a Newtonian part stands with linear post-Riemannian corrections.

Splitting torsion and nonmetricity into Lorentz components exposes their separate signatures in the tidal tensor. Some can be told apart; others remain entangled, and the paper maps which. Future tidal measurements could be turned into benchmark bounds on the post-Riemannian terms. Tidal physics becomes a hunting ground for geometry beyond Einstein's.
arxiv-2606-27533:
Vahanwala records a clean equivalence: continuous-time Markov chains and linear dynamical systems are the same thing at different sizes. A Markov chain's states evolve by fixed transition rules; a linear dynamical system evolves a vector by repeated linear maps or a generator. For discrete time the correspondence was known. This short note proves the continuous-time analogue. In 2026, the dynamics of a chain with any number of states is governed by a linear system of dimension at most one less.

Conversely, any linear dynamical system of a given dimension embeds into a Markov chain with one more state. Probability distributions and stochastic generators translate exactly between the two languages. Results proved for one formalism therefore transfer to the other without loss. The note is brief by design: a dictionary entry, not a treatise. Two literatures gain a shared border crossing.
arxiv-2606-27633:
Fisher information measures how much data reveal about an unknown parameter. It anchors the famous Cramér–Rao bound in statistics and quantum metrology. Xin-Zhu Liu and six colleagues extend that foundation in 2026. They define a new measure based on higher-order Fisher information. Higher order means using more derivatives of the estimating function. The measure leads to a generalised uncertainty relation for estimation.

The new relation extends the Cramér–Rao bound. The authors apply it to quantum phase estimation with a single qubit. They compare their bounds with established hierarchical bounds. A photonic experiment then tests the framework in practice. Simulations show the bound behaving like Fisher information for large samples. It converges to the quantum Cramér–Rao bound for repeated independent data. The authors argue the method handles complex distributions well. That is where the classic bound is weakest.
arxiv-2606-27733:
Bash scripts run system administration and deployment pipelines everywhere. Bad scripts threaten stability and security directly. Language models that write Bash act as black boxes, though. They explain nothing, and their code often carries robustness flaws. Lei Yu and nine colleagues propose BashCoder-R1 in 2026 to fix both problems. The framework aims at robust and explainable Bash generation.

Training runs in three stages. Continual pretraining specialises the base model on Bash idioms. Long chain-of-thought fine-tuning uses thousands of expert-validated reasoning-and-code samples. A reinforcement stage then rewards syntax correctness, robustness checked by shellcheck, and format correctness. Evaluation used BashBench, a new benchmark of 952 real-world automation tasks. Results were strong on both single-line commands and multi-line scripts. Full success reached about ninety percent on single-line tasks. It reached about seventy-three percent on multi-line scripts, beating state-of-the-art baselines.
arxiv-2606-28033:
Meta-analyses often compare two diagnostic tests. Standard models assume the tests are independent given true disease status. That assumption is often unrealistic. Breaking it biases accuracy estimates for tests used together. Vera Hudak and three colleagues propose a Bayesian model in 2026 that handles the dependence head-on. Dependence is captured through study-specific log-odds ratios. Studies that lack joint data on both tests are still included.

The model extends to varied study designs. Studies without a gold standard are included. So are studies with partial verification, where not everyone gets the reference test. Imperfect reference standards are not assumed error-free. Two example meta-analyses show the framework in action. The computations stay stable, unlike some earlier dependence models. No imputation step is needed first. The examples show a clear warning. Ignoring strong dependence yields biased joint accuracy estimates. Modelling it directly is the safer course.
arxiv-2606-28233:
Julie Veschambre and nine colleagues, including Jean Dalibard and Raphael Lopes, measured the Feshbach spectrum of dysprosium, a strongly magnetic atom used in ultracold gas experiments. Feshbach resonances are magnetic field values where atoms interact especially strongly, and their pattern of energy levels had been linked to quantum chaos.

Veschambre's team calibrated the spectrum precisely and measured the magnetic moments of bound states tied to more than eighty resonances. Level patterns turned out to be mixed rather than uniformly chaotic. Resonances in the middle of the magnetic-moment spread showed strong level repulsion, a hallmark of chaos. Those near the lower edge stayed close to the pattern expected for orderly, non-interacting levels, revealing hidden regular structure.
arxiv-2606-28433:
Matthew Vandergrift, Esraa Elelimy, and Martha White wrote this position paper to separate two jobs that reinforcement learning researchers often blur. Simulators can be the thing being solved, or a stand-in used to learn about decision-making in the real world. Chasing a high simulator score quietly converts the second job into the first.

Vandergrift and colleagues argue the two uses differ in what an agent may do with the simulator, which algorithms suit, and which metrics mean anything. Conflating them produces misleading conclusions about deployed learning, a risk they document with examples and simple experiments. Solving simulators is worthwhile research, they stress, but it answers a different question. Their call is for authors to state plainly which use they intend, so readers can judge the evidence correctly.
arxiv-2606-28533:
Zikun Cui, Renzhi Wu, Junjie Yang, and ten colleagues at Meta rethink how recommenders read a user's history. Leading systems feed the whole history as one chronological sequence, mimicking a sentence. But a user's past is not a sentence: it is a tangle of unrelated interests, and forcing them through one attention budget lets noise pollute the signal of real intent.

Their Constructive Multi-Sequence Learning instead builds several coherent sequences in latent space. A learnable construction module disentangles the history into pure thematic strands, and linear attention models those strands efficiently at scale. The pollution problem fades because unrelated behaviors no longer compete inside a single stream. The system is not a prototype: it has been deployed across ranking and retrieval on four major Meta surfaces, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-28833:
Xu, Miroszewski, Zeng and Zhao tackle the cost of quantum kernel estimation, where each matrix entry must be sampled with few circuit runs. Their setting is Gaussian process regression, a flexible prediction method whose uncertainty and likelihood depend on the whole kernel, so errors bite harder than in classification. They derive three closed-form measures of how sensitive the result is to each pair of points.

Those sensitivities feed a Neyman-style rule, which spends the sampling budget where it cuts variance most. A uniform coverage floor stops the budget piling onto a few entries when early estimates are noisy. On benchmarks and controlled studies, the allocator cut test error by ten to twenty-one percent over uniform allocation at moderate budgets. Gains transferred to several downstream tasks and genuine quantum kernels on suitable data. They vanished on ordinary features forced into a quantum kernel.
arxiv-2606-28933:
Tan, Li, Wang, Chen and Zhang present FinInvest-GTCN, a model that helps venture capital investors judge start-ups with numbers rather than recommendations. Venture decisions mix many data sources, unstable time series and high stakes with little data, and investors need predictions they can explain. The architecture combines a graph encoder for the investment ecosystem's network of links, a temporal module that fuses patterns at several time scales, and a causal decision head that outputs risk-adjusted predictions.

Each prediction comes with explanations of which factors drove it. A meta-causal strategy fine-tunes the model for new, data-poor sectors, keeping updates aligned with plausible causal structure. On private venture datasets, the model lowered its main risk-adjusted error from just over three to about two and a half. A simulated portfolio's total return rose by nearly a fifth. Ablations confirmed each component mattered.
arxiv-2606-29033:
Dietz presents a prototype tool that splits the work of judging AI outputs between humans and language models in a way meant to keep the human signal real. Reliable evaluation needs human judgment, but common setups either anchor experts, nudging them to rubber-stamp model verdicts, or leave them unsupported in noisy labelling tasks where answers vary wildly.

Her design gives each side the job it does best. Humans identify nuggets, the pieces of information that matter for a good answer. Language models then handle the high-volume work of matching those nuggets against many system outputs. The workflow runs in three phases, and the exported nugget banks plug into automated judges, scaling the human decisions across large test sets. Dietz describes the key design choices behind the split. The aim is genuine oversight: accountability stays with the humans, while the tedious matching is automated.
arxiv-2606-29133:
Sun and Chan borrow a quantum computing idea, shadow tomography, to make classical simulations of quantum states cheaper. Shadow tomography estimates many properties of a quantum state from few samples. Tensor network states are a classical way to represent quantum systems, but estimating their observables can still demand many costly contractions, especially for long-range interactions.

Adapted to tensor network contraction rules, shadow-inspired estimators improve sample scaling by factors growing with system size, up to its cube, depending on task and type. The team develop strategies for spin and fermionic systems. For expectation values of long-range Hamiltonians, they reach essentially constant scaling at fixed error, the best possible up to small factors. Shadow estimators also give more stable gradients than standard Monte Carlo ones. Demonstrations include a long-range Heisenberg model and a chemistry Hamiltonian.
arxiv-2606-29433:
Choi and Baccelli build a math framework for low Earth orbit satellite networks that mix several altitudes and orbit types. Such Walker constellations, named patterns where satellites spread evenly over circular orbits, have tangled spatial and temporal structure. Older tools struggle to predict downlink performance, meaning how well a ground receiver can hear a satellite.

Their orbit-aware stochastic geometry model treats the whole network as a dynamical system. The state follows from a starting setup plus the rotation speeds of the satellites and of Earth itself. When those speeds are rationally commensurable, the system repeats periodically. When they are rationally independent, the system is ergodic, so long time averages match averages under a fixed spread. The authors derive the nearest-satellite distance spread for a typical receiver at a given latitude. They also obtain coverage probability for the signal quality measure SINR and the ergodic throughput of the downlink.
arxiv-2606-29533:
Rivkin and five colleagues at Cornell study forecasting for many downstream agents whose objectives are unknown. Each agent best-responds to the forecaster's predictions. The goal is one forecaster that guarantees sublinear swap regret, a measure of how much each agent wishes it had swapped its choices, for all agents at once.

For two-dimensional outcome spaces, they give a polynomial-time algorithm with a much better swap regret bound than previously known. It also avoids the exponential runtime of earlier algorithms in that setting. The algorithm extends to other low-dimensional environments, keeping the same time scaling while dimension raises other exponents. For arbitrary dimension, a second algorithm guarantees a bound that improves on prior results, which had worse time dependence and needed extra behavioural assumptions. The forecaster must know an upper bound on each agent's action count, and runtime in high dimensions stays long.
arxiv-2606-29933:
Samanta, Holtzman, and West argue that alignment research should borrow ideas from physics, in particular phase transitions, to describe how language models change during post-training. Their case study uses crystallization, the freezing of a liquid into a crystal.

For tasks such as random number generation, they describe three phases. The pretrained model is a high-entropy liquid, with many sampling behaviours reachable by prompting. Supervised finetuning nucleates behaviour onto a single seed distribution already present in the model. Reinforcement learning then settles that collapsed distribution, shifting probability among mostly the same options. The authors propose simple metrics for spotting the transitions and validate the picture across a range of random tasks.
arxiv-2606-30233:
Mozib Bin Awal and Prabwal Phukon explore the phase structure of Euler-Heisenberg black holes beyond their critical points. Black hole thermodynamics mirrors ordinary matter, with phases and transitions. These anti-de Sitter black holes turn out to have unusual structure. Their supercritical region hides more than the usual single Widom line. The authors use Lee-Yang phase transition theory to map it.

The system admits two distinct critical points, with four thermodynamic phases. A degenerate higher-order point appears where the two criticalities merge. Extending thermodynamics into complex values locates the Lee-Yang singularities. Their distribution shapes the complex phase diagrams the authors construct. At the degenerate point, a Widom line emerges without any coexistence curve. It acts as a stability boundary in the supercritical regime. Elsewhere, two distinct Widom lines can coexist. The formalism also reproduces single-critical and non-critical cases correctly.
arxiv-2606-30333:
Debraj Banerjee, Santanu Mahapatra, and Kunal Chaudhury turn a family of hard discrete problems into smooth ones without creating fake solutions. The generalized Ising problem covers MAX-CUT, number partitioning, and independent set. Such problems have huge discrete search spaces. Continuous relaxations smooth them for gradient methods. Ordinary relaxations add spurious local minima that mislead solvers. Their relaxation provably adds none.

The key notion is the one-flip local minimum of the Ising problem. Their polynomial relaxation mirrors exactly those minima, no more, no fewer. A landscape equivalence theorem proves the one-to-one match. Solving the discrete problem becomes finding minima of a smooth function. Standard gradient optimizers like ADAM then apply directly. Benchmarks include spin-glass models, MAX-CUT, and number partitioning. Performance stays strong across all of these hard cases. The method also scales to large problem sizes.
arxiv-2606-30533:
Dilina Dehigama and six colleagues keep cloud services fast under spiky load without paying for idle machines. Online services face load swings within single seconds. Strict service-level objectives demand low response times throughout. Operators usually over-provision, wasting money and utilization. Autoscalers and serverless platforms each fail one side of the trade-off. Spandana splits the problem into two decoupled parts.

A lightweight controller sits beside each application virtual machine. It steers every arriving request between the machine and serverless functions. Requests that can meet the objective stay local. The rest overflow to a stock serverless layer like Lambda. A separate allocator sizes the machine pool for cost. It weighs machine cost, serverless cost, and traffic volatility together. Evaluation shows strict objective adherence throughout the tests. Processor utilization reaches seventy-six to eighty-six percent. Costs fall five to forty-four percent against three strong baselines.
arxiv-2606-30633:
Xiaosheng Huang and fourteen colleagues present GIGA-Lens 2.0, a major upgrade of their strong-lensing modelling framework. Strong lensing occurs when a massive galaxy bends light from a background source, and fitting such systems with full Bayesian inference, a method that maps all plausible parameter values, is computationally heavy. The first GIGA-Lens ran on graphics processors; the new version spreads one model across many GPU nodes at once.

The team ran the framework on 128 nodes holding 512 top-end A100 graphics cards. They demonstrate the speed gains on one hundred simulated lens systems. They also model one real system, a DESI survey lens, end to end. Other changes to the framework brought further performance gains beyond the multi-node scaling. The work targets the growing samples of lenses that upcoming surveys will deliver, where slow per-system fitting would bottleneck dark-matter and cosmology studies.
arxiv-2606-30733:
Marah Brinjikji and twenty-eight colleagues report a young brown dwarf companion found by the C-BASS survey, which snapshots B and A type stars looking for companions. The host, HIP 17453 A, is a chemically unusual A-type star about eighty-one parsecs away. Ten years of high-resolution imaging with the Keck II telescope showed a faint neighbour moving together with the star, marking it as a true companion rather than a background object.

Follow-up spectroscopy with the Gemini-North telescope classified the companion as an L2-type brown dwarf, give or take one subtype. The system is roughly two hundred eighty million years old. Matching its spectrum to evolutionary models gave a temperature near nineteen hundred fifty kelvin and a mass near fifty-three Jupiter masses, only about two point four percent of the host's mass.
arxiv-2606-30833:
G. Vietri and six colleagues lay out SUNRISE-3D, a survey of active galaxies at cosmic noon, the peak era of galaxy growth. The science case asks how outflows driven by a central black hole heat or sweep up gas across a galaxy, and whether that feedback throttles star formation. Answering needs a sample with spectroscopic coverage of emission lines.

The coming SHARP instrument on the Extremely Large Telescope will map outflow properties across each galaxy in three dimensions. From those maps the team can derive outflow mass and energy rates pixel by pixel, without assuming the outflow's geometry. Pairing outflow maps with star-formation maps of the same galaxies allows a local comparison. The target sample spans redshifts one point five to two point five and stellar masses from dwarf scale to the massive end. The authors aim to reveal how feedback regulates star formation at small scales.
arxiv-2606-30933:
Liqiang Hou simplifies the design of fuel-optimal, low-thrust spacecraft transfers under realistic dynamics. Indirect methods need costate equations. Those are built from partial derivatives of the motion, step-by-step rates of change. Deriving them gets painful once fine effects enter the model. Examples are solar radiation pressure, the Sun's slight bulge, Jupiter's gravity and relativistic corrections. Hou rewrites the costate equations using state transition matrix sensitivity. The complex effects are then treated as black boxes. No explicit derivative derivations are needed.

A standard optimiser solves for the best costates and transfer parameters. The method matched the conventional approach on a classic Earth-Mars case. Hou then applied it to a high-fidelity Earth-Mars transfer. A multiple-revolution Earth-Venus transfer followed.
arxiv-2606-31033:
Kazuaki Furumai, Shuichiro Haruta, Kazunori Matsumoto and Daisuke Kamisaka hunt hallucinations inside retrieval-augmented answers one token at a time. In long RAG outputs, invented content usually sits in local spans, not spread through the whole answer, so whole-response verdicts are too coarse. Their method, CORTEX, rests on a simple intuition: tokens truly grounded in the retrieved documents should be shaped by those documents more than invented tokens are. CORTEX compares the model's internal representations with and without the documents in context.

It also tracks how document influence propagates through earlier tokens, which cuts false alarms on tokens whose evidence was already absorbed. A smoothing step then exploits how hallucination labels tend to persist across neighbouring tokens. On two RAG benchmarks and three language models, CORTEX substantially improved token-level detection, with each component contributing gains.
arxiv-2606-31333:
Cenci and two colleagues propose using quantum light to adjust DNA at a single chosen spot. Hydrogen bonds hold the DNA bases together, and changing them locally could aid genetic work without cutting the molecule. Their tool is a plasmonic cavity, a tiny metal structure that traps light and couples it strongly to matter.

Calculations with quantum electrodynamics coupled cluster methods, a high-grade simulation of light and electrons together, show small but clear local changes in how bases interact. The changes appear under standard strong coupling and touch nothing else, and they should grow if ultra-strong coupling can be reached. Unlike collective coupling schemes that act on many molecules at once, this route aims at one local site, opening a path to optical DNA handling.
arxiv-2606-31433:
Pelosi and five colleagues present a new model for forecasting galactic cosmic rays over long spans. The solar wind and the Sun's magnetic field change the flow of cosmic rays, so the flux near Earth rises and falls with solar activity. Good forecasts matter for radiation risk in space and for cosmic-ray science itself.

Their model solves a one-dimensional form of the Parker transport equation. It includes diffusion, solar-wind advection, and adiabatic energy loss. Solar proxies, delayed in time, are tied to the model parameters through filtering and cross-correlation. The model was checked against flux data from PAMELA, AMS-02, and ACE. The checks span particle species, energy ranges, and phases of the solar cycle. The model matches the data well within its stated uncertainty.
arxiv-2606-31533:
Bali and Aydin present MV-GEL, a system that finds named geometric parts on 3D meshes from plain language. Picking out an edge, a flat face, or a curved surface by description is basic to computer-aided design, robotics, and simulation. Vision language models can ground phrases in images, but a mesh looks different from every viewpoint, and the target may hide in any single view.

Their GELviews module ranks viewpoints by how interpretable the queried entity looks from each, guided by the prompt itself. A vision language segmentation backbone then marks the entity in the chosen views, and geometry-aware ray casting lifts those masks onto the mesh. The method needs only the mesh, works across CAD sources, and improves results up to about 1.7-fold in their tests.
arxiv-2606-31633:
Zhu and three colleagues ask why some magnetic skyrmions, tiny whirling spin patterns eyed for future memory devices, survive heat better than standard theory predicts. Micromagnetic models tie stability to skyrmion size or exchange stiffness, the strength of coupling between spins. The team tests whether long-range frustration, competing couplings acting over longer distances, can raise stability on its own.

Mapping the smooth model onto an atom-level spin lattice, the authors find that skyrmions with identical micromagnetic settings can face very different collapse barriers, depending on the underlying atomic exchange. The gap comes from saddle point textures, strongly twisted spin patterns that feel the long-range frustration. An optimization framework then predicts that this frustration can double the collapse barrier under realistic conditions, without growing the skyrmion.
arxiv-2606-31733:
Fontana proposes a conceptual model that gives transposable elements, stretches of DNA that can move and copy themselves, a central role in ageing. The model builds on the Evolvable Soma Theory of Ageing, which treats development as a lifelong process rather than a phase that ends early. In that view, genes keep driving change in body cells across the whole lifespan.

Transposable elements, Fontana argues, helped gene regulatory networks grow by supplying binding sites where transcription factors attach. Cells keep these elements tightly repressed early in life through epigenetic marks, chemical tags that silence DNA. Age-linked loosening of that control then adds random noise to gene activity and feeds age-related decline. The model thus links one mechanism to both regulatory innovation and later deterioration, and it sets out predictions that still need testing.
arxiv-2606-31833:
Huang and seven colleagues present BRIDGE, a compiler and hardware fabric that keeps data atoms still on neutral-atom quantum computers. Most compilers shuttle qubit atoms during execution to create connectivity. Each move adds handoff errors, motional heating and atom-loss risk, which steadily erode fidelity in deep circuits.

BRIDGE instead interleaves non-encoding buffer atoms into a fixed two-dimensional array. Long-range links pass through buffer relays using tuned Rydberg channels, while a lazy-move compiler adds motion only at selected hotspots. On a 22-circuit matched suite under one shared error model, total fidelity runs about ten times higher than ZAP and sixteen times higher than Enola. Data-atom movement falls from thousands of events to zero.
arxiv-2608-00033:
Belikova and co-authors present SIRIN, a toolkit for spotting contextual hallucinations. Such errors are fluent replies with no support in the given evidence. They appear in retrieval-augmented and memory-grounded systems. SIRIN joins three detector styles under one interface. It also tests if a query can be answered before generation.

The three styles are representation probing, uncertainty estimates, and judge-style checks. A web UI shows scores, marks unsupported spans, and compares detectors side by side. It works at both reply level and span level, in white-box and black-box modes. A plug-in design lets new detectors join easily. The team shows SIRIN on detection, answerability, and memory faithfulness gates. Code is public for reuse.
arxiv-2608-00233:
Gadeyne, Vishnoi, and Ruchon push optical vortices into the extreme ultraviolet. These pulses, called STOVs, carry transverse orbital angular momentum. That momentum is debated despite their clear topological charge. Past work sat at standard optical wavelengths. Their route uses high-harmonic generation to upconvert the pulses.

A custom pulse shaper makes infrared STOVs of charges plus or minus one and two. Focused in argon, they drive harmonics that form rings in the far field. Ring size shifts with harmonic order and input charge as expected. That pattern points to XUV vortices of charge equal to order times input charge. Focus position gives control over their making. XUV STOVs open new probes for ultrafast spectroscopy.
beach-american-practice-vol1-1833:
Wooster Beach founded the eclectic school, and Volume I of The American Practice of Medicine, from 1833, is its founding textbook. Beach broke with the harsh dosing of his day, the bleeding and calomel of heroic medicine. In its place he taught botanic practice, cures drawn from plants.

The first volume lays out his system and the diseases it treats, with plant remedies at the center. Beach wrote for American doctors facing American conditions, and his school trained thousands. Readers today find in these pages the opening shot of a medical movement that rivaled regular practice for decades.
beach-american-practice-vol2-1833:
Volume II of Wooster Beach's American Practice of Medicine, from 1833, carries his founding textbook forward into daily work. Beach built the eclectic school on a simple protest: regular doctors bled too much and dosed too hard with harsh drugs. Plant remedies, chosen with care, form his answer across these pages.

The volume works through more diseases and their botanic treatments in Beach's plain teaching style. Students at his school learned practice from books like this one, then carried the method west with them. As the middle third of the set, it shows eclectic medicine finding its feet as a system of its own.
beach-american-practice-vol3-1833:
With Volume III in 1833, Beach's American Practice of Medicine stands complete in three volumes. Wooster Beach wrote as the head of a young school, the eclectics, who picked the best remedies from every system. Botanic cures stand at the center of his teaching from first page to last.

The closing volume rounds out the course of diseases and treatments the set set out to cover. Together the three gave American country doctors a full practice guide that trusted plants over the lancet. The set marks the start of organized eclectic medicine in the United States.
cia-0000009033:
Major C. J. Ramsay's name anchors photo comparison case number 10,407, reported in April 1969. Specialists compared images that might show the missing major against his known photographs. The case number and name together show the system's two faces: bureaucracy and one officer's fate.

Results in such cases were phrased with care, since families and commanders read them closely. A finding could direct searchers, or tell them a lead was dead. Ramsay's file was one among thousands, yet each got the same measured treatment. The paper preserves that treatment at the level of a single named man.
cia-0000009833:
American prisoners were moved through Cambodia, a January 1967 CIA report tracks. Captives taken in South Vietnam's border regions were often marched west into Cambodian sanctuaries. From there, some were sent north; others stayed in border camps.

Movement through a third country hid prisoners from the war's official geography. Officials in Washington had to follow men across a border their own maps treated as closed. Each transit report added a segment to a captive's route. This file records the Cambodian segment early in the war, when the cross-border sanctuary system was still taking clear form.
cia-0000009933:
Twelve American prisoners of war were sighted in the Rung Dau jungle, in Dinh Quan district, a November 1971 report states. Dinh Quan lies northeast of Saigon, in country where rubber plantations meet jungle. Twelve men together formed one of the larger southern groups on record.

A dozen prisoners in one place implied a camp, a march, or a gathering for transfer. Each possibility pointed officials toward different checks. Group size also shaped the report's credibility: big claims drew big scrutiny. This file preserves the sighting as claimed, a large number in a jungle district, in the southern record.
cia-0000011833:
In November 1966 the CIA forecast what would follow a United Nations resolution to end a mandate. The resolution of that season concerned South West Africa, which the General Assembly voted to take back from South Africa. Pretoria had ruled the territory since the First World War and refused to give it up.

The paper weighs the likely results: legal fights, pressure on South Africa, and unrest inside the territory. It also judges how far the world body could push a defiant member state. The forecast opens the long struggle that ended with Namibia's freedom in 1990.
cia-0000013233:
Procedures for detaining and executing prisoners in Tuyen Duc province fill a CIA paper from January 1971. The procedures come from the Viet Cong system in that southern highlands province. Their order is chilling to read today. Capture, judgment, and death are reduced to plain steps. They were applied in that province to men whose names the file may never fully recover for their families.

The paper sets the system's darkest rules down without flinching. That plainness makes it hard to read, and necessary to keep. For readers, it is the southern system's lethal logic, preserved so the record cannot be softened later.
cia-0000013833:
A captured American pilot is the subject of a CIA item from November 1966. The item preserves the incident's bare facts in the file's plain form. Somewhere over Vietnam an airman's war ended in a parachute and a capture. The item records what was known at the time. It notes the loss and the place as reported. It also marks the man's entry into the prison system this file maps in such detail.

The bare facts were all the files had, and they were entered with care. Every name in the accounting began as a note like this one. For readers, the item is the capture note in its plainest form.
cia-0000015333: A letter to Joseph Karth from Lawrence Houston fills a CIA file dated May 5, 1961. It concerns Karth's inquiry of June 30, the title notes. Karth sat in Congress, where saucer questions carried a member's weight. Houston, the agency's top lawyer, handled such mail at the very top level. Houston's letter to Karth is held in the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000015433: Photo experts examined UFO photography for the CIA in a record dated January 5, 1967. Their craft was reading grain, light, and angle to judge whether a picture showed a real object. Most saucer photos of the era were too blurred to prove much either way. A formal analysis entry shows the agency still testing camera claims with lab methods in the late sixties.
cia-0000022333: The Powers trial depicts the pilot as a criminal, in a Soviet line kept by a CIA record dated in 1969. Nine years after the trial, Moscow's telling still cast Powers as a common offender. The agency filed the echo, not just the event. Long afterlife in enemy print was part of how a Cold War case kept its shape.
