Durante and co-authors dissect eye melanoma one cell at a time, revealing unexpected complexity. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Uveal melanoma spreads aggressively and, unlike skin melanoma, rarely answers to checkpoint immunotherapy. Its tumour neighbourhood held many unknowns.

The team profiled 59,915 cells from eight primary tumours and three metastases. Cancer cells showed new subclonal variety and shifting gene states. Immune cells proved diverse too. Killer T cells there mainly carried the checkpoint LAG3, not the usual drug targets PD1 or CTLA4. Those T cells had multiplied clonally, proof they could mount a response. One slow-growing liver metastasis brimmed with antibody-making plasma cells. LAG3, the authors propose, is a fresh candidate for checkpoint blockade in high-risk patients.
europmc-pmc7055033:
Prince and co-authors compare self-reported sitting time with device measurements in the International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. Sitting too much raises the risk of chronic disease and early death. Studies often ask people how long they sit, but how far those answers stray from what accelerometers record was unclear. The team ran a systematic review and meta-analysis to settle the gap.

The review included 185 studies. For general validity, 123 studies with 55,199 participants supplied comparable pairs of self-report and device data. On average people underreported their sedentary time by about 105 minutes a day, roughly 1.74 hours, compared with devices. Workplace sitting showed the opposite bias, reported about 40 minutes higher than devices measured. Single-question measures performed worst. The message for researchers is blunt: questionnaires alone distort the true picture of how much adults sit.
europmc-pmc7069833:
Clark and co-authors test a search translation tool in the Journal of the Medical Library Association. Systematic reviewers must search several databases, and each database speaks a slightly different search dialect. Translating a search string by hand is slow and error-prone. The Polyglot Search Translator was built to automate that chore, and the authors ran a randomised trial to check it.

Twenty participants each translated database search strings, five with the tool's help and five by hand. Sixteen participants finished the set, producing 174 assisted and 192 manual translations. Assisted work averaged 31 minutes per string against 45 minutes manually, a saving of 14 minutes, or about 32 percent. Errors also fell, from a mean of 14.6 per translation to 8.6. The authors conclude the translator truly speeds the work without trading away accuracy, a practical gain for evidence synthesis teams.
europmc-pmc7105733:
Vendrik and co-authors review fecal microbiota transplantation for neurological disorders, in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology. The treatment moves gut microbes from a healthy donor into a patient. It already works well for repeated Clostridioides difficile infections. The authors ask what it might do for the brain.

From 541 reports, 34 met their rules. Trials in autism showed gains in gut and behavioral symptoms. For multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's disease, animal studies and a few case reports looked hopeful. Evidence for epilepsy, stroke, and Alzheimer's disease stayed thin or animal-only. One stroke study even found higher deaths after transplant. The authors call for large blinded trials. Readers get a sober map of promise and proof in gut-brain medicine.
europmc-pmc7139933:
Ting, Yang, and Tsai review the role of interleukin-6, an immune signalling molecule, in depressive disorder, in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Major depression is a leading psychiatric illness worldwide and raises suicide risk. Blood and brain levels of IL-6 are often raised in patients, especially when depression accompanies physical illness.

Higher IL-6 activity may drive depression by switching on the body's stress hormone axis or by disturbing neurotransmitter metabolism. IL-6 levels also relate to prognosis and to how well treatment works, though genetic studies disagree. The authors suggest pairing IL-6 with other immune markers to define biological subtypes of depression, then matching patients to treatments, from standard antidepressants to agents that dial IL-6 down.
europmc-pmc7151633:
Saginala and co-authors review the epidemiology of bladder cancer, in Medical Sciences. Bladder cancer accounts for 3% of cancer diagnoses worldwide and ranks sixth in the United States. Ninety percent of cases are diagnosed at age 55 or older, and men are affected four times as often as women.

Tobacco smoking is the dominant risk factor, behind 50 to 65% of cases. Workplace and environmental toxins add an estimated 20%, and a parasitic infection, schistosomiasis, drives cases in parts of Africa and the Middle East. Average five-year survival in the United States is 77%, but only 5% once the disease has spread. With 81% of cases tied to known risks, the authors stress prevention.
europmc-pmc7170333:
Lin and co-authors review immune changes in viral pneumonia and propose a hypothesis for how SARS-CoV-2 makes people ill, in Emerging Microbes and Infections. Most patients have mild disease, but some deteriorate into multi-organ failure and die. No specific antiviral existed, and the disease process was unclear.

Drawing on SARS, MERS, and other viral pneumonias, they piece together the immune pattern: lymphocyte loss, inflammatory surges, and clotting problems. For severe patients they recommend two treatments for consideration: high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin, pooled donor antibodies, and low-molecular-weight heparin against clotting. The paper is openly a hypothesis built from neighbouring diseases, offered while direct evidence was still gathering.
europmc-pmc7212533:
Hua reviews advances in oral drug delivery aimed at specific regions of the gut. The article appeared in Frontiers in Pharmacology. Swallowing medicine is the route patients prefer most. It is easy, painless, and allows self-treatment at home. Formulations can also be tuned to release in the upper or lower gut.

The gut, though, is a hard place for drugs to survive. Acid, enzymes, and poor absorption block many compounds. Hua sorts the obstacles into body factors, disease factors, and formulation factors. Disease can change how a region absorbs medicine. Particle size and coatings can steer delivery to diseased tissue. Studies sometimes disagree between animals and humans. The review helps designers match a drug to its gut target.
europmc-pmc7222033:
Pertea and Pertea present two open-source tools for working with gene annotation files. Their article appeared in F1000Research. Files in GTF and GFF formats store where genes and transcripts sit in a genome. Nearly every genome pipeline handles them. Awkward files can slow or break that work.

GffRead converts, sorts, filters, and clusters entries in such files. GffCompare checks one annotation against another and can merge them. It reports accuracy statistics at several levels, from bases to whole transcripts. Both programs are written in C++ for Linux and Mac systems. They are released under an MIT license on GitHub. The authors aim to make routine annotation chores fast and dependable.
europmc-pmc7264033:
Messner and co-authors build a fast platform for measuring proteins in blood and use it to find markers of COVID-19 severity. Their study appeared in Cell Systems. Standard protein testing is slow, which limits its use during a fast-moving pandemic. Their workflow follows an international quality standard so clinical laboratories can adopt it.

The low-cost setup handles up to 180 samples per day with precise measurements and fewer batch effects. Run on samples from early hospitalized COVID-19 patients, it found 27 potential biomarkers whose levels varied with the World Health Organization severity grade. The markers include clotting and complement factors and signals tied to interleukin 6. All protocols and software are freely available to support routine testing and new treatment ideas.
europmc-pmc7274033:
Christgen and co-authors find a protein platform that can set off three kinds of cell death at once. Their study deals with cells that die by design to stop invaders. The three paths are pyroptosis, apoptosis, and necroptosis. They were long seen as apart, but new work shows they cross and mix. The mixed form is called PANoptosis.

The team infected mouse immune cells with flu virus, a second virus, and two kinds of bacteria. The cells died with signs of all three paths at once. Cutting one death gene gave little shield. Cutting four key genes at once gave strong shield. Tests of how the proteins touch each other showed a shared platform, the PANoptosome, that runs all three paths as one.
europmc-pmc7299433:
Madhi and co-authors report a trial of vaccinating pregnant women against respiratory syncytial virus to protect their newborns. Their trial report appeared in The New England Journal of Medicine. RSV is the dominant cause of severe lower respiratory infection in infants, worst in the youngest. The randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 4,636 pregnant women across several countries, immunized between 28 and 36 weeks of pregnancy.

The vaccine was safe and raised antibodies in the mothers, which crossed to their babies. The main goal missed its strict protocol target, though vaccine efficacy against medically significant infection in the first 90 days was 39.4%. Against infection with severe low oxygen, rates were 58.8% lower. Eighty-eight women needed vaccination to prevent one significant infant case in the study's accounting.
europmc-pmc7312633:
Rayego-Mateos and co-authors review how inflammation drives diabetic nephropathy, the kidney harm that comes with diabetes. Their review notes it is the top cause of chronic kidney disease. It pushes many patients toward kidney failure. Proof from health data and lab work ties its start and growth to the body's inflammatory response.

Some inflammatory markers can flag which diabetic patients face the most kidney risk. In lab models, drugs that block set parts of the response cut protein leaks and kidney scars. Targets range from sticky molecules that draw in immune cells to the signal paths inside cells. The team maps the key players and sums up new cures aimed at them, and calls inflammation a fair target to slow kidney harm.
europmc-pmc7337733:
Huang and co-authors present a research article in National Science Review on air pollution in China. It studies the COVID-19 lockdown that followed the 2020 New Year holiday. Travel and business fell sharply, and so did many emissions. Yet heavy haze still formed in eastern China.

The team combined ground measurements with model simulations. They find that secondary pollution grew and offset much of the cut in primary emissions. Sharp drops in nitrogen oxides from transport raised ozone and night-time radical formation. That boost in the air's oxidizing power helped form fine particles. The authors argue that haze control needs a balanced plan across many pollutants. Cutting one pollutant alone can backfire, their results show.
europmc-pmc7410833:
Van Nostrand and co-authors present a large-scale map of human RNA-binding proteins in Nature, built within the ENCODE project. These proteins grip RNA and control splicing, editing, transport, stability, and translation. The team mapped where hundreds of them bind, in two human cell lines.

Five kinds of assay combine binding sites on RNA and chromatin, lab-measured binding preferences, functional effects, and each protein's location in the cell. The result is 1,223 replicated datasets covering 356 RNA-binding proteins. The authors chart the spectrum of binding across all transcripts and connect interactions to downstream processing steps. Readers get an atlas of the post-transcriptional control layer, the stage where much gene regulation actually happens.
europmc-pmc7415433:
He and co-authors review microRNAs in cancer in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. MicroRNAs are tiny non-coding RNAs, about 22 letters long, that tune gene activity. When their tuning goes wrong, cancers can follow; many microRNAs shape tumor growth, immunity, and response to sponges that soak them up.

Two decades of research have produced candidate biomarkers for cancer screening, diagnosis, and prognosis. MicroRNA-based therapies are in development across cancers, including combinations designed to work synergistically. A third theme is resistance: many microRNAs help tumors shrug off treatment, through tangled mechanisms. Understanding that web, the authors argue, can sharpen prognosis and guide clinicians. Readers get a broad progress report on very small molecules.
europmc-pmc7422733:
Srinivasan and co-authors profile microglia, the brain's own immune cells, from people who died with Alzheimer's disease. Mouse studies had shown a distinct damage-linked state in these cells. The team asked whether human microglia show that same state.

They built a method to purify cell types from frozen brain tissue for RNA sequencing. The human profile they found barely matched the mouse damage profile. Instead, the cells showed strong signs of aging plus disease-linked shifts such as raised APOE. Checks in other datasets backed the result. The gap held for Alzheimer's tissue but not for other brain diseases. The findings warn that mouse models may mislead Alzheimer's drug work.
europmc-pmc7482833:
Harrison and co-authors link prior conditions with death in United States adults with COVID-19. Records came from 24 healthcare organizations in a shared network. The cohort covered January 20 to May 26, 2020.

In all, 31,461 patients aged 18-90 years entered the study. The median age was 50 years, and chronic lung disease and diabetes were the most common listed conditions. Older age, male sex, and Black or African American identity each raised the odds of death. Heart attack history, heart failure, dementia, and lung disease also raised risk. Kidney disease, stronger liver disease, and spread cancer showed high odds as well. Which conditions mattered most shifted across age groups in the stratified results.
europmc-pmc7644933:
Hossain, Sultana and Purohit umbrella-review mental health outcomes of quarantine and isolation. These measures limit movement and social contact for people. Their mental effects needed a global evidence check.

The team searched nine major databases and more sources. From 1,364 citations, eight reviews met the criteria. Most primary studies came from high-income nations. Many were done in hospital settings at the time. Problems included depression, anxiety and psychological distress. Trauma symptoms, insomnia and fear were also common. Stigma and low self-esteem appeared in reports too. Patients, caregivers and health workers all showed burden. The authors urge stronger mental health services worldwide. Psychosocial support for high-risk groups is also urged.
europmc-pmc7657933:
Roozenbeek and co-authors survey belief in false claims about COVID-19 in five countries. Samples came from the UK, Ireland, the USA, Spain, and Mexico. The team tested how well people judged common false statements about the virus.

Belief in false claims was not widespread, but many people rated some false claims as highly reliable. People prone to false claims were less likely to follow health guidance. They were also less keen to get a vaccine or urge it on others at risk. Trust in scientists and strong number skills linked to lower risk of being misled.
europmc-pmc7661733:
Kalam and co-authors review a common but little-known group of soil bacteria. The group, Acidobacteria, turns up in nearly all soils in large numbers. Its members are hard to grow in the lab, which has slowed study of what they do.

Gene studies show these bacteria hold tools for many chemical tasks. They may drive nutrient cycles, break down plant polymers, and help plants grow. Their genes may also help them live in the zone around plant roots. The authors map what is known and point to future uses in farming and biotechnology.
europmc-pmc7668533:
Ma and co-authors test a natural compound against obesity in mice, with human data for context. The compound is spermidine, found in food, which prompts cells to recycle their parts. Obesity often comes with a leaky gut wall and shifted gut microbes. The team asked if spermidine could repair both.

Mice fed a rich diet lost weight on spermidine and handled insulin better. Their gut wall grew stronger and toxin leak fell. Gut microbe makeup changed too. Moving those microbes into other mice passed on the protection. One microbe group that rose with treatment tracked closely with the stronger gut wall.
europmc-pmc7782833:
Dobie and Skropeta review how added sialic acid on tumor cell surfaces helps cancer spread. Enzymes called sialyltransferases attach sialic acid to growing sugar chains. Many tumors make too much of these enzymes. The result is heavy sialic acid coating on 40–60% of the tumor cell surface.

That coating aids spread in several ways. It helps tumor cells dodge the immune system. It supports cell survival, invasion, and migration. The authors trace the mechanisms behind each effect. They also survey drugs in development that block sialyltransferases. Blocking sialylation is presented as a possible new anti-metastatic strategy.
europmc-pmc7815633:
Stelzle and co-authors estimate the global share of cervical cancer linked to HIV. HIV speeds the cancer-causing action of human papillomavirus. The population-level size of that link was unmeasured. The team set out to quantify it.

The authors assessed cervical cancer risk in women living with HIV. They then scaled that risk to world population data. Regional patterns matter, since HIV rates vary widely. Sub-Saharan Africa carries the heaviest HIV burden. The estimates show where prevention can do the most good. Cervical screening and HPV vaccination gain extra weight for women with HIV. The work gives planners a firm basis for joint programs.
europmc-pmc7874133:
Piret and Boivin present a review of pandemics across human history. They trace how diseases with pandemic spread have struck again and again over the centuries. Their account runs from plague and cholera to flu and the coronaviruses behind SARS and MERS.

The review explains how many pandemic diseases start in animals and reach people through farming, hunting, and trade. It covers old public health tools such as isolation, quarantine, and border control. Those tools still mattered during COVID-19, when no drugs or vaccines were ready at first. The authors also call for strong surveillance of water-borne, vector-borne, and animal-linked threats. They argue that fast tests, contact tracing, and new vaccine platforms are needed for the next pandemic.
europmc-pmc7939333:
Larsell presents a biographical sketch of Anders Adolf Retzius, the Swedish anatomist and anthropologist. The paper was read before a medical history club in Oregon in January 1923. Retzius lived from 1796 to 1860. He was born in Lund on October 13, 1796. His father held a chair of natural history at the university there. The son grew into one of Sweden's many gifts to science.

Larsell frames Sweden as a land where learning has long burned bright. Chemistry, botany, physics, and geography all owe debts to Swedish workers. Retzius mixed the old Norse urge to explore with a scholar's patience, Larsell writes. His field was the hidden structure of the human body and the variety of humankind. The sketch follows his family roots and early life. It sets up the career that made his name known across Europe.
europmc-pmc8012333:
El Ansari and Elhag map what is known about weight regain after bariatric surgery. Bariatric surgery is the most durable treatment for severe obesity. Yet some patients regain much of the weight, and others never lose enough. The authors undertook a scoping review of both problems. They searched for work on definitions, causes, predictors, and care.

The pair found many definitions of weight regain, and fewer for insufficient loss. That spread makes reported rates hard to compare. About 20–25% of patients struggle with considerable regain. Causes look complex and layered, spanning behavior and biology. The review ends with the open questions. Better definitions, the authors argue, would sharpen counseling and patient selection.
europmc-pmc8044133:
Muto and co-authors pair two single-nucleus methods to redraw the cell map of the adult human kidney. Gene activity alone leaves some cell states hidden. The team added chromatin accessibility profiles from the same tissue. Each cell type thus got a matched pair of readouts. Together they sharpen where one cell state ends and another begins.

Most open chromatin regions sat at gene promoters. Many sat near genes that differed between cell types. Binding site patterns pointed to specific transcription factors at work. NF-κB stood out in a subset of proximal tubule cells. It switched on VCAM1 and drove those cells into a distinct state. The combined approach redefined variety in two segments: the proximal tubule and the thick ascending limb. Kidney atlases gain a regulatory layer.
europmc-pmc8071133:
John and co-authors review why uncontrolled diabetes and severe COVID-19 form a perfect storm for mucormycosis. This mold infection has turned up again and again in COVID-19 patients. The team gathered every published case they could find. The total came to 41 cases with enough detail to judge. Risk factors, symptoms, and outcomes were then compared.

Diabetes appeared in 94% of the cases, and it was poorly controlled in 67% of those. Severe or critical COVID-19 showed in 95% of the patients. Most infections hit the nose, eyes, and brain, as they do in diabetes alone. Nearly all cases, 93%, were proven by firm criteria. That sets them apart from COVID-linked aspergillosis, where proof stays thin. The authors urge high suspicion in diabetic patients with rhino-orbital signs.
europmc-pmc8096433:
Sabnis and co-authors overturn the standard account of how colistin kills bacteria. Colistin is an antibiotic of last resort with weak real-world results. Up to 70% of patients fail to respond to it. The drug was known to tear the outer membrane by targeting its lipopolysaccharide. How that tear killed the cell stayed unclear. The team traced the resistance gene MCR-1 in E. coli.

Resistance turned out to hinge on modified lipopolysaccharide at the inner, cytoplasmic membrane. That is where colistin does its lethal work, not only at the surface. The team then turned the insight into a tactic. A transport blocker, murepavadin, traps more lipopolysaccharide in the inner membrane. Pseudomonas aeruginosa grew far more sensitive to colistin as a result. Treatment worked better in living models too. The mechanism suggests fresh pairings for a failing drug.
europmc-pmc8138533:
Erdbrügger and co-authors issue a position paper on urinary extracellular vesicles for the field's international society. Urine carries tiny vesicles shed by kidney, bladder, and prostate cells. Their cargo mirrors the state of the tissues that made them. That makes them a tempting liquid biopsy source. Labs isolate and read them in wildly different ways. Results across studies rarely line up as they should.

The Urine Task Force wrote this paper to impose order. Its members span nephrology, urology, cardiology, and basic biology. They survey the state of the art method by method. Gaps in separation, characterization, and normalization get named plainly. Normalization of results draws special concern throughout. Concrete recommendations close each section of the paper. Rigor, reproducibility, and interoperability are the stated goals. Clinical translation depends on that groundwork. A promising biomarker field is told to grow up.
europmc-pmc8202033:
Spackman and co-authors present CrystalExplorer, a program for studying molecular crystals. Designing useful materials needs insight into how molecules bind in a solid. Hirshfeld surface analysis helps reveal those forces.

The program visualises crystal structures and maps their surfaces. It produces fingerprint plots and measures interaction energies. Quantum-mechanical properties can be computed inside it as well. The software runs natively across platforms. It links packing patterns to the forces that drive them. Chemists can use it to reason about crystal design rather than guess. Worked examples in the text show the tools in action.
europmc-pmc8308533:
Djuricic and Calder update the evidence on omega-6 and omega-3 fatty acids and human health. Oxidative stress and inflammation raise chronic disease risk. These fatty acids can tune antioxidant signals and inflammatory paths.

Long cohort studies link moderate linoleic acid intake to lower heart disease risk. Lower blood cholesterol likely explains much of that link. Raising arachidonic acid to 1500 mg per day showed no adverse effect. The review also covers liver lipid handling and heart responses. Omega-3 sources get their own weighing. The update aims to settle a long public argument with data.
europmc-pmc8395333:
Wang and co-authors review jasmonic acid, a plant hormone that helps plants answer stress. Plants cannot move away from harm, so hormones carry much of their defense work. Jasmonates help plants respond to both living attackers and harsh conditions.

The review covers how jasmonic acid is made, broken down, and sensed. It sums up recent work on drought, cold, salt, heat, and heavy metal stress. It does the same for attack by pathogens, insects, and plant-eating animals. The hormone also talks with auxin, ethylene, and other signals. That crosstalk sets the balance between growth and defense. The authors close with open questions.
europmc-pmc8674133:
Cho and co-authors trace how antibodies evolve in memory B cells after mRNA vaccination in people with no past infection. Infection-driven antibodies keep growing broader for at least a year. The team asked if vaccine-driven cells follow the same path. Samples came five months after Moderna or Pfizer shots.

Between the first and second doses, cell antibodies grew stronger. After that, strength and breadth did not rise further. Cells found at five months made antibodies much like the first wave. Single vaccine antibodies were weaker than top infection antibodies. Yet blood from vaccinated people neutralized the virus better overall. The authors expect boosters to raise that blood activity more.
europmc-pmc8779633:
Najmi and co-authors review modern approaches to finding and developing plant-based natural products as drugs. Natural sources gave many of today's key medicines. Drug firms largely turned away from them for decades due to their complexity. New technology has revived interest in this route in recent years.

The review covers each step of the modern pipeline. It spans plant selection, identity checks, extraction, and biological screening. Analogue building from a lead compound gets its own account. One core route tests fractions by their activity step by step. The authors argue for an integrated approach across fields. A brief history and major drug wins frame the survey.
europmc-pmc8866433:
Tuo and co-authors link a clotting enzyme to a distinct form of brain cell death after stroke. Ischemic stroke kills neurons as blood flow stops and returns. Which death program dominates is still debated. Ferroptosis, an iron-driven death, is a rising suspect. The team used multi-omics profiling in rodent stroke models. Thrombin and the gene ACSL4 stood out as sharply altered. Their lipid products rose together.

The authors show thrombin freeing arachidonic acid inside cells. ACSL4 then builds that fat into ferroptosis-driving lipids. Blocking the pathway at several points eased injury. The rescue held in cell models and in living animals. The authors name the thrombin-ACSL4 axis a drug target. It could limit ferroptotic damage when flow returns. New stroke treatments are scarce, so the lead matters.
europmc-pmc8891333:
He and co-authors design a tandem catalyst that turns waste nitrate into ammonia with electricity. Making ammonia today leans on the harsh Haber-Bosch process. Pulling it from nitrate waste would be greener. The reaction, though, needs many electron and proton steps. Single catalysts stall or waste energy. The team paired two metals in one system. Copper and cobalt phases each handle part of the chain.

The catalyst forms core-shell structures under working voltage. Inner copper phases reduce nitrate to nitrite. The cobalt shell then rushes nitrite onward to ammonia. The split labor dodges the usual scaling limits. Nitrate-to-ammonia Faradaic efficiency reached 93.3%. The yield rate beat most prior reports. Half-cell energy efficiency reached about 36%. The authors present tandem design as a general trick. Cascade reactions beyond ammonia could borrow it.
europmc-pmc9252733:
Zou and co-authors update ChIP-Atlas, a data-mining suite for exploring epigenomic landscapes. The service gathers public sequencing data on protein binding and chromatin state. This update adds all ATAC-seq and whole-genome bisulfite-seq data for six model organisms. Together with ChIP-seq data, users can now read three layers at once.

A peak browser shows accessibility, methylation, and protein binding at any chosen locus. An enrichment tool characterizes sets of genes or regions in the same way. One example found disease-linked variants most under-methylated in neutrophils. All data sets are free to download by button or API. The authors call the result a panoramic view of the epigenome.
europmc-pmc9420733:
Wen and co-authors map the signaling pathways that drive obesity and the drugs that target them. Obesity is a chronic disease marked by excess body fat. It raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and fatty liver disease. Diet and exercise help, but lasting weight loss stays hard.

The review covers pathways that govern food intake and glucose balance. Others shape fat cell growth, heat output, and chronic inflammation. Named routes include MAPK, PI3K/AKT, JAK/STAT, and AMPK. A second half turns to treatment. It surveys approved anti-obesity drugs and compounds in clinical trials. GLP-1 based drugs get close attention. The authors frame pathway knowledge as a path to precise care.
europmc-pmc9465933:
Nikanjam, Kato, and Kurzrock review liquid biopsy tools and their clinical uses in cancer care. A liquid biopsy reads tumor signals from blood and other fluids. Targets include cell-free DNA, tumor DNA, and whole circulating tumor cells. The method is far less invasive than tissue biopsy.

The authors sort the lab methods for each target type. Droplet digital PCR and deep sequencing lead the DNA side. Cell capture by markers or physical traits leads the cell side. Uses span early detection and prognosis checks. Serial samples can track response and resistance to targeted drugs and immunotherapy. Hard to reach tumors can be profiled this way too. Limits include scant shed material and confounding by clonal blood changes. Future work may add fluids like urine and spinal fluid.
europmc-pmc9832433:
Zhang and co-authors review neutrophils, their extracellular traps, and vessel lining failure in sepsis. Sepsis is organ failure driven by a misdirected infection response. Vessel lining damage is one of its hallmarks. Neutrophils are the first innate defenders on the scene.

Beyond eating germs, neutrophils cast web like traps outside themselves. The traps are tangled DNA laced with killing proteins. They snare bacteria moving through the blood stream. Excess trap release turns that defense against the host. The traps push lining cells toward clotting and inflammation. They also strip the lining's slick sugar coat away. The barrier then leaks and blood flow falters in small vessels. Tissue starvation and organ failure follow in late sepsis. The review weighs drugs that block trap formation. Blocking cell fuel use is another route it surveys.
europmc-pmc9981733:
Wu and co-authors trace epigenetic control in metabolic diseases and its clinical promise. Epigenetics shapes gene activity and many metabolic conditions. Listed diseases include diabetes, obesity, and fatty liver disease. Osteoporosis, gout, and thyroid disorders appear as well.

Four main routes anchor the review. They are DNA methylation, histone change, chromatin remodeling, and noncoding RNA. Aging, diet, and exercise interact with these systems. Together they help form a person's traits and disease risk. The authors first sketch the field's history since 1942. Research methods come next, then clinical uses. Those uses include biomarkers, new drugs, and gene editing. The review links basic routes to bedside aims in plain order.
frus-1861-d133:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 22 June 1861, the day Seward also wrote to him. The dispatch is document 133 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The same day crossing in the Paris file mirrors the London one. Neither man could shape his words to the other's last page. Their trust in each other had to bridge that gap, and in the Dayton file it plainly did. Their bond, built by mail, held firm through the storms of the autumn. The storm of the Trent would strain that bond and, in the end, prove it.
frus-1861-d233:
The mail from abroad brought Seward a letter from Mr. Murphy, dated 10 April 1861. Congress received it as Document 233 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It was written in the month the Civil War began, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d33:
To Brussels on 5 August 1861, William H. Seward sent a letter for Henry Sanford. It is document 33 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

August brought hard lessons about the length of the war ahead. Seward shifted to a longer game abroad, built on patience and firm law. His letter to Sanford in Brussels forms part of that shift, guiding a keen envoy through a changed season. A firm letter to Brussels also spoke, by echo, to Paris and London beyond it. An echo in Paris and London gave a Brussels letter a reach beyond its size.
frus-1862-d133:
Writing home was Charles Francis Adams's duty, and his letter of 22 August 1862 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 133 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d233:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, addressed William Stuart on 5 September 1862 in a letter printed as Document 233 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Stuart handled Britain's Washington business while Lord Lyons was away.

Five days into September, the Maryland campaign was under way and no one knew its outcome. Stuart had to report that uncertainty home while keeping his dealings with Seward smooth. Letters from these days are valuable because they were written without knowledge of Antietam, the battle that would soon change the terms of every discussion. Stuart had served at the legation for years before he took charge of it.
frus-1862-d33:
A State Department letter of 15 March 1862 told Charles Francis Adams what Washington wanted done. Congress received it as Document 33 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The date falls in the winter of the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d333:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 10 October 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 333 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mid-October brought Gladstone's Newcastle speech praising Southern nationhood, which echoed in Paris as a sign Britain might move. Seward's mail that week countered the impression with the administration's steady line. This dispatch is part of the paper battle that ran beside cabinet meetings in two capitals, each side reading the other's press for clues. France's Mexican venture shared the court's attention with the American war all year. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d433:
On 7 August 1862 Gabriel García Tassara addressed a note to Secretary of State William H. Seward from the Spanish legation in Washington. It is Document 433 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Spain's minister wrote in a month when Union fortunes looked thin and European capitals debated whether to step into the war. Tassara's business ranged over the standing questions of the two governments, with Cuba and the Mexican affair never far away. For the reader, his notes pair with the Madrid reports of Perry and Koerner: the same relationship seen from both capitals. Together they explain how Spain stayed out of the war while keeping its empire intact.
frus-1862-d533:
Roest van Limburg wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 June 1862, carrying the Dutch exchange into its second week. His note is Document 533 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

By the second week the June matter had a shape: statements made, answers given, points still open. Van Limburg's persistence was his government's instruction, since Dutch commerce felt every extension of blockade law. Seward met the pressure with courtesy and firmness in roughly equal parts. The note is worth reading as part of the whole run from 5 June. There the reader can watch a diplomatic question being narrowed, letter by letter. It narrows toward the ground both governments could accept.
frus-1862-d633:
On 16 October 1862 Edward Joy Morris wrote from Constantinople to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is Document 633 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the Turkish file's last paper of the year.

By October the news of Antietam was reaching the eastern Mediterranean. Morris could report its reception at the Porte. He could also report the post's autumn business. The Ottoman government, itself an empire of many peoples, watched national rebellions with professional interest. His closing report for the year rounds off a file that shows the Civil War's diplomacy at its widest stretch. The same conflict was discussed in the same season at both ends. The line ran from Madrid to the Bosphorus.
frus-1863p1-d133:
On 27 March 1863, Charles Francis Adams sent a second dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 133 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, the middle piece of three sent that day.

Adams's middle sheets often bore the weight of a day's set: the fullest talk, or the claim worked out in depth. This letter holds that place in the 27 March three. Seward read such mail to judge Britain's next step on the war. Filed in the volume, the set shows a post doing in one day what lesser posts did in a month.
frus-1863p1-d233: Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 13 July 1863. It is document 233 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, within the orders that steered American policy toward Britain during the Civil War. Through such letters Washington told its man in London what to press, protest, or let pass.
frus-1863p1-d33:
On 16 January 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams held the London legation. The letter is document 33 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, one of three he sent on that date.

An envoy split his mail so that each sheet could be filed, read, and acted on by itself. Adams's triple mail of 16 January shows that craft at full stretch. This letter is the middle piece of the set. With its mates, it gives a full day's view from the post that stood between the Union and the world's strongest sea power.
frus-1863p1-d333:
From the British legation in Washington on 9 December 1862, Lord Lyons sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 333 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d433:
Document 433 in the volume is a letter of 30 March 1863 from Secretary William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d533:
25 May 1863 is the date on a letter from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d633:
Writing on 28 October 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons in an official letter. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d133: A third Early letter in three days, dated November 16, 1943 and addressed to the same four officials, stands as Document 133 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Two Early letters sharing one date and one set of names suggest split business, perhaps security and schedule, though the record does not divide their topics. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series. The cluster shows how much summit work ran through staff paper.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d233:
President Roosevelt received a short secret telegram from Secretary of State Cordell Hull, sent from Washington on 18 November 1943 about the crisis in Lebanon. French authorities there had seized the country's leaders, and Britain was asking for American backing of the policy it had ordered its minister, Richard Casey, to follow.

Under that policy, if General Catroux had not freed the Lebanese political prisoners by that night, Casey would fly to Beirut the next day with an ultimatum. Unless the prisoners were released and the French delegate Helleu recalled by ten on Sunday morning, Britain would declare martial law. It would free the prisoners itself and let the Lebanese parliament meet again. It would insist the step was a military need with no political meaning.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d33: Stalin wrote to Roosevelt and Churchill jointly on September 12, 1943, and the message stands as Document 33 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Three-way letters were the exception in a correspondence that usually ran in pairs, and they marked points where the whole alliance had to move at once. The record gives the date and the three names. The message is printed in the Foreign Relations series among the September summit papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d333:
President Roosevelt wrote a warm personal letter to Dr. H. H. Kung, China's minister of finance, from Cairo on 26 November 1943. Kung had sent him a gift of Chinese tea with a letter of 17 November, forwarded from Washington, after Roosevelt had earlier sent cigars to Chungking by Madame Chiang.

Roosevelt thanks him for the tea, saying he is glad of it since he is substituting tea for coffee more and more. The Cairo visit with the Generalissimo and Madame Chiang, he reports, has been delightful and a true success, and the beginning, he hopes, of many such conferences. The Chiangs have raised China's inflation problem with him, and will pass Kung a suggestion of Roosevelt's on their return; he will take it up with Treasury Secretary Morgenthau once home.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d433:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent Harry Hopkins a secret, urgent telegram from Tehran on 3 December 1943 about securing a Soviet representative for the Cairo meeting with Turkey's president. Molotov, his first channel, had left Tehran the morning before.

Harriman is therefore sending Molotov the substance of Hopkins' cable through the Soviet Embassy at Tehran. But time is so short, he warns, that Cairo should also have someone in Algiers inform Vyshinsky directly and offer him air transportation to Cairo. Molotov had stated at Tehran that he would name Vyshinsky to represent the Soviet government at the conference. Harriman has told Molotov of the probability that a plane will be placed at Vyshinsky's disposal in Algiers, if he still wishes him to attend.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d533:
Ambassador Averell Harriman reported to President Roosevelt from Moscow on December 27, 1943, his third direct report in a week. The frequency itself tells a story about the temperature of Soviet-American business that month. The State Department printed the cable in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Harriman had pressed at Tehran for candor between the allies, and his late-December reports tracked how Moscow responded once the talking stopped. Roosevelt relied on these cables to judge whether Tehran's warmth was real. For readers, the report is part of the earliest evidence historians use to date the alliance's high point, and the first strains that followed it.
frus-1944-quebec-d133:
Roosevelt answered Taylor's appeal three days later, on September 3, 1944, in a top-secret telegram routed through Allied headquarters in Italy. The whole message is one sentence. It shows the president acting on the Vatican envoy's advice about Italy's relief crisis just before leaving for the Quebec Conference with Churchill.

Roosevelt asked Taylor to have General O'Dwyer report to him as soon as possible. The general should reach Washington by Friday morning, September 8. If that proved impossible, he was to come to Quebec on Monday the eleventh instead. In the event, O'Dwyer made Washington in time and met the president on September 8.
frus-1944-quebec-d233:
Harriman cabled Roosevelt and Hull from Moscow on September 13, 1944, about the Warsaw operation's tangled start. Hull's instructions reached him only late that night. Acting on an earlier air force message, he had already spoken to Molotov, who approved the American operation after telephoning the Red Army General Staff. The Western side of the plan was moving.

The Soviet side was not. Deane asked a Red Army staff officer what the Soviets intended to do on their own account and was told the Red Army had nothing planned. Deane and the British mission head would jointly press the General Staff the next day to carry out Moscow's own promise of assistance. If no satisfactory answer came, Harriman would see Molotov himself.
frus-1944-quebec-d33:
The third Hopkins message to Prime Minister Churchill dated August 28, 1944 completes that day's set in the Quebec 1944 volume. Three papers in a day mark August 28 as a working summit in miniature.

By then the conference's outline was set: Roosevelt and Churchill would meet at Quebec City in mid-September, with Germany's future and the war against Japan at the top of the list. Hopkins's messages carried the American preparation across the Atlantic. For readers, the trio shows the staff process at its most intense, in the last days before the principals took the stage.
frus-1945-50-intel-d133:
Byrnes answered Vandenberg on 8 January 1947. The secretary of state replied to his director of central intelligence within five days, at the very end of Byrnes's own tenure. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Byrnes left the State Department that month, so his answer is among his last acts in this long story. He had been present at the creation. The OSS order landed on his department in 1945. He had signed the secretaries' letters that built the authority. Readers get a fitting symmetry here. The secretary had received the analysts in the wreck of one agency. Now he writes to the director of its heir, days before both men leave the stage.
frus-1945-50-intel-d233:
On 24 April 1948, the President’s Assistant (Steelman) sent a memorandum to President Truman. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 233, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d33:
Russell wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 24 October 1945, carrying the State Department's administration view to the top. He had written to McCormack on the intelligence office's needs two days before. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

An assistant secretary writing to his chief usually asks for a decision or reports a problem too big for his own level. Russell's pair of papers that week shows a manager working both ends of a build-out. One went down to the intelligence office. One went up to the secretary. Readers get the State Department's internal strain in plain form. A new duty, landed by a president's order, that the house had to find room and money for.
frus-1945-50-intel-d333:
The Chairman of the Research and Development Board (Bush) addressed a memorandum to Secretary of Defense Forrestal on 5 December 1947. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 333 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Security Act had just taken effect. The CIA had replaced the old group, and the Council had just begun to meet.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d433:
National Security Council Intelligence Directive No. 13 was issued on 19 January 1950, the same day as a new No. 1. It is document 433 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

A high number beside a fresh base rule shows a system both growing and being re-founded at once. The Council was widening the rule book while it restated first principles. This directive belongs to that busy January, when the lines of the intelligence world were drawn once more. The pairing of a new base rule with a new high number sums up the whole series in one day.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d133:
Ambassador Harriman sat down with Soviet official I. M. Maisky in Moscow on 20 January 1945 to sound out Moscow on Germany. His memorandum of the conversation is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Maisky, an assistant people's commissar for foreign affairs, was readier than most to trade early views.

No precise Soviet decisions exist yet, Maisky said, but the leanings were clear. Germany should be broken up; the Rhineland with the Ruhr might stand alone, and a Catholic republic might join Bavaria and Württemberg. German heavy industry would be cut down, steel perhaps to a quarter of its former output. Farm output and light industry should be encouraged, and Germany would need some export trade to live.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d233:
Soviet pressure on Iran, and Britain's plea for a joint stand, are laid before the President on 6 December 1944. Stettinius's memorandum, headed “Soviet-Iranian Relations,” is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It asks for authority in advance, to be used only if events demand it.

London has taken the question up with Moscow again. Soviet pressure forced the Iranian prime minister out; it eased for a time, and now seems to be renewing. Britain rests its plea on the Declaration of Iran of 1943 and on the three-power treaty with Iran. Eden hopes Washington will press the Russians too, on respect for Iranian sovereignty. Stettinius holds back from acting at once, but he wants the President's approval ready so the Department can move fast if the need arises.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d33: Churchill closed the year in this correspondence with a message to Roosevelt on 29 December 1944. It stands as document 33 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, issued by the Department of State. Greek fighting and the Ardennes battle filled that week, yet the letter also belongs to the longer build-up toward the Malta stop and the Yalta Conference.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d333:
Matching the timing of attacks in east and west filled this tripartite military session at Yalta on February 5, 1945. At General Antonov's suggestion, Field Marshal Brooke took the chair. The day before, Antonov had laid out Soviet needs: Allied armies in the west should attack during February.

Brooke, citing Marshall, answered with dates. The northern offensive would start on February 8, with the Ninth United States Army attacking some eight days later. More operations would run through most of the month. For once, the alliance's two great fronts were being geared to the same calendar, in the same room.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d433:
Matthews's shorthand boils over in these notes of the late session of February 9, 1945. Eden said he had done the work and put together a piece of work. Molotov objected to a new text and wanted the old one. Eden answered with his War Cabinet cable, objecting to his own text of three days before and to how far the talks had drifted from it.

Frankly, Eden said, without something like this text there was no chance of British approval. Molotov said he could not talk from a new text. Eden replied that Molotov had held it for two and a half days. The scraps preserve a quarrel the smooth minutes soften.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d133:
Ambassador Winant cabled the full British delegation list from London on July 9, 1945. The urgent telegram is document 133 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Downing Street had supplied the names of everyone traveling with Churchill to the Big Three meeting.

Churchill brings his daughter Mary and a personal staff of twelve, and Attlee is going. Around the Foreign Office team stand the chiefs of staff, Brooke, Cunningham, and Portal, plus figures such as Lord Leathers, Sir Hastings Ismay, Lord Cherwell, and Sir Walter Monckton for reparations questions. An interpreter staff serves the Prime Minister. Winant puts the whole British delegation at roughly 250 people, a traveling government larger than the American party.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d233:
Ambassador Winant sent Byrnes a history of the European Advisory Commission in a letter dated July 12, 1945. The letter, with its summary report enclosure, is document 233 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Winant had represented the United States on the commission in London for eighteen months.

He tells the Secretary he has long felt the time would come to ask whether the commission had any further function. Its work had narrowed to German and Austrian questions. And it cannot sensibly sit beside the Control Council. The Control Council will hold the widest knowledge of Germany. It will also hold full responsibility for what is done there. Winant assumes the heads of government will close out the commission once the Control Council is running. But its members' experience might serve the planned Council of Foreign Ministers.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d33:
Eight hours alone with Churchill fill Joseph Davies's supplemental report to the President, dated June 12, 1945. Davies writes in detail, he says, so the report may prepare Truman for the atmosphere and attitude that may still confront him at the coming meeting. At Chequers, the two talked from 11 o'clock Saturday night until 4:30 Sunday morning.

They resumed in Churchill's bedroom at 11 on Sunday, the Prime Minister sitting up in bed, until lunch at 1:30. Talks continued that afternoon, and again on Tuesday at 10 Downing Street. The report's scene-setting alone tells Truman much about the man he would meet at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d333:
When and how civil government should return to Germany is the subject of a memorandum by the Joint Civil Affairs Committee. American policy, it states, was to rebuild state, town, and local offices as fast as possible. Those offices were to be purged of Nazi staff and habits, then run under close military supervision.

At the center, though, no German government existed. On June 5, 1945, the four allied powers had taken supreme authority over Germany. Their commanders, sitting as the Control Council, held that authority jointly for matters touching Germany as a whole. The memo maps a country run from the top by occupiers and from below by Germans.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d433:
Food for Berlin is pledged in Murphy's cable from Hoechst of July 12, 1945, relaying the Berlin meeting of July 10. Murphy and General Clay had attended. Clay and General Weeks each accepted commitments, starting July 15, to supply 20,000 tons of food monthly to Berlin's civilian population. The British commander gave a like pledge for his sector.

The meeting stressed that every effort would be made to draw food from indigenous resources. Immediate needs, though, would partly be met from imported stocks. Each supply was proportioned to the size of the sector, and each commitment stayed subject to review by the governments concerned. The question, Murphy notes, would probably reach the coming conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d533:
Harriman presses the Berlin air link in a letter to Vyshinsky dated July 7, 1945. He has told General Eisenhower of their last talk. The talk concerned opening a civil air lines link at Berlin, between Soviet and American planes. He has suggested that Eisenhower, or his representative, discuss the matter with Marshal Zhukov, or with Zhukov's representative.

He hopes Zhukov will be told of the link's value. He hopes Zhukov will be authorized to work out the technical details. The link, he writes, should be set up promptly. Every day adds to the inconvenience, and to the difficulties of contact with the United States and other American missions in western Europe. He closes by asking Vyshinsky's cooperation in a speedy conclusion.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d633:
Joseph Grew, signing as Secretary of State ad interim, wrote a short secret letter to Stimson on June 28, 1945. It is document 633 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The letter closes the exchange on U.S. forces in Iran begun earlier that month.

Grew acknowledges Stimson's letter of June 19, which set out the War Department's views. He thanks the War Department for the military points it raised. Those points, he assures Stimson, will be borne closely in mind. They will guide any talks with the Iranian government on pulling U.S. forces out. The brief letter matters less for new facts than for the record it seals. State and War were now aligned on a slow, staged withdrawal from Iran.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1033:
Assistant Secretary James Dunn reported to the Secretary of State on July 27, 1945. The day before, the European Advisory Commission had signed its agreement amending the 1944 protocol on occupation zones. The agreement creates a French zone in Germany, as promised at Yalta.

Dunn notes the terms were worked out in full line with guidance agreed between the Department and the Joint Chiefs. He suggests the President now approve the agreement and tell Ambassador Winant. The agreement takes force once all four governments approve it. Its terms, Dunn adds, are already being carried out by the military authorities on the ground. Truman's approval is dated July 28.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1133:
George Kennan, the senior American diplomat in Moscow, wrote to the United States team at Potsdam on 22 July 1945. Kennan ran the embassy there while the ambassador was away. His post gave him a rare close view of Soviet conduct and mood.

The team in Germany prized his reading of Moscow's aims while they bargained with Stalin in person. A year later Kennan would write the famous Long Telegram that shaped America's Cold War course. This dispatch shows him earlier, as an insider feeding word to his own side. It is prized evidence of how the Moscow post saw the summit from afar.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1233:
Togo instructed Sato on 25 July 1945, on the eve of the Potsdam Declaration. Tokyo's foreign minister still pushed the Moscow errand. His government wanted a special envoy heard in Moscow before the Allies spoke, and it wanted terms that kept the imperial house safe.

The timing gives this cable its sting. Within a day, the summit would publish terms demanding Japan's surrender, with the throne's fate left vague. Togo wrote in ignorance of that text but in fear of something like it. His message is the last Tokyo instruction of the exchange before the declaration changed the board.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1333:
President Harry Truman sent a message to General George Marshall, chief of staff of the United States Army, on 27 July 1945. Truman was then at Potsdam, in the closing days of the Potsdam Conference, where Truman, Churchill. Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945. Marshall stayed in Washington and ran the Army from there.

The message links the president at the summit with the senior soldier directing American forces around the world. Late July 1945 was a crowded moment: Germany had fallen, the war against Japan still ran on, and plans for the peace were being set. Short papers between the two men show how tightly the political and military sides of the war were joined at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1433:
The last Soviet text in the closing run is dated 29 July 1945, the fifth of that date printed in the volume. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Five texts in one day close the Soviet drafting campaign at Potsdam with a flourish. Two days later the leaders signed the protocol that fixed the settlement these papers had fought over. Readers who work through the run gain something the summary histories cannot give. The feel of a negotiation's final hours, when paper flew and every clause had a price. This text ends the volume's drafting trail, a fitting last word before the results.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-133: This editorial note stands in the unnumbered run after document 710 in the second Potsdam volume. The historians of the Foreign Relations series inserted such notes to guide readers through tangled files. A note of this kind states a source or links the nearby papers to each other. It keeps the published record open and checkable.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-33:
Robert Murphy, political adviser in Germany, set down Soviet economic ideas for Germany in a memo of July 20, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The ideas came from the Soviet delegates Maisky and Sobolev in the experts' talks.

Murphy lists their main points in order. The Control Council's chief task is the elimination of the German war potential. Heavy industry, the basis of that potential, should be kept from recovering in all zones alike. Agriculture and light industry, by contrast, would get a free hand. Two guiding ideas would rule the council and the German administration. One was the reparation obligation, under a plan to be set. The other was the needs of the occupying armies. Murphy notes the aim beneath the wording. Reparations, not imports, should stand as the first principle.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d733:
The Soviet delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 20, 1945, as document 733. Soviet texts entered the talks in their own style: firm opening lines, held with patience. Each delegation's drafts revealed its aims. This one was printed among the numbered papers of the second Potsdam volume.

Reading the other side's draft is half the work of a conference. The Soviet text lets readers do the same. Its lines show what Moscow put on paper early. Later bargaining can be tracked against it. The document balances the volume's many American drafts. It keeps the record honest: three sides wrote Potsdam, not one.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d833:
Yost wrote this memorandum on August 8, 1945, in document 833. The Central Secretariat's executive secretary was still closing the conference's accounts a week after it ended. His memo belongs to the wrap-up papers of the second Potsdam volume. The secretariat had served three delegations' paper needs throughout.

Post-conference memos by the secretariat are the archive's own diary. They record how texts were gathered, checked, and stored. Readers interested in how history gets kept will value this one. The document also shows the long tail of a summit. The leaders left in a day; their paper took far longer to settle.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d933:
American staff worked out this undated memorandum on the reparations shares during the Potsdam talks. It starts from the Soviet claim to 50 percent of total reparations. The Russian zone, the paper notes, holds about 45 percent of Germany's wealth. A gap of 5 percent would remain to come from the other three zones.

The Ruhr holds about half of all removables in the western zones. The paper proposes offering the Russians a tenth of western removables. Half of that offer would be free, to close the 5 percent gap. The other half would be traded for food, coal, and supplies from the Soviet zone.
frus-1964-68v06-d33: Another 1964-1968 FRUS editorial note from the 1968 Vietnam volume. The turning year. This note provides that context. Coming generations can find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Readers can find it here.
gao-gaoreports-b-296533: Jess Bruner Fire Suppression took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298533: Celadon Laboratories took its November 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Lab deals get the same full hearing as the rest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299433: Weidlinger Associates doubled its May 2007 protest — two case numbers, one engineering fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both claims for good. The firm challenged the awards as unfair; the call weighs each claim. Engineering bid wars get the full technical hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299533: Battelle Memorial Institute took its May 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict. The research giant said the agency's award was unfair; the call tests the claims against bid law. Even nonprofit research powerhouses must play by the bidding rules.
gao-gaoreports-b-316533: This 2008 GAO ruling is about transfer of Support Function for Principal Federal Officials at Department of Homeland Security. The decision answers a legal question about spending public funds. The library keeps it in the public record of federal fiscal decisions.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-233: Services buying reform got a progress report in 2005, and GAO's review tracks the 2003 reform act's implementation. The review checks the follow-through. The government's service contracts deserved the discipline. The progress was tracked. The government's service contracts deserved the discipline.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-433: Base power deals needed minding in 2005, and GAO's report says the handover questions had to be watched. The findings demand the attention firmly. The report warns that the bases' utilities deserved sound management. The bases' utilities deserved sound management. The handover had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-633: Pacific compacts' new requirements were underway in 2005, and GAO's report says implementation of funding and accountability rules progressed. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the island nations deserved honest aid. The implementation had to continue. The island nations deserved honest aid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-833: Defense space personnel needed performance measures in 2005, and GAO's report says management guidance was required to develop the workforce. The findings demand the metrics. The report warns that the star warriors deserved good bosses. The measures had to be developed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-133: Intercountry adoption needed further enhancements in 2005, and GAO's report says agencies improved the process, though more work was required. The findings balance credit and need. The report warns that the adopted children deserved smooth journeys. The enhancements had to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-733: The mail's delivery grades needed work in 2006, and GAO's report says performance standards, measurement, and reporting wanted improvement. The findings target the metrics. The report warns that the nation's letters deserved honest grades. The standards had to be real. The grades had to be honest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-733: The Pentagon's business computers were slowly getting governors in 2007 — GAO's report says corporate-style controls were finally taking hold. The findings credit the progress while noting the distance left. The report's hope: run the back office like a business, and the waste will shrink.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-33: This 2007 GAO report looks at the SEC's watch over self-run trade groups — the stock exchanges and broker clubs that police their own members. GAO found holes in how the SEC kept tabs on these groups and urged fixes. The report pulls back the curtain on an odd setup: an industry that grades itself while a federal agency grades the graders.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-333: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at governmentwide Purchase Cards: Actions Needed to Strengthen Internal Controls to Reduce Fraudulent, Improper, and Abusive Purchases. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-633: GAO published its findings on telecommunications: FCC Needs to Improve Performance Management and Strengthen Oversight of the High-Cost Program in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
goethe-faust-hayward-1833:
Abraham Hayward published his English Faust in 1833, the first complete English version of Goethe's dramatic poem in prose. Goethe's Faust, Part 1, had appeared in German in 1808 and Part 2 only in 1832. Hayward, a lawyer and man of letters, gave English readers the whole work at once.

Faust, a scholar weary of knowledge, bargains with Mephistopheles and is led through love, ruin, and striving. The Gretchen tragedy at the heart of Part 1 became the best known part in English. Hayward's prose was plain where verse translations had failed or cut. His version introduced Faust to the English-speaking world and shaped its picture of Goethe for decades.
govdocs-archive_org-TheOrderOfMelchisede:
Michael Davies, the best-known English writer of Catholic traditionalism, published The Order of Melchisedech in 1979, with a later edition in 1993. Its subject is the Catholic priesthood, defended against both Anglican claims and the changes that followed Vatican II.

Davies argues what a priest is by nature, examines the question of Anglican orders, and attacks the new rite of ordination introduced after the council. He writes as an advocate with deep learning in liturgy and doctrine. The book sets out the traditionalist case on the priesthood in full, and it shaped debate among traditional Catholics for decades.
henrici-cornelii-agrippae-ab-nettesheym-: Henrici Cornelii Agrippae De occulta philosophia, 1533. The three occult books. This book preserves that classic. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
hildegard-physica-1533:
Hildegard of Bingen, the twelfth-century abbess, visionary, and composer, wrote the Physica on the natures of created things. This text is the first printed edition, from Strasbourg in 1533. Nine books treat elements, plants, trees, stones, fish, birds, and beasts, with the healing use of each spelled out.

Hildegard writes from monastery practice and sharp observation. A plant's warmth or cold, its juice and season, decides how it heals. Her medicine joins prayer and herb craft in one system. The 1533 printing carried her natural lore beyond the convent walls. It remains a remarkable woman's guide to the healing world around her.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-low-asher-ben-a:
Asher ben Aryeh Löb, chief rabbi of Carlsruhe, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906. Born at Minsk in 1754, he studied under his father, Aryeh Löb, rabbi of Metz. He helped run his father's rabbinical college when the older man's sight failed. He later served as rabbi at Niederwerrn and then at Wallerstein.

The article traces his rise under the Grand Duke of Baden, who reorganized Jewish congregations on the Napoleonic model. In 1810 Asher joined the consistory and became chief rabbi of the grand duchy, a post he held until his death in 1837. The entry describes him as a strict Talmudist of the old school, yet tolerant toward other views. It also records his responsa, published after his death, and notes his son's rabbinate at Bühl.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malka-ben-aha-1: Malka ben Aha, gaon of Pumbedita from 771 to 773, is given a brief entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. The article admits that only one fact is known about him. He joined Haninai Kahana ben Huna in opposing Natronai ben Habibai. Natronai had tried, for unknown reasons, to push out the exilarch Zakkai ben Ahunai. The two geonim prevailed, and Natronai was forced to leave Babylonia. He probably settled at Kairwan. The notice rests chiefly on the letter of Sherira Gaon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-me-ati-ha-10533:
Ha-Me'ati is the name of a Roman family of translators, traced in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Ismar Elbogen. They worked in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, turning Arabic science into Hebrew. The name itself is a pun: Me'ati is the Hebrew form of Cento, "one hundred," the town the family's founder came from.

Nathan ben Eliezer, at Rome from 1279 to 1283, leads the entry and was called the Prince of Translators and the Italian Tibbonide. His stated purpose was to replace the medical literature Jews had lost and to answer Christian mockery that Jews had none. His translations include Avicenna's "Canon," writings on the eye, and the aphorisms of Hippocrates and of Maimonides. His son Solomon and grandson Samuel finished and extended his Galen translations, so the entry becomes a three-generation record of one family's workshop.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-messina-10733:
Messina, the Sicilian city on the strait facing Calabria, had a Jewish community that may reach back before the destruction of the Second Temple. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its history for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The community is first named in the letters of Gregory I, and Benjamin of Tudela counted 200 Jews there about 1170.

The article records hard centuries: Jews executed in 1347 on a false ritual murder charge, a riot bought off in 1475, and full expulsion from Sicily in 1492. Messina was also the seat of the highest Jewish court of appeal on the island, and Moses Ḥefeẓ became its chief justice in 1439. Lists of scholars, physicians, and tax figures fill out the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milhau-moses-be:
Moses ben Michael Milhau was a French scholar and poet of Carpentras in the later eighteenth century, and apparently the father of Joseph Milhau. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. The family link rests on the genealogy Joseph printed in his own book, and the entry treats it as probable, not certain.

Three of Moses' works appeared together at Leghorn in 1787: a philosophical essay on Job, a rhymed paraphrase of Ruth with reflections, and a rhymed letter of consolation for the sad. A poem honoring Napoleon, printed at Paris in 1806 under the name Moses Milhau, is doubted here, since Joseph's father would hardly still have been living then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-molko-solomon-1:
Solomon Molko, born a Christian in Portugal about 1500 under the name Diogo Pires, is the Marrano cabalist whose career Isidore Singer and Philipp Bloch recount in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906.
