pmc-13289233:
Linda Ng Fat, Robert West, and Sarah E Jackson authored a 2026 cross-sectional study on healthy habits and life satisfaction in England. They used the Health Survey for England from 2017 and 2018. The sample held 6978 adults aged 35 to 64, and life satisfaction was scored from 0 to 10.

Models compared people who met guidance on smoking, alcohol, activity, and fruit and vegetable intake with those who did not. Eating five or more portions a day, having quit smoking, and being highly active each linked to higher odds of scoring 7 or more. Gains added up when people met several habits at once. Meeting all three habits tied to the largest rise, which suggests broad lifestyle support could lift well-being at population scale.
pmc-13289733:
Laura G Schaerer and colleagues track a 2026 shift inside a waste bioreactor that stopped making methane to make acids instead. Such arrested digestion turns organic waste into building blocks for fuels, bioplastics, and medicines. Product mixes vary wildly because microbe control is hard, and lactic acid bacteria often take over and sour the tank with short acids.

When feed changed from manure and paperboard to food waste, caproic acid output rose from an average of 3.9 g/l to 12.3 g/l in the reactor. Time-series gene data showed the dominant lactic species swapped, diversity rose, and a likely chain-lengthening genus reached 26.2 percent share overall. Bacterial weapons called bacteriocins and resistance to them may steer who wins.
pmc-13289933:
Tom A. Bond led a 2026 cohort analysis on whether parent body size truly causes child body size, or whether shared genes explain the link. Data came from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort, covering births from 1999 to 2009 at most maternity units in Norway. Mother weight before pregnancy was compared with father weight for effects on birth weight, child size to age eight, and eating behavior at eight.

Questionnaires captured appetite traits at age eight, while records tracked size from six months onward. A twin-based structural model then separated causal paths from genetic confounding shared within families. Adjustments covered parity, age, smoking, schooling, income, and language background of parents and grandparents. The design isolates nurture from nature more cleanly.
pmc-13290333:
Parita Noisamran and colleagues link house conditions to lameness in Thai broiler chickens in a 2026 field study. Lameness hurts both bird welfare and farm income in fast-growing flocks. Records covered 296 flocks, about eleven and a half million birds, on five farms in Eastern Thailand during 2023. The team matched culling records against temperature, humidity, light, and ammonia by bird age.

Median lameness sat near one percent of birds, with wide differences between farms. Heat on the first day of life predicted later lameness, and day-to-day temperature swings on day seven mattered too. Light intensity at day fourteen showed the strongest single link in mid-growth. Ammonia joined the risk list from day twenty-eight onward. A combined model explained about 43 percent of flock differences. The authors advise tight climate control in the first two weeks, when legs are most vulnerable.
pmc-13290433:
Real-world scan results confirm which high-risk prostate cancer patients are likeliest to have hidden spread, Amy Sharkey and colleagues report in 2026. They studied baseline staging with gallium-68 PSMA-11 PET/CT, a scan that lights up prostate cancer deposits.

The cohort held 525 newly diagnosed men who had at least one of three risk factors: PSA of 20 or more, MRI stage T3 or higher, or biopsy grade 3 or higher. Overall, 22.1% already had nodal or distant metastases on the scan, and the share climbed steeply as risk factors stacked up. Each factor, plus the share of positive biopsy cores, independently predicted spread. Sharkey and colleagues say the findings validate the eligibility rules used by the ProPSMA trial.
pmc-13290533:
A coronary artery ballooned to about 15.6 cm squeezed a woman's heart until surgery relieved it, Zhi Wen and colleagues recount in a 2026 case report. The 53-year-old had no usual cardiovascular risk factors, yet she arrived with acute chest pain, a squeezed right heart, and superior vena cava syndrome.

Imaging showed a giant right coronary artery aneurysm packed with clot and pressing on the right atrium, right ventricle, and the great vein. Tests ruled out vasculitis, and the wall showed non-atherosclerotic degeneration of unclear origin. Surgeons removed the aneurysm and its clot, tied off the artery, and added a saphenous vein bypass. Her venous pressure fell, symptoms cleared fast, and the graft stayed open at three months.
pmc-13290833:
The mathematics of malaria's sleeping liver stage gets a tractable shortcut from Somya Mehra and Peter Taylor in a 2026 modeling paper. Plasmodium vivax parasites bank dormant hypnozoites in the liver that later reactivate, and overlapping infections from new bites complicate any realistic epidemic model.

Their earlier stochastic model handles both features but is hard to analyze, so here they approximate its early phase with a multitype branching process. A coupling argument bounds the approximation error, and the branching version yields the chance that the disease dies out rather than settling into endemic spread. Two test cases follow: vivax reintroduced into a region that had eliminated it, and a mass drug campaign draining the hypnozoite reservoir population-wide. The work gives elimination planners a computable handle on relapse-driven risk.
pmc-13291133:
Pain control first, with sleep-inducing sedatives held back, is the plan set out in a 2026 study protocol led by Yu-Mei Wang for intensive care after brain surgery. Patients who have had a craniotomy need agitation and pain managed while doctors still watch alertness and nerve signs closely, a balance that heavy sedation can blur.

Sixty-five adults expected to stay in intensive care over 24 hours will receive structured non-drug measures plus a remifentanil infusion tuned to keep them calm and pain free within set score ranges. Rescue sedation with standard drugs stays available whenever safety demands it. Success means managing the first 24 hours without protocol failure, and the single-arm design tests feasibility before any larger comparison is attempted.
pmc-13291233: Junhua Xu and co-authors issued a brief author correction in 2026 to a study on sound-driven drug delivery through skin. Only the correction note is present here, and it is very short. One mouse image in a figure was a duplicate by mistake. A stray data point in another panel has also been removed. The corrected figure now appears in both online versions. No results can be judged from this note alone.
pmc-13291733:
Nozhan Ghoreishi and co-authors ask which fall risk factors a wearable system should measure, in a 2026 analysis. Clinical guidance under the STEADI program screens gait, balance, strength, fear of falling, and fall history. Most wearables, though, track gait alone. The team built a dataset of twenty-four older adults labeled low or high risk by two standard tests. Eighteen features were drawn from plantar pressure recordings.

A random forest using all features sorted risk with about eighty-eight percent accuracy. Importance analysis crowned a fear-of-falling feature, the right foot flat phase ratio, as the top signal. A strength measure came second, while classic gait features missed the top ten entirely. Single-factor models told a similar story, with fear of falling matching the full model. Differences between factor models were not statistically clear, though. The authors present the work as preliminary design guidance for clinically aligned wearables.
pmc-13291933:
Lisa Heß, with co-authors, reports a 2026 mouse study on how low levels of the enzyme DPP9 change the way triple-negative breast tumors answer treatment. Tumors lacking DPP9 grow faster and spread more, and patients with low DPP9 fare worse. The team grew human MDA-MB-231 tumors with switchable DPP9 deficiency in the mammary fat pads of mice.

DPP9-deficient tumors grew heavier and sent more metastases to the lungs, apparently helped by extra blood vessel growth. Radiation at two doses of 9 Gy slowed all tumors at first, but the deficient ones regrew faster. Adding the PARP inhibitor Olaparib at 25 mg/kg to radiation shrank tumors further, with the strongest extra benefit in DPP9-deficient tumors. Spread to other organs, though, gave mixed results.
pmc-13292033:
Benjamin Taton and colleagues report a 2026 letter presenting a cohort study of shingles in kidney transplant recipients at one center. The study followed 1,101 adults transplanted between 2004 and 2015 who kept a working graft past day 30. Follow-up ran to January 2017, totaling 6,092 patient-years, with cases confirmed by expert review of medical records.

Eighty-nine recipients developed herpes zoster, an incidence of 14.5 cases per 1,000 patient-years, and the median onset came 5.3 years after transplant. Rates in these patients ran about 3.6 times those of the general population across age groups, even among the young. Older age at transplant, rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin induction, and more HLA class II mismatches each raised the risk independently. The authors argue the numbers support offering the recombinant zoster vaccine to all adult recipients.
pmc-13292333:
Abdolvahab Ebrahimpour Gorji and a large team feed a 2026 question to forty-five dairy cows: can farm by-products cut methane while shifting rumen microbes? Mid-lactation Holsteins spent 24 days on a control diet, apple pomace, or hempseed cake. The team measured intake, milk, fermentation, methane, and sequenced rumen contents with shotgun metagenomics.

Both supplements lifted Bacteroidota abundance and lowered the Bacillota-to-Bacteroidota ratio compared with controls. Apple pomace enriched propionate pathways and cut methane per unit of feed intake from 24.27 to 20.33 grams per kilogram in the reported values. Hempseed cake boosted fiber-degrading microbes and xylanase gene families and also lowered methane intensity. Total methane output and feed efficiency details round out a case for circular feed ingredients.
pmc-13292433:
Ben Bepouka and Mardoche Kafua write in 2026 on the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, focusing on how hospitals themselves amplified early spread. Early WHO regional reports described infected health workers, spread inside facilities, feeble triage, scarce isolation space, and missing infection control supplies. Early symptoms of filovirus disease are vague, which makes test certainty arrive late.

The authors argue that waiting for a named pathogen before acting is the core mistake. They propose an IPC-first response: trigger full infection control steps and symptom-based isolation on suspicion alone, before test results land. Frontline awareness, they say, must persist between declared outbreaks. Their warning is blunt: slow infection control can be as dangerous as slow diagnosis.
pmc-13292533:
Miguel A Labrador-Espinosa and co-authors sort a 2026 group of symptom-free, amyloid-positive older adults by two tau tests that do not always agree. Plasma p-tau217 flags early tau trouble, while flortaucipir PET reads advanced tangles. Among 330 A4 Study participants, the team formed four profiles from the two results and followed brain scans and cognition for about five years.

Most people, 57 percent of the cohort, tested negative on both, while 19 percent were positive on both and the rest split. The double-positive group carried the heaviest amyloid load, the fastest tau spread across fronto-temporo-parietal cortex, the quickest tissue loss, and the steepest cognitive slide. Discordant profiles sat between the extremes. The authors argue pairing a blood test with a scan sharpens early risk sorting for future prevention trials.
pmc-13293433:
Vasile Chasciar and co-authors survey, in a 2026 study, Romanian construction workers in Brașov County about work changes and plans to move abroad during the COVID-19 pandemic. Building work stayed fairly active in Romania while travel was tightly curbed.

A total of 384 workers answered an online survey in February and March 2022 about conditions, hardships, and migration plans. Most saw little change in workload, with masks, hygiene rules, and longer project times as main strains. Few planned to work abroad overall, yet those hit harder in money terms were more willing to move. The study adds worker-level views from a key sector.
pmc-13293733:
Enrique Barrueco-Otero and co-authors report an unusual lung reaction to a Parkinson's drug, in a case published in 2026. A sixty-two-year-old man developed headache, dry cough, chest pain, fever, and breathlessness three weeks after starting apomorphine injections under the skin for advanced Parkinson's disease. Scans showed lung infiltrates in a pattern resembling organizing pneumonia, a form of lung inflammation.

Extensive testing of lung washings found no bacteria, fungi, or viruses, and broad antibiotics brought no improvement. Suspicion shifted to the drug, which was stopped while steroid treatment began at a moderate dose and tapered. He improved quickly, and imaging cleared fully within a month. The timing, the negative infection workup, and the recovery after withdrawal together support apomorphine as the probable cause.
pmc-13293833:
Zhong-yu Kang and coauthors review passenger lymphocyte syndrome in a 2026 literature synthesis. In that rare complication, B cells carried with a transplanted organ or stem cells make antibodies that attack the recipient red cells. The team searched PubMed and Embase through August 2025 for case reports, series, and cohort studies.

They found 64 studies covering 135 cases across kidney, liver, lung, intestinal, heart, and stem cell grafts. Reported rates ranged from about 9% after kidney grafts to over 50% after lung grafts. Most illness began within one to three weeks, often settled on its own, though severe cases needed transfusion, plasma exchange, or rituximab.
pmc-13294433:
Feng-Ping Zhang and coauthors compare storage bulbs and roots across orchid species in a 2026 anatomy study. Dendrobium orchids live on trees where water arrives in bursts, relying on fat pseudobulbs to store water and thick roots to grab it. Seven bulb traits and 13 root traits were measured in 37 species, with family tree corrections to separate shared ancestry from true links.

Bulb traits varied more freely than root traits, hinting at diverse water strategies. Bulb thickness tracked inner storage tissue and vessel traits, while root thickness tracked cortex and velamen layers. Matching traits across the two organs rose together, showing coordinated evolution for canopy drought.
pmc-13295233:
Alexander Pachanov and co-authors update a review on surgical volume and the Norwood heart operation in a 2026 article. The high-risk procedure for newborns may go better at busier hospitals or with busier surgeons. A 2013 review was refreshed with newer comparative studies through late 2024.

Eight added studies brought the total to 18, with 15 feeding the final summary. Most short-term and long-term analyses of death favoured higher hospital and surgeon volumes, though often without firm statistical strength. Teaching hospitals also showed lower deaths in two older studies. Overall certainty was rated very low because definitions and data varied widely between studies.
pmc-13296033:
Noshin Farzana and co-authors review, in 2026, loneliness among people who care informally for relatives with chronic kidney disease. Searching four databases to May 2025, they gather first-person studies on how caregiving cuts people off socially.

Nineteen studies covering 598 caregivers in 28 countries yielded four themes. Lives were confined by the patient's needs, and too little help deepened isolation. Other themes covered damaged relationships and lost identity, plus coping through peer, service or faith support. Carers described skipping outings, clashing with family and hiding struggles from stigma. The authors call for services aimed at carers' social needs.
pmc-13296133:
Cornelia Fursenco and colleagues optimise, in 2026, how to pull useful compounds from Canadian goldenrod, a common plant rich in flavonoids. They compare microwave-based extraction with warm soaking. Conditions were tuned with a set design, and the extracts were dried for testing.

Microwave extraction gave the highest flavonoid levels, while soaked extracts scored stronger on tests against cell damage. Both kinds killed tumour cells from liver and gut lines selectively, sparing normal kidney cells. Chemical profiling tied activity closely to the plant compound mix. The authors say the tuned extracts suit further development for health products.
pmc-13296433:
Jan Soukop and co-authors compare drug-processing enzyme genes across four non-obese rat models of metabolic syndrome in a 2026 study. Each model carries a different dominant trait, from high blood fats to high blood pressure or lost oestrogen. Liver and intestine samples were measured for two enzyme families that help the body clear drugs.

Patterns differed sharply by model, especially in the liver. One strain switched some enzymes almost off while raising others several fold, and inflammation changed expression in yet another direction. Oestrogen loss lowered two liver enzymes in females. Because these enzymes shape how drugs are handled, the strain chosen for a preclinical test can change its results.
pmc-13296833:
Katherine Yaacoub reviews, in 2026, immunogenic cell death, a way of killing cancer cells that wakes the immune system against the tumour. Dying cells release alarm signals that recruit defenders and train them, turning a local treatment into body-wide anti-cancer memory.

The review explains the death pathways and alarm molecules involved, surveys which drugs can trigger this kind of death, and weighs pairing such triggers with other immunotherapies for stronger effect. Faults in cell death routes underpin many cancers, the author notes, so exploiting them offers wide promise. Better grasp of the process is framed as key to new treatments.
pmc-13296933:
Iris M. De Cuyper and colleagues show that blood plasma from leukaemia patients on strong drug treatment can blunt healthy donor platelets in a 2026 study. Such patients get frequent platelet transfusions to prevent bleeding, yet bleeding still occurs. Past work hinted that something in their plasma harms the given platelets once inside the body.

Lab tests confirmed that plasma from acute myeloid leukaemia patients weakened platelets from other donors. A protein scan of the plasma then flagged parts that might drive the block. Naming those parts could let doctors tailor transfusion support for each patient. The team also sees use in care such as bone marrow transplants.
pmc-13297133:
Rosa Devesa-Rey and colleagues test, in 2026, printed plastics for custom braces after soaking in salty fluids mimicking sweat and washing. Four materials, two corn-based plastics and two resins including a soy-based one, were varied by thickness, salt strength and soak time under a structured design.

Standard blue resin kept its surface hardness steadiest. Plant-based materials drank in more moisture, especially when thin. Fitted models predict absorption and hardness from the three factors, giving designers a selection tool. The authors aim at braces that stay strong, clean and comfortable over long wear.
pmc-13297433:
Two catheter-based liver cancer treatments perform much alike, concludes a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis headed by Priyanka Gogna. The authors pooled trials and real-world studies from 2018 to 2025 comparing chemoembolization with radioembolization for hepatocellular carcinoma.

Fourteen studies fed the survival analysis, giving a pooled hazard ratio of 0.99 with a confidence interval from 0.70 to 1.39, essentially no difference. Response rates and progression-free survival also showed no significant gap, and serious side effects occurred at similar rates with both approaches. Given the parity, the authors argue that choice between the two should rest on each patient's anatomy, liver reserve, and preferences rather than assumed superiority.
pmc-13297733:
Nearly all kids treated for chest and throat bugs at commune clinics in north Viet Nam got an antibiotic, Hai Nguyen-Tran and his team found in a 2026 chart review. They read 35,675 visit records from 112 commune health centres for the year 2019.

Drugs went out in 97.2% of visits, and 12.3% used Watch-group drugs on the WHO list. Sore throat was the top cause of visits, at 59.6% of all cases. It drew a drug in 97.9% of its visits. Judged by local rules, many of those sore-throat scripts were not called for. The team says staff need the rules in hand, and the rules need to stay up to date, if use is to fall and drug pushback is to slow.
pmc-13297933:
Under brutal heat in the 2024 vintage, two vineyard tactics rescued a Greek red grape in different ways, report Despina Lola and colleagues in a 2026 study of Avgoustiatis. They compared regulated deficit irrigation with drying the grapes after harvest, against untreated control vines.

Irrigation more than doubled yield to 2.75 kg per vine while keeping berry size, and dehydration shrank berries to 93 g while concentrating sugars to 27.3 °Brix. Both approaches protected acidity that heat destroyed in controls and deepened wine color. Dried-grape wines turned tannic and structured with plum aromas, while irrigated wines smelled fruitier and more floral. The authors present dehydration as a premium option as irrigation water grows scarce.
pmc-13298133:
Lucía Quinde, Victor López-Guerra, and Sandra Guevara-Mora study psychological capital and mental health among Ecuadorian university students, in a 2026 one-time survey. Psychological capital combines hope, self-efficacy, resilience, and optimism. Checked survey forms reached more than seventeen hundred students at three campuses, and structural equation modelling tested whether negative stress carries part of the effect.

Higher scores on that capital measure linked to lower negative stress, while stress linked strongly to anxiety-depression symptoms and rigid thinking. Indirect paths through stress were significant, and direct effects stayed smaller, supporting partial mediation. The authors suggest campus programmes should build personal strengths while also teaching stress reduction.
pmc-13300033:
Yezo virus, a tick-borne pathogen first found in Japan, causes acute fever in people but remains poorly mapped at the molecular level. In a 2026 structural study, Anastasia V. Gladysheva and colleagues produced the first solution structure of domain 1 of its nucleoprotein. The protein came from the native sequence of a clinical isolate.

The team paired small-angle X-ray scattering with AlphaFold 3 predictions and molecular dynamics simulations. Their model shows a stable, mostly alpha-helical fold that stays as a single unit under near-body conditions, with moderate flexibility. Knowing this shape should aid blood-test design and structure-guided drug work against Yezo virus and related orthonairoviruses.
pmc-13300833:
Imran Siddiqi and co-authors present a stepwise, navigation assisted technique for lumbar laminectomy in a 2026 surgical paper. Removing the back of the spinal canal relieves pressure on nerves, but bone removal varies widely between surgeons, and both underdone decompression and facet damage cause failures. Their six-step method builds paired troughs with a small matchstick burr and thins the shell further with a diamond burr. It then lifts the lamina out in one piece, using navigation checks at set points.

A worked example follows a seventy-year-old man with multilevel stenosis whose three-level decompression took about fifteen minutes of troughing, lost little blood, and sent him home on the third day without complications. The authors argue the staged burr sequence lowers the risk of tearing the membrane around the spinal cord while keeping the operation teachable for residents. They call for prospective testing in larger cohorts.
pmc-13301533:
Fatty liver tied to metabolism hides in plain sight among ordinary outpatients, Nicolás Ortiz-López and colleagues find in a 2026 cross-sectional study. They enrolled 182 adults sent to a tertiary hospital for abdominal ultrasound for non-liver reasons, screening out heavy drinkers and known liver disease. A subgroup also received elastography to grade scarring.

Ultrasound found liver fat in 57.6 percent of patients, and nearly all of them met the full MASLD definition. Higher body mass, hypertension, and glucose disorders each raised the odds, while regular physical activity lowered them. Among seventy-four elastography patients, eight percent already had fibrosis. The authors back opportunistic ultrasound screening with early risk sorting.
pmc-13302133:
Research on gender affirming voice care has exploded while staying small and lopsided, Kayen Tang and colleagues chart in a 2026 scoping review. From 3,231 screened papers, 290 met the entry bar across four databases. The team mapped who gets studied, which treatments dominate, and how outcomes get measured in this young literature.

Yearly output climbed from an average of 2.7 papers in the late 2000s to 31.3 in the early 2020s span they charted. Most work was cross-sectional or retrospective, rarely randomized, and centered on transgender women. Anterior web glottoplasty and cricothyroid approximation led the surgical reports. Trans men and nonbinary people remain barely studied, the authors warn.
pmc-13302233:
A sieve-like growth pattern in prostate tumors often travels with a hidden dash of the worst grade, Sayeh Fattahi and colleagues report in a 2026 pathology study. They re-read digitized prostatectomy slides from 303 patients for cribriform architecture, then checked the original reports for tertiary Gleason pattern 5. Adjusted models weighed age, PSA, stage, and margins alongside.

Tertiary pattern 5 appeared in 15.5 percent of the men. Cribriform growth showed in seventy percent of those tumors, against twenty-one percent of the rest. After adjustment, cribriform architecture carried an odds ratio of 9.46 for harboring the minor high-grade component. Pathologists, the authors suggest, should hunt harder for pattern 5 whenever the sieve pattern appears.
pmc-13302333:
Ruizhe Wang and co-authors make glowing carbon dots from lactic acid in a 2026 materials study aimed at detecting iron ions. The tiny nitrogen-doped particles dissolve well in water and fluoresce under light, and three nitrogen sources from a family of related chemicals gave three distinct products. Sizes stayed around ten nanometres across all three.

Each version glowed at a different colour, spanning blue to yellow-green, and the middle variant gave the brightest output. Fluorescence held steady across a wide acidity range, resisted salt, and survived six months of storage. Iron ions quenched the glow in a straight-line relationship across the tested range, with a low detection limit. The authors propose the dots as cheap, stable probes for iron sensing.
pmc-13303133:
Blood tests built from several markers outperform any single one for diagnosing recurrent implantation failure, Mojtaba Moradi and colleagues conclude in a 2026 systematic review. Eighteen studies survived screening of more than three thousand records across four databases. Blood, uterine fluid, and menstrual fluid were all in scope, though blood studies dominated the haul.

Immune-cell profiling panels and cytokine-plus-clinical models reached diagnostic accuracy up to 0.94 on the AUC scale. Lone markers sagged, one lymphocyte count managing only 0.577. A single uterine-fluid study showed promise, and menstrual fluid had none at all. The authors want prospective validation in standardized cohorts before clinics adopt any panel.
pmc-13304333:
Ming Cheng and colleagues tune protein digestion for studying membrane proteins in a 2026 methods study. These water-shy proteins form most drug targets, yet they resist the cutting steps that mass spectrometry analysis depends on.

A single two-sided membrane protein served as the test case while enzyme and additive pairs were compared. A filter-based cleanup removed detergents well before measurement. The best recipe covered over nine tenths of the protein sequence with pieces of useful length. Fancy breakable soaps proved needless for single-protein work. Careful cleanup, enzyme choice, and piece size matter most, the authors conclude.
pmc-13304533:
Anna Elisabeth Hentrich leads a 2026 survey comparing vitamin knowledge between pregnant women and their care providers in Germany. Enough key nutrients in pregnancy protects the growing baby, yet shared understanding between patients and staff was unmapped.

Parallel anonymous surveys at one large center drew 132 pregnant women and 105 providers, with 80 full provider replies used in comparisons. Providers knew more on most nutrients, and the widest gap covered vitamin B12 effects on the baby. Beliefs about diet alone being enough clashed most on that same vitamin. Supplement habits and advice patterns also diverged widely.
pmc-13304633:
Akira Takamata, Natsumi Kosugi, and colleagues test, in a 2026 human study, whether fizzy or salted drinks rehydrate better after mild dehydration. Fifteen young adults lost about one percent of body weight through stepping exercise, then drank freely for three hours. Four drinks crossed two factors: carbonation and added sodium.

Plain water produced the largest total intake, while carbonated water alone ended with the poorest fluid recovery because fizz cut how much people chose to drink. Sodium-bearing drinks reduced urine output and raised the share of fluid retained. Adding electrolytes to sparkling water rescued its retention but never beat the still drinks, since intake stayed low. The authors conclude plain water wins for casual rehydration, with electrolytes helping mainly by curbing losses.
pmc-13304833:
Simon K. Joseph heads a 2026 operations report on making carbon-11 tracers for PET brain and body scans. Short-lived tracers demand tight teamwork between cyclotron crews, chemists, quality staff, and clinicians.

Extra carbon-12 sneaking into the product dilutes tracer strength and dulls scan quality, a risk when separate groups run the machine and the chemistry. A university team and an industry partner share target upkeep routines, remote module service schedules, and a liquid test that tracks a key impurity over time. Tracer strength stayed above the recommended floor for human studies.
pmc-13304933:
Sujan Kumar Mondal, Elizabeth Kenyon, and co-authors develop, in a 2026 study, zinc-loaded liposomes aimed at prostate tumors. Healthy prostate cells hoard zinc, which throttles their energy metabolism, but cancer cells lose the transporter that imports it and thrive on the freed metabolism. Swallowing zinc cannot help, since the tumor cells refuse free zinc at the door.

The team's liposomes carry a homing molecule for a prostate cancer surface marker and ferry zinc inside through that receptor instead. The particles were uniform, stable in storage, and leaked little zinc. Cancer cells took them up, died more readily, and shifted toward programmed death. In mice, the liposomes circulated long and gathered in tumors, delaying growth during early and middle stages before the effect faded, hinting at combination use.
pmc-13305333:
Anni Feng, Qilong Li, Ning Jiang, and Qijun Chen review regulatory B cells, immune cells that calm rather than attack, in a 2026 synthesis. Their calming signals keep the body in balance, but the same dampening can shield germs and tumors.

The cells work chiefly through a calming messenger called IL-10, plus IL-35, growth signals, and direct cell contact routes. Roles are traced across infections, cancers, autoimmune diseases such as lupus and arthritis, and organ transplants. Calming cells protect against self-attack and graft rejection while letting long infections and cancers grow, a double edge that shapes therapy ideas.
pmc-13305433:
Zeeshan Umar and colleagues coat sodium vanadium oxide with a conducting polymer to improve water-based zinc batteries in a 2026 study. Such batteries are safe and cheap for grid storage, but vanadium cathodes conduct poorly and wear out fast.

The polymer skin sped charge transfer at the surface while keeping zinc ion paths open inside the layered frame. The cathode stored strong charge at gentle rates and held up through cycling tests. Speed analyses showed faster zinc movement and lower energy barriers. Post-test scans showed the frame flexing and recovering rather than collapsing, a good sign for durability.
pmc-13305633:
Christine Patterson and colleagues carried out a qualitative study in 2026 on how pandemic visiting bans changed care in Canadian intensive care units. They spoke with patients and relatives who had lived through those bans, asking how separation affected communication, advocacy and support.

Sixteen people took part, eleven relatives and five patients, recruited across Canada from January 2021 to April 2022. Four patterns stood out, covering how context shaped each experience, how information stopped flowing, how distance blocked family care roles, and how inventive workarounds helped. The authors argue that human, digital and practical fixes offered by participants could protect family-centred care in later crises.
pmc-13305833:
Attilio Giacosa reviewed 28 studies in 2026 on moderate wine drinking and type 2 diabetes, covering both new disease risk and outcomes in people already diagnosed. Heavy drinking is clearly harmful, yet the picture at low intake has stayed disputed.

Across the studies, risk of developing diabetes followed a J-shaped pattern, with lower risk at low intake in the authors' summary. Red wine taken with meals looked most favourable, likely tied to its polyphenols, and diagnosed patients showed fewer heart and kidney problems in several reports. The authors still warn about low blood sugar risk with glucose-lowering drugs and advise avoidance for vulnerable people.
pmc-13308133:
Petra Ricijaš, Petra Dmitrović, and Boris Pirkić standardise a keyhole-style spinal operation in 2026 for dogs with a fluid pocket pressing on the spinal cord. Eleven dogs with slowly worsening walking problems had the diagnosis confirmed by advanced imaging. Surgery removed a small window of bone and cleared the tissue squeezing the cord, all under magnification.

Every dog but one improved neurologically within a month of surgery. Breeds prone to the condition include pugs, French bulldogs, and Rottweilers, though causes range from inherited forms to old disc disease. Longer-term durability was not assessed in the series, which the authors state openly. Even so, a single repeatable technique with consistent early results helps surgeons counsel owners. Quality of life for affected dogs, they argue, can improve quickly when pressure is relieved.
pmc-13310733:
Yergen N. Kenzhegulov led a 2026 case report on a rare spine tumor that came back years after full removal. A man aged 39 years had a growth inside the neck spine that pressed on the cord and caused weakness. Surgery removed the whole mass, and lab tests graded it as a mid level solitary fibrous tumor.

Scans stayed clear for five years of checks. In 2026 pain and numbness returned, and scans showed a new growth at the same site with no spread elsewhere. A second operation removed it fully. Lab tests now showed faster growth and dead tissue, which raised the grade. Close scan checks were advised.
pmc-13310833:
Ganesh Janarthanan and colleagues survey food safety knowledge among poultry butchers in Chennai, India, in a 2026 study. Butchers guard against meat borne illness, yet training is rare. The team asked what butchers know and what they actually do during slaughter and cutting in city shops.

Interviews covered 375 butchers from November 2022 to July 2023. All slaughter work was done by men, most had only basic schooling, and almost none had formal safety training. Most knew hand washing helps, yet glove and mask use was uneven, rodent presence was common, and all handled cash while cutting meat. Knowledge alone did not ensure safe practice.
pmc-13310933:
Fazilet Zeynep Yildirim-Keles and co-authors test whether mental imagery sharpens side vision in a 2026 study. Nearby objects crowd side vision and blur recognition. Past work showed a matching center item can ease crowding, which raised the question of whether a merely imagined match could do the same.

Volunteers judged a crowded side target while imagining items in mind. Accuracy rose only when the imagined item matched the target in exact visual form. Imagining a different item or one with shared meaning alone gave no gain. Detailed inner pictures seem to blend with weak outer signals, which may aid training for sport and clinic use.
pmc-13311133:
Ying Gu and co-authors track small RNA markers across pregnancy after gestational diabetes diagnosis in a 2026 pilot study. No proven early blood test foretells pregnancy diabetes, and single time point finds may shift as pregnancy moves. Ten candidate RNAs were followed over time in matched groups.

Blood came from 18 diabetic and 18 healthy mothers at four points, from diagnosis to the day before birth. Four placenta linked RNAs ran higher in diabetic mothers at most points, while several other RNAs ran lower across all points. One RNA rose early then fell before birth. Time aware panels may sharpen early screening.
pmc-13311333:
Md Ahsan Karim and co-authors release a 2026 image dataset of farm crops and flowers from Bangladesh for training classification software. The set is named AMCD, short for Agricultural Multidisciplinary Collection Dataset.

The set holds 5405 photos sorted into four groups: fruits, vegetables, flowers, and crops or grains, with 77 subgroups in all. Photos were taken with phone cameras at farms, markets, and gardens in three districts near Dhaka in early 2025. Images were cleaned, squared, and lightly boosted where a class ran short. The set can train farm apps, test models, or serve as healthy-plant reference pictures.
pmc-13311933:
Georgina Krebs and Elizabeth Hogg comment on a 2026-cited study of body dysmorphic symptoms in pregnancy and their tie to poorer quality of life. The disorder fixes sufferers on imagined flaws in their looks.

The discussed study by Gibson and colleagues used a cross-sectional survey to link such symptoms with body image and life quality across pregnancy stages. About 2 percent of the general population has the disorder, and it often starts in the teen years, when bodies change fast. The commentators urge close monitoring of pregnant women with these symptoms. They call for long-term studies in women meeting full diagnostic rules to chart the course.
pmc-13312533:
Jaime M Moore and colleagues offer a 2026 practical guide for clinicians seeking obesity drug coverage for young patients under Medicaid. Coverage of these medicines varies sharply by state. The federal EPSDT benefit requires Medicaid to pay for medically necessary care for people under 21 even when a state plan omits it, and few clinics know how to invoke it.

The guide distills federal policy, state-by-state differences, and workflows from centers that have won approvals into a step-by-step framework. Its core moves include framing obesity as a chronic disease with documented risks, wording records in EPSDT's statutory language, dividing tasks across the care team, and running structured appeals after denials. Sample necessity letters, documentation templates, and workflow algorithms are supplied so clinics in varied settings can copy the process.
pmc-13313233:
Andres H. Gutierrez and co-workers analyze a new flu strain in a 2026 paper on subclade K, an influenza A H3N2 type that took over world spread. It caused more than 90 percent of flu A cases in the 2025 to 2026 season by the count given in the report.

Seasonal shots still raised antibody defense judged protective, but T cells also guard against infection and severe illness, and they act on epitopes shared between shot and wild strains. The team used a tool called EpiCC to check how well T cell epitopes were shared between subclade K, other H3N2 strains, and recent vaccine strains, working from 706 HA sequences. Their claim is that changes in the HA protein erased some shared epitopes, which may have helped subclade K rise, and that shot design should weigh T cell match too.
pmc-13313933:
Chu Thi Thanh Huong and colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, drug resistance in E. coli from pigeon droppings in Bac Ninh, Vietnam. Pigeons can harbor bacteria that resist drugs, and their meat and eggs are increasingly farmed and eaten. The team collected 128 fresh fecal samples from pigeon farms. They confirmed isolates in the lab, ran disc diffusion tests, and screened quinolone-resistant strains for movable genes.

Three quarters of samples, 75.8 percent, carried E. coli. Resistance ran highest against ampicillin at 69.1 percent of isolates, with sulfonamide and tetracycline close behind. Two-thirds of isolates qualified as multidrug-resistant. Every quinolone-resistant strain carried at least one movable gene, led by qnrS in 65.6 percent of them. A worrying 11.3 percent of isolates were even suspected of meropenem resistance. The authors warn that pigeon farming can seed resistant bacteria into the wider livestock environment and food chain.
pmc-13314733:
Asim A. Khan and colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, whether redo shoulder replacement can safely go home the same day. Primary shoulder replacements already moved outpatient, but revisions are surgery with risk. Reviewing revisions at one institution from 2015 to 2024, the team matched nineteen same-day cases against nineteen admitted ones by components exchanged, age, and gender. They then compared problems, returns, re-dos, and outcomes.

Both groups improved clearly on outcome scores over a follow-up of twenty-one months. Problems numbered nine in each group. Same-day patients needed one re-do and had zero returns, against three re-dos and two returns among admitted patients, differences the statistics did not separate. Admitted patients did carry more smokers and higher surgery risk grades at baseline. Nearly half the revisions were full component exchanges, not touch-ups. The authors conclude outpatient revision is safe and effective for selected patients.
pmc-13315033:
K. Mahalakshmi and Sivakumar Nagarajan design a learning-guided lock for medical images, in their 2026 paper. Devices of the Internet of Medical Things send and store scans on weak hardware under rising cyber attack, so locks must be strong yet light and fully undoable.

Their color image framework lets a Deep Q-Network pick scrambling moves based on stats of the half-locked image. Layers include a SHA-512 key stream mask, a shape-keeping Arnold scramble, and chaotic mixing, as listed in the report. Tests scored high randomness, near-best change rates against the original, faint pixel ties, and near-zero likeness to the plain image, all as reported. Clean recovery on unlock matters in medicine, where a lost pixel can mislead care.
pmc-13315533:
James M. Jurica and co-authors argue, in a 2026 commentary, that hospitals should retire contact precautions for COVID-19 patients. Gowns and gloves were layered onto mask protection at the pandemic's start, when transmission routes were unmapped and surfaces were feared. The authors review what the evidence has since established: the virus travels overwhelmingly through small droplets and aerosols, and contaminated surfaces play no meaningful role in spread.

Keeping contact precautions anyway, they contend, is not harmless caution. It burdens patients with isolation's mental and care-quality costs, consumes enormous quantities of disposable equipment with waste fallout, and taxes a stretched health system, all for no demonstrated benefit. Three years after the pandemic's declared end, the authors advocate that national guidelines be rewritten to match the science. They sketch a streamlined approach to caring safely for infected patients without the gown-and-glove ritual.
pmc-13315633:
Tomás Hernández and colleagues survey, in a 2026 study, what Spanish glaucoma patients prefer about their eye drops, and how those preferences steer adherence. Glaucoma destroys vision, pressure-lowering drops cut progression, yet patients skip doses for a disease that usually has no symptoms. The survey ran across Spanish centers in 2024 in patients treated for over six months, and 169 of 200 responses proved usable.

Most respondents were between 51 and 74, on treatment long-term. Nearly all, 93.5 percent, knew preservatives matter, but only 36 percent recalled an ophthalmologist discussing them. Container preference split evenly, multidose bottles at 42.2 percent against single-dose units at 37.0 percent, with younger women favoring single doses. Ease of handling depended on what patients were used to, and nearly four in five valued environmental impact, where bottles won. Adherence was mixed, and nonadherent patients wanted reminder systems. The authors argue care should match the patient, packaging too.
pmc-13315733:
Kirito Kojima and colleagues report, in a 2026 case report, rebuilding a burn-damaged ear with tissue from the patient's other ear. The ear's thin, shaped cartilage and skin make it prone to exposure and deformity after injury. Local flaps often fail when surrounding burn scarring leaves no usable skin. Their patient, a 27-year-old man, had lost the third of his right ear's helix and its crus in a flame burn earlier, leaving him unable to wear glasses.

The team transferred a free flap from the opposite ear, carrying crus helix cartilage, to rebuild the defect. Outcomes were favorable, with no complications and flap survival. Feeling returned, measured at 2.44 on the Semmes Weinstein scale at two years of follow-up, and the patient could wear glasses again. The authors offer the method as both visual and functional reconstruction when scarring rules out local options.
pmc-13316133:
Nawfal Hasan Siam and co-authors review in 2026 medicinal plants and their active compounds as possible treatments for Alzheimer's disease. The illness advances through amyloid buildup, tau tangles, mitochondrial failure, oxidative stress, inflammation, and barrier breakdown, while approved drugs give only modest symptom relief and do not stop progression.

Gathering cell, animal, and clinical studies, the review covers plant extracts and isolated compounds with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anti-amyloid, anti-tau, and cholinesterase blocking actions. Multi-target effects, favorable safety, and long traditional use make plant compounds attractive candidates, though stronger clinical proof is still needed.
pmc-13316633:
SD Blacksell and co-authors offer a 2026 structured review of safety evidence for Hendra and Nipah viruses, two deadly bat-borne germs that spill into animals and people. New global lab guidance demands risk-based containment choices, yet the proof behind many current rules is thin.

Gathering outbreak reports, lab studies, and official guidance, the team found big unknowns. No set infectious dose for people exists, spread routes are only partly mapped, and many killing or cleaning methods were never formally tested in real materials. Clustering of Hendra cases in place and time also lacks an explanation. The gaps endanger vets, nurses, and lab staff most. A One Health lens, joining human, animal, and lab safety, frames their call for better data.
pmc-13317933:
Sowmya Gatram, Viswanathan Pandurangan and Devasena Srinivasan report, in 2026, intestinal tuberculosis that looked like colon cancer in a 32-year-old woman in India. Tuberculosis of the ileocaecal area, where the small and large bowel meet, is the commonest gut form and can form mass-like growths that narrow the bowel.

The woman had fatigue, major weight loss and swollen feet, with severe anaemia and raised inflammation markers. Colonoscopy showed a friable ulcerated growth narrowing the passage. Whole-body imaging showed thickening across several bowel segments with nearby lymph nodes. Tissue examination found granulomatous inflammation and acid-fast bacilli, and a rapid molecular test confirmed tuberculosis. Weight-based treatment brought strong improvement, weight gain and normal blood counts.
pmc-13318033:
Arnold Fredrick D'Souza and co-authors explore, in a 2026 interview study, how people with Parkinson's disease felt about TELEPORT-PD. The low-cost home exercise program is guided remotely by physiotherapists to improve balance and daily movement. Eight participants finished a two-week trial, then sat for deep interviews.

Everyone reported good experiences and most hit no major snags. Many said daily tasks grew easier and rated the live therapist demonstrations above their usual clinic therapy. A few asked for small tweaks. All wanted to keep going, and most would urge peers to join. The small group and praise bias temper the findings, yet home-based, low-resource rehab clearly has an audience among patients far from clinics.
pmc-13318633:
Sergio Díaz-Fernández and a large international team review, in 2026, immune markers for tuberculosis studied in animal models, and how those findings translate to people. Tuberculosis still kills over a million people yearly. Markers that signal disease state could improve diagnosis, prognosis and treatment monitoring, but human studies face cost, ethics and sampling limits.

Animal work offers a controlled and cheaper setting, including access to lung samples that human studies rarely obtain. The review ranges from invertebrates to large mammals, summarising host-pathogen immune interactions, methods and the strongest findings for each model. Species differences are a recurring caution. The authors conclude that combining animal and human data is essential to speed better tuberculosis management.
pmc-13319033:
Guang-Hui Gao and co-authors give a 2026 preliminary report of a new operation for hand flexion spasticity after stroke. Fifteen patients with one-sided hand spasm had the T1 nerve root cut between November 2023 and December 2024. Surgery used an approach above the collarbone. Follow-up lasted at least one year.

All operations finished without major complications. Some patients had brief numbness or mild forearm pain that cleared within three months. Spasticity scores fell from a mean of 3.07 before surgery to 1.20 at final follow-up. Hand function grades and daily living scores also improved clearly. Two patients partly relapsed, while thirteen held a two-grade gain. The authors call the method safe and effective, pending longer study.
pmc-13319733:
Muhammad Ronuq Hasan and his team track, in 2026, which bacteria colonise burn wounds over the first ten days at a national burn centre in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Burned skin invites opportunistic microbes, and infections prolong stays and add problems, most of all in poorer countries. Knowing local germs and drug sensitivity guides safer antibiotic use.

The study followed 110 patients with burns covering a tenth to half of their body surface, swabbing the same wounds on days one, five and ten. Children under ten formed the largest group, and flame injuries led. Bacterial growth rose sharply by day five and stayed high. Gram-negative germs dominated throughout, led by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. No tested antibiotic kept high effectiveness throughout, though colistin did best of the set.
pmc-13320333:
Mattson Ogg and co-authors build a flexible test for how closely smart software thinks like people in a 2026 methods study. As large language models take on bigger social and choice roles, their match to human thought needs a scale that works across tasks and media. Pair ratings of how alike two items feel were used to draw thought maps for people and models side by side.

Two named closed models matched human word ratings most closely, and one open model led its class in the tests reported. Still, no model caught how much people differ from each other, and match to any one person stayed middling. The method works across words, sentences, and images and gives labs a shared yardstick for alignment work.
pmc-13320433:
Rachel Cockburn and co-authors describe one man treated in 2026 for a rare gland cancer of the urine channel. A 65 year old man came in with blood in his urine and a blocked flow, and a tumor was found in the lower channel where a past narrowing had sat. Tissue checks showed a gut type gland cancer grown from a frilled benign growth with high grade early change.

Scans ruled out spread or a second source, a key step since the tumor mimics bowel cancer under the scope. Most of the channel was removed and a new urine opening was made below, with clear edges on the cuts. A mild narrowing later eased with plain care, and at one year no return had shown.
pmc-13320533:
Ruqiao Duan and colleagues use gene data to test cause and effect between irritable bowel syndrome and brain wiring in a 2026 study. Gut and brain links in this common bowel condition are often noted, but which side drives the other stays unclear. The team used Mendelian randomization, a method that uses gene variants as natural clues to direction.

Forward checks suggested the bowel condition raised links between movement sensing areas and the cerebellum, and lowered other frontal and deep brain links. Reverse checks also tied brain patterns back to bowel risk, so influence may run both ways. Gene follow-up pointed to shared pathways that could guide joint gut and brain treatment ideas.
pmc-13320833:
Tangqiaochu Gan, Zhou Fu and Chao Niu review, in 2026, the airway lining as a pivotal player in childhood asthma treatment. Inhaled steroids are first-line therapy and normally calm inflammation while protecting the airway barrier. A significant minority of children, especially with severe asthma, respond poorly, a problem called glucocorticoid resistance.

The review argues that barrier damage itself helps drive resistance and progression to severe disease. Steroids may even harm the barrier in some settings by promoting surface cell death and dysfunction. Infections, nutrition including vitamins A and D, and immune maturation all interact with barrier health in growing airways. The authors urge barrier-focused strategies alongside steroids to improve control for children whose asthma resists standard treatment.
pmc-13321833:
Aaron C. Nolan and co-authors show how a natural molecule boosts older antibiotics against MRSA in a 2026 study. Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus resists both wall targeting and folate targeting drugs, two pillars of care. Guanosine, a purine building block, had earlier restored wall drug sensitivity in this germ.

New tests show guanosine drains thymidine inside MRSA cells and strengthens antifolate drugs such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, plus two pyrimidine blocking drugs. Adding a wall drug, oxacillin, deepened killing of both free and biofilm germs. Thymidine loss came with higher reactive oxygen and fading membrane charge, which helps explain the lethal effect and widens the adjuvant idea.
pmc-13323233:
Laura Cox, Sarah A Gutin and Ifeyinwa V Asiodu interview people living with HIV in the United States about infant feeding choices, in a 2026 pilot study. United States guidance changed in January 2023 to support breastfeeding through shared decision-making for people with suppressed virus, after years of advising against it.

Ten pregnant, postpartum or parenting participants, aged 27 to 40 years and all on antiretroviral treatment, gave in-depth interviews between October 2023 and March 2024. Four themes emerged: need for support, fear of passing HIV to the baby, stigma and desire for real feeding options. Fear drove formula choices, while those who breastfed stressed infant preventive medication and support from family, clinicians and community.
pmc-13324033:
Hyesung Lee and colleagues showed that two phospholipase D enzymes help tumors hide from the immune system. Their 2026 study examined PLD1 and PLD2 in a syngeneic melanoma model, where tumor cells shape their surroundings through macrophages, regulatory T cells, checkpoint pathways, and suppressive signals. The enzymes were already linked to tumor growth, but their direct role in sculpting the immune landscape had stayed largely undefined.

High PLD expression drew in M2-like macrophages, weakened eat-me signals, and dampened killer T cell attack. Mechanistically, PLD1 and PLD2 raised secretion of the chemokine CCL19, pushed macrophages toward a suppressive state, and switched on PD-L1 through the PI3K-Akt-NF-kB axis. Blocking or deleting the enzymes reversed each effect, cutting macrophage infiltration and boosting CD8 T cell entry. The authors propose PLD inhibition as a route to overcome resistance to cancer immunotherapy.
pmc-13324533:
Karl J. Wittmann and Pierre Chevaldonné catalogue mysid shrimp from Caribbean sea caves in a 2026 monograph. Material came from the PACOTILLES-2 cruise to the Lesser Antilles, added sampling, museum holdings, and past records.

The survey found 27 cave species: five strict cave dwellers, 13 cave-loving forms, and nine casual visitors. DNA barcodes covered six species, and family trees helped sort close kin. The authors revise the tribe Mysidetini and the genus Palaumysis, name three new species, and move one species into a new genus, Chelitrapezura. A male of Platyops sterreri is described for the first time, from Guadeloupe. Keys and range notes cover all 27 species.
pmc-13324833:
Hanan Mohammed Shamrani reviews bladder testing in women with lower urinary tract problems in a 2026 study of past cases. Urodynamic studies measure bladder pressure and flow, but how well they match symptoms in non-neurogenic cases is debated.

Records covered 89 women seen between 2020 and 2025. About 60.7 percent were grand multiparous, and many had a prior cesarean birth. Most women showed normal bladder compliance, and only a few had reduced compliance. Few had stress incontinence that matched both testing and symptoms. Symptom links were mostly weak, apart from hesitancy and straining. Birth and surgery history showed no firm tie to results.
pmc-13325033:
Riley E. Cornwell and a large student team report the full genome of a new virus that infects Rhodococcus equi bacteria in a 2026 genome announcement. The host can sicken farm animals and people with weak immune systems, yet its viruses are little studied.

The phage, named Nova53, came from soil in Grand Rapids, Michigan, and shows the long-tailed siphovirus shape under the microscope. Its genome spans 137,941 base pairs and likely encodes 250 proteins plus 31 transfer RNAs. Gene content places Nova53 in cluster CG, a group with only two other known members. In plate tests it made tiny round plaques about 0.5 mm across. Calvin University students isolated and annotated the virus.
pmc-13328033:
Fernanda Cristina Poscai Ribeiro and co-authors compare neuroendocrine tumors across humans, dogs, and cats in a 2026 literature review. These rare tumors can release hormones or stay silent, delaying diagnosis, and pets share homes and tumor forms with people, making them promising natural models. The review searched PubMed through December 2025.

Dog and cat tumors matched many human features in look, markers, symptoms, imaging, and course, above all for pancreatic, liver, and gut tumors. Gaps remain wide, though: weak pet disease tracking, unvalidated markers, uneven imaging standards, and few prospective treatment studies. Coordinated multi-center work with shared reporting rules could improve pet care while sharpening animal models for human research.
pmc-13328133:
Yaşar Aluç and co-authors test electric waveforms as growth boosters for a commercial microalga in a 2026 study. Most electro-technology work on algae uses direct current or high-voltage fields, so the team tried alternating waveforms on Chlorella vulgaris instead. Pulse, sine, square, and triangle patterns were compared with an untreated control.

Growth readings rose 40 percent in the Pulse-10 group and 33 percent in Pulse-90 on their optical density measure. Sine reached 26 percent, square 24 percent, and triangle 19 percent against control. Chlorophyll-a climbed most in Pulse-10 as well, up 54 percent, and protein, fat, and pigment yields also gained. Tuned pulses could raise output for food, feed, cosmetics, and biodiesel uses.
pmc-13328433:
Guoyi Xue, Junhong Yang, and Hui Zhu build a radar gesture reader in a 2026 article. Ultra-wideband radar spots hand movements without cameras, protecting privacy and ignoring light, but a single viewpoint loses information to blocking and angle. Their network merges time-range maps from three viewpoints early on.

Twin branches then read fine local motion texture and long-range timing patterns side by side, and an adaptive fusion module blends them with both simple gating and second-order interaction. On a public twelve-class gesture dataset, tested on unseen people, the method reached 98.29 percent average accuracy, beating the rival systems compared. Multi-view fusion may make touchless control dependable enough for daily devices.
pmc-13330233:
Hai Long and a large team assess doravirine-based HIV therapy in routine care in China in a 2026 study. Charts from seven hospitals covered adults who started such therapy between August 2021 and September 2023, with follow-up to September 2024. Both new starters and switchers were included, whatever their starting virus level.

In total, 352 people took part, with a mean age of 40.0 years in the reported baseline data. Among 271 people with virus data at about week 48, suppression reached 93.7 percent overall in the results given. New starters and switchers both scored above 90 percent in those summaries. Adherence was high and side effects matched the label. The authors call the therapy effective in real-world use.
pmc-13330633:
Anita Szloboda and team built a streamlined method to estimate macroinvertebrate body length from digital images. Their 2026 study notes that exact length measurement is key for gauging biomass, growth rates, and trophic links in aquatic ecosystems. Yet full datasets remain scarce because manual work is labor-heavy and error-prone, especially for bulk mixed-species samples spanning orders of magnitude. The team adapted a Fiji protocol with the Labkit plugin for high-density bulk processing.

Novelty lies in hands-on segmentation to beat computational limits, standard bulk workflows, and skipping the large labeled sets and heavy machine work deep learning needs. The original plugin struggled with high density, taxonomic diversity, and variable image quality, sometimes causing crashes, memory strain, or wrong detection in images with up to 80 individuals. Adapted to these cases, the method offers routine monitoring a non-destructive, accessible route to body length data.
pmc-13330733:
José Castro-Gamboa and team placed orforglipron among marketed GLP-1 agonists. Their 2026 narrative review notes that orforglipron is an oral, nonpeptide, small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes and obesity. The team searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials, and prescribing information with citation tracking, screening 245 records and keeping 35. Synthesis was grouped by molecular structure, receptor pharmacology, early clinical pharmacology, direct and context evidence, and dosing.

Findings appear mixed, maybe helpful, broadly on par, or still unclear against marketed agonists. The review looks at molecular and receptor-level traits setting orforglipron apart from peptide-based agonists, sums up its early pharmacology and oral dosing, pulls together direct comparative evidence against dulaglutide and oral semaglutide. It also weighs prescribing issues. By grouping evidence around structure-function links, direct versus second-hand comparisons, and prescribing ease, the review aims to offer clearer value than another general benefit and safety summary.
pmc-13331033:
Krish Relan and team reviewed the interplay between periodontal health and kidney function. Their 2026 full review examines literature from 2015 to 2025 on dental health and renal function, keeping select foundational studies from 2008 to 2014 for mechanistic context, openly stated as such. Chronic kidney disease and periodontal disease are both big global health burdens with a complex link that is still being mapped.

Shared mechanisms include body-wide inflammation, oxidative stress, impaired neutrophil function, and altered vitamin D metabolism, with a key gap: which causes which. Data suggest periodontal disease nearly doubles renal decline risk compared with gum-healthy controls, while the uremic setting of kidney disease often worsens mouth damage, creating a cycle of decline. Both burden people with diabetes and cardiovascular disease. The review pulls together epidemiology, causes, biomarkers, and care challenges to guide future long-term research and team-based preventive care.
pmc-13332033:
Kunal Singh and colleagues report a 2026 non-contact method for naming waste plastics by their heat signatures. Sorting waste plastics at speed has lagged because rapid, accurate, and scalable naming tools are scarce. Their transient thermal barcode shines tunable mid-infrared light on a sample: when the light matches a polymer's absorption band, the energy turns to local heat that a thermal camera records. Scanning across wavelengths yields a thermal spectrum that tracks the standard infrared spectrum of the plastic.

Just six mid-infrared wavelengths proved enough to give distinct thermal barcodes for all six major commercial plastic classes in waste. For recycling plants, that could mean faster, cleaner sorting lines and less material sent to landfill or incineration. The work shows a path from lab optics to automated sorting at real plant scale.
pmc-13332333:
Hallewell and colleagues ask if dietitians should join children's dental teams in primary care. Diet drives both tooth decay and poor growth. Dental staff give food advice, but time and training are short. The team spoke with ten dental staff, six dietitians, and seven carers. Talks ran across the south west of England and the wider United Kingdom. Four themes shaped the views they heard.

Most backed the idea, if done with care. Staff wanted clear lines on who does what. Carers wanted kind talk, not blame, about food and weight. All groups said shared trust made the plan feel right. Support from clinic leads was key too.
pmc-13332433:
Yihang Zhou and colleagues develop a 2026 collagen coating for heart closure devices to cut clots and speed healing. Catheter-delivered occluders are a mainstay for congenital heart defects and for blocking the left atrial appendage to prevent clots. Yet long-term results suffer from device-related clots, lingering inflammation, incomplete lining regrowth, and slow tissue healing. The team grafted recombinant humanized type III collagen onto biodegradable polymer surfaces through stable covalent bonds.

Lab tests showed the coating curbed clotting, improved lining and heart muscle cell function, and steered macrophages toward a calm, anti-inflammatory state. In animal work, the coating also improved lining regrowth on the device. The coating combines strong cell adhesion with low immune reactivity. Device designers gain a surface strategy that may lower clot risk while helping the implant blend into heart tissue faster.
pmc-13333233:
Yu-Dong Zhao and colleagues detail a fatal drug reaction case in 2026 involving two antimicrobials often paired together. A 60-year-old man with nephrotic syndrome on steroids was treated for Aspergillus and Pneumocystis lung infections.

He started voriconazole and co-trimoxazole on day 6 and went home on day 9. He then restarted co-trimoxazole on day 37 after a 20-day break, and broke out in widespread skin and mouth redness within hours. By day 42 the diagnosis was toxic epidermal necrolysis, with skin detaching over more than 30 percent of his body, alongside stage 2 kidney injury. His voriconazole level measured 9.81 mg/L, well above the 5.5 mg/L ceiling, and gene testing showed he metabolized the drug at an intermediate pace. Causality scoring rated co-trimoxazole highly probable and voriconazole probable. Dialysis began on day 49, but he died on day 63. The authors urge drug level checks, gene testing, and organ monitoring for such combinations.
pmc-13336233:
Herica Silva Dutra and co-authors measured intention to quit among nursing staff at three Brazilian federal university hospitals in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Workforce loss threatens care quality, so knowing who wants out, and why, guides retention policy.

Data collected between October 2018 and September 2022 covered 429 nursing professionals, mostly women and mostly technicians, with an average age of 38.9 years. Intention to leave ran higher among staff with more education, the job-dissatisfied, those who judged staffing inadequate, and the younger and less experienced. Low job satisfaction tripled the odds of intending to leave, with an odds ratio of 3.519 in the analysis. The results point managers toward satisfaction and staffing as the levers that matter most.
pmc-13336433:
Kiho Sung and Sungchul Shin programmed aerogels with fibers aligned along several axes in a 2026 materials study. Living materials gain toughness from multi-axial order, but freeze-casting normally aligns pores in one direction only, leaving the cross direction weak.

Their technique, SHIFT, separates scaffold making into two freeze-casting rounds: a primary structure forms first, then an infiltrated solution is frozen again using the first scaffold as a template. The second alignment angle can be dialed from 0 to 90 degrees with adjustable density. Orthogonal alignment cut the anisotropy ratio to 2.87, nearly matching natural cuttlebone at 2.89 in their comparison, while oblique angles between 30 and 60 degrees improved recovery over repeated compression cycles. Radial and vertical freezing can be blended in as well.
pmc-13336733:
Yuseok Kim leads a big 2026 team reporting the first growth of single-layer platinum diselenide films by an optimized vapor process. The material draws interest for future tiny electronics thanks to high predicted charge speed and good air stability. Even, clean single layers, though, have been hard to grow at useful sizes.

Adding oxygen during growth burned away carbon impurities and raised film quality. Uniform layers covered an area of 1.5 cm by 1.5 cm in the reported work, checked by several optical methods. Arrays of transistors built on the film showed low off-current and a top on-off current ratio of 8.31 × 104 for the best device in the array tests. Industry-ready growth moves this channel material closer to real devices.
pmc-13336833:
Marcel Jung heads a very large 2026 team redefining a long-watched neutrophil marker, CD177. These white blood cells were thought to switch CD177 on when activated. Instead, cells lacking it form a stable group that never gains it, and each person's ratio of the two groups stays steady over time.

After stem cell transplants, the donor marrow set the pattern in new cells. The CD177-free cells looked similar yet carried distinct proteins, made more arginase, and helped tumors grow. They were enriched in head-and-neck cancer tissue and matched worse outcomes. pmc-13339633:

pmc-13341333:

pmc-13341533:

pmc-13341733:

pmc-13341933:

pmc-13342233:

pmc-13343133:

pmc-13343833:

pmc-13344033:

pmc-13350633:

pmc-13350733:

pmc-13351133:

pmc-13351933:

pmc-13352433:

pmc-13352633:

pmc-13355033:

pmc-13356733:

pmc-13359533:

pmc-13363833:

pmc-13375533:

pmc-13380433:

pmc-13384533:

pmc-13385433:

pmc-13385533:

pmc-13386533:

pmc-13393733:

pmc-13394033:

pmc-13394133:

pmc-13395833:

pmc-13396233:

pmc-13400733:

pmc-13401533:
