Unlike its protein-coding parent transcript, the circular form helped drive drug resistance. Switching it off made cells and animals respond to crizotinib again. It works by soaking up a small regulatory RNA, miR-25-3p, which releases a downstream gene, PIP5K1C, to act. The authors name circZBTB46 as a treatment target.
pmc-13421533:
Franciszek Gorski and colleagues built a Polish medical-text tagger in 2026 by distilling a large multilingual language model into small classifiers. Annotating enough Polish clinical texts by hand was infeasible, so the team let Llama3.1 label a large corpus across radiology, oncology, cardiology, hypertension, and pathology, verifying only a portion for testing.

Trained on those labels, a distilled DistilBERT model beat BioBERT and Polish HerBERT variants, topping F1 scores of 0.80 in every category and 0.93 in three, at a fraction of the size and compute. Polish health-data teams gain fast, cheap classifiers for sorting clinical text without a giant model.
pmc-13422133:
Moretto and colleagues test whether variants in PDCD1, the gene for the PD-1 immune brake, predict how hard COVID-19 hits. The brake tunes T cell attack, so inherited settings could tilt the fight against the virus. Their 2026 study genotypes four variants in 366 Brazilian patients, classed as mild, moderate, or severe. It also checks the combined variant strings, called haplotypes, that travel together on one chromosome.

First pass tests flashed signals: one variant tracked with moderate disease, and two others with severe disease under some genetic models. Yet none of the links survived as independent predictors once the models were tested. Five haplotypes differed in frequency across severity groups, but they too failed to predict severity or death. The authors close with a negative verdict, valuable in itself: these variants, whatever their role in immune biology, should not be used as biomarkers to triage COVID-19 patients.
pmc-13422333:
Yu-Ling Huang and colleagues settled a bamboo naming dispute in 2026 with morphology and DNA evidence for Indosasa solearis of northern Vietnam. The bamboo had been moved to Sinobambusa, yet its position stayed controversial for lack of vegetative data.

Field study at the type locality plus gene and SNP trees showed it matches Indosasa diagnostic traits. It sits with Indosasa parvifolia and jinpingensis, so the authors reinstate it in Indosasa and synonymize those two names under it. Bamboo taxonomists gain a clarified genus boundary and a hybrid-origin clue for Sinobambusa.
pmc-13424833:
Evangelos Koutsoukos and Mircea-Dan Mitroiu describe five new species of parasitic chalcid wasps from Cyprus, each belonging to a genus never before recorded on the island. The family Pteromalidae is vast and poorly inventoried in southeastern Europe and the Middle East, and the finds underline how much remains unknown about these tiny insects.

Two of the new species sit in the genus Ablaxia, joined by one each in Erythromalus, Hemitrichus, and Janssoniella, the last named for Aphrodite. Nothing is yet known of any of their life histories. The authors supply and illustrate the diagnostic features separating each species from its known relatives, so future collectors can recognise them, and they frame the work as inventory-building for an understudied region.
pmc-13425533:
Md Abu Sayeed and coauthors studied weather and rotavirus hospitalizations in Bangladesh in a 2026 time series analysis. Weekly admissions for children under five came from seven surveillance hospitals covering August 2013 to June 2017, matched with national weather records. A distributed-lag nonlinear model centered on maximum temperature estimated risk while accounting for seasonal patterns.

Beyond describing past links between heat and admissions, the authors projected hospital burden for 2040 under different climate pathways. Health planners gain a locally grounded view of how warming could change a major cause of childhood diarrhea hospitalization in Bangladesh.
pmc-13425633:
Reema Ashrafi and colleagues tested potting mixes and stacked, vertical growing to raise vegetable output on Bangladesh's flood-prone river islands. These sandy islands, called chars, offer little safe land, so growers need methods that yield more from small plots.

A mix of worm compost, soil, and sand in equal parts grew the sturdiest tomato and cauliflower seedlings. For harvest crops, worm compost with rice husk at a 70 to 30 mix gave the best spinach and capsicum yields per pot. Joining vertical growing with normal farming more than doubled garden output, from about 112 to about 308 kilograms. Net earnings also more than doubled, which Ashrafi reads as proof the approach suits poor char farmers.
pmc-13425833:
Hádila da Silva Veras Sousa and coauthors compared two PET tracers head to head in advanced head and neck cancer in a 2026 pilot study of 14 patients. Fluorodeoxyglucose imaging, which marks sugar use, is standard for staging, while PSMA imaging marks new blood vessel growth and had an unknown role here. Each patient received both 18F-FDG and 18F-PSMA-1007 PET/CT scans for direct comparison.

Tumors were detected better by the FDG scan, according to the study highlights, while uptake of both tracers showed sugar use and vessel growth coexist in these cancers. The pilot guides whether PSMA imaging deserves larger trials in this setting.
pmc-13425933:
Degaga and colleagues published a 2026 meeting report on malaria's comeback in Ethiopia. Malaria cases have climbed again, and the relapsing vivax form drives more of them. New cure options exist, including stronger drug doses and one-dose treatments. A two-day meeting in Addis Ababa gathered 38 program and research leaders.

Funding gaps, service breaks, and climate pressures topped the challenge list. No one could yet say how much illness comes from relapses versus new bites. Full cures need a gene test first, which raises cost and fairness questions. Drug prices and rollout costs stayed too unclear for firm planning. The group called for tighter teamwork between researchers and policy makers. Better counting of relapse cases is the key evidence step ahead.
pmc-13427233:
Thomas and Lipton described in 2026 a class of engineered materials that can change shape in many planned ways and then hold the new shape without steady force. The materials are built from bistable elements, parts that rest in one of two stable positions, joined in a repeating grid. Earlier shape-changing materials could reach only a few set forms, or had no clear way to pick one form from a very large set of options.

Thomas shows that coupling the elements lets users steer through this large set of states and encode varied, targeted profiles. The force needed to set a shape is kept apart from the force that holds it, so small inputs produce large, stable movements. A matching method finds the right element states for a wanted profile, and an automatic machine writes those states into real samples, forming flat profiles and layered three-dimensional surfaces.
pmc-13427433:
Anisha Mittal and colleagues report a stubborn fungal brain infection in a 2026 case study of Cryptococcus gattii. A 63-year-old man came to emergency care after a ground-level fall, with declining physical and mental activity and general symptoms. He also had slow heart rate, high blood pressure, low sodium, and malnutrition-related immune compromise. MRI showed a multicystic, necrotic enhancing mass with a soap-bubble look, about 2.1 centimeters across, spanning thalamus, tectum, and the periaqueductal region.

The lesion blocked spinal fluid flow, dilating the lateral and third ventricles, and fluid diversion proved refractory in management. This rarer cryptococcal species can strike even without classic immune suppression, the authors remind clinicians.
pmc-13427533:
Caner Gunerbuyuk and co-authors report a 2026 study from one center on spine surgery for slipped lumbar discs. Sixty patients had a small disc operation, and half also received heat treatment on the torn disc wall during surgery. The two groups were matched closely on age, sex, pain scores, and disability before surgery. All patients had one of two smaller tear types, named in the Carragee system.

Both groups felt much less leg pain and back pain after a year, and both regained function. Patients who also had the heat treatment improved more, returned to work sooner, and reported higher satisfaction. No extra complications appeared. The authors note that larger trials run ahead of time are still needed to confirm the gain.
pmc-13428433:
Axel Sannö and colleagues test, in a 2026 pilot study, whether pregnant pigs choose cooled floors when summer heat rises. Pigs cannot sweat well and cope with heat mostly by behavior, such as lying on cool surfaces. At a Swedish research center in July 2025, 31 pregnant sows shared a pen with three concrete resting zones. Chilled water ran under two zones, holding them at two set temperatures, while the third stayed uncooled.

Cameras logged where sows lay for three days before cooling began and three days with cooling on. Beforehand, the zones drew equal use. With cooling running, sows crowded onto the cooled concrete at nearly double the density of the plain zone. The hotter the day grew, the stronger the pull of the cool floor. Farmers weighing barn upgrades get direct behavioral evidence that sows value floor cooling.
pmc-13429133:
Noy Norman Kambuaya, Iwan Fuadi, and Annisa Isfandiary Ismandiya review, in a 2026 paper, anesthesia choices for emergency cesarean birth in a dangerous pregnancy syndrome. HELLP syndrome combines blood breakdown, liver strain, and low platelets, and low platelets can make spinal anesthesia risky. The team searched three databases through September 2025 for studies reporting both technique and outcomes. Seven observational studies qualified, covering 369 cesarean deliveries.

Technique could be pinned down for 328 births, split nearly evenly between general and spinal-region anesthesia. Reporting of outcomes varied so much that the team dropped a planned head-to-head pooling and described results instead. No study reported a spinal blood collection injury or lasting nerve harm after regional anesthesia. Death rates ranged widely, driven by how sick each group was at entry. Certainty across every outcome rated very low, a frank verdict on how thin the data are.
pmc-13429733:
Mawadah K Alnaseri and colleagues compare three contrast dyes for spotting cracked teeth on cone-beam CT scans, where fine cracks often hide. Thirty-nine extracted premolars with induced micro-cracks were scanned before and after each dye, with micro-CT as the truth standard.

Two blinded readers counted cracks, and statistics compared the dyes. Micro-CT found an average of 19.9 cracks per tooth, while cone-beam CT found 5.6 with ioversol and 5.8 with barium sulfate. Meglumine ioxitalamate found fewer, at 3.4 per tooth. Dentists learn that dye choice matters, yet even the best dye still misses most fine cracks.
pmc-13430733:
Imran Ahmed and colleagues chart the rise and genomes of Listeria monocytogenes, the food-borne germ behind listeriosis, in Pakistan from 2017 to 2023. Local information on human cases was sparse, leaving doctors and food-safety teams with little to go on.

Cases were found in laboratory culture records and in spinal-fluid PCR tests, with whole-genome sequencing on randomly chosen isolates from 2022 and 2023. Typing, serogrouping, family trees, and core-genome typing mapped the strains. Isolations rose from none before 2017 to 142 across the period, marking an emerging threat that genomic tracking can now follow.
pmc-13430933: Wojtaszek and colleagues saw their 2024 article in the journal Foods retracted in 2026, with their agreement. The study had tested beef burgers enriched with açaí and sea buckthorn juices. After publication, the authors alerted the journal that the ethics statement in the article was wrong. It claimed approval for research involving human subjects that had not in fact been granted. No valid approval could be supplied afterward. The journal's investigation agreed, found a breach of its human-subjects policy, and the editor-in-chief approved the retraction.
pmc-13431433:
Ricardo L Cruz and co-authors laid out a short route in 2026 for building a whole family of fungus-fighting natural compounds in the lab. The family shares a ring core with an oxygen-rich pattern. Rather than craft each member from scratch, the team first made one shared core that carries two halogen handles at set spots.

From that core, step-by-step coupling rounds attach new parts at one handle at a time, with care for which spot reacts first. A final joining step, modeled on how nature may build these compounds, links a complex ring fragment with strong control over shape. Five natural members came out of the route, each in a modest chain of steps and with fair overall yield. The authors say the shared-core plan opens the family to deeper study of its effects on living cells.
pmc-13431733:
Gagan K Sawhney, Brittany Bowman, and Brad Hall looked back in 2026 at five-year results for a tiny eye stent placed during cataract surgery to ease glaucoma strain. The stent helps fluid drain from the eye, which lowers inner pressure. Charts covered 280 eyes of adults with the common open-angle form of the disease, each tracked for at least a year.

Drop counts fell from a mean above two at the start to near one and a half through year four, then rose past the start point at year five. Inner eye pressure dropped from the mid-teens to near thirteen and held there across all five years. Sight test scores held steady through year four, a sign the disease stayed in check. The authors warn that heavy loss of patients by year five clouds the late reads.
pmc-13432833:
Kohei Fujita and co-authors charted in 2026 how eleven lung cancer patients at one center fared on chains of targeted drugs built for a gene fusion fault. Chain care of this kind is common, yet reports on real picks, gains, and harms stay rare. Each patient took two or more drugs from the class over their course.

One drug led as first pick, with two more close behind in use counts. Time before the cancer pushed back shrank with each round, from near two years on the first drug to five months on the fourth. Life span from the first drug hit near five years at the mid point. Stops for side harm struck six rounds in all, and five of those six rounds traced to one drug. The authors urge care with that drug's harm load.
pmc-13433333:
Maryam Mohamed and co-authors surveyed health workers in 2026 at four public hospitals in Omdurman, Sudan, on grit, felt danger, and showing up for work inside live war zones. The war that broke out in April 2023 has gutted care in the land. Forms went to doctors, nurses, lab hands, and drug staff in early 2025.

Of 325 workers, three in five had home goods wrecked, near half saw kin hurt, and two in five lived through security spikes. Show-up rates ran higher for men, the unwed, the crisis-trained, and those spared harm to self or kin. Mid grit scores sat low, with two in five in the low band. Felt danger ran high and tied to security spikes. Grit and danger rose in weak step with each other.
pmc-13433833:
Chen and a large team hunt for the drivers of drug resistance in liver cancer in this 2026 study. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors are a mainstay for hepatocellular carcinoma, but tumors commonly become resistant. The team ran a genome-wide CRISPR screen. They knocked out genes one by one to see which losses changed drug response. They also integrated twenty datasets covering 322 samples. That built a response landscape for this cancer.

Four pathway families shaped sensitivity: RNA splicing, ubiquitination, membrane trafficking in and out of cells, and the cell cycle, all closely tied to anti-tumor immunity. Six genes stood out as resistance drivers, including GPATCH4 and CCT3, and all were highly expressed in tumors and linked to worse prognosis. Their expression levels also tracked with how tumors responded to the drugs and with how much immune infiltration they showed.
pmc-13433933:
He Shao and co-authors built a voice-print chip in 2026 from a graded metal-halide film. The chip learns to sort speakers in noise. Sound wobble and room clatter trip stock gear at that task. Voice prints guard doors and accounts, so reads must hold in real halls. The film's mix grades on its own from face to base.

That grade lets the chip tune its gates and shuffle face charge with care. Replies land in millionths of a second, and clean reads beat past marks by a wide step. Bench tests hit near-total right calls on voice prints. In true room noise, right calls held above nine in ten. The authors pitch the chip as a lean, tough ear for safe voice gates.
pmc-13434133:
Igor Kozlovskii and Petr Popov introduce BiteNetI in 2026, a deep learning tool that finds where ions bind on proteins. Ions help proteins cut, signal, and change shape, yet lab mapping of these sites is slow and costly. Their model reads the three dimensional form of a protein to locate binding spots.

Training used more than 10,000 known protein and ion pairs across 14 ions. On two test sets the tool beat older tools and a broad structure tool used for the same task. For calcium, sodium, and potassium its accuracy rose two to three fold. The gain should help labs plan focused tests first.
pmc-13434233:
Giovanni Santacatterina and coauthors set out a 2026 Bayesian method for finding genes that differ between groups in single cell data. Cells from one person are not free standing data points, so older tests can mislead. Their method restores fair tests by working at the level of each patient.

Fast math on graphics chips lets the method handle more than ten million cells at once. It held up across varied study designs in the tests shown. Large clinic groups, cell atlases, and drug screens with thousands of donors can now be studied as one data set. The shift should cut false gene hits that come from pooling cells.
pmc-13434633:
Yueyue Xu's team tested rapeseed pollen extract in mice with alcohol-linked liver harm in 2026, seeking both protection and a mechanism. Chemical scans found 64 compounds in the extract, chiefly flavonoids, triterpenoids, alkaloids, lipids, and sterols. Mice given the extract showed lower blood markers of liver damage, fats, and inflammation, while liver enzymes that clear alcohol and fight oxidation rose and a damage marker fell.

Tissue checks showed less liver injury, and a stress-defense pathway involving Keap1, Nrf2, and NQO1 was more active after treatment. The authors frame the extract as a candidate for liver-support foods, not a proven medicine. Nutrition teams get a detailed animal case for further study, with human proof still missing.
pmc-13435733:
Francesco Baccelli and coauthors review a fungus shield drug in children with blood cancers in 2026. Isavuconazole was given as first line prevention to 21 patients, most after stem cell transplant. Doses were set by weight, with blood level checks for all.

No severe side effects were tied to the drug, and no breakthrough fungus illness struck. Blood levels hit the target range in 95.2 percent of first checks. Dose tweaks were rare, which hints at steady drug handling in children. Other drugs that share liver paths did not upset levels. Formal trials should now test the drug head to head.
pmc-13435933:
Juliana Theorell's team tested in 2026 how allergy-type immune signals reshape nasal lining and its defense against colds in chronic sinus disease. Chronic rhinosinusitis often involves Th2 immune skewing and extra viral susceptibility, and Th2 remodeling was suspected to ease viral entry. Nasal cells from patients with and without sinus disease were grown at an air-liquid surface, exposed to Th2 cytokines during maturation, then infected with rhinovirus.

Th2 exposure dampened cilia genes and function and lowered viral reads, while shifting cytokine release toward a calmer profile, with similar trends in both patient groups. Male-derived cultures ran hotter on inflammation when unexposed. Sinus teams get a nuanced picture: Th2 remodeling quiets cilia and inflammation together, complicating simple stories about susceptibility.
pmc-13436033:
Kesong Wu, Amanda J Oliver, and Zewen Kelvin Tuong highlight a Chinese immune atlas that corrects a Eurocentric skew in 2026. The atlas profiles over ten million blood immune cells from 428 Chinese adults. Paired gene and chromatin reads map control switches cell type by cell type.

A linked model blends DNA shape with cell context to forecast which DNA stretches stay open. Noncoding variant effects can then be scored, shown for guardian T cells. Prior atlases drew mostly on European ancestry, which hid group specific immune wiring. The new resource joins Japanese and pan Asian efforts to widen the map. Drug and vaccine work gains a broader base.
pmc-13437433:
Dongdong Yang and colleagues tested a deeper placement for chest ports in very thin cancer patients. Such ports give lasting vein access for chemotherapy, yet in wasted patients the shallow pocket under the skin can erode, expose the device, or infect. Their 2026 study reviewed 188 patients at one Chinese hospital with body mass index below the underweight line, with fat at the site no thicker than five millimeters.

Surgeons set each port above the chest muscle rather than in the thin fat layer, guided by ultrasound and X-ray checks. Problems touched eleven patients: four pocket infections, three misplaced tubes, two exposures, and two fiber sheaths on the line. Four ports had to come out, while the rest kept working until follow-up ended or the patient died. The authors call the method workable and safe enough short term for this fragile group, while noting the single-center design.
pmc-13439333:
Banks and colleagues describe a surge of a tropical bacterial disease during record rains in this 2026 case series. Melioidosis, caused by a soil bacterium, spikes after heavy rainfall in northern Australia. Townsville's 2024-2025 wet season brought record rain and a wave of cases. The team reviewed all confirmed patients who first came to the hospital's emergency department. The window ran from November 2024 to April 2025.

Fifty-seven patients presented, forty men and seventeen women, and nearly nine in ten carried a risk factor, most commonly diabetes, present in about 47 percent of the group overall. Blood cultures grew the bacterium in two-thirds of those tested, lungs were involved in about four-fifths, and one in five patients needed intensive care. Eight patients, about fourteen percent, died in hospital despite treatment.
pmc-13439533:
Lei Hong and co-authors report a protective role for the protein NPM1 inside tumour-associated macrophages, publishing mouse cancer work in 2026. NPM1 is famous as a leukaemia gene, but its part in solid tumour immunity was little known. Blocking or reducing NPM1 sped growth of colon and lung tumours implanted in mice. Tumours in those mice drew in more suppressive M2-like macrophages, a wound-healing type that shelters cancer, while killer T cells worked poorly.

Gene tracing showed NPM1 partners with the signal protein STAT3 to switch on CCRL2, a regulator of macrophage behaviour. Raising NPM1 levels in mice flipped the pattern: tumours grew less, suppressive macrophages fell away, and killer T cell attack strengthened. The authors frame the STAT3-CCRL2 axis as a lever for rearming immunity inside solid tumours.
pmc-13439833:
Tiet-Hanh Dao-Tran's team validated proxy reports in 2026 on a quality of life scale used in Australian residential aged care. Many residents cannot answer the EQ-5D-5L themselves, so staff answer for them, yet how trustworthy those proxy scores are was unclear. Data from 281 residents in a twelve-month deprescribing trial were used to test convergent validity, known-group differences, reliability between raters, and responsiveness to change.

Staff proxy scores tracked residents' cognition, physical function, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and frailty, separated known groups sensibly, and moved with changes in those domains over a year. Aged care teams get support for proxy use of the scale, with rater agreement details to weigh. Proxy scores complement, but do not replace, resident voice where it can be heard.
pmc-13439933:
Sagadiev and colleagues pin down how a muscle protein anchors itself to the cell membrane in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans. Their 2026 paper studies RRC-1, a protein needed to assemble integrin adhesion complexes, the anchor points linking muscle cells to their surroundings. The team suspected one region of RRC-1, its PX domain, grips membrane fats directly.

Tests confirmed the predicted PX domain binds phosphoinositides, a family of membrane lipids, in the test tube. Worms engineered to lack just that domain could not position RRC-1 correctly at the muscle cell boundary, and normal placement also required the scaffold protein GIT-1. Extra-copy experiments showed both the lipid-binding domain and the protein's enzyme domain contribute to proper function. The authors conclude membrane contact through the PX domain is essential for building working adhesion complexes.
pmc-13440133:
Jorge González-Prieto and colleagues build rabbit versions of two nerve-interface muscle targets used to drive prosthetic limbs, reporting a 2026 feasibility study. Regenerative peripheral nerve interfaces wrap a cut nerve in a free muscle graft, while vascularised denervated muscle targets keep a muscle flap on its blood supply after detaching its nerve. Both let prostheses read muscle signals, yet rodent models are too small for testing implantable recorders. Eight rabbits were split between the two builds and followed for eight weeks.

The flap-based targets kept their tissue fully alive, with no dead areas on microscopy, and showed electrical activity in three of four cases. Graft-based interfaces suffered heavy tissue death and produced no signal in this run. Painful nerve bundles called neuromas formed in all graft cases and half the flap cases. The authors offer the rabbit platform for preclinical testing of implanted neuromuscular devices.
pmc-13440733:
Kiyotaka Wakatsuki and colleagues report two trauma cases where a scope, not open surgery, emptied blood clots inside the brain, publishing in 2026. Traumatic intracerebral haemorrhage often arrives with other head injuries, complicating the choice to operate. Open craniotomy is the classic route for pressing clots, while endoscopic removal promises a smaller footprint with thinner evidence. Both patients declined because a single clot's pressure threatened the brain, suiting focal decompression.

Working through a burr hole with a clear sheath and rigid scope, the surgeons removed enough clot in each case. Scans confirmed satisfactory clearing, pressure stayed controlled, and no bleeding complications followed the procedures. Both patients later died of severe body-wide problems unrelated to the head surgery, with no clot-driven decline in between. The authors call the method technically feasible for selected clots, while refusing survival claims from two cases.
pmc-13441833:
Yuan Qing and colleagues store prized truffles at four temperatures and read the chemical fallout, aiming to pin down the best cold chain, in a 2026 study. Truffles from Huidong County in Sichuan were held at minus four, zero, four, and twenty degrees. Decay rate, membrane leakiness, breathing rate, and enzyme activity were tracked, and metabolomics mapped shifting chemistry inside the fungi.

The coldest store, minus four, gave the lowest rot rate and the strongest protective enzyme activity in the first three weeks. That same cold, though, bruised cell membranes more, shown by higher leakiness and damage markers late in storage. Warmer cold stores kept energy enzymes livelier later on. Chemical contrasts were richest between the coldest and the four-degree groups, touching amino acid, glutathione, and steroid pathways. The authors frame the coldest setting as best against rot, with a membrane cost worth managing.
pmc-13442433:
Jianwei Guo and colleagues build a visual tool for post-match study of table tennis in a 2026 paper. Match data packs stroke order, landing spots, shot types, player names, and point results into long rallies. Plain charts show those layers poorly, so the team paired two views that track both shot traits and landing paths.

One view groups like strokes with a clustering step to cut line clutter and reveal player habits. The twin view stacks landing points rally by rally, which exposes repeat paths and hot zones as rallies grow. Two matches with checked labels tested the pair of views. Five experts scored the tool on a seven-point scale and rated it clear and useful. The authors offer the pair as a shared frame for coaches who face fast, dense match records.
pmc-13442633:
Xuan Luo and colleagues mine a soil microbe for pest-fight goods in a 2026 study from Cangma Mountain. The new strain, Pseudoduganella sp. D-3-1, fought fungi hard and grabbed iron with strong grip. Its full gene map spans 6,875,892 letters and holds 6,035 gene parts, plus a full path for a purple pigment called violacein.

Gene hunts found many clusters that build microbe goods, led by one cluster the team named pseudodubactin. That cluster builds an iron-grab tool kin to turnerbactin, a known compound of the same class. Mass scans, gene knockouts, and host swaps helped pin the product to the cluster. The authors pitch the strain as a farm biocontrol lead that could cut spray use. Work of this kind also widens the known map of iron tools in a little-studied microbe order.
pmc-13442833:
Ju Young Lee and colleagues tune mist and feed for aeroponic Centella asiatica in a 2026 greenhouse study. Roots hang in air and take pulsed sprays of feed in a closed loop, so nozzle choice steers root wetness and air. Six nozzle types faced laser checks, and three spray plans faced growth screens.

Fine mist types led on dry-mass output per feed unit in the screens. A plan of five-minute rests with 288 spray events per day beat the rival plans across nozzles. At 53 days after transplant, the finest mist gave the most fresh and dry mass per bed area. Stage-matched feed, tuned to leaf growth then bulk growth, beat two fixed feeds on mass and feed thrift. The authors share their bed data to help farms scale this herb with less waste.
pmc-13443333:
Nathaniel Dunckley and colleagues test whether Alzheimer marks run heavier in women with Parkinson disease in a 2026 study. Brain bank cases from an Arizona aging program gave 230 autopsy-proven Parkinson cases with full clinic histories. Plaque loads in the cortex were scored side by side for women and men.

Women held higher mean plaque scores, at 6.5 points out of 15 on the total scale, against a mark of 4.9 points for men. Dense plaque marks also ran higher in women in the set. A high plaque load showed in 56.8 percent of women, against 39.7 percent of men in the cohort. Adjusted models gave women more than twice the odds of a high load. Gene and age checks did not erase the gap.
pmc-13443933:
Mauricio Oliveira and colleagues map which messages neurons translate in the first hour of memory settling in a 2026 study. Long memories need fresh protein, yet most past maps came hours or days after training, when settling is done. Their team caught translation in three neuron types of the dorsal hippocampus, a core memory zone.

Each neuron type ran its own translation program in that first hour. Hard-coded traits in the messages themselves explained much of the split. The maps show how mixed neuron crews rebuild their molecular kits in step to hold a memory. The authors share the landscape as a resource for memory work in health and disease. Their frame links cell type to timing in a field that often pools both.
pmc-13446133:
Mohammad A. ALMohiza and Ravi Shankar Reddy compare platform measures of sway with standard clinic tests of balance and walking in people with chronic stroke, in a 2026 study. Poor balance drives falls and lost mobility after stroke, and clinic tests may miss hidden control faults. Fifty-six adults who could walk took part.

Each person stood on a force platform with eyes open, eyes shut, and on foam, while the team logged sway path, speed, and area. Platform scores worsened sharply when sight or footing was challenged. Sway speed with eyes shut tracked the standard balance scale and the timed stand-and-walk test most tightly. People who had fallen scored worse across the board, which supports platform checks in rehab planning.
pmc-13446333:
Jiang Zhou and colleagues test a reshaped form of silybin, a milk thistle compound, against oral submucous fibrosis, a stiffening mouth disease that can turn malignant, in a 2026 study. Current care gives only brief, partial relief. The derivative, named B1, was built to sharpen the parent compound's anti-scarring power.

In dishes, B1 cut the scar proteins that mark overactive fibroblasts and slowed their crawling. In mice with drug-induced mouth scarring, it eased the disease in the living tissue. Gene reading pointed at the Wnt relay, with one gene, DAAM2, dialed down most. Follow-up tests pinned the effect to a side branch of that relay. The authors pitch B1 as a helper drug for early disease care.
pmc-13447833:
Xiangyu Meng, Wenbin Zhou and Yifan Peng advance full three-dimensional holographic displays through mesh-based hologram synthesis in 2026 work. Near-eye holography promises natural depth cues that fix the focus conflict causing fatigue in current headsets. Layer-based methods blur tilted views and focus cues, while point and light-field methods demand heavy computation, and encoding phase-only holograms remains mathematically awkward.

Their framework represents scenes as meshes, models wave travel at tilted angles, and optimises the full complex wave rather than phase alone. A learning-based calibration scheme uses camera feedback to correct the physical display. Tests on a prototype near-eye display produced smooth focus blur and view-dependent effects with quality the authors call unprecedented for full three-dimensional scenes. Immersive virtual and augmented reality are the target uses.
pmc-13448333:
Fecci and colleagues investigated why immune T cells lose strength inside brain and body tumors, reporting their laboratory findings in 2026. T cells pass from a renewable early state, which responds best to immunotherapy, into a worn-out final state. The team used mouse tumor models to find which cells and signals push T cells along that path.

Fecci found that immune cells called macrophages, which gather inside tumors, supply the contact that drives this wearing-out process, rather than the tumor cells themselves. Blocking it improved tumor control and boosted checkpoint drugs in tumors under the skin and inside the skull, pointing to two drug targets worth testing.
pmc-13449233: Frontiers Production Office issued this 2026 correction for an article on how Chinese users build kinship-like ties with AI companions in resilient communication. The notice is a correction only: a paragraph meant to be cut during production was left in by mistake and has now been deleted from the second paragraph of the introduction. The removed passage discussed AI taking parental roles and the anxieties that raises. The original article has been updated accordingly.
pmc-13450233:
Tingting Zheng and colleagues build in 2026 a simple forecasting rule to help fertility clinics decide, for older patients, whether embryos should be cultured to the blastocyst stage. Women of advanced maternal age produce fewer good embryos, and a failed blastocyst run can leave nothing to transfer. The retrospective study mined 6,840 cleavage-stage embryos from 1,102 retrieval cycles, testing which day-two and day-three features predicted high-quality blastocysts five days in.

One count dominated the model: the number of high-quality day-three embryos. pmc-13451233:
Mark Fedyk and others studied perceived clinician autonomy support in pregnancy before and after COVID-19 in 2026, using a California cohort. Autonomy support means clinicians helping patients grasp choices, pose questions, feel listened to, and decide in line with their values. Whether pandemic care shifts changed those perceptions was unknown.

Participants in the PETALS-2 pregnancy cohort answered a short validated healthcare climate survey, with pre- and post-pandemic onset responses compared and patterns checked by participant traits. The analysis shows whether autonomy support held, fell, or rose as care moved and strained. Maternity services gain a window into the patient-clinician relationship during a period of rapid change.
pmc-13452233:
Chu-Hao Liu and a very large team read in 2026 urine protein snips for signs of exercise intolerance in people at risk of heart failure. The HOMAGE trial gave 268 such patients a shuttle walk test and a urine scan, first at entry and again nine months on. Thousands of urine peptides were matched to the proteins they came from.

Sixty peptides tied to weaker exercise power after strict checks. A lean model kept a core set of proteins, from blood and muscle parts to five collagen kinds. Path reads pointed to oxygen balance, rust control, and fuel use. The authors offer urine scans as a window on why hearts tire, with no needles or biopsies.
pmc-13452333:
Cristelle Obeid and co-authors tell in 2026 of a woman whose wrinkle toxin shots wore off with each period, and of a hormone drug that fixed it. Botulinum toxin shots are the world's top nonsurgical beauty fix, with effects that last three to six months. Hormone swings had rarely been blamed for short effects.

Their patient, a woman aged 45 with regular cycles, first saw a full toxin effect bloom by two weeks in 2019. Three days into her next period, the effect vanished whole. The pattern held across later rounds. Care with tamoxifen, a hormone path drug, at last held the effect in place. The case flags cycle timing as a hidden factor in toxin care.
pmc-13453533:
Charlotte B Christiansen and ten co-authors test whether two gut hormones can slow bone loss in children living with cerebral palsy or with spinal muscular atrophy. Both conditions leave children with weak bones and high fracture risk. The hormones, GIP and GLP-2, curb bone breakdown in adults, but their effect in these children was unknown before this 2026 study.

Just three children took part, each trying a liquid meal, a hormone dose under the skin, and a placebo on separate rounds. The meal clearly lowered a blood marker of bone breakdown over four hours. The hormone dose, by surprise, moved neither the breakdown marker nor a bone building marker. It did lower parathyroid hormone, a separate bone signal. The authors call for larger, age matched studies of the gut and bone link in these groups.
pmc-13453633:
Kyunghee Lee and Hideaki Kawaguchi link home visit dental care use with pneumonia death rates across Japan's regions. Pneumonia is a top killer of older adults, and mouth care helps prevent it. Their 2026 study uses public data from 335 medical areas in 2023, with a spatial model that accounts for how neighboring areas resemble each other.

Against first guesses, areas with more home dental care had slightly higher pneumonia death ratios, at a relative risk of 1.04. The authors read that pattern as a sign the service clusters where frail, high risk elders live. Local poverty showed no firm link to death ratios, yet poorer areas logged fewer claims per patient. That gap hints that preventive dental visits reach deprived areas unevenly, and the authors urge access plans shaped to local need.
pmc-13454133:
Qi Zhao and fourteen co-authors show that the metal at a framework's heart sets how well it changes color under voltage. These two dimensional metal organic frameworks suit smart windows and displays, yet past work blamed color change on the organic parts alone. Their 2026 study screens metal catecholate systems with machine learning and lands on zinc, nickel, and copper versions.

All three shift from green to blue to purple, but zinc and nickel switch in about 5 seconds against copper's 14.4. Their cycle life also runs two orders of magnitude longer. Copper's electron hungry setup, the authors show, demands extra electrons and strains the structure, which slows and degrades it. Test pieces in camouflage, display, and wearable forms back the design rule: pick a calm metal center for speed and life.
pmc-13454233:
Kunyi Wang and eleven co-authors build a risk index for papillary thyroid cancer from protein modification patterns, the chemical tags added to proteins after they are made. Their 2026 study joins bulk and single cell gene data with clinical records from two public databases, screening 17 kinds of modification. Twelve machine learning methods compete to build the best predictor of cancer free time.

A 12 gene index emerged, and patients sorted into three molecular clusters with distinct outlooks. The index tracked immune features of the tumors in detail. High index patients answered well to approved drugs and chemotherapy, yet resisted radioactive iodine, the standard add on for this cancer. One gene, TYMS, stood out as the functional core of the signature in lab checks. The authors offer the index for personal treatment planning.
pmc-13454433:
Lauren Nicol and seven colleagues measure, in a 2026 plant study, where exactly leaves dump excess light energy as heat. This safety valve, called non-photochemical quenching, protects the photosynthetic machinery in bright light. Quenching sites sit in several parts of the Photosystem II complex, but their shares were unmeasured.

The team timed fluorescence flashes in wild Arabidopsis plants and in mutants missing parts of the light-harvesting antenna. Combining flash data with steady light readings let them assign a quenching rate to each part. More than 70 percent of quenching happened in the main antenna trimers. Under 10 percent occurred in the minor antenna, and the rest sat in the core. The split gives modelers firm numbers for how plants guard themselves against light damage.
pmc-13454733:
Hussain and Malcolm ask how teenage grassroots soccer players like to learn about sports related concussion, a brain injury caused by force passed to the head during play. Their 2026 study used focus groups with 20 players aged 14 to 18 at one inner city club in the United Kingdom. The players helped shape the work throughout, sharing how they find and judge health information.

The players mostly got concussion facts from short videos on TikTok and Instagram, and they trusted elite athletes or peers who had lived through a concussion most. They favored short, structured lessons with hands on, visual teaching over lectures, plus online quizzes. The authors suggest building future teaching with young players as co-designers, while noting that one club alone cannot speak for all youth sport.
pmc-13455233:
Han and colleagues built Korea's first evidence-based practice guideline for pediatric anorexia. Here anorexia means poor appetite and low food intake in young children. The guideline covers Korean medicine treatments that families often use without guidance. The team pooled systematic reviews and meta-analyses, plus a Delphi expert consensus. Evidence was graded with the standard GRADE approach.

It issues 15 key rules spanning herbal medicine, acupuncture, Chuna manual therapy, and herbal patches applied to acupoints, alone or mixed with conventional care. Most treatments rested on moderate-to-low certainty evidence, yet showed meaningful gains in appetite-related outcomes across the reviewed trials. Adverse events were infrequent, supporting a low-risk profile for the recommended treatments in children treated under the guideline. Reported rates run 14 to 50 percent in preschoolers, making the guidance broadly useful in pediatric practice in Korea.
pmc-13455333:
Sebastian Jugl and colleagues sift the findings on THC cannabis for inflammatory bowel disease in a 2026 systematic review. Many patients already use cannabis for gut symptoms, yet trials and real-world reports disagree, and recent reviews skipped real-world studies. The team searched four databases under Cochrane and PRISMA rules, keeping only peer-reviewed studies with a control group and a measured effect or safety outcome.

Eight studies qualified, four trials and four non-interventional studies, but bias ran high across them, and the non-interventional work was too biased to grade. One trial reported gains in bloating and appetite at low evidence quality. Disease activity, bowel frequency, quality of life and pain gave mixed results. Remission, weight, endoscopy scores and nausea showed no meaningful gap. The review therefore calls the findings inconclusive and asks for stronger trials before cannabis can be judged as a bowel treatment.
pmc-13457033:
Yun Joon Lee and seven colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a lung cancer patient whose chemotherapy began working again after a stool transplant. The transplant was aimed at a stubborn gut infection, not the cancer. Their patient was a 64-year-old woman with advanced lung cancer on her eighth line of chemotherapy, weakened by repeated Clostridioides difficile attacks that antibiotics could not cure.

After colonoscopic transplant of donor stool, her diarrhea stopped and she completed the next chemotherapy cycle. Chest scans then showed her lung consolidation shrinking from about 91 to 77 millimeters. Stool sequencing found a friendlier balance, with helpful Bifidobacterium rising and a Klebsiella species fading. The authors suggest, cautiously, that resetting the gut may have refreshed her response to platinum drugs through the gut-lung axis. One case cannot prove it, and they frame the report as a lead for trials.
pmc-13457233:
Marijn A. J. Hiep and colleagues test a real-time navigation system that helps surgeons find suspected cancerous lymph nodes during robot-assisted operations in the pelvis and retroperitoneum. Nodes vary in position and sit near vital structures, so a node seen on a preoperative scan can be hard to locate once surgery starts. Their 2026 prospective study enrolled 20 patients with 40 target nodes and registered a patient-specific 3D model to the body using tracked ultrasound over bone.

Navigation displayed the model on the console as a 3D view or augmented-reality overlay, guiding a tracked pointer to each node. Surgeons located 39 of the 40 nodes; one para-aortic node was out of reach in a patient with a body mass index of 52. Median accuracy was 0.8 millimeters, setup took seven minutes, and usability scored 70 on the standard scale. No navigation-related complications occurred, and the authors see wireless tracking widening adoption.
pmc-13457833:
Jason Tan and co-authors report the case of a 32 year old man whose sarcoidosis first showed itself as severe inflammation inside both eyes. Sarcoidosis is an inflammatory disease that forms clusters of immune cells in organs. Their 2026 case report describes how he arrived with a body wide inflammatory illness and swollen lymph nodes after travel to Southeast Asia. Infection was suspected first. Two days later he developed worsening central blind spots, floaters, and light sensitivity in both eyes.

Eye examination found inflammation throughout both eyes with many deep retinal lesions, and scans showed retinal swelling and fluid. Standard clues misled the team, because his blood ACE level and chest imaging, both commonly used in sarcoidosis, were normal. High dose steroids rapidly improved his vision. A groin lymph node biopsy showed the characteristic granulomas, confirming the diagnosis. His eyes settled within three weeks, and vision recovered fully by two months.
pmc-13458333:
Ilkin Aygün and colleagues catch a protein-trimming enzyme breaking its family's rules inside a living animal. Dipeptidyl peptidases of the DPP4 clan are supposed to snip two amino acids off protein ends only after proline or alanine. Earlier test-tube work hinted the worm enzyme DPF-3 accepts more. Their 2026 study applies an isotopic labeling technique called TAILS to hunt DPF-3's targets in Caenorhabditis elegans.

The search surfaced MEP-1, cut after a threonine, confirming the wider appetite operates in vivo and not just in vitro. The cut matters: when the team engineered MEP-1 to resist cleavage, the protein grew unstable, gonads migrated wrongly, and reproduction suffered. The human relative DPP4 is a diabetes drug target, so loose specificity in this family carries weight. The authors argue these enzymes' physiological reach is broader than textbooks assume and that substrate hunting in whole organisms maps it best.
pmc-13458733:
Shuo Shi and Petros Christopoulos comment on a two-drug strategy for the EGFR-mutant lung cancers standard targeted drugs serve worst. Beyond the classic sensitizing mutations lies a zoo of atypical variants, hundreds known, each structurally distinct and less responsive to kinase inhibitors. The piece examines Tomasini and colleagues' CHRYSALIS-2 cohort, pairing the third-generation inhibitor lazertinib with amivantamab, a bispecific antibody hitting EGFR and MET together, in 105 patients.

The pairing produced a 52 percent response rate, with benefits lasting a median of 14.1 months and progression-free survival of 11.1 months. Treatment-naive patients did better still, responding at 57 percent with progression-free survival stretching to 19.5 months. Overall survival remains immature. The authors read the data as proof that stronger, dual-route EGFR blockade can deliver for a group precision oncology has left behind. They place the regimen within two decades of EGFR drug work, still widening its reach.
pmc-13458933:
Yucheng Zhong and colleagues present in 2026 the pivotal trial of Neonova, a new catheter system that clips the mitral valve leaflets together to reduce leakage. The prospective trial enrolled 123 high-risk Chinese patients with symptomatic primary mitral regurgitation of at least moderate severity. Treatment took place at 23 centers between April 2022 and March 2024, with follow-up lasting two years.

Event-free survival reached about 93 percent at one year, well above the preset 60 percent goal, and stayed near 85 percent at two years. Almost every patient kept leakage at a mild level, functional class improved markedly, and the heart's pumping chamber shrank back toward normal. Death from any cause remained low at two years.
pmc-13459233:
Yan Huang and co-authors examined two immune checkpoint proteins in colorectal cancer tissue to see whether their levels predict survival in advanced disease. The proteins, B7-H3 and PD-L1, help tumors evade immune attack, and drug developers are racing to target B7-H3. Their 2026 study built a tissue microarray from 388 patients of several racial and ethnic backgrounds. It stained the samples for marker proteins and linked results with clinical records, focusing survival analysis on 258 patients whose cancer had spread.

Tumors on the left side of the colon were tied to better survival, with a hazard ratio of 0.52 in the adjusted model. Patients whose tumors expressed low levels of both proteins also lived longer, while high expression of either marker signaled worse prognosis. The cohort was notably diverse, including 159 non Hispanic Black and 147 Hispanic patients. The authors see the pair as a prognostic platform for future targeted therapy trials.
pmc-13459333:
Xinran Fang and co-authors built a tool to predict recurrence in HER2 positive breast cancer from patterns in ordinary ultrasound images. HER2 positive tumors are aggressive but treatable, and knowing who relapses would help guide therapy choices. Their 2026 study enrolled 148 patients treated between 2017 and 2021. It extracted image measurements, called radiomic features, from the tumor itself plus rings of tissue five millimeters inside and outside its border. The best features were then fused with clinical risk factors into a scoring nomogram.

The combined model outperformed both the image only and clinical only versions. It reached an accuracy score of 0.905 on the standard curve measure, against 0.820 for the best radiomic only comparison reported. The clinical inputs that added power included irregular mass shape, abnormal echoes behind the tumor, and lymph node spread. Tests confirmed the fusion added real predictive value rather than noise, supporting ultrasound based planning without extra scans.
pmc-13460533:
Katherine L. Mason, Tabrez Hussein, Miku Wake, Nicholas West, and Gillian Lauder report in 2026 a supplemental analysis of a prospective trial. The trial tested intravenous lidocaine during spine surgery for teenagers with idiopathic scoliosis. During posterior spinal fusion, electrical monitoring of nerves guards against injury, and anesthetic drugs can distort those signals. Earlier chart-review work from the team found no harm from lidocaine infusions, yet dosing varied and allocation was not random.

It used a standard anesthetic plan and a fixed lidocaine regimen beginning with a weight-based bolus. Reapplying the earlier analysis to this cleaner dataset offers firmer evidence on whether lidocaine can ease pain without blinding the nerve monitors that protect these patients.
pmc-13460633:
Matthew Hart, Alexandra Batinic, and Justin Skowno measured in 2026 how common anemia is before major surgery in Australian children, and what it predicts. Their retrospective study at a tertiary children's hospital included 582 children with a hemoglobin reading in the three months before surgery, applying the World Health Organization's 2024 thresholds. Demographics, other illnesses, transfusion, and recovery outcomes were all extracted.

Anemia affected about twenty-one percent of the children, roughly one in five. It clustered in girls, in sicker children, in emergency cases, and in those with chronic conditions. After adjustment, anemic children had nearly triple the odds of receiving a transfusion and almost double the odds of a postoperative infection. Because anemia was common even in planned surgery, the authors back screening and treatment programs before operations.
pmc-13461833:

Lambert-Eaton syndrome causes near weakness, reduced reflexes and body-auto symptoms through loss of pre-nerve calcium channels, and up to 60 percent of cases are tumour-linked, most often with small cell lung cancer. pmc-13462033:

In their 2026 study, single cell data from healthy lung, methylation sequencing, and tumor datasets were combined. The aim was to locate where FAM83A is legitimately active in non cancerous airways.

Its promoter sits unmethylated in basal cells as a standing state. A germline cancer gene used for contrast stayed silent and methylated everywhere in lung. pmc-13462133:

The enzyme's tail end proved crucial for controlling KEAP1 stability. pmc-13462233:

The team asked how brain rhythms and the opposing muscle's reflex response link up during the illusion. Volunteers took part under two setups, hand covered or uncovered, and paired vibration rates were applied to the wrist muscles.

Muscle reflex activity differed between setups at one setting, while a broad brain rhythm measure did not separate them. The illusion grew stronger in the covered-hand setup at two settings than at the matched-rate setting. Only in covered-hand conditions did brain rhythm changes at head sites track reflex activity. The authors read the pattern as condition-specific engagement: covering the hand, removing sight of it, changes how senses combine to shape the illusion.
pmc-13463633:
Ming Zhou and four co-authors review the devices and sealed containers used to give antibody drugs in pairs. Giving two biologics together, mixed or side by side, can beat single-drug care for chronic disease. The review follows these systems from clinical trials to market use.

Settled tools get weighed on design, dosing action, and fit for dual-molecule products. Hard points include drug-to-drug reactions, clean sterilizing, seal strength over shelf life, and ease of use for patients. New tools and fresh chances for progress close the survey. Drug makers gain a practical guide to the choices and trade-offs in paired antibody delivery.
pmc-13465133:
Mohadeseh Sadat Khorashadizadeh built a phone app in 2026 for heart rehab in cancer patients, whose treatments can damage the heart. As survival improves, heart disease has become a leading late threat, yet rehab support for patients lags. Needs came from 31 heart-cancer doctors, then a prototype was tested by 27 patients with heart problems and eight experts.

Wanted features included heart-risk education, smoking and exercise guidance, personal and clinical tracking, fatigue and anxiety checks, and messaging with doctors. Usability scored 8.19 out of 9 from patients and 8.22 from experts, a good rating. The app offers a practical bridge between cancer and heart care, though trials must show it improves heart outcomes, not just user ratings.
pmc-13465233:
Zheng and co-authors trace how amyloid clumps overactivate a neuronal enzyme in Alzheimer's disease. Their 2026 paper studies extracellular oligomers of amyloid-beta 42, the sticky protein fragments that damage nerve cells, in neuronal and glial cell lines and in Alzheimer's model mice. The focus is ROCK2, a kinase controlling the actin skeleton that gives neurites their shape.

The oligomers switched ROCK2 into overdrive through two routes at once: an integrin and RhoA pathway from the cell surface, and processing linked to the enzyme granzyme B. The hyperactivation tangled the actin skeleton, stunted neurite growth, and reduced cell survival. But the dose relationship cut both ways: blocking ROCK2 too hard caused excessive neurite outgrowth, itself disruptive to brain networks. The authors conclude the therapeutic target is restoring moderate ROCK2 activity, not abolishing it, and offer that balance as a strategy for Alzheimer's drug design.
pmc-13465333:
Ekaterina Sergeevna Prokopenko and four co-authors silence two stress sensors in leukemia cells to see which one keeps them alive. Muting PERK woke the cell death program, raising Bax, caspase-3, and CHOP at gene and protein level. Cleanup markers for self-digestion stayed flat under PERK loss. Muting IRE1-alpha did nearly the mirror image: death signals fell or held, and self-digestion markers dropped across the board. The split shows PERK guarding survival in this leukemia, which nominates it as a drug target.
pmc-13465433:

The brain tumor is the deadliest of its class, and the barrier locks out most candidates. Gene and network analyses traced its punch to STAT3, a signal switch that patient tumors overuse and that marks poor outlook. Blocking the switch lifted harmful oxygen forms inside tumor cells and fired their self-kill program. Patient tissue checks confirmed the switch runs high in the worst-grade tumors.
pmc-13465533:
Ghenciu and co-authors argue that diabetic eye disease dims vision before standard tests notice. Across the searched literature, diabetic patients showed reduced contrast sensitivity even with no visible retinopathy and normal acuity. The impairment tracked with retinal neurodegeneration, ganglion cell dysfunction, vessel changes, and the severity of macular swelling. Imaging correlations backed the functional findings: thinner retinas, capillary dropout, and poorer perfusion on advanced scans accompanied worse contrast performance. pmc-13466033:
Otsuka and co-authors tested in 2026 how much plaque add-on cleaning tools remove from between teeth, using a lab jaw model. Fake plaque was painted on a molar's inner side. The toothbrush alone removed less than half the plaque, about 44 percent. Every add-on routine did significantly better. Holder-type floss helped but trailed string floss combinations. No single add-on matched the full trio. The findings support layering tools rather than relying on one device. The authors note real mouths, with their varied gaps and angles, still need testing.
pmc-13466133:
Ulrich and co-authors reviewed in 2026 whether pesticide exposure on farms links to high blood pressure and obesity in workers. Farm workers face some of the heaviest chemical exposure of any job. The team searched the medical literature for observational studies of adults with farm exposure. Screening narrowed 355 records to 14 studies. Most measured general pesticide use rather than single chemicals.

Obesity showed the clearer signal. It rose with organophosphate insecticides in three studies and with the herbicide atrazine in one. General exposure linked to obesity in five studies, though two found the opposite. Blood pressure findings were mixed, with only three studies tying general exposure to hypertension. The authors want long-term studies with precise exposure measures on today's pesticide mixes.
pmc-13466233:
Jie Chen and colleagues sort irritable bowel syndrome patients by how their symptoms travel over time, then ask whether gut microbes predict the pattern, in a 2026 analysis of trial data. Sixty-two participants with repeated measures over twelve weeks formed two groups. One group showed a constrained response, the other a broader, adaptive improvement across many life areas.

Measures spanned quality of life, pain, mood, thinking, fatigue, and sleep. A flexible tree-based model searched starting gut microbe types and pathways for signals of later change. The two response patterns differed in microbial makeup, hinting that a stool profile might one day help match patients to self-management programs with better odds of success.
pmc-13466333:
David Fernández-Morales and colleagues ask whether a brief course of the heart drug esmolol leaves lasting protection in artery walls strained by high blood pressure, in a 2026 rat study. Earlier work from the group showed two days of treatment reversed some wall remodeling in the chest aorta. Animals here were checked right after treatment or after breaks of a week or a month.

The short infusion lowered blood pressure and thinned the aortic wall, trimming its diameter, cross-section, and collagen content. Later checkpoints tested whether those gains survived once the drug stopped. Wall stiffness behavior was measured alongside shape and matrix makeup. The design separates a true lasting effect from a benefit that fades with the drug.
pmc-13467033:
Robinson Rúa-Patiño and five colleagues published this 2026 study on greener mortars for flooring layers. They replaced part of Portland cement with fly ash, a power-station residue, and activated the mix with potassium hydroxide solutions. Flooring needs more than strength: the surface must also resist wear from abrasion. The team tested three cement-to-ash blends at two activator strengths, and compared them with plain cement mortar.

Plain cement mortar still came out strongest and wore least. Among the hybrid mixes, the blend with 10 percent ash and the stronger activator performed best. The 20 percent ash version with the same activator gave the best balance, cutting cement use while keeping fair strength and wear resistance. The 30 percent ash mix fell behind, as the activator could not offset the lost cement. The authors ranked all mixes with a combined index covering strength and surface wear together.
pmc-13467133:
Wang and colleagues tested a 2026 concrete made from coal gangue and slag, industrial wastes bound into a geopolymer instead of cement. Basalt fibres reinforce the mix, and tiny silica particles, called nano-SiO2, might tighten its pores and slow cracking. The team varied the silica dose and watched strength, water uptake, and crack growth.

A half percent dose performed best by a wide margin in Wang's tests on the hardened material. Compressive strength rose about eighteen percent and splitting strength about forty percent over the plain reference mix. Water absorption fell, total porosity dropped from near fourteen percent to about five percent, and peak crack width more than halved. Higher doses helped less, which the authors link to poorer particle dispersion.
pmc-13468133:
Zeng and colleagues report a 2026 physics study naming a new effect, the piezochiral effect, in which squeezing or stretching a crystal gives it a handed twist. Flipping the strain direction, or switching from squeezing to stretching, flips the induced handedness. A strain dial for handedness could serve fields from spin electronics to chemistry that must favor one mirror form of a molecule over the other.
pmc-13468333:
Palafox and co-authors analyze a chemically tweaked building block of RNA in this 2026 computational and spectroscopic study. Their molecule is 6-chloro-3-methyluracil. It is ordinary uracil with a chlorine atom and a methyl group attached. Those changes raise its chemical reactivity. They make it interesting as a possible drug ingredient.

The team measured the molecule's infrared and Raman spectra in solid form. They matched the readings against quantum-chemical calculations. The models covered the isolated molecule, a three-molecule crystal, and the molecule inside a short double-stranded RNA helix. Swapping the modified base into the helix in place of uracil noticeably deformed the structure. That hints it could interfere with cancer-related or viral RNA. Computer docking also suggested the molecule fits the active site of a protein complex. The complex involves beta-catenin, a known cancer target.
pmc-13468633:
Sebastian W. Simon and colleagues report in 2026 a simple route to highly active supported catalysts for hydrogenation, the workhorse reaction behind fuels, foods, and fine chemicals. The complex is parked on SBA-15, a porous silica, and finished with hydrogen treatment at elevated temperature.

The resulting materials hydrogenated a wide range of olefins under mild conditions with high activity. Photoelectron spectroscopy on the palladium version showed only part of the metal fully reduced to the active state. Remarkably, the remaining oxidized fraction barely changed after the catalyst was recycled ten times. A catalyst that is easy to make, easy to fish out of the product, and stable across many reuses attacks the main cost of hydrogenation chemistry, which is the precious metal itself.
pmc-13468833:
Górecka and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the gene OXCT1 and its enzyme SCOT, the gatekeeper letting tissues burn ketones for fuel. Ketones are backup fuel molecules made during fasting. The enzyme passes a chemical tag between molecules, unlocking ketones for the cell's main energy cycle. Long treated as a simple metabolic worker, the gene now looks like a wider regulator, and the review pairs published work with database analysis across cancers and tissues.

Several layers of control emerged. The gene also produces non-coding RNAs, copies that regulate rather than build proteins, appearing in multiple cancers. Chemical tags on the enzyme tune its activity with nutrient and stress signals. Gene activity swings widely across cancer types and metabolic states, fitting a role in fuel adaptation. Beyond cancer, faults here touch metabolic disorders, brain disease, and heart muscle disease, and the authors nominate OXCT1 as a drug target.
pmc-13469233:
Tomas Oppenheim and co-authors build in 2026 a wearable hand tracker that costs about a hundred dollars and can be put on by a naive user in five minutes. The system combines soft stretchable electronic skin sensors that read finger bending with inertial measurement units for the wrist, giving quantitative hand kinematics outside the laboratory. Stroke rehabilitation needs exactly that: therapists urge patients to reuse the weakened hand at home, yet almost nothing measures how much or how well it is used there.

The team demonstrated multi-hour tracking out of the lab, robust operation, and an estimated device cost of 111 dollars, falling to about 55 dollars at scale. Fast, unaided setup is the headline feature, because a rehabilitation wearable that needs a technician will stay in the clinic. Continuous, affordable hand measurement could finally show whether home practice is happening and working.
pmc-13469833:
Yu and colleagues described in 2026 the co-design of ENHANCE, a coach-supported phone app for dementia prevention in underserved older adults. The team built the programme with 162 community people, public helpers, and design experts between 2023 and 2025. The app targets ten changeable dementia risk factors, from blood pressure to hearing.

Co-design produced module plans for each risk factor and guiding rules for low-literacy, culturally fitting content. The final app has a meadow theme, tailored check-ins, short videos, brain-training games, and in-app messaging. A structured coaching model adds human onboarding and brief follow-ups by phone or message. Testing rounds simplified menus and language, cut text load, and kept game formats familiar. One week of testing with coaching support left a prototype ready for pilot trials.
pmc-13470333:
Li and co-authors review how molecular classification is reorganising endometrial cancer treatment. Their 2026 paper surveys one of the commonest gynaecological cancers, where early-stage disease does well but advanced and metastatic cases still face limited options and poor outcomes. The review covers the standard pillars of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy before turning to classification-driven strategies.

One is the PI3K and AKT and mTOR chain. The other is the RAS and RAF and MEK and ERK chain. Both are frequently disturbed in this cancer. Immunotherapy and combination regimens are presented as the emerging frontier. The authors argue that respecting the cancer's molecular heterogeneity is the route to individualised treatment selection and better outcomes.
pmc-13471033:
Jie Qiu and co-authors warn in 2026 that climate change is shifting China farm nitrogen pollution toward its driest regions. Fertilizer runoff from cropland supplies over forty percent of the nitrogen reaching rivers worldwide, feeding algal overgrowth. The team fused close to fifteen hundred field observations into maps that balance runoff against how well waterways retain nitrogen.

Today the humid south exports the most cropland nitrogen to rivers, roughly double the arid share. Under two future climate paths, southern exports dip slightly by 2050 as warmer waters retain more nitrogen. Northern dryland exports instead surge, rising by a fifth to over a half, because runoff amplifies nonlinearly there. The authors urge policy to follow the moving hotspot, cutting nitrogen at the source in arid and semi arid farmland first.
pmc-13471133:
Zeeshan Ahmad Bhutta, Dohee Ahn, Hong Kyu Lee, and Kyung-Chul Choi evaluate in 2026 a pomegranate compound as a candidate treatment for endometrial cancer. This womb cancer is growing more common, and advanced or returning cases have few options. The compound, punicalagin, was tested on two endometrial cancer cell lines and in mice carrying human tumors.

Rising doses slowed cell growth and colony formation, and the compound blocked cell migration while restoring a marker of cells staying put, a shift against spread. Treated cells lost mitochondrial voltage, built up reactive oxygen, and died by programmed death with raised death signals. Signs of self digestion appeared too, strongest in one cell line. In mice, tumors shrank in volume and weight while body weight held steady. The authors call for further preclinical and clinical study.
pmc-13471233:
Alisa Hamilton and colleagues offer in 2026 practical guidelines for building infectious disease models that take sex and gender seriously. Biology and social roles both shape who gets exposed. They also shape who seeks care and who is reached by services. Yet many outbreak models ignore those forces. Their guidance was adapted from an established evaluation framework. It lists five moves: split populations by sex or gender, add a second social divider, and keep the split in reported results. It also asks modelers to answer the needs of each group and ground the model with local participation.

A scoping review then tested how often modelers actually do this. Of more than seven thousand papers screened across HIV, COVID-19, and malaria, only forty five qualified. Nearly all modeled HIV. Most discussed local care access, stigma, and gender norms in partnership patterns and occupational risk.
pmc-13471333:
Chuah and co-authors asked what helps or blocks heart-health screening for children in Malaysian primary care clinics. Their 2026 qualitative study drew on interviews and group discussions with 51 people, including policymakers, clinic staff, teenagers, and parents.

Barriers appeared at every level: clinics lacked staff time, child-specific training, and money for tests such as cholesterol and glucose checks. Parents often saw little need to screen a child who seemed well, and teenagers struggled to answer questions on diet, sleep, and exercise. On the positive side, staff said the checks were simple to run and could build on existing school and adolescent health programs. Two coders working independently reached 93.1% agreement on shared transcripts, which supports the reliability of the coding.
pmc-13471433:
Baspinar and co-authors surveyed doctors and nurses in five Istanbul hospitals about why medical errors so often go unreported. Their 2026 cross-sectional study gathered 705 healthcare professionals, 43.7% physicians and 56.3% nurses, and modeled how workplace rank and fear of judgment shape reporting attitudes.

More than half the respondents, 51.9% of them, had witnessed a medical error in the past year, yet only 4.5% held positive attitudes toward reporting errors. Mediation analysis showed fear of negative evaluation carried part of the effect of power distance, with a standardized path of 0.020 linking the two. The authors argue that easing steep rank gaps and softening blame could open up safety reporting.
pmc-13471633:
Zeyu Ye, Sai Yu, Leming Liao, Zebin Zhang, and Li Lv pool in 2026 the trial evidence on structured exercise after hip replacement surgery. Twenty two studies with more than seventeen hundred participants compared planned exercise against standard care after a first hip replacement for arthritis.

Exercise clearly improved hip abduction strength in the first six months, with the benefit fading to uncertainty beyond a year. Hip flexion strength showed no real gain. A standard hip function score improved at every early checkpoint through twelve weeks, though the one year estimate was too scattered to trust. Motion range results were likewise inconclusive. The reviewers grade the early strength and function gains as moderately certain.
pmc-13471833:
Chae Yeon Kim, Sunghun Kim, and Bo-yong Park split in 2026 autism into subtypes using the left right imbalance of brain activity. Social and communication differences in autism tie closely to brain lateralization, so the team measured how unevenly each brain region sits in the connectivity network. One subtype, marked by atypical asymmetry along the sensory to default axis, carried the heaviest clinical severity. The rightward leaning subtype showed underconnection across sensory and association regions and a profile tied to self reference and motivation. The leftward subtype showed overconnection and a profile tied to memory and language systems. The authors argue asymmetry offers a cleaner sorting lens than symptoms alone.
pmc-13471933:
Melanie Penner and Rebecca McNally Keehn argue in 2026, in a commentary, for a lifespan approach to autism assessment that replaces the single big evaluation. Their framework rests on three principles for organizing assessment as a lifelong, precision service.

First, assessment should not be a single, uniform event; it continues across the life course. Second, each assessment should answer questions relevant to the person current stage and needs. Third, community based expertise should be engaged wherever possible, so people get a fitting assessment when and where they need it. The authors claim the shift would ease access backlogs while serving needs that change from childhood through old age.
pmc-13472033:
Francesco Romano and colleagues image in 2026 the walls of retinal veins in eyes where dye tests show leakage, comparing two causes side by side. Twenty nine eyes with leakage from a blocked retinal vein or from active uveitis were scanned with a high resolution form of optical coherence tomography along the leaking veins. Healthy matched vessels served as the comparison.

Forty veins were measured in all. Blocked vein eyes showed wider vein lumens, thicker inner retina, and fluid like spaces, with the outer wall largely spared. Uveitis eyes instead changed most in the outer wall, a contrasting signature the authors detail with thickness numbers. A subset of uveitis eyes was rescanned after the inflammation settled into remission, letting the team watch the wall changes evolve. The patterns may help separate causes without dye.
pmc-13472933:
Gonzalez Santa-Catalina and colleagues explored in 2026 whether patterns in tumor DNA floating in blood can predict who resists immune checkpoint drugs in advanced lung cancer. Standard markers, PD-L1 levels and mutation burden, leave much of the variation unexplained. The team sequenced blood tumor DNA from 37 patients starting first-line immune therapy.

Median progression-free survival was nine months and overall survival twenty months in this group. Mutation burden looked similar in patients with good and poor outcomes. Copy-number signatures, which summarize large gains and losses in chromosomes, separated the outcome groups most clearly. One signature tied to unstable genomes ran higher in poor-outcome patients, while another marked the best responders. None survived strict statistical correction, so the authors call the work hypothesis-generating.
pmc-13473033:
Fang and co-authors investigated NRAV, a long noncoding RNA, as a possible warning flag in liver cancer, combining database mining with cell experiments. Their 2026 study compared NRAV levels across cancer genome cohorts, paired tumor and normal samples, and independent validation sets, then knocked the RNA down in liver cancer cells.

As a diagnostic marker it discriminated cancer from normal tissue with an AUC of 0.901 on the standard scale. Tumors rich in NRAV also showed reduced CD8 T cell presence, tying the marker to an immune-colder microenvironment, and silencing it blunted malignant behavior in vitro.
pmc-13473333:
Hui Ying Khoo and two colleagues tested in 2026 a breast-conserving technique designed to hide scars and protect shape after tumour removal. Breast-conserving surgery plus radiotherapy matches mastectomy for survival, but clear margins and a good cosmetic result stay difficult for deep or awkward tumours. Their method, called S-SMARTS, marks tissue with sutures, minimises visible scarring, and fills the defect by sliding fat flaps from the armpit and side of the chest.
