Clear margins were reached at first excision in 95.5 percent of cases and in every case after frozen-section checks during surgery. Independent cosmetic scoring rated 76.2 percent of results good or excellent and 23.8 percent fair. No factor reliably predicted a positive margin. The authors call the approach feasible with acceptable early results, while noting that one surgeon's cases need wider, comparative testing.
pmc-13474833:
Wei Zhang and co-authors pool studies in 2026 on exercise during pregnancy and depression before and after birth. Twenty-three studies from ten countries held nearly one hundred twenty-three thousand people. Dose-response math asked how much activity links to how much protection. Both straight-line and curved fits were tested.

Each added block of weekly activity tied to about a six percent lower risk of depression before birth. The curve bottomed out at a moderate weekly dose and faded at very high doses. Late pregnancy showed the clearest gain, while mid-pregnancy and after-birth links were not firm. The dose curve helps shape safe activity advice in pregnancy.
pmc-13475233:
Wolbink and colleagues externally validate a widely used breast cancer prediction tool in older Dutch women in this 2026 population study. PREDICT version 3.1 estimates survival and treatment benefit, but older women face more competing causes of death, which can skew its forecasts. Using the Dutch Cancer Registry, the team compared predicted and observed survival for 11,041 women aged 70 and over, with a median age near 76 years.

The tool overestimated survival at both horizons checked. At five years it ran about seven percentage points high. At ten years it ran about twelve points high, against the observed outcomes in this cohort. Its ability to rank patients was moderate, with discrimination scores near 0.75, but the forecasts themselves were systematically too optimistic. The overestimation grew with age and with the number of other health conditions a woman had.
pmc-13475533:
Federspiel and colleagues present a 2026 review of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the most common inherited heart muscle disease, in which the left ventricle wall thickens. Faulty variants in muscle fiber genes explain many cases, yet genetic and non-genetic causes converge on the same picture: stiff filling and over-strong contraction. The review asks whether heart development explains that convergence.

The authors compare immature and mature heart muscle, cell by cell and trait by trait. Young heart tissue differs in metabolism, structure, and growth signals, and disease tissue appears to fall back toward some of those young patterns. Early adaptation later turns harmful, priming the thickening that defines the disease. If diseased hearts partly re-run a development program, treatments might target the switch points of that program, not only its end-stage mechanics.
pmc-13475833:
Iskander and colleagues studied in 2026 whether a gentler catheter technique protects the tricuspid valve during ductus closure in tiny preterm babies. Valve leakage progressed in about a third of babies with the old technique, but in only about seven percent with the new one. Progressions in the new group were mild only, while the old group included jumps to moderate leakage. The difference was statistically significant despite the small sample. The authors conclude the softer crossing technique reduces harm to the tricuspid valve.
pmc-13478033:
Matteo Ferrari and coauthors published a 2026 cultivation study on Chrysotila, a marine microalga that builds chalky shell plates called coccoliths. Because the organism uses carbon dioxide for both growth and shell building, it interests researchers working on biological carbon capture. Best growth came at 600 milligrams per liter of nitrogen under strong light, reaching about one gram of biomass per liter per day. Calcium additions and light schedule changes barely moved the shell-to-biomass ratio, a tension the study maps for future process design.
pmc-13478633:

pmc-13479533:
Kirsty Roberts and coauthors published a 2026 commentary arguing that translation and interpreting must be planned across the whole life of a clinical trial, not sprinkled at recruitment. pmc-13479733:
Miłosz Miedziaszczyk and coauthors published a 2026 study of the triglyceride-glucose index as a prognostic marker in peritoneal dialysis patients. Heart disease kills more of these patients than any other cause, and insulin resistance feeds that risk. The index, computed from routine fasting labs, served as the exposure in two cohorts: 278 patients new to dialysis and 178 already established on it.

Average index values ran higher in the established cohort. Among new patients, two-year survival fell step by step across index quartiles, from about 84 percent in the lowest to about 74 percent in the highest. After adjustment for other factors, the index lost independent predictive power for survival. The authors report a marker that stratifies risk crudely but adds little beyond standard variables.
pmc-13479833:
Su Shuxia and coauthors published a 2026 five-year evaluation of a school dental policy in Dongying District, China. In 2018 the city began offering free fissure sealants and school-based oral health education. Permanent teeth told a better story, with clear declines in both decay rate and the decay index, while baby teeth barely moved. Filling rates for decayed teeth also rose across the period. The authors read the pattern as real but modest progress, strongest where sealants physically protect new permanent molars.
pmc-13480033:
Eric Yi-Liang Shen and co-authors report a 2026 study of a cell surface protein called HEPACAM2 in rectal cancer. pmc-13480233:

pmc-13480833:

pmc-13483033:

The new version also lets users change island size and spacing rules that were fixed before. pmc-13483433:

Those twin novelties let them seize the new alpine ground, and species poured in. Andean barberries stayed evergreen and faced less high ground, so their count grew modestly. Fresh traits meeting fresh land, the authors argue, is the pairing that builds a hotspot.
pmc-13483533:

pmc-13483633:

pmc-13483833:
Jing Zhang and colleagues track how Mongolian gulls cross a dry plateau with few wetlands on long migrations between central Asia and East Asian coasts. Published in 2026, the study uses satellite tracking from 2018 to 2025, covering dozens of coastal and inland legs in both spring and autumn. pmc-13485133:

pmc-13486633:

pmc-13487433:

pmc-13488133:

pmc-13488233:

pmc-13488333:

pmc-13490433:

pmc-13490733:

pmc-13491733:

pmc-13492033:
Nasibe Soltaninejad and others examine the link between working memory and grammar in Persian-speaking children with high-functioning autism. In 2026, the study recruits twenty monolingual children and assesses grammar from speech samples scored with a Persian developmental sentence system. The strongest link appeared between overall grammar scores and repetition of three-syllable non-words, while most grammar subtests correlated clearly with memory tasks, ranging from weak to strong. pmc-13492433:
Al-Taei and colleagues report a 2026 case of Erdheim-Chester disease, a rare disorder where abnormal immune cells build up in organs, showing itself as complete heart block. In complete heart block the electrical signal that sets the heartbeat fails to pass between the heart's upper and lower chambers. Scans showed tissue infiltrating the heart, and the team argue the disease belongs on the list of possible causes when conduction problems have no clear explanation.

Care for such patients, the authors stress, needs cardiologists, radiologists, cancer specialists, and pathologists working together, supported by advanced imaging and biopsy to confirm the diagnosis early. Drugs that target the BRAF and MEK pathways, which drive growth in many of these cases, can improve outcomes, and interferon alfa is another option. Even on targeted treatment, heart block can still develop, so the authors call for close rhythm monitoring and follow-up.
pmc-13492833:
Falahchai and colleagues assessed in 2026 how dental students at Guilan Dental School in Iran rate their educational environment. Learning climate shapes performance, especially in clinical training. The team surveyed 168 students across all six years using the fifty-item DREEM questionnaire. It scores five domains: learning, teachers, academic self-perception, atmosphere, and social self-perception.

The mean total score was about 102 out of 200, a middling rating. The teacher domain drew the most positive responses, with students most often saying things were moving in the right direction. Overall quality ratings did not differ significantly by age or gender. Academic self-perception, though, fell as students advanced through the years, a significant negative trend. The authors conclude some domains are rated positively while social self-perception needs improvement.
pmc-13493933:
Laura Sierra Heras and Christophe Danelon present autocatalytic selection, a way to evolve gene functions inside a minimal DNA self-replicator. In 2026, the method inserts a gene of interest into the replicator and links its action to gene copying, protein building, or DNA copying through positive feedback. More active variants then copy themselves more and take over the group.

The authors demonstrate selection for gene copying, for regenerating a DNA building block from a precursor, and for beta-galactosidase action, a function unrelated to the central dogma. Metabolically active replicators were also enriched from a randomly mutated library. The work streamlines building complex man-made cells and engineering useful enzymes by Darwinian evolution in vitro.
pmc-13494033:
Šimková and colleagues ask how strongly the shapes of human back teeth vary together, a question that matters for evolution studies and dentistry alike. Working from micro-CT scans of 526 teeth belonging to 136 people, their 2026 analysis measured the three-dimensional shape of the inner dentine crown in premolars and molars, skipping wisdom teeth. They then computed how closely each tooth's shape predicted every other tooth's shape within the same mouth.

Teeth in the same jaw tracked each other most closely, with neighbouring premolars in the lower jaw showing near-lockstep covariation. Biting partners also matched strongly, the upper and lower first molars most of all, while some non-biting pairs surprised the team with high scores. Teeth doing similar chewing jobs covaried more than chance pairs. Crown height and proportions drove most of the pattern, beyond simple size effects.
pmc-13499733:
Pasquinelli, in a 2026 philosophical essay, proposes reading artificial intelligence through three organising metaphors of modern thought: the machine, the organism, and language. Philosophy of science usually stresses the organism-machine analogy, from early clockwork analogies to cybernetics. Pasquinelli shifts attention to the language-machine analogy. It runs from the telegraph through the Turing machine and information theory to today's large language models.

Against the story of AI as mathematics or as imitation of biological brains, the essay argues that AI systems automate something social. What they automate is the patterns laid down through human cooperation, work's division, and culture itself. Language models, on this reading, are machines built from language understood as collective work. That history of formalising labour explains both their power and their limits. The conclusion urges judging AI as a mirror of the social order that produced it rather than a technical marvel.
pmc-13500033:
Bruna Elise da Silva Messias leads a randomised trial testing whether adding a breathing exercise device to standard cardiac rehabilitation helps patients recover after heart surgery. Incentive spirometry coaches deep breaths through a volume-based gadget meant to reopen lungs, while rehabilitation followed a seven-step graded activity protocol. The trial ran in two hospitals and enrolled 46 inpatients, assigned to rehab alone or rehab plus the breathing device, each delivered twice daily.

Both groups lost respiratory muscle strength and walking distance after surgery, as expected in early recovery. Adding the device brought no significant advantage on any main outcome, since lung complication rates, grip strength, and hospital stay all matched the rehab-only group within the reported comparisons. One imbalance deserves note, because the device group spent longer on the heart-lung machine during surgery, yet outcomes still converged, and the authors conclude the device added nothing measurable here.
pmc-13500533:
Sai Li and others compare two 7-tesla MRI sequences for visualizing dorsal nigral hyperintensity, a swallow-tail sign whose loss supports Parkinson disease finding. In 2026, the forward-looking study enrolls thirty-three patients and fifty-two healthy controls, each scanned with CLEAR-DESS and susceptibility-weighted imaging, assessed by four blinded observers plus quantitative signal tests.

CLEAR-DESS outperformed susceptibility imaging at both lesion and patient levels, with rightness scores up to 0.96 versus 0.85, sensitivity up to ninety-six percent versus seventy percent, and better signal and contrast ratios. Inter-observer agreement was excellent for both. The authors propose CLEAR-DESS as the preferred sequence for evaluating this Parkinson marker.
pmc-13500733:
Ruixi Liu and others develop and validate a scale testing first-visit dental patients' experience with AI question-answering systems. In 2026, the Chinese-language study builds an initial item pool from literature and expert panels and refines it through two Delphi rounds. It then tests it in 305 first-visit patients at a Chinese hospital, split for exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis. No dedicated tool existed for this setting.

The final scale holds ten items in a single dimension, with strong content validity, high factor loadings, and excellent reliability, including a Cronbach alpha of 0.981, though one fit index for error approximation was weaker. Clinics gain a same-form way to judge AI waiting-room services on explanation rightness, anxiety relief, personalization, and willingness to recommend.
pmc-13501533:
Alexandru Vlad writes a 2026 commentary on a route for recycling fluoropolymers, the plastics built around strong carbon-fluorine bonds. PTFE, the toughest example, resists breakdown so well that recycling has meant pouring in energy through heat, grinding, or electrochemistry. Vlad discusses a study by Liu and co-workers in National Science Review, where touching PTFE with a liquid sodium-potassium alloy starts the chemistry instead. Contact triggers electron transfer at the surface, launching a Wurtz-type defluorination cascade that then sustains itself.

Once started, the heat-releasing reaction keeps breaking carbon-fluorine bonds with no further energy input. The process converts PTFE into fluorine-doped porous carbon plus alkali-metal fluorides, turning stubborn waste into something useful. The carbon performed well in supercapacitor tests and captured carbon dioxide. Vlad frames the lesson as reaction-network design: arrange the chemistry so the waste supplies the force for its own conversion.
pmc-13503433:
Jennifer Bolton leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 pilot trial of Baby-Feed, a website that scores what infants eat and coaches their caregivers. Early diet quality is often poor, and rapid weight gain forecasts later obesity. At a health centre, fifty caregivers of term infants aged four to twelve months were randomized for three months to usual care or the website. The site assesses the baby's diet from a food frequency questionnaire, returns results, and gives feedback.

Both groups' diet scores slipped as babies aged, but the website group slipped far less: a change of minus 2.95 against minus 7.69 points for controls, a real difference on the analysis. Healthy weight gain was commoner among website babies, 95 percent against 58 percent in the control group. Caregiver confidence gains tracked fruit and juice score improvements only in the intervention arm. The authors call for a larger, longer trial to confirm the signal.
pmc-13503733:
Camille M Montalcini and Thomas W Crowther ask what drives a country to protect animals, in a 2026 study. They built two scores for each country, one from laws and enforcement and one from how much animal product people make and eat. Wealth was long thought to be the main driver.

Their analysis found that free speech and citizen voice in public life beat wealth as a guide. A measure of voice and accountability alone explained 59 percent of the spread in protection scores, against 44 percent for income per person. The result held across rich and poor states alike. The authors argue that open civic life lays the ground on which animal laws can grow.
pmc-13503933:
Dwi Sendi Priyono leads a team reporting the first full mitochondrial genome of the Javan hawk-eagle, in a 2026 paper. The bird is Indonesia's national symbol and an endangered top predator on Java. Habitat loss and illegal trade press it hard, yet no gene data existed for it.

Reading machines assembled a circular genome of nearly 18,000 letters. It holds the standard bird set of 37 genes, plus two control zones, one with a string of repeats. Letter use leaned toward A and T bases. Family tree analysis placed the eagle in a subfamily that split off about twelve million years ago, with a Malayan eagle as its closest kin. The data now support population studies, forensic work on traded birds, and protection plans.
pmc-13504833:
Cara G Ghiglieri leads a team asking ICU survivors and staff how remote rehab after critical illness feels, in a 2026 interview study. Survivors often face long physical and mental recovery with patchy support at home. A UK trial tested a remote program with several parts against standard care.

Thirty-five survivors and six staff from twenty-four hospital sites were interviewed. Those in the remote program valued its structure, steady contact, and help in building confidence and self-care skills. Standard care often felt scattered, with survivors left to steer recovery alone. Digital delivery and peer support pleased many but not all; readiness and home context shaped the fit. The authors back structured, flexible rehab paths built into post-ICU care.
pmc-13507133:
Tamoghna Saha leads a 2026 team that built a smart ring able to track body chemistry from sweat, not just pulse and sleep signals. The ring draws sweat without effort or skin shocks and reads glucose, ketone, vitamin C, uric acid, lactate, and alcohol at once. Flexible zinc-silver batteries and compact electronics send data wirelessly.

The ring ran for about twelve hours per charge, and personal calibration held for about two months. Glucose and ketone readings matched blood meters and standard glucose monitors in healthy users and in people with type 1 diabetes. Trials covered varied daily settings. Multi-chemical tracking could sharpen daily choices for diabetes care.
pmc-13507333:
Yebao Wang, Junyi Zhang, Feng Lv, Ting Zhang, and Yafeng Zhou test, in 2026 work, whether the drug finerenone directly shields heart and vessel cells after heart attack. Finerenone blocks a hormone receptor that drives scarring, and trials suggest benefit, but direct cell protection was unproven. Starved-oxygen cell models mimicked attack conditions, and mice received the drug daily for four weeks after induced infarction.

Treated heart and vessel lining cells survived better, cleared waste sacs faster instead of clogging, and died less by programmed death. Vessel cells also migrated and formed tubes more readily. In mice, pumping improved, scar size shrank, and inflammation and fibrosis eased. Growth signals for new vessels rose in heart tissue.
pmc-13508233:
Achyoot Sharan Koirala and four co-authors describe a 72-year-old Nepali man whose long-standing gout had formed hard lumps, and who died after a brain bleed, in a 2026 case report. He had lived with high blood pressure for 15 years and poorly controlled gout for 12 years. He arrived after a fall with reduced awareness, very high blood pressure, and weakness on his left side. Exam found gout lumps at his elbows, knuckles, big toes, one heel tendon, and both knees. Blood uric acid was markedly high.

Brain imaging showed a deep bleed that had broken into the fluid spaces. Despite intensive care he worsened, left against medical advice, and died five days later. Doctors judged the bleed came from the blood pressure crisis itself. The case warns that untreated high uric acid signals wider damage, and it stresses steady urate-lowering treatment plus heart risk control in gout patients.
pmc-13508433:
Shuang Hou, Hexin Shen, and Yong Zhang rebuild the test used to judge computer tools that predict droplet-forming proteins, in 2026 work. Such proteins clump into liquid droplets that organize cell chemistry, a process called phase separation. Predictors are ranked on benchmark sets, but the authors show a recent benchmark is rigged by accident. Its droplet proteins and its ordinary proteins differ in species origin and in floppy region content, so tools can score well by learning those shortcuts instead of droplet behavior. The team built a fairer benchmark matched on both traits.

On the clean test, scores dropped to honest levels and varied widely by species group. Raw feature values of droplet proteins differed sharply across species, yet their shifts against local background stayed similar. Proteins without floppy regions proved hardest for every method. Testing nineteen predictors this way gives developers a truer target.
pmc-13509533:
Zhongjie Wang, Xinyang Xu, Qiuli Pan, Yajuan Li, and Liya Huang report a seven-day diary study of stress and thoughts of suicide among college students, published in 2026. Sixty-one Chinese students with valid records supplied 427 daily entries in total. Each day they rated felt stress, sense of connection to others, feelings of disgust toward themselves, and thoughts of suicide.

On days when a student felt more stress than usual, connection to others tended to dip and self-disgust tended to rise the same day. Higher self-disgust went with stronger thoughts of suicide that day, and the chain through lower connection and higher self-disgust held as well. These links appeared within single days for the same person, not across students as steady traits. The authors say daily support may matter most on high-stress days.
pmc-13510033:
Mohamed and colleagues studied in 2026 how low vitamin D tracks with blood health in Sudanese patients with sickle cell disease. In that inherited fault, red blood cells bend into a sickle shape. Low vitamin D is common in these patients, but data from Sudan, where the disease is widespread, were scarce. The team recruited 50 patients at a blood clinic.

Blood tests showed that over half the patients lacked enough vitamin D, and only about one in six had healthy levels. Patients with lower vitamin D had less hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen, and suffered more pain crises each year, when blocked vessels cause sharp attacks. The link held even after age, sex, and drug use were taken into account. The authors advise routine vitamin D checks and trials of supplements.
pmc-13510633:
Zeina Radwan and ten co-authors test an extract from a red seaweed as a helper for chemotherapy in colorectal cancer cells, in 2026 work. Standard drugs for this cancer often cause heavy side effects and meet resistance. The extract, drawn with a solvent mix from the alga Jania rubens, had already shown direct growth-slowing effects in earlier work by the team.

Paired with either of two standard drugs, the extract killed more cancer cells and slowed their spread in two of three cell lines tested. The pairing also cut long-term colony growth, hinting at action against stubborn cell pockets. Cell death rose in a dose-linked way, a key survival protein fell, and genes for inflammatory signals shifted. The authors present the extract as a candidate add-on that may deepen drug response, while noting all tests so far are in lab cell lines.
pmc-13511433:
Bennett O. V. Shum and six co-authors test gene sequencing as the first step of newborn screening for three rare diseases, in 2026 work. Current heel-prick screening for severe combined immune deficiency and cystic fibrosis flags many healthy babies, sending families into anxious follow-up. The team ran targeted sequencing on 3025 newborns alongside the standard tests for those two diseases plus spinal muscular atrophy.

Sequencing found one baby with cystic fibrosis whom the standard test had missed, and it caught the spinal condition case the standard panel found. It produced zero false alarms across all three diseases. Standard screening, by contrast, produced roughly nine false alarms for each true case found. The authors say swapping in sequencing could cut false positives sharply and may raise detection for cystic fibrosis, though a larger trial must settle accuracy and cost.
pmc-13511533:
Teresa Ravizza and colleagues review in 2026 how gut microbes and their chemical products may shape acquired epilepsy, seizures that arise after brain injury or illness. Two product families take center stage: short-chain fatty acids from fiber fermentation, and compounds made from the amino acid tryptophan.

The review gathers evidence that disturbed gut communities alter both families, which in turn sway inflammation, the blood-brain barrier, and how excitable brain cells become. Animal studies that adjust the microbiota change seizure patterns and related brain damage. Still, the authors stress that the two-way traffic between gut and brain is far from mapped. They frame these pathways as candidate sources of new treatments and warning markers.
pmc-13512033:
Phassorn Khumfu and five co-authors test a heat-responsive wound gel blending aloe vera extract, silk protein, and chitosan, in 2026 work. Test cells mimic chronic diabetic wound conditions. Such wounds stall under lasting inflammation and heavy oxidative stress. The team exposed macrophage-like cells and diabetic skin fibroblasts to the mix and the gel, both at rest and under a cocktail of inflammatory triggers.

Both forms kept cell survival high, showing good compatibility with living tissue. Under inflammatory pressure, treated cells held far less reactive oxygen and released less of two key inflammatory signals. A central inflammation switch quieted in both cell types. Macrophages also shifted toward a repair-oriented form marked by low attack signals and high healing markers. The authors present the gel as a multi-action candidate for calming diabetic wound cells.
pmc-13514233:
Bianca Liana Grigorescu and colleagues review how artificial intelligence could fuse the flood of data from intensive care patients into one live picture. Critically ill patients change fast, with many failing systems at once, so their data outgrow human tracking.

AI tools can merge body signals, lab results, and clinical notes to flag decline earlier and tailor bedside choices. The review finds the tools promising yet little used in real practice so far. Hard proof is missing: few prospective studies and few checks that the tools work when deployed live. Sepsis care ranks among the most relevant uses the review names. Grigorescu insists doctors must give the output clinical meaning, with biology, not software, as the base.
pmc-13515433:
Shen introduces the second edition of a journal special issue on how food shapes the gut microbiota, the community of microbes living in the digestive tract, in a 2026 editorial. The first edition appeared in 2023, and the follow-up gathers eight articles from scientists in five countries. The studies span farm animals, laboratory models, and human subjects, covering forages, dietary supplements, probiotics, and traditional herbs.

Four of the eight studies concern livestock, linking feed types and growth patterns to gut health. One highlighted trial fed laying hens dried olive pulp and found more beneficial Megasphaera and Megamonas bacteria in 59-week-old birds than in controls. Hens on the higher dose also laid eggs with the darkest yolks at 39 weeks of age. Broken eggshells fell by between 15 and 34 percent in the olive pulp groups compared with controls.
pmc-13515833:
Cheol Woong Kim, Geonwoo Park, and Hae June Lee simulate a plasma used to pattern atom-thin MoS2 in a 2026 study. Etching such films without damage means controlling which ions arrive, how hard, and at what angle. The team modelled an argon-oxygen discharge driven at low voltage, varying the gas mix from argon-rich to oxygen-rich. They tracked particles, electric potential, and the energy and angle of ions striking the centre and edge of the electrode.

More oxygen thinned the electrons, swelled negative oxygen ions, and flipped the main positive ion from argon to oxygen. Ion energies mostly rose with oxygen, though unevenly, and edge fields tilted the incoming angles. Linking ion and oxygen-radical flows through a simple surface scheme exposed a trade-off: very argon-rich and very oxygen-rich mixes both look damaging.
pmc-13517433:
Khondoker Mohammad Iftekhar Zahan leads a seven-author survey of gut parasites in Thai cattle in a 2026 study. Kanchanaburi province sits on the Myanmar border, where traded cattle cross freely and parasites travel with them. The team tested local and cross-border herds for worm and protozoan infections and looked for the farm practices that raise risk.

Just under thirty-six percent of cattle carried gut parasites. Strongyle-type worms, the thread-necked roundworm family, were the commonest find, and border herds showed both high infection rates and rich parasite variety. Farmers dewormed often, yet nobody checked whether the drugs still worked, a blind spot the authors flag hard. Zahan's team calls for routine checks of drug performance and tighter parasite control along the border trade routes, where one region's herd health quickly becomes the other's.
pmc-13517833:
Amalia Papanikolopoulou, Ilektra Tseliou, and Helena C Maltezou review the thin shelf of measles treatments in a 2026 article. A vaccine exists, yet measles still killed about ninety-five thousand people in 2024, and no licensed drug treats it: care is supportive only. The authors survey a decade of work on candidate agents, from repurposed antivirals to immune proteins.

Ribavirin leads the pack from severe-case use, though no randomised trial backs it, and new polymer and nanoparticle carriers sharpen its punch without added cell harm. Two younger families, blockers of the virus's fusion protein and of its copying enzyme, performed well in animals. Interferons matter most for brain infection, and scattered reports describe stubborn brain disease steadying briefly under repeated courses. Papanikolopoulou's team calls progress extremely slow and the need urgent, since lab promise has yet to become ward-ready proof.
pmc-13518033:
Potalivo and colleagues reported a 2026 emergency department case in which ultrasound revealed a tension hydrocele. A tension hydrocele is a fluid sac around the testicle grown large enough to squeeze off its blood supply. A 57-year-old man arrived with right scrotal swelling. ultrasound, scanning done by the treating clinician at the bedside, showed a large hydrocele with reduced blood flow inside the testicle, a pattern that threatens the organ's survival.

Potalivo describes how the emergency physician drained the fluid with a needle under ultrasound guidance, after which the man's symptoms resolved and normal testicular blood flow returned on repeat scanning. The authors present the drainage as a potentially testicle-saving measure when urology help is delayed. They present the case as the first report of ultrasound-guided aspiration for this condition, widening the list of causes emergency clinicians should consider in sudden scrotal pain.
pmc-13518933:
Yu Zeng leads an eleven-author team tracing in 2026 how low oxygen inside glioblastoma tumors breeds resistance to the frontline drug temozolomide. Circular RNAs, ring-shaped RNA molecules, were a missing piece of that resistance puzzle. Multiomics profiling plus experiments in patient-derived cells, mouse tumors, and clinical samples spotlight one ring, circSPECC1.

Oxygen shortage switches circSPECC1 on through the HIF-1 alpha factor. The ring then scaffolds a partner protein, IGF2BP2, to stabilize the message for PGK1, an enzyme that speeds sugar burning. Faster glycolysis blunted drug-induced DNA damage and protected the tumor. Silencing circSPECC1 restored drug sensitivity and extended survival in mouse models, marking a targetable weakness.
pmc-13520333:
Jinmin Su and colleagues traced a molecular chain that drives liver cancer aggression. Published in 2026, the study measured three molecules in 179 paired tumor and nearby tissue samples plus cell lines. They were a long noncoding RNA called MIR9-3HG, a small RNA called let-7c-5p, and a protein called THBS1. Liver cancer is often found late and moves fast, so markers that flag aggressive disease carry real value.

MIR9-3HG ran high in tumors, tracking with advanced stage, higher grade, vessel invasion, and poorer survival as an independent risk marker. Lab tests showed it soaks up let-7c-5p, freeing THBS1 to rise, and silencing MIR9-3HG slowed cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion. The authors propose the RNA as both a prognostic marker and a future drug target. Readers get a complete chain from tissue signal to cell behavior.
pmc-13521033:
Muhammad Talha Sami and colleagues report a study, published in 2026. It counts hepatitis B and C in chronic kidney disease patients. The setting is a teaching hospital in Lahore, Pakistan. Both viruses are common in Pakistan. They add serious liver risk to kidney patients. The team reviewed past records. They counted infections and looked for links with patient traits.

Hepatitis C was highly common in this group. Hepatitis B was much rarer. Testing positive for C tied to male sex and city living. Longer kidney disease and later stage also tied in. Heart disease, past transfusions, and dialysis history mattered too. Testing positive for B linked to female sex and diabetes. The authors call for routine screening and tighter infection control.
pmc-13522533:
Franchi and colleagues introduce BayFlood in 2026, a method that detects flooded streets from dashboard camera images using a vision-language model, an artificial intelligence system that interprets pictures. Cities now rely on sparse sensors and resident reports, which miss many neighborhoods. Dash cameras already record street scenes at huge scale, and the team asked whether that footage could fill the gaps without hand-labeled training data.

They validated the method on 1,440,184 images, and its flood detections lined up with known predictors of flood risk across several cities and time periods. Applied to New York City, the analysis found flooding in neighborhoods that current methods overlook, exposed demographic biases in existing detection, and suggested locations where new flood sensors would help most. The authors argue that dense street-level imagery can make flood monitoring faster and fairer, and that the same approach could spot other street incidents.
pmc-13523533:
Sakurako Nomura and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, sugar decorations on human IgE, the antibody class central to type I allergy. The tail region of IgE carries four possible attachment sites for glycans, branched sugar chains. One site, Asn394, mainly holds a high-mannose type, whose role was poorly understood.

The team expressed normal IgE tail constructs and mutants in mammalian cells. Removing the Asn394 sugar sharply impaired secretion, showing it is needed for proper folding and release, while a mutant lacking complex sugars was secreted normally. Stripping high-mannose sugars lowered thermal stability. Mass spectrometry showed the sugars on the two heavy chains pair without selectivity. The authors conclude this single sugar site underpins both secretion and stability of the antibody tail.
pmc-13524133:
Kim and Jeong reported in 2026 a case that shows how two kidney function estimates can disagree in a telling way. A woman in her seventies had a kidney fornix rupture, a tear where urine collects, caused by a blocking ureter stone, with urine leaking behind the abdomen lining. Such leaks can raise creatinine in the blood because spilled creatinine is reabsorbed, faking kidney failure.

Kim tracked both creatinine-based and cystatin C-based filtration estimates through her surgery to relieve the blockage. The gap between them started large and positive, flipped negative on the morning of surgery, and settled to a small positive value a week later. Creatinine alone had fallen to near normal and could have faked recovery, while the other marker disagreed. The authors show the moving gap helped separate fake azotemia, raised waste levels without true failure, from real kidney function.
pmc-13525133:
Amponsah and colleagues study what drove COVID 19 prevention habits in Ghana's informal settlements in this 2026 paper. Crowded settlements with poor services saw uneven uptake of protective behaviour during the pandemic. The team used a model linking information, motivation, and practical skills to action. They surveyed residents of three informal settlements in Ghana.

The survey covered 496 people, and only about three in ten answered every knowledge question correctly. Both personal motivation and social motivation were directly linked to preventive behaviour. Knowledge alone showed no direct link, because its effect ran entirely through practical skills. Amponsah argues that future outbreak plans should build skills and motivation, not just hand out information, in vulnerable settlements.
pmc-13525833:
Heinecke and colleagues check whether a first-year self-test predicts dermatology board success. Their 2026 paper uses deidentified American Board of Dermatology data for 1,585 residents from 2018 to 2023. Under the new certification model, residents take a self-assessment Basic Exam in year one. Core Exams follow during training and an Applied Exam afterwards. The authors asked if the early score forecasts the later outcomes.

Residents who eventually passed the certification exams scored significantly higher on the Basic Exam than those who failed. Optimal warning thresholds varied by exam, with total scores between about 76 and 80 and percentile ranks between about 22 and 38 percent. Using an average threshold of about the 31st percentile would have flagged 77 percent of eventual failures. Demographic data were unavailable, a stated limitation. The authors support using the early exam to target help at struggling residents.
pmc-13526833:
Christensen and colleagues reported a 2026 structural biology study of the sodium potassium pump, a protein that moves sodium out of cells and potassium in. That pumping keeps the electric gradients animal cells depend on. Variants of the pump are tuned to each tissue, including a neuron specific form found in brain cells.

Using cryo-electron microscopy, a method that images frozen proteins, Christensen captured the pump while it was actively working. Structures covered the common human form and the neuron specific form across four shapes in the pumping cycle. One shape held sodium just before its release, revealing a key rearrangement. A mutant linked to alternating hemiplegia of childhood, a movement disorder, damaged a fat binding pocket and weakened stimulation by certain fats.
pmc-13528033:
Zhongting Huang and ten colleagues build a pathway-level model of DNA methylation for asthma in a 2026 study. Single methylation sites are hard to interpret. This team grouped sites into biological pathways instead. Data came from 908 people across one training group and three check groups. A classifier learned from pathway scores, and a method called SHAP ranked each pathway's weight.

The model sorted asthma well in two airway tissue groups. It did moderately well in blood samples. Top pathways involved amino acid use, airway development, and nerve-immune signaling. Some pathways acted through eosinophil cells and nitric oxide inflammation. Two pathways acted directly, bypassing those middle steps. The authors say pathway scores tie severity to biology in a readable way. That may guide more targeted asthma research.
pmc-13528133:
Yuanhua Dai, Jun Chang, and Jing Guo compare two blood thinner families after a heart plug procedure in a 2026 meta-analysis. The plug seals the heart's left atrial appendage, where clots form in atrial fibrillation. Patients still need thinners for a while. The team pooled studies from 2017 to 2025 comparing newer direct drugs with older vitamin K blockers.

Twenty-one studies entered the pool. The newer drugs cut serious bleeding modestly, with odds about twelve percent lower. A combined bad-event measure also favored them by a similar margin. Stroke and body-wide clot rates did not differ clearly. Leaks around the device and clots on it matched too. The authors warn most studies were not randomized. Certainty sits at moderate to low. They call the newer drugs a reasonable pick, not a proven winner.
pmc-13528333:
Xie and colleagues built an artificial intelligence system to predict why surgical patients end up back in theatre unexpectedly, information hospitals need to fix quality problems. Most earlier work mined records retrospectively for single diseases. Their 2026 system, called MPSUR, learned from 2,922 cases across 15 departments in eight hospitals between 2015 and 2024. It fused structured data like age and laboratory series with free clinical text through graph and recurrent neural networks.

In a reader study, the system beat surgeons at naming the true cause of reoperation, reaching mean accuracy around sixty percent while the human readers scored lower across every department tested. Removing the procedure performed and the department from its inputs hurt performance most, which tells developers where the predictive signal concentrates. The authors present the tool as decision support for quality review boards, triaging which reoperations deserve deep case review.
pmc-13529133:
Hsu and Chiu reported a 2026 eye case in which a pet bird's bite damaged a corneal flap fourteen years after laser vision surgery. A 40-year-old woman came in a week after the bite with blurred vision and irritation in her left eye. LASIK flaps, the thin corneal layers cut during laser in situ keratomileusis, never regain full strength and can shift after trauma even decades later.

Hsu describes examination findings of a displaced flap with ragged edges, surface cells growing underneath it, and a full-thickness hole near the center of vision. Surgeons repositioned the flap the same day, and later episodes of cell ingrowth were managed with lubricating drops made from the patient's blood serum plus repeated laser treatments. Her corrected vision improved from 20/50 to 20/25, with no further ingrowth over long follow-up, showing that prompt repair and staged follow-up can salvage flap injuries.
pmc-13529633:
Sumaiya Binte Khalid and three colleagues survey depression in Bangladeshi women who live with polycystic ovary syndrome in a 2026 study. The hormone disorder is common and often distressing. Four hundred seventeen women aged eighteen to thirty took part. They came from clinics, digital health services, and online support groups. A standard nine-question scale scored depressive symptoms.

About two-thirds showed moderate to severe symptoms. Moderate cases were the largest band at thirty-six percent. Severe symptoms hit about thirty-one percent. pmc-13530233:

A large share of cases carry underlying liver disease, matching the patients who most need major liver surgery. The dataset was validated for preoperative planning of major hepatectomy and supports model building, vessel-shape research, and patient-specific 3D vascular roadmaps. The authors present it as a foundation for AI that helps surgeons navigate complex liver anatomy. Readers get a clinically grounded dataset, with model performance to be proven next.
pmc-13530633:

Position players returned at nearly ninety-three percent and took about 285 days, while pitchers returned at under forty-four percent and needed about 493 days to reach a major league mound. pmc-13531533:
Sinéad Teresa Jennifer McDonagh and colleagues weigh in 2026 whether wearable devices should join blood pressure care in primary practice. Undiagnosed high blood pressure keeps rising, while the recommended day-long cuff test sees uneven use. Watches, wristbands, and rings now estimate pressure from light pulses on the skin.

Continuous readings could even catch pressure drops on standing, a fall risk that clinics test poorly today. The authors urge clinicians and systems to prepare now for handling wearable data well.
pmc-13531833:
Nandita Chowdhury, Indranil Bhattacharjee, and Goutam Chandra report in 2026 a mosquito-killing bacterium found inside dead larvae of a filariasis-carrying mosquito. pmc-13531933:

pmc-13533833:
Marie-Renee El Kamouh and colleagues study in 2026 how venous blood flow in the brain affects pressure and waste clearance. pmc-13535733:
Sahan D Chandrasekara and Matthew T Naughton update in 2026 knowledge on central sleep apnoea, a pattern of paused breathing during sleep driven by brain control rather than a blocked airway. Care should target the cause first, the authors stress. For leftover cases, options such as breathing stimulants, tailored pressure therapy, added oxygen, or nerve pacing remain debated without strong proof. One pressure mode raised deaths in weak-heart patients, so caution guides current practice.
pmc-13536633:
Zhihao Han, Zheyi Jiang, and Xiaoqin Ma sort in 2026 early-career operating room nurses in China into career growth profiles using resources theory. pmc-13538333:
Takuya Mino and colleagues build a learning model to predict dental implant placement error before guided surgery in a 2026 study. The authors suggest the model can support pre-surgery review of expected accuracy, helping clinicians adjust plans before operating rather than discovering drift afterward.
pmc-13540833:
Ping Wang and colleagues simulate screw placement in a 2026 imaging study. The screws go into the top neck vertebra, called C1. Some people are born with a bony bridge over the groove of that bone. CT scans from 141 people fed a planning program. The program tested screw sizes and paths on screen. Tight clearance was commonest when the bridge sat on both sides. Medium screws stayed feasible in most cases. Bigger screws caused more simulated artery violations. Two simple measurements predicted safe placement well in this exercise.
pmc-13540933:
Jeanette Finderup and six colleagues build, in a 2026 Danish Delphi study, expert-agreed guidance for managing physical symptoms in advanced kidney disease. Patients and kidney professionals both need help choosing among the many drug and non-drug options on offer.

A literature search produced 216 options, and panellists added eighty more from practice. Over seventy percent agreement, the consensus bar, was reached for 242 interventions. The final round ranked them by importance and how often they are used. The authors present the guidance as groundwork for support tools that clinics can test next.
pmc-13543433:
In a 2026 study, Jianying Liu and colleagues asked whether simple blood ratios can predict vein clots, or death, in advanced lung cancer patients receiving immune checkpoint drugs. Clots are a serious complication in this group, and inflammation and clotting systems are entangled. The retrospective cohort held 206 patients treated between 2020 and 2024. The other two ratios did not predict clots, though the analysis also explored mortality pathways separately. Cheap routine labs, the authors suggest, may outperform established clot scores in this specific treatment setting.
pmc-13543533:
Wenhui Wang's team studied ozone nano water in 2026, a green disinfectant carrying ozone in microscopic bubbles, against drug-resistant Escherichia coli, a foodborne germ troubling farms and clinics. Four germ strains were tested, three of them clinical isolates resistant to many drugs. The team checked the product's bubble sizes and stability. They then timed killing speed and biofilm suppression, and viewed cell damage under several microscopes and a light-scattering technique.

Images showed torn membranes, and molecular patterns of walls, membranes, genes, and energy stores all faded, pointing to multi-target oxidative injury rather than a single weak point. Exposed bacteria kept their drug sensitivity across three generations, a sign the disinfectant kills without training resistance. The authors propose it for medical and farm hygiene where resistance is a growing fear.
pmc-13543633:
Liqi Yi and colleagues published a 2026 study building a urine test strategy for watching non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, which returns so often that patients face lifelong scope examinations. It also cut the second test's workload by about a third, and a negative combined result was right about ninety-one percent of the time. pmc-13545633:
Xinwei Cheng and colleagues presented in 2026 a lung cancer case where one lesion on a scan did not behave like the others, and that mismatch changed the diagnosis. A 67-year-old man with advanced lung adenosquamous carcinoma had a PET/CT scan after four rounds of chemotherapy. His main tumor and the lymph node spread around it still took up the radioactive tracer strongly.

A nodule in his left armpit took up far less tracer and had not changed size. Knowing the man had previously lost part of that arm, the team suspected something benign, and tissue examination proved a traumatic neuroma, a tangle of regrowing nerve fibers. The authors argue that uneven tracer uptake between lesions, read alongside the patient's history, can prevent benign growths from being misread as metastasis.
pmc-13548533:
Candice Babarit and a large team of collaborators study muscle damage markers in Pompe disease, a 2026 investigation spanning mouse tissue and patient biopsies. Biopsies from people with late-onset disease showed matching patterns in moderately affected muscle, fading where damage was most advanced. Mature myostatin, a brake on muscle growth, also built up persistently. The findings point to stalled membrane repair and altered growth control as features of the disease's muscle remodeling.
pmc-13548933:
James Laurence Ruello and colleagues present a flexible film that adjusts how much heat it radiates, switching itself between keeping warmth and shedding it, in a 2026 materials paper. The film embeds tungsten-doped vanadium dioxide, which changes phase near room-side temperatures, plus transparent conductor particles inside a polyethylene sheet backed with aluminum. Tuning the particle loading and thickness produced an optimal recipe for infrared modulation.

In the key nine to eleven micrometer band, the film's transmission swung by up to about forty percent. Around forty degrees Celsius it flipped between heat-conserving and radiative-cooling modes with no power input, venting heat toward the sky when warm. Repeated heating cycles left performance intact, thanks to the tough plastic base. The authors pitch the scalable film for buildings, enclosures, and mobile systems aiming at zero-energy temperature control.
pmc-13549133:
Bauckneht and co-authors published a 2026 review on frailty in older men receiving a targeted radiation drug for advanced prostate cancer. Decisions should rest on life expectancy, other illnesses, and frailty, which means reduced strength and reserve. The review presents geriatric assessment tools that grade frailty in clinic and matches treatment advice to each frailty level.
pmc-13554433:

They found Rg3 binds ORAI1 directly, raising calcium inside cells and loosening contacts between the membrane and the endoplasmic reticulum. Mutating two key channel residues erased the calcium influx, weakened a protective AMPK-NRF2 pathway, and dulled the anti-senescence effect. The work names ORAI1 as the compound's mediator and offers a concrete target for ginseng-based ageing research.
pmc-13554633:
Chih-Chung Lin and colleagues pooled trial evidence on diabetes drugs called SGLT2 inhibitors for heart outcomes in chronic lung disease, publishing the meta-analysis in 2026. These drugs already protect heart and kidney in diabetes and heart failure, but their value in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease was unclear. Treatment cut the combined risk of cardiovascular death and heart-failure hospitalisation by about a quarter, driven mainly by fewer hospitalisations, while overall mortality and cardiovascular death only trended downward. Adverse events were similar between groups. The authors urge caution given only three trials, but the result supports larger studies of these drugs in lung-disease patients at cardiac risk.
pmc-13558333:
Richard Kellermayer and five colleagues rethink dolichocolon care. Dolichocolon, a long winding colon first noted in 1820, stays missed in clinical care. Their 2026 review looks at PubMed and Scopus studies from 1900 to 2024. It sums up anatomy, case rates, and possible clinical meaning.

Estimates place dolichocolon in 10 to 20 percent of people, linked to constipation, volvulus, and possibly gut inflammation. Proposed causes include stasis and ischemia in redundant loops, altered nerve-muscle signaling, and added mucosal surface driving immune-microbe contact. pmc-13558633:
Manuel Alonso Dos Santos and three colleagues trained in 2026 machine learning models to predict how satisfied gym members feel, and to name what drives that feeling. Random forest won clearly, with the strongest discrimination and overall accuracy near eighty-nine percent. The factors carrying the prediction were the centre's overall environment, trust in employees, staff quality, and how waiting times are handled. The authors argue that machine learning gives managers an interpretable ranking of service levers, not just a score. Investment in atmosphere and staff, their results say, buys more satisfaction than equipment alone would suggest.
pmc-13558733:

pmc-13560133:

pmc-13560233:

pmc-13560333:

pmc-13560433:

pmc-13562333:

pmc-13562533:

pmc-13562633:

pmc-13569433:

Brain effects without craving change suggest the method engages its target but needs more work, perhaps repeated sessions, to help patients.
pmc-13569833:

Predicted vibration behavior and surface error met targets, and shake tests matched the models within about ten percent for most readings. pmc-13574333:

pmc-13575133:

pmc-13575233:

pmc-13576033:

pmc-13576133:

pmc-13576233:

Extracted data will be grouped into themes, mapped by region, and scanned for gaps. pmc-13576733:

pmc-13578333:

Two of the seven linked only to aggressive forms, while the rest tied mainly to slower forms. The authors call for larger studies to confirm the list and work out what drives the links.
pmc-13578433:

pmc-13579733:
Jesús Alejandro Ríos-Solis and colleagues review the wild plant trade in Mexico's traditional markets, in a 2026 paper. The tally reached nine hundred two species across one hundred thirty one plant families, with orchids and cacti near the top. pmc-13580633:
Shreya Jha, Julie Birrell, and Karen Leslie tell how songwriting lessons took root in a hospital day program for teens with substance use trouble, in a 2026 narrative piece. Jha, who trained in music composition before medicine, had seen self expression through music steady her own mind and lift children in a free lessons program for poor youth. A medical school project opened the door to try it in care.

The Toronto program pairs treatment with school credit, five days a week. A team of a trainee doctor, a physician, a teacher, music therapists, and youth counselors adapted a classroom songwriting course for the group. The piece reflects on what making songs offered young patients: a voice, a finished thing to own, and relief that words alone had not given.
pmc-13582033:
Aneta Aleksova and colleagues find a split story for heart attack patients whose hearts stop inside the hospital, in a 2026 study. Restart speed was the hinge, the authors argue, which puts all weight on instant response teams and drills.
pmc-13583133:
Emma Whyte, Theophilus I Emeto, Frances Snowden, and Vinay Gangathimmaiah describe how one Australian hospital used a nose-spray sedative for children in its emergency department. The drug, dexmedetomidine, calms children without a needle, which matters when the planned task itself is a drip line, a cut repair, or a burn dressing. Townsville University Hospital had just put a new guide for the spray into practice.

Over seven months, 114 children aged 1 to 16 received the spray, most often for drip placement or stitching. It worked on its own in about four of five cases, and younger children did best of all. Side effects arose in roughly one child in eight, mostly a slow heart rate that stayed mild, while parents and staff rated the care highly.
pmc-13587433:
Nurit Dessau and colleagues grade fifteen years of Israeli health policy aimed at closing the north-south health gap. Israel's Northern District has long trailed the center in beds, doctors, and outcomes, despite repeated ministry plans. Their 2026 study paired hard counts from 2009 to 2024 with a close reading of ten policy papers from the same years.

The counts showed the gaps holding firm: fewer hospital beds, physicians, and allied health staff per person in the north at the end than fairness would demand. Of the ten policy papers, only four spoke to the northern district at all. The authors blame three habits: weak seats for the periphery at the decision table, choices made centrally, and a fading focus on place-based gaps. Without a stronger voice for the north, they argue, the pattern will persist.
pmc-13589133:
Hechuan Wang and nine colleagues read the chemical marks on goose DNA for clues to longer egg-laying runs. A clutch is the string of eggs a goose lays without a break, and the trait's regulation was nearly unmapped. From 280 individually housed Zi geese with daily laying records, the team picked three long-clutch and three short-clutch birds and profiled their ovary tissue with two sequencing methods in 2026.

One method mapped methylation, the DNA's dimmer tags, finding over six hundred thousand differing regions; the other mapped open, readable DNA, finding about nine hundred differing stretches. Genes near the marks clustered around egg-cell support growth, hormone readiness, and the remodeling that precedes laying. One gene, RERE, was backed by both layers of evidence, and spot checks of gene activity matched the marks. The authors call the atlas a starting resource, not a finished answer.
pmc-13591833:
Yaxin Xu leads a 2026 review of biased signaling at the beta2 adrenergic receptor, a switch on cell surfaces that answers adrenaline like signals. A drug that flips the switch can favor one downstream route over others, giving distinct effects in the body. The review traces how this bias works and where it matters: heart and lung health, brain control, immunity, and tumor growth all feature.

Classic signaling runs through G proteins, while routes via beta-arrestin and other arms can protect or harm in different settings. Drugs tuned to one arm could treat asthma or heart failure with fewer side effects, the authors argue. Xu and the team call for clearer maps of the switch's shape and fresh biased drug candidates.
pmc-13591933:
Fei Yang and Haitao Xiong build, in 2026, a planning method for sharing energy and labor across China's provinces to lift output while cutting carbon. Their approach starts from efficiency analysis and adds two twists: it credits future technology gains, and it lets each region be judged against its own peer group frontier. Targets are set centrally yet kept within reach, province by province.

Applied to 30 provinces, the best shuffle of energy use and workers raised total output by nearly seven percent over 2023 levels, with vast carbon savings on paper too. Labor sat badly shared between eastern and central regions. Yang and Xiong advise giving growth modestly more weight than emission cuts when setting the plan's balance.
pmc-13592633:
Lin Qin and five colleagues test a greener binder for expansive soil, the kind that swells when wet and shrinks when dry, cracking foundations. Their mix, called LSP, blends lime and sodium silicate into phosphogypsum, a factory waste. Lab samples were packed, soaked, and put through repeated drying and wetting rounds while strength, swelling, and water flow traits were tracked. Microscopy and pore scans probed why the traits moved.

Treated soil packed denser, swelled far less, and held together better at the start. Repeated wet dry cycles still wore every gain down: strength fell about a quarter after fifteen rounds and water passed more freely. Filling of pores by the waste powder did the early good, Qin and the team found, while tiny cracks drove the later decline.
pmc-13592833:
Stefania Spina and colleagues read all gold-standard trials of body-based care for arm pain after stroke. Such pain hits a big share of stroke survivors and curbs arm use, rehab, and life quality. Twelve trials with 567 people made the cut, with six on electric care, three on shock-wave care, and three on laser care, searched through July 2025.

Most trials showed clear pain drops versus sham or plain care. Electric care gave pain relief that held, shock-wave care eased both pain and tissue faults, and laser care eased pain and daily use. Harms were mostly mild, but harm notes were patchy. Proof strength was low to very low, so these tools fit best as one part of mixed rehab, not as lone cures.
pmc-13593633:
Dimitrios Charemis and colleagues built a model of how dead-space pockets in the brain block drug transport in Alzheimer's disease. Lab tests show these pockets hinder drug entry, but most models capture them only sideways through maze-effect settings. Their 2026 model treats dead space as sealed blocks in the outside-cell space, tuned against lab spread timing.

Drug-arrival delays hinged strongly on drug size: the target level contour reached a vein 11 seconds late for memantine, 14 seconds late for donepezil, and 80 seconds late for aducanumab. Overall uptake missed these local delays. Checks showed transport stays spread-ruled under sick-brain states. The authors present the model as a base for forward-looking brain drug-transport models.
pmc-13596933:
Timothy Brandt, Dhara D. Shah, and Gina Cassel-Choudhury report a quality improvement project in a 26-bed pediatric intensive care unit that set out to cut prescriber medication errors by forty percent over about two years. Children with complex chronic conditions were the focus, since their long home medication lists make admission ordering error-prone.

Five improvement cycles attacked the drivers: no standard process for reconciling medications, high-risk drugs silently expiring, and the difficulty of rebuilding home lists for complicated children. The headline error rate per thousand orders stayed flat, with no special pattern over time. Yet admission reconciliation errors for the complex chronic group fell by a mean of forty-three percent with a clear downward shift, helped by pharmacist-supported reconciliation and standardized workflows. The authors claim the narrower, process-level win for the highest-risk children.
pmc-13597633:
Yella Hewings-Martin and colleagues studied how orgasm rates and sexual variety relate to satisfaction in sex with a partner and solo sex. Orgasm rates with a partner are known to predict satisfaction, but solo orgasms and variety were less understood. Their 2026 survey covered 27,931 Flo app users, nearly all women, averaging about 28 years old, reporting on 13 with-partner and 13 solo activities over six months.

Orgasm rates with a partner and variety with a partner both went with higher satisfaction. Solo orgasm rates showed a weak negative link, and solo variety went with neither satisfaction nor orgasm rates. Solo orgasms ran highest with vibrator or dildo use, porn or erotica, and hand stimulation. Partnered peaks came with sex toys, vaginal sex with clitoral touch, and self-touch with a partner present. For matched acts, solo orgasm rates ran higher throughout.
pmc-13600633:
Prajakta Kakde and five colleagues present a 2026 case of Heyde's syndrome, a little-known cause of gut bleeding in the elderly. The condition joins a severely narrowed aortic valve, fragile vessel tangles in the bowel, and loss of a clotting protein, von Willebrand factor. Their patient, a 72-year-old man, had passed black stools for six months, growing anemic and tired despite several hospital stays.

Standard stomach and colon scopes found no bleeding source. A heart ultrasound showed severe calcified valve narrowing, blood tests confirmed the missing protein, and a swallowed camera found the fragile vessels in the upper small bowel. Supportive care and scope treatment failed to stop the bleeding, so surgeons replaced the valve. Afterward the bleeding stopped for good, his blood counts recovered, and the clotting protein returned. Check for this trio, the authors stress, when gut bleeding in an older person defies the usual search.
pmc-13601633:
Jhalak Singhal leads an eleven-author team reporting a 2026 host-targeted strategy against two parasites. Leishmania donovani causes visceral leishmaniasis, and Plasmodium falciparum causes the deadliest malaria; both exploit a human signaling protein, p38-MAPK, to survive inside our cells. Rather than attack the parasites directly, the team used a designer molecule, NR-7h, that tags the host protein for destruction: a PROTAC.

NR-7h removed p38-MAPK from host cells, dose by dose and hour by hour. As the protein fell, parasite loads fell with it. In Leishmania infection, treatment also shifted immune signals tied to parasite death, and it strengthened the standard drug amphotericin B. In malaria parasites, growth slowed and red cell invasion faltered. Destroying a host protein the parasites depend on, the authors argue, could sidestep drug resistance: the target belongs to the patient, not the pathogen.
pmc-13602033:
Matias and de Freitas describe in 2026 CaDENCE, a very large dataset of call disconnection events harvested from consumer Android phones. It was built to study why mobile calls drop. The records began as routine quality telemetry collected by the phones themselves.

An instrumentation layer in the operating system logged signal quality, network type, and service state whenever a call ended, and the events flowed to a manufacturer warehouse. The researchers filtered, standardized, anonymized, and labeled the records, keeping those for packet-switched voice services over modern mobile and Wi-Fi calling. The release holds over 125 million event records gathered across 98 days in spring 2024 from phones running two recent Android versions. Each record carries timing, device, network, and signal fields plus a label marking dropped calls, and the files ship with schema documentation and processing scripts.
pmc-13602533:
Gina Madera leads a six-author team evaluating in 2026 a United Kingdom 'passport' for acute oncology skills. Cancer patients can become urgently ill anywhere, yet no standard test of acute oncology competence existed for the staff who meet them. Clinicians and cancer educators co-designed a digital competence assessment attached to an introductory e-learning module, forming the Level 1 Acute Oncology Passport.

The passport was piloted across the UK, with 376 staff answering before and 176 after completing it. Confidence in acute oncology knowledge and skills rose significantly. Learners judged the material relevant, correctly pitched, and a fair measure of competence. The main complaint was lack of study time, and many wanted workplace support to keep building skills afterward. The co-designed passport is engaging and acceptable, the authors argue, but protected time is essential if e-learning is to mean safer care.
pmc-13612933:
Keiko Mori, Miina Yamazaki, and Yoshiyuki Haruna examine how immersive virtual reality can turn nursing students' awareness of disasters into real readiness to act. Knowing about flood and landslide risks does not always lead people to prepare, a gap the authors place at the centre of their study. Twelve nursing students in Japan, from undergraduate and graduate courses, took part in virtual reality simulations of floods and landslides.

After the simulations, each student sat for a one-to-one interview about their feelings, their sense of risk, and what they felt moved to do. The authors trace how a vivid, first-person experience can shake the calm distance that lectures often leave intact. Their findings speak to teachers who want disaster training to change behaviour, not just to inform, in future health and critical care practice.
pmc-13616233:
Shiyuan Zheng leads a team presenting in 2026 a glowing reporter system. It tracks, moment by moment, how a signal protein called STAT6 switches macrophages into their healing mode. Macrophages are a type of immune cell. Two messenger chemicals, interleukin 4 and interleukin 13, flip that switch, and the resulting cell state matters in wound repair, immune calming, and tumour growth. The team built human immune cells carrying a light-making gene wired to STAT6's docking sites.

The reporter faithfully mirrored the protein's real activity, checked against several standard lab methods. A systems model then tied the glow's time pattern back to the steps of the signalling chain inside the cell. Reading cell change as a light signature over time gives drug testers a live dial for a process they used to sample only in snapshots.
pmc-13616333:
Michael Leonidas Chikindas leads a large team arguing that fish farming should move beyond live probiotics to postbiotics, preparations of dead microbes and their products, for keeping farmed fish healthy. Live probiotics are popular as antibiotic use tightens, yet their effects swing wildly with fish species, gut shape, and water conditions like salt, acidity, and heat. Living doses also risk disturbing wild microbes and spreading antibiotic resistance genes.

Postbiotics keep the helpful chemistry without the living risk: they are stable, dose-controlled, and safer by design. The review weighs the trial record for both approaches across aquaculture. For an industry feeding a growing world population under strict drug limits, a shelf-stable, predictable health additive could be the difference between a promising idea and daily practice on the farm.
pmc-13616633:
Jae Woo Lee and colleagues ask which cut-off on the caloric balance test best matches the video head impulse test when judging one-sided inner ear failure in patients with sudden vertigo. The two tests probe the balance organ at different speeds and often disagree. The standard caloric cut-off of 25 percent weakness on one side may not line up with the quick head-turn test. The team reviewed patients seen within 72 hours of vertigo onset who took both tests at a referral centre.

They compared several candidate cut-offs against the head impulse verdict, excluding patients whose picture suggested common mimics like positional vertigo or Ménière's disease. Choosing the threshold that agrees best helps clinics read the older caloric test in the terms of the newer one, cutting confusion when the two answers clash at the bedside.
pmc-13618933:
Rubing Huang and two colleagues design a neural network that spots industrial surface defects from a handful of labeled examples, a chronic problem. Defect photos are scarce, defect sizes vary wildly, and textured metal backgrounds trigger false alarms. Their Prototype-Aligned Multi-Scale Attention Network fuses features at several scales. It applies attention over space and channels, and classifies regions by matching them against class prototypes inside a two-stage detector.

On the NEU-DET steel defect benchmark with five examples per class, the network reached mean average precision above ninety-two percent at the overlap threshold. It also showed strong small-object accuracy and a false response rate near four percent. It beat a Faster R-CNN baseline on every headline measure. Cross-domain testing on a second dataset, GC10-DET, held precision in the mid-eighties. The authors support region-level prototype alignment for limited-label metal inspection.
pmc-13620133:
Zanhong Chen and thirteen colleagues issued an author correction to their 2026 Nature Communications article on nanoscale magnetic tunnel junctions that act as artificial synapses and neurons for brain-like computing. The correction fixes a series of mismatches between figures, figure legends, and text in the first published version. Several labels had been swapped or worded wrongly.

Corrected items include dashed line directions on a microscope image annotation. Two percentage values appeared in reverse order, and a swapped pair of color labels and several legend names needed fixing. Some methods passages also gain missing units or drop a wrong field direction. The authors state plainly that the experimental results, the interpretation of the data, and the article's main conclusions stand unchanged. Updated wording now appears in both the HTML and PDF versions.
pmc-13620833:
Yi Ding, Fan Tong, Jing Zeng, and Chun-Ping Cui review glutamine, the most plentiful amino acid in blood and tissue, and the web of jobs it performs. Glutamine feeds cell growth, steadies acid balance, supports immunity, and supplies building blocks for DNA and proteins. Textbooks call it nonessential, yet during illness and stress the body can run short, making it conditionally essential.

Disease states rewire how cells grab and burn glutamine. Cancer cells lean on it especially hard to keep dividing, hold their chemical balance, and make new material. The review walks through glutamine's synthesis, transport, and use, then its roles under heat, hunger, oxidation, and DNA damage stresses. Later sections cover immune control, treatment resistance, and therapies that block glutamine use alone or in combinations, plus imaging tools that watch this metabolism in patients.
pmc-13621333:
Bo Sun and four colleagues review how broken zinc transporters cause human disease. Zinc is a trace element the body needs for more than a thousand enzyme reactions and thousands of gene switches. Yet cells cannot store it, so daily intake and tight transport rule everything. Two protein families do the hauling: one moves zinc out of the cell fluid, the other pulls it in.

The review catalogs disease-linked variants across both families, ten members on the export side and fourteen on the import side. Each transporter sits in particular tissues and compartments, so a single broken gene can scar one organ system while sparing others. Beyond listing diseases gene by gene, the authors look for converging signaling pathways the variants disturb. They frame that shared map as scaffolding for the next round of mechanism studies and, eventually, targeted treatment ideas.
pmc-13621433:
Angela S Bruzina and five colleagues tested whether uneven limb loading explains why exercise rehab disappoints after volumetric muscle loss, an injury where a chunk of muscle is simply gone. One suspicion was that animals spare the injured leg, starving it of the loading that drives recovery. Twenty-four young mice were split into uninjured runners, injured non-runners, and injured runners with free wheel access for six weeks.

Injured runners did even out their weight bearing until it matched healthy runners, exactly the adaptation coaches would want. Muscle function, though, stayed stubbornly impaired, and the bone next to the injury gained nothing either. Loading, the authors conclude, was never the bottleneck. Something inside the remaining muscle blocks recovery despite normal use, so future rehab research should hunt that mechanism instead of chasing symmetry.
pmc-13623133:
Henry Mollel leads a team counting women in health leadership across Tanzania, where women form most of the health workforce yet hold few top posts. The study uses government data from 2022 covering twenty of the mainland's twenty-six regions. It examines management teams at regional, council, and facility levels, the three tiers that run the public health system.

The data covered 9,120 leadership positions. Women's share came close to half at the facility level, then fell at each higher tier, reaching its lowest in the regional teams. The drop was steepest for the most powerful clinical roles: women held nearly thirty percent of facility chief posts but only about eleven percent of regional medical officer posts. Smaller, lower-level facilities looked more balanced than larger ones. The authors recommend mentoring, fairer promotion, and workplace cultures that open leadership to women, rather than treating the gap as a pipeline problem alone.
pmc-13624033:
Ashley J P Smit and colleagues survey Dutch paediatricians about screening families for poverty during child care visits. Children in poverty get sicker more often and their families miss appointments or struggle to reach support, so children's doctors are well placed to spot trouble. What those doctors actually do was unknown.

Fifty paediatricians answered the 2024 survey. Nearly all had seen money worries block families' access to care. Asking about finances and referring families onward varied widely, and neither step belongs to standard practice today. Doctors named the blockers: few clear places to refer, little knowledge, and no handy tools for spotting poverty or opening the conversation. Even so, a large majority said doctors should play a role here. The authors call for practical support: referral routes, training, and screening tools that fit a busy clinic.
pmc-13624833:
Hadley Ross and six colleagues, publishing in 2026, look back at integrative medicine visits for patients hospitalized during pregnancy. At one large center, between January 2024 and July 2025, some 207 patients asked for or were offered therapies such as aromatherapy, meditation, breathwork, sound therapy, and relaxation coaching. Nurses scored each patient's discomfort on a five-point scale just before and after a visit.

Aromatherapy reached nearly every patient, and mind-body work reached about half. Among 174 patients with paired scores, discomfort typically eased by one step, and three in four reported some relief while none felt worse. With no comparison group, the authors call the gains suggestive rather than proven, and they offer the pattern as a base for controlled trials.
pmc-13628133:
Song and colleagues engineered in 2026 a tweak to antibody-drug conjugates that fixes how many drug units each antibody carries. Conjugates with a uniform drug-to-antibody ratio act more alike in the body. Making a uniform ratio of six drugs per antibody, called DAR6, has been hard. The team mutated one cysteine, a sulfur-bearing amino acid, in the antibody hinge region of a dual-target anti-c-Met antibody.

During testing, extra mass species appeared, traced to mucin-type sugar chains attached at a hinge serine.
