That sugar modification, called O-glycosylation, also appeared in other antibodies with similar hinge mutations. It was therefore not a quirk of one antibody scaffold. Cutting the open sites made the joining step yield uniform DAR6 products every time. The authors present hinge engineering as a flexible route to such conjugates.
pmc-13628533:
Kristina A. Kostadinova and eleven colleagues present a modular kit for assembling medicines that switch on several hormone receptors at once, a strategy behind the newest obesity drugs. Published in 2026, their system replaces the usual one-off construction of each large fusion peptide with a flexible scaffold onto which parts can be clicked in sequence.

The scaffold is built on solid phase without intermediate purification and accepts up to three components, such as therapeutic peptides or units that extend a drug's life in the body. As proof, the team combined GLP-1 and amylin receptor activators into dual-acting constructs with adjustable dosing balance. The leads proved potent at both receptors in cell assays, and the authors offer the platform as a general route to multifunctional peptide medicines.
pmc-13629233:
Peng He and six colleagues extend kinship theory to ask how the size of an animal's social group changes its relatedness to groupmates across its life. Published in 2026, the modelling study builds on the idea that shifting relatedness steers when helping or harming kin pays off, a mechanism invoked to explain menopause in humans and some whales.

Within one connected population split into smaller and larger groups, the models show relatedness running higher and changing faster in small groups, favouring stronger helping or harming, especially among the young. In whale-like systems, the predicted female shift from harming to helping arrives earlier in small groups. The authors trace these effects to a tug between ancestry dilution and lineage merging across the whole population.
pmc-13629533:
Haang Jeung-Maarse and seven colleagues propose a global framework for open science in basic medical training. Medical teaching drills students in judging published proof. Yet it says little about how research is truly made, governed, and shared. That gap matters more as failures to repeat results shake public trust.

Their framework rests on three domains. They cover openness about how knowledge is made. They cover duty in research conduct. They cover how a doctor's identity forms. Together they describe how students should engage with knowledge making, doubt, and duty. The authors do not dictate course plans. They offer flexible principles schools can map onto current structures. Openness, in their view, is part of becoming a doctor. It is not a technical add-on.
pmc-13632533:
John Howieson wrote this commentary on the energy budget of nursing humpback whales. Humpback mothers leave food-rich polar waters for warm tropical breeding grounds, then fast while nursing fast-growing calves. A research team tracked whales off Hawai'i between 2020 and 2025 to price that strategy. Tags on twenty mothers and thirty-one calves recorded swim speed, dives, and tailbeats, while drones filmed behavior and body size from above.

Resting dives, where whales drift below the surface, saved a large share of energy compared with other diving. Older calves rested more as they grew, likely to offset the cost of rapid growth. Mothers burned huge amounts of energy each day while eating nothing. Computer simulations showed that human disturbance could raise daily costs enough to demand far more feeding later. The piece argues that quiet breeding grounds are an energy issue, not just a comfort.
pmc-13632933:
What patients actually want when they message an internet hospital is decoded by Xu and colleagues. They used language tools on real enquiries. Rigid online menus often mismatch what patients mean. That wastes triage time and sends resources to the wrong place. The team analysed more than twenty-eight thousand messages from a large Chinese internet hospital, first clustering them without labels to discover intent types, then training a specialised language model to classify them.

Clustering revealed eight distinct intents, with clear overlap between rehab and follow-up requests. The tuned small model beat two large language models on a gold-standard set of marked records. It also held up better on a separate nationwide dataset. Department patterns differed sharply, since prescription renewals dominated neurology enquiries while first symptom questions dominated dermatology, giving hospitals a measurable basis for redesigning digital services.
pmc-13645233:
Yunfei Wei and twelve colleagues present a study of how a Staphylococcus aureus toxin factor, Sph, drives mammary gland inflammation in mastitis, a costly disease of dairy animals. The enzyme was known to injure host cells, but its pathway to tissue damage was unclear.

Deleting the factor sharply reduced ferroptosis, an iron-linked cell death, during infection. The team traced a chain: the factor binds a mitochondrial organizer, breaks the organelle's inner folds, and spills mitochondrial DNA into the cell. A DNA sensor pathway then sends the protective enzyme GPX4 for destruction, removing the brake on ferroptosis. Blocking the factor could become a mastitis treatment strategy.
pmc-13647133:
Jiang-Bo Li and seven colleagues build a framework linking depression with shorter survival in cancer patients through the body's stress and immune wiring. Depression is common in cancer and tracks with earlier death, yet the biology between mood and tumor has stayed murky. The review joins clinical, population, and lab evidence into one system. The nerve network that sets fight-or-flight tone, the hormone axis that releases stress steroids, and the immune network talk to each other in reinforcing loops.

Together, the trio can create conditions that favor tumor growth, the authors argue. They grade the support at each node and flag open fights, above all about which direction cause runs. Three patient subtypes are proposed, dominated by hormone, inflammation, or immune-killing patterns, to guide future trials. Any therapy built on the framework, they insist, stays experimental until large trials with survival endpoints test it.
pmc-13648633:
Madhu Singh and eleven colleagues link a family of membrane fats called ether lipids to how cells dispose of peroxisomes, the small compartments where those lipids are made, when oxygen runs low. Inherited ether lipid shortages cause severe disease, yet the lipids' everyday roles remain murky.

The team found that the rate-limiting enzyme of ether lipid production doubles as a docking point for the cell's autophagy machinery during low oxygen, making peroxisome breakdown possible. Blocking the pathway stalled breakdown in cells and animals, while feeding lipid precursors switched autophagy on and protected mouse hearts from ischemic injury. The work casts the enzyme as a guardian of peroxisome balance under oxygen stress.
pmc-13649733:
Run Yuan and two colleagues used a 2023 national survey to probe how exercise links to low mood in older Chinese adults. The sample held 2,233 people aged 60 and up. The team tested a chain model in which how people rate their own health, and how good life feels, carry part of the exercise effect.

More exercise tied to fewer signs of low mood, both head-on and through the chain. Over half of the total link ran through the side paths: exercise lifted self-rated health, which lifted life feel, which eased mood. The direct share was just under half. The authors say exercise plans for older adults should feed body and mind at once.
pmc-13649833:
Kai Wai Lee and three colleagues write to the editor in 2026 with sharp doubts on a pooled study of two lupus drugs. The study set the drugs side by side with no head-to-head trial, a method called indirect comparison. The letter says sturdier takes on the same trials, built on single-patient data, are already in print.

The flaws they list are plain. Some end points were read as yes-no counts when the source trials told them as change scores. The chief trial of one drug was left out of the main run. Rules that drug agencies had thrown out were used for the trial that stayed. The writers could not check parts of the data from the paper. They ask what new light the study casts.
pmc-13650433:
Jianan You and one colleague review how lasting changes in gene control help lock in chronic pain. Pain that persists past three months is maintained across sensory nerves, spinal circuits, immune cells, and brain regions, and the review separates three regulatory layers that are often blurred together.

The strongest pattern is not a single mark rising or falling, but targeted reprogramming at specific places in specific cells, silencing pain-dampening genes while switching on pain-promoting and inflammatory ones. Evidence is firmest where experiments changed one site and watched pain behavior shift. Human blood and tissue studies offer candidate signatures, yet none is ready for routine diagnosis or treatment choice. Broad gene-control drugs ease pain in animals, while one targeted drug already failed a mid-stage human trial, a gap the authors say only cell-level, long-term human studies can close.
pmc-13650533:
Guang Ta and six colleagues argue that sarcopenia, the age-related loss of strength, should be studied through the whole muscle-tendon unit rather than muscle alone. Strength and physical performance often fall faster than muscle mass predicts, which suggests the tissues that transmit force matter as much as the tissue that generates it.

Aging processes such as metabolic dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and poor blood supply strike muscle, tendon, and their junction at different rates. That mismatch can leave strong-enough muscle pulling through a weakened junction, wasting force and magnifying disability. Evidence for muscle signaling to tendon is reasonably firm, while tendon-to-muscle effects rest mostly on laboratory co-culture work. The authors propose that the unit view can sharpen exercise prescription and functional testing, while staying compatible with current diagnostic criteria. Tendon changes in diagnosed sarcopenia, they note, remain poorly described.
pmc-13650933:
Neha Mohiuddin and four colleagues optimize a spongelike material for capturing carbon dioxide from wet industrial flue gas, the humid exhaust that defeats many sorbents. Their base is a zirconium metal-organic framework, and they loaded it with an amine called TETA, a chemical known to grab carbon dioxide even in moisture.

Simulated flue gas blended carbon dioxide with water vapor and oxygen. A statistical design method varied temperature, amine loading, sorbent amount, and contact time together. The aim was to find the sweet spot, landing near a moderate temperature with a fifth of the material's weight in amine. The fitted model matched the best measured capacity closely. Capture time and temperature mattered most, while amine loading showed a curved effect with a clear optimum. The material kept most of its capacity after ten reuse cycles, and standard kinetic and isotherm models fit its behavior well.
pmc-13651533:
Xi Chen and eleven colleagues build chemical tags that both locate and count lipid isomers in a single photochemical step. Fat molecules differing only in where a double bond sits can behave very differently in the body, yet ordinary analysis sees one blended mass and cannot separate them.

Their duplex tags latch onto double bonds under light, forming a four-membered ring handle. Hard collisions then release reporter ions that measure the total amount, while softer fragmentation produces bond-position fingerprints carrying the reporter, and a third stage reads each isomer's quantity. The tags quantified fatty acids accurately across a wide concentration span and messy mixtures. Applied to fat tissue from mice on ordinary or high-fat diets, the method found eighteen fatty acids and thirty-seven double-bond variants. It exposed diet-driven remodeling, including opposite shifts within one fatty acid's variants, that total-level analysis had hidden.
pmc-13651633:
Ya-Ru Kuo and seven colleagues feed mice broccoli fermented by a friendly bacterium and watch metabolic disease retreat while muscle holds firm. Fat-and-fructose diets drive the modern pairing of muscle loss with obesity, and fermentation was expected to add useful metabolites to an already healthy vegetable.

Chemical profiling of the fermented broccoli found several new small molecules. Mice on the damaging diet who received the supplement carried less belly fat, less fatty liver, and better insulin sensitivity, and their grip strength survived. Inside the calf muscle, protein-building pathways ran hotter while the tagging enzymes that mark muscle protein for destruction quieted. Gut sequencing showed richer populations of a butyrate-producing species and a bifidobacterium. The authors read the package as gut remodeling plus fermentation chemistry protecting muscle quality, while stopping short of claiming any single ingredient did the work.
pmc-13651833:
Alba Iglesias-Fente and four colleagues screen bubble-like carriers called niosomes for delivering genes into aged stem cells, a delivery problem that blocks many anti-aging gene therapies. Their target cells are senescent stem cells from umbilical cord stroma, coaxed into aging with a cancer drug, with young cells from the same source as controls.

Two formulation families were built around the same charged lipid, varying the soap-like surfactant and helper ingredient across a few ratios. One family clearly outperformed the other in cells from four different donors, in both aged and young states. Its best ratios produced the highest gene expression in senescent cells, beating a leading commercial reagent, while escaping the cell's digestive compartments efficiently and leaving viability intact. The authors present niosomes as sturdy vehicles for genetically modifying senescent cells in future healthspan therapies.
pmc-13652533:
Baptiste Godrie examines how the worth of scientific research gets measured, and who gets to decide what counts. Funding agencies increasingly ask researchers to prove the impact of their work with indicators presented as objective. Those measures justify public spending and let universities display their influence, yet they differ widely in what they capture. From citations and journal prestige inside science to effects on policy, practice, and public well-being outside it.

Health research shows the split clearly, since a finding can be famous among scientists and still never change a single treatment. Godrie argues that choosing indicators is a political act, not a technical one, because each measure rewards some kinds of work and hides others. The essay asks readers to question whose interests a metric serves before treating its numbers as the value of research itself.
pmc-13661533:
Daniela Stastna led a 2026 dual-center study that trained machine-learning models on MRI pattern analysis to tackle three hard problems in skull base chordoma care. These rare, locally invasive tumors mimic cartilage tumors on imaging, hide among post-treatment changes after surgery, and recur often, yet no noninvasive tool addressed all three tasks together. The team studied sixty-one patients operated on between 1998 and 2023, using pre-surgery contrast MRI with nested cross-checks.

Gradient boosting reached 90 percent accuracy separating chordoma from cartilage tumors and background, 91 percent for telling true residual tumor from treatment change, and 87 percent for two-year survival without progression. A neural network performed similarly, slightly better on survival at 93 percent. Clinicians get a candidate tool for pre-surgery assessment, post-surgery watch, and risk grouping, with future validation needed given the small, varied cohort.
pmc-1534033:
van den Berg, Hoefsloot, Westerhuis, and co-authors explain how data handling choices shape metabolomics results. Drawing real biological meaning from huge datasets is a core challenge in modern genomics work. Raw values can mislead, for instance when some molecules differ in amount by thousands of times.

The authors compare centering, scaling, and related transforms that adjust data before analysis. Each choice boosts some signals and mutes others, so picking well matters. Their guidance helps researchers avoid methods that bury true patterns or invent false ones. Cleaner data handling leads to safer claims about health and disease.
pmc-3246833:
Hübschle, Sheldrick, and Dittrich present ShelXle, a graphical interface for the crystallography program SHELXL. SHELXL refines crystal structures, adjusting atomic models to fit X-ray data. Working with it meant editing text files by hand, which is slow and error-prone.

ShelXle features an editor that highlights SHELXL syntax, plus an interactive three-dimensional display of the structure. Seeing the model while editing helps crystallographers spot mistakes at once. The friendly interface made a respected but austere program accessible to far more users.  Colour-blind-safe palettes and export options were added with everyday laboratory users in mind.
pmc-4822133:
Swatek and Komander reviewed ubiquitin modifications in 2016. Ubiquitin is a small protein that cells attach to other proteins to change their fate. This shifting tag plays a part in almost every process in eukaryotic cells, from division to defense.

Once attached, ubiquitin itself can be modified further, creating a multitude of distinct signals. Chains of different shapes tell the cell to destroy a protein, move it, or change its activity. This code-like system is called the ubiquitin code by many researchers. The review maps its forms and readers, knowledge that underpins drugs targeting protein disposal in cancer.
pmc-4849733:
Bowden, Davey Smith, Haycock, and their co-authors proposed a weighted median estimator in 2016 for Mendelian randomization. Summary genetic data had made such analyses relatively straightforward to run. Getting reliable results, though, remained hard when some variants used as instruments are invalid.

Their estimator gives consistent results even when up to a share of the instruments break the rules. It takes a weighted median of the variant-level estimates, so outliers cannot dominate. That robustness matters because invalid variants are common and hard to spot one by one. The method joined the standard checks that causal claims from genetic data must pass.
pmc-5506233:
Burgess and Thompson explained in 2017 how to interpret findings from Mendelian randomization using the MR-Egger method. MR-Egger is a way to run Mendelian randomization tests from summarized genetic data. It consists of three parts: a test for directional pleiotropy, a test for a causal effect, and an estimate of that effect.

Pleiotropy, where variants affect the outcome through other routes, is the main threat to such analyses. The authors set out what each part of MR-Egger can and cannot show. Conventional methods fail when pleiotropy is directional, so a robust option matters. Clear interpretation guidance helps researchers avoid overstating causal claims from genetic data.
pmc-5661633:
Ting Liu, Lingyun Zhang, Donghyun Joo, and coauthors wrote this review of NF-kappaB signaling in 2017. NF-kappaB is a protein complex that switches on genes tied to immune defense and swelling. It sits at the center of how the body reacts to infection and injury.

The review explains how the pathway turns on, which signals control it, and what happens when it stays active too long. Long-lasting activity is linked to chronic swelling and several diseases. By pulling the known steps into one account, the authors give researchers a base for designing drugs that calm harmful inflammation without blocking needed defense.
pmc-5711033:
Gibran Hemani, Kate Tilling, and George Davey Smith wrote this methods paper in 2017. Researchers often want to know which of two related traits causes the other. Genetic data can help, because genes are fixed before either trait appears.

The authors show that sloppy measurement of a trait can flip the apparent direction of cause. They then present a way to use summary data from large genetic studies to judge direction more safely. Getting direction right matters for choosing which trait to treat. The paper warns readers that a strong link alone never proves which side drives the other.
pmc-6148333:
The GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators published this global analysis of alcohol use in 2018. Drinking ranks among the top causes of death and disability worldwide. Its overall effect is tangled, since light drinking has been linked to small gains for some conditions.

The study estimates use and harm across nearly two hundred countries from 1990 to 2016. It weighs deaths and disability from injuries, cancers, liver disease, and heart conditions together. The authors conclude that the level of drinking that cuts overall harm most is none. That blunt result drew wide debate and shaped later drinking guidelines.
pmc-6323933:
Annalisa Buniello, Jacqueline MacArthur, Maria Cerezo, and coauthors described the GWAS Catalog in 2019. The catalog curates every published genome-wide association study in one place. Such studies link DNA variants to traits and diseases.

Curators extract the top associations, the samples used, and the traits measured, all in standard terms. The scope has grown to summary statistics and new study designs. Researchers use the catalog to check whether a variant was already linked to other traits. That cross-checking helps spot shared biology between diseases that look unrelated. All curated records can be downloaded freely for large offline studies.
poe-ms-found-in-a-bottle-1833:
Edgar Allan Poe won a prize with MS. Found in a Bottle in 1833. The tale is told by a man on a doomed ship in the south seas. His ship is struck by a storm and sunk save for him and one mate. A vast black ship then bears down on their wreck.

He boards the black ship and finds its crew old, blind to him, and bound south. He writes his tale, seals it in a bottle, and casts it to the sea. The ship drives toward a vast whirl at the pole as he writes. The tale is the root of Poe's polar dread.
priest-american-antiquities-1833:
Josiah Priest sold the lost race idea to all America in 1833. American Antiquities, and Discoveries in the West was the first popular book of its kind and a bestseller of its day. Priest was a harness maker turned author with a sharp nose for what readers craved.

He tells readers the great earthworks of the West were raised by a civilized people who then vanished. Giants, ancient coins, and Old World scripts crowd his proof. The book launched the mound-builder craze that gripped the young republic. A century of American guesswork about its past starts on these pages.
pushkin-eugene-onegin-1833:
Alexander Pushkin published Eugene Onegin in full in 1833, his verse novel in fourteen-line stanzas. Onegin, Lensky, and Tatyana people the poem that is Russia's national poem in the judgment of Russians. Pushkin wrote it over seven years, and its digressions sparkle with wit, weather, and literary talk throughout.

Onegin, a bored Petersburg dandy, inherits a country estate and befriends the young poet Lensky there. Tatyana Larina loves Onegin, writes him a frank letter, and is coldly lectured for her pains at once. A name-day ball and a foolish quarrel lead to a duel that leaves Lensky dead in snow. Years later Onegin loves the married Tatyana, now a great lady, and she refuses him in turn. The poem's ease and depth made Pushkin the founder of modern Russian literature.
roys-chilam-balam-chumayel-1933:
In the towns of colonial Yucatan, Maya scribes kept books of history, prophecy, and ritual in their own language. The book from Chumayel is the best known of these Books of Chilam Balam. Ralph L. Roys translated and edited it, and the Carnegie Institution published his work in 1933.

Inside are creation accounts, calendar lore, and chronicles that run from mythic times into the Spanish conquest. Prophecies tied to the turning katun cycles frame the town's past and future. Roys added notes that help readers follow names, dates, and rites. For scholars of the Maya, the Chumayel book stays a core native source on colonial Yucatan.
schmerling-recherches-ossemens-fossiles-:
Philippe-Charles Schmerling, a Belgian physician, published the first volume of his cave researches in 1833, in French. Digging in caves near Liege, he found human bones beside remains of extinct animals. The Engis skull came from those same deposits.

Schmerling argued that humans had lived alongside mammoths and cave bears. Most scholars of his day ignored or rejected the claim. A generation later, the Neanderthal finds proved his basic point. Volume one presents the caves, bones, and reasoning in detail. It stands as the first scientific case for fossil humans.

Volume two of Philippe-Charles Schmerling's cave researches appeared in 1833, in French. The Belgian doctor turned from his headline finds to the supporting evidence. Animal bones, cave geology, and careful site descriptions fill these pages.

Schmerling shows that human and extinct animal remains shared the same undisturbed layers. Plates illustrate the bones and cave sections he describes. Together, the evidence made contemporaneity hard to dismiss on fair reading. Contemporaries dismissed it anyway, and Schmerling died unvindicated. Later prehistorians restored his name as a founder of their science. The two volumes together run to hundreds of pages of observation.
sextus-empiricus-outlines-pyrrhonism-bur:
Sextus Empiricus, a Greek doctor of the late second century, set down the fullest account of Pyrrhonism, the school that doubted all claims to knowledge. R. G. Bury translated his Outlines of Pyrrhonism for the Loeb series, and the volume came out in 1933. Bury also wrote a long opening essay on the rival schools of his day.

The three books lay out the skeptic's method: for every claim, set an equal claim against it, then rest in doubt. Sextus gives the famous modes, the stock arguments used to unsettle any firm belief. The first book defines the school, and the later books attack logic, physics, and ethics in turn. No other ancient text states the skeptical case so fully.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5033:
William H. Taft gives four yearly addresses in one set. Their dates run from December 7, 1909, to December 3, 1912. Three stars part each address from the next. The first reports on ties with foreign governments. Those ties hold on a normal base of friendship. They are in the main pleasing, Taft says. Under a head for Europe, he takes up one quarrel. It turns on fishing rights on the North Atlantic Coast.

A general treaty of 1908 with Great Britain frames the case. A special pact of January 27, 1909, sent the questions onward. A court at The Hague was to hear them. Its members came from the Permanent Court of Arbitration. Each government filed its printed case on October 4 last. The American counter case is now in hand. American rights rest on the Treaty of 1818. Its fisheries clause has split the two lands for near seventy years.
the-constitution-of-man-considered-in-re: George Combe's Constitution of Man Considered in Relation to External Objects appears here in its second American edition, from Allen and Ticknor, with a quote from Butler's Analogy at the front. The title page is worn and hard to read. A preface written for American readers praises Combe's essays on phrenology and his zeal for the subject. The preface argues that this study of the head and mind rests on nature and could aid the study of thought itself. Only the title page and that preface are present here.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: No. 33 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is dated June 24, 1897. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a premium offer. The premium is a Scientific Box Kite, sent to any one who sends one new subscriber. Its inventor is H. H. Clayton, who serves as chief observer at the observatory on Blue Hill, near Boston. Kites of this type have reached 9,200 feet, nearly two miles.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2-part:
The Ormsby Don Quixote, Cervantes' tale in English, opens Volume 2, Part 33 here. Chapter forty-nine tells of what happened to Sancho in making the round of his island. The great governor is left angered and irritated by a portrait-painting farmer who tried to practise upon him, coached by the majordomo at the duke's orders.

Fool, boor, and clown as he is held to be, Sancho holds his own against them all. Turning to Doctor Pedro Recio and the company, he declares that he now sees plainly what judges and governors must be. Cervantes gives the joke government real weight, as plain sense in office shames the tricksters who staged it.
the-mahabharata-of-krishna-dwaipayana-vy:
Book 3 of the Mahabharata, the Vana Parva, continues in this record of Kisari Mohan Ganguli's English prose translation, made from the Sanskrit between 1883 and 1896. A heading warns that section CXLV is continued from a previous eBook, so the record starts mid-episode. Bhimasena, the mighty son of the wind-god, is loose in a forest among panicked animals: geese, ducks, parrots, herons, lions, and elephants flying in all directions. Bhima slays one elephant with another and one lion with another, and dispatches the rest with slaps.

Then, shouting so that all sides resound, he reaches a beautiful plantain tree on the slopes of the Gandhamadana. He uproots trunks as tall as stacked palm trees and hurls them on every side. The passage gives the epic at full stretch: superhuman strength, terrified nature, and a hero compared to a mad lion.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, November 14, 1829, No. 398, turns its Naturalist division to curiosities of nature, led by the praying mantis and a branched starfish. Castles and cathedrals have filled so many recent frontispieces that the editors choose relief from artificial monotony. Nature's economy, they argue, surpasses the proudest works of men's hands in intricacy.

The mantis is classed as a species of cricket in the second order of insects. Blumenbach's four varieties run from a gigantic Amboyna kind, a span long and eaten locally, to the religious mantis pictured here. A Cape variety is considered sacred by the Hottentots, the article says, using the period's term. The pictured mantis goes on four legs, holding two shorter ones raised. Its wing covering mimics a dry willow leaf, earning it the name of walking leaf. Readers trade architecture for entomology for one number.
three-expeditions-into-the-interior-of-e: Major T. L. Mitchell's Three Expeditions into the Interior of Eastern Australia appears here as volume two of the revised second edition, published by T. and W. Boone at London. The sibling record in this slice presents volume one instead. This volume's contents cover the 1836 expedition to the Darling and Murray rivers. Chapter headings list the proposed route, equipment, the men, and an agreement with a native guide. Only the title and contents pages are present here, so Mitchell's journal itself does not appear.
tob-0033:
Project Blue Book was the United States Air Force program that logged reports of unidentified flying objects. Special Report No. 14, prepared with the Battelle Memorial Institute and issued in 1955, took thousands of cases and tested them with statistics rather than opinion.

Analysts sorted sightings into known and unknown and asked whether the two groups truly differed. On qualities like shape, color, and motion, they found the unknowns did stand apart, a result quoted ever since. The prose is dry and methodical. Skeptics and believers both cite the study, which makes it a rare shared piece of ground in a loud debate.
tob-0133:
King Chandakapali asks the sage Gheranda how a person can master the body and reach liberation, and the Gheranda Samhita records the answer. Gheranda lays out a sevenfold path, broader than the limbs of Patanjali. The teaching proceeds as a calm dialogue between king and sage.

Purification rites come first, then postures, then breath work, withdrawal of the senses, meditation, and final absorption. Each stage gets practical detail meant for use, not mere theory. The Samhita stands with the Hatha Yoga Pradipika among the root manuals of hatha yoga. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10033:
After the Metamorphoses, Ovid turned to the Roman calendar and wrote the Fasti, a poem that moves month by month through the year. Frazer's translation is the version named here. Ovid finished only January through June before exile cut the work short.

For each festival he gives the rite, its origin story, and the gods and heroes tied to the day. Readers learn why Romans honored strange old gods and how myth explained custom. The poem is a rich store of Roman religion and folk practice, told with the same wit and speed that mark all of Ovid's verse.
tob-10233:
Four hundred twenty-three short verses, in F. Max Müller's translation tradition, gather sayings attributed to the Buddha in the Dhammapada. Buddhism's most beloved scripture, it has been memorized by monks and householders for two thousand years. No single story carries it; each verse stands as counsel that can be recalled in daily life.

Verses are arranged by theme, including anger, craving, folly, wisdom, and the awakened person. The teaching is practical: master the mind, speak truthfully, harm no living thing, and watch where desire leads. Because the language is brief and concrete, readers can enter anywhere, though the cumulative picture is a full discipline of attention and kindness.
tob-10333:
Heinrich Kramer, with Jacob Sprenger named as co-author, published the Malleus Maleficarum, the Hammer of Witches, in 1486. Kramer was a Dominican inquisitor whose witch trials had met resistance. He wrote the manual to win backing and guide other judges.

Three parts argue that witchcraft is real and mostly women's work, list the harms witches were said to do, and set out trial steps, torture, and sentencing. Print spread the manual across Europe, and it fueled witch hunts for two centuries. Historians read it today as key proof of how fear, law, and print fed a persecution.
tob-13333:
James George Frazer reshaped the study of myth and religion with The Golden Bough, his vast study of magic and religion. The title comes from the golden bough at Nemi, where a priest ruled until a challenger killed him. Frazer ranged across the whole world to explain that rite. He returned to the riddle again and again as his evidence grew.

Frazer argues that magic came first, that religion grew from its failure, and that science later grew from both. He piles up cases of taboo, sacred kings, and dying gods. Later scholars corrected much, but the book's sweep still stuns readers.
tob-4214-10833:
Two friends argue about faith in Religion: A Dialogue, the best-known piece in Saunders's Schopenhauer selection. Philalethes, the lover of truth, presses the case against natural religion. Demopheles defends faith as a useful cloak for truths the crowd cannot bear directly.

Around the dialogue stand essays on government, free will, ethics, and the emptiness of worldly striving. Schopenhauer writes with unusual wit for a German thinker of his weight. He mocks cant, praises honesty, and returns always to his core claim that will drives the world. Readers meet the atheist at his most combative and most entertaining here.
tob-4333:
Volume two of Augustine's Confessions, in William Watts's translation of 1631 as reprinted in the Loeb series, carries the autobiography into its searching later books. The stolen pears and the Milan garden lie behind; what remains is harder. Augustine turns his mind on memory itself, and on the riddle of time.

What is time, he asks, if no one asks me, I know; if I must explain, I cannot. The final book reads Genesis as a figure of the church and the soul's rest. Verified from the 1919 edition record, Watts's old English suits the old bishop. The restless heart's inquiry completes itself here.
un-ga-res-33: How long should the first members of UN councils serve? Resolution 33, passed on 13 February 1946, settles the point for the men and women picked in January of that year under stopgap rules. They would hold office for twelve months. Fresh votes for their successors would fall at the second part of the first regular session, and the Secretary-General had to report any rule changes needed to make that work.
un-ga-res-a-69-33:
Small arms kill on a vast scale in the Sahel and Sahara lands. Resolution A/69/33, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session, deals with help for states that fight their spread. The text recalls the vote of the year before on the same aid. It voices deep worry at the toll of such arms, above all among children, and at the harm they do to the fight against poverty.

African states had set a shared stand on the illicit flow of small arms at Bamako in the year 2000. World reports had warned that states must fight small arms as hard as the great arms of war. The vote backs aid to Sahel-Saharan states to curb the trade and to gather the arms in.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 33, adopted on 13 February 1946 at the thirty-second plenary meeting, is a short ruling on terms of office. The Assembly stated its sense that members of councils elected in January 1946 under the provisional rules should serve twelve months. Votes for their successors would come at the second part of the first regular session. It asked the Secretary-General to report what rule changes that would need.

General Assembly resolution 69/33 (2014) supports help for states trying to curb the illicit traffic in small arms and light weapons and to collect such weapons. The text stresses the human cost of illicit small-arms spread, especially in the Sahelo-Saharan region. It backs the Economic Community of West African States convention on small arms. The Assembly encourages the Secretary-General's advisory missions, national commissions against illicit proliferation, and civil-society work. It invites continued technical and financial assistance to affected states that request it.
un-sc-res-1033: Catalogue data places Resolution 1033, a United Nations Security Council text, in the year 1995. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-133: Cameroun sought a seat at the United Nations. Resolution 133 records the Council's reply. The Council adopted it on 26 January 1960. No member dissented. The meeting was the Council's 850th. The record states that the Council examined the application. It recommends that the General Assembly admit the Republic of Cameroun. The text is one formal sentence. It is kept in the official record.
un-sc-res-1333:
Resolution 1333 addressed Afghanistan under the Taliban when the Council adopted it on 19 December 2000. The Taliban still sheltered Usama bin Laden and let his network run training camps. Opium taxes paid for much of that activity. The Taliban had ignored earlier demands to hand him over for trial.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council sets an arms embargo on Taliban-held territory. States must close all Taliban offices and all offices of Ariana Afghan Airlines. Funds of bin Laden and his associates, including Al-Qaida, are frozen at once. Flights to Taliban areas are barred unless cleared for aid or peace talks. The Taliban must close the camps and halt the drug trade.
un-sc-res-1433: Under number 1433, the catalog lists a Security Council resolution dated to 2002 in the official UN record. The Council is the UN body charged with world peace and security, and it speaks formally through texts like this one. For students of the UN, the record offers the Council's language itself rather than a summary written later. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-1533:
Congo's arms embargo gained its own watchdog committee on 12 March 2004. Armed groups and militias still held ground in North and South Kivu and in Ituri. Weapons kept flowing in against the ban set by resolution 1493 (2003). Experts had tied the war to the illegal mining and sale of Congo's natural wealth.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council restated the demand that all states block arms supplies to the eastern groups. MONUC was told to keep seizing weapons found in breach of the embargo, within its means. All parties had to give MONUC staff free and instant access. The Council set up a sanctions committee of all its members to watch the embargo. States, above all in the region, were urged to end illegal resource trading, using courts where needed. The machinery here became the base of the Congo sanctions regime for years after.
un-sc-res-1633:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1633, adopted on 21 October 2005. The crisis dragged on and conditions kept getting worse. Elections set for 30 October 2005 could not be held. The African Union had ruled that President Laurent Gbagbo could stay on for at most twelve more months.

The Council backs the African Union plan in full. A new prime minister, accepted by all sides, must be named by 31 October 2005. The prime minister gets full power over the cabinet, defense, and election work. An international working group will draft a road map toward free elections by 31 October 2006. Militias must disarm at once, and anyone blocking peace faces targeted sanctions.
un-sc-res-1733: Resolution 1733, a 2006 Security Council text, is preserved in this collection through a Wikisource copy of the official record. Its number fixes its place among the year's decisions, between its neighbors 1732 and 1736. The entry holds the complete act at that address: findings, decisions, and the reporting instructions that typically bring the text to a close.
un-sc-res-1833: Kept under number 1833, a formal Security Council resolution is preserved through a Wikisource transcription of the official record. The Council's fifteen members, five permanent and ten elected, stand behind the text. What they jointly decided is the entry's content: findings stated in order, then operative paragraphs that put the decision into effect.
un-sc-res-1933:
Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1933, adopted on 30 June 2010. The last presidential election had taken place in October 2000. The vote promised under the Ouagadougou peace deal kept slipping, with no date set. Unrest in February 2010 showed how fragile the calm remained.

The Council renews the United Nations Operation in Côte d'Ivoire until 31 December 2010. Ivorian leaders must publish the final voters list and name the election date without more delay. The Secretary-General's envoy will certify each stage of the vote. The mission guards civilians, watches the arms embargo, and backs reunification and disarmament. Hate speech in the media could draw targeted sanctions.
un-sc-res-233:
War broke out in the Near East at the start of June 1967. On 6 June, one day into the fighting of the Six-Day War, the Security Council acted. The Secretary-General had briefed the Council on the situation. Members had heard statements from the parties. The Council said it was concerned at the outbreak and at the danger in the region.

Its demand was short and direct. It called on the governments concerned to stop all military activity at once. That halt was meant as a first step, not a settlement. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed without delay. The fighting in fact ran on for four more days.
un-sc-res-33: The Council settled a point of procedure with the General Assembly in 1947. The issue was how membership applications would be handled under the two bodies' rules. On 27 August 1947 the Council accepted its experts' advice. A sub-committee would negotiate matching changes to the Assembly's rules. Some Assembly proposals on the Council's own rules were accepted as well. The dry text aligned the paperwork of admissions between the two organs.
un-sc-res-333:
Rhodesia's sanctions net was tightened on 22 May 1973. The sanctions committee's second special report lay before the Council. Measures so far had not ended the illegal regime. Some states had failed to stop trade with it, against resolutions 232 (1966) and 253 (1968). South Africa and Portugal refused to help apply the sanctions at all.

The Council approved the committee's recommendations and pressed for urgent action on them. States whose laws allowed imports of Rhodesian minerals and goods had to repeal those laws at once. All states were called to pass laws with harsh fines and jail for sanctions breakers. Contracts with South Africa and Portugal had to carry clauses barring Rhodesian goods from the deal. Insurance firms were to be barred from covering flights into and out of Rhodesia. Marine insurance contracts had to state plainly that no Rhodesian cargo was covered.
un-sc-res-433: At number 433 in its series, the Security Council decision is catalogued here as a 1978 record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-733:
Somalia collapsed into civil war at the start of 1992, and Somalia itself asked the Council to take up its case. The fighting was taking a heavy toll in lives and property. The Council was gravely alarmed at how fast the situation was getting worse. It treated the collapse as a threat to peace and security in the region. Resolution 733 was adopted unanimously on 23 January 1992.

All parties in Somalia were strongly urged to stop fighting at once. They had to agree a cease-fire and work for reconciliation and a political settlement. The Secretary-General was asked to expand aid to the people affected. Working with African and Arab partners, he also had to press the factions to end hostilities and let relief supplies through. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council imposed a general and complete arms embargo. All deliveries of weapons and military equipment to Somalia were banned.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1033, adopted unanimously on 19 December 1995, concerns Western Sahara and the stalled identification of voters for its self-determination referendum. The Council repeats its commitment to holding the referendum without further delay, under the Settlement Plan accepted by Morocco and the Polisario Front. It notes both parties' responses to the Secretary-General's proposal for moving the identification process forward.

The Council stresses that the Identification Commission can work only if both parties trust its judgement and integrity. It welcomes the Secretary-General's decision to intensify consultations aimed at an agreed plan. It asks him to report urgently. If those consultations fail, he is to give the Council options. They include a programme for the orderly withdrawal of MINURSO, the United Nations Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara.

Cameroun's path into the United Nations runs through this short text of 26 January 1960. The Council had looked at the new Republic of Cameroun's request to join. Its answer was yes: it told the General Assembly that Cameroun should be admitted. Under the Charter, that step by the Council is the required step before the Assembly can vote a new country in. This brief text is the formal gate through which Cameroun's membership passed.

Sanctions on the Taliban are sharply widened by Resolution 1333, adopted unanimously on 19 December 2000. The Taliban still sheltered Usama bin Laden, indicted for the 1998 embassy bombings in Nairobi and Dar es Salaam. The Taliban let terrorist training camps operate on Afghan soil despite the demands of Resolution 1267 (1999). Opium taxes helped pay for it.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands the Taliban hand over bin Laden for trial, close all terrorist camps, and end sanctuary for terrorists. It imposes an arms embargo on Taliban-controlled territory and bans military advice to the Taliban. It orders states to freeze the funds of bin Laden and those associated with him, including the Al-Qaida organization, as listed by the Sanctions Committee. Taliban offices and Ariana Afghan Airlines offices must close, flights to Taliban territory are banned, and sales of the heroin-making chemical acetic anhydride to that territory are banned.

Angola's long civil war had ended months earlier when, on 15 August 2002, the United Nations Office in Angola was replaced with a fuller mission. The peace rested on the Lusaka Protocol and its addendum. A stronger United Nations presence, the Council judged, could help lock in the peace while the remaining steps were completed.

The new United Nations Mission in Angola, UNMA, is set up for six months, until 15 February 2003. Its work spans political, military, human rights, humanitarian, and economic goals, and its staffing includes a Child Protection Adviser. Whether the mission would be extended, changed, or ended was to turn on an assessment of progress in finishing the Lusaka Protocol.

Resolution 1533, adopted unanimously on 12 March 2004, gives Congo's arms embargo a referee. Militias still roamed the east, in North and South Kivu and Ituri, and weapons kept flowing into the Democratic Republic of the Congo despite the embargo imposed in July 2003. The Council also tied the fighting to the illegal stripping of Congo's natural resources, which an expert panel had documented the year before.

The Council created a sanctions committee of its own members to oversee the embargo. It further set up a group of experts to gather and analyze information on arms flows, name violators, and suggest ways to make the embargo work. That committee-and-experts pairing became the template for modern UN sanctions.

Côte d'Ivoire's transition is restructured by Resolution 1633, adopted on 21 October 2005. Elections due on 30 October could not be held. The African Union Peace and Security Council had decided on 6 October that the president's mandate had ended. It decided he should stay as head of state for at most 12 more months.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council endorses the AU decision and demands all Ivorian parties implement it at once. A new prime minister acceptable to all signatory parties must be appointed by 31 October 2005. He will have full authority over security, defence, disarmament, and elections. Ministers will be accountable to him. A new International Working Group must draw up a road map for elections by 31 October 2006 and report any obstruction of the prime minister. Militias must disarm at once, and sanctions stay ready against spoilers.

A tribute closes the year on 22 December 2006. The text honours Kofi Annan at the end of his time as Secretary-General of the United Nations. The central role he had played in guiding the organization is recognized, along with his sustained work toward just and lasting settlements of disputes and conflicts around the world. The reforms he launched and his proposals for strengthening the United Nations system are commended, and deep appreciation is expressed for his service to peace, development, and human rights.

The International Security Assistance Force in Afghanistan, ISAF, is extended for another year on 22 September 2008. Afghan authorities hold the main duty for security across the country, with ISAF assisting the government. The force's work is linked to the broader world effort in Afghanistan, including the United Nations mission.

ISAF's authorization is extended, and the states taking part may use all necessary measures to carry out its mandate. ISAF is told to work in close consultation with the Afghan government and the United Nations mission's head. Its leadership is to report regularly through the Secretary-General. More trainers and resources for the Afghan army and police are also pressed for, so Afghans can take over security themselves.

Côte d'Ivoire's election clock is pressed in Resolution 1933, adopted on 30 June 2010. The last presidential election had been in October 2000. The provisional voters list of November 2009 was still not final, and no first-round date was set. The February 2010 unrest showed how fragile the Ouagadougou peace process remained. Sexual violence and other abuses continued with impunity.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council gives UNOCI a mandate to 31 December 2010 focused on stability, protection of civilians under imminent threat, monitoring the arms embargo, and election support. It urges the Ivorian parties to publish the final voters list, certified by the Secretary-General's Special Representative, without further delay. It urges them to announce the election date, holding them fully accountable. It reaffirms the certification role for every stage of the vote and warns it is ready to impose targeted sanctions, including on media actors inciting violence.

Resolution 233 is the UN Security Council's first ceasefire call of the Six-Day War, adopted unanimously on 6 June 1967, the war's second day. The Secretary-General had given an oral report, the Council had heard statements, and it recorded its concern at the outbreak of fighting and the menacing situation in the Near East.

The resolution calls on the governments concerned to stop all military action in the area at once, as a first step. It asks the Secretary-General to keep the Council swiftly and steadily informed. The fighting ran its course before diplomacy caught up, and the war's outcome set up Resolution 242 five months later.

Rulebooks, not wars, fill this early text. In 1947 the Council and the Assembly were still shaping how they worked. Their rule drafts clashed in spots. Rule 58 dealt with bids by new states to join. A team of the Council's own rule experts had views on the text. Resolution 33 passed on 27 August 1947 by ten votes to none. Australia held back.

The rule team was told to treat with the Assembly's match body. It could deal on the Council's revised rule 58. Side shifts in the Assembly's rules were part of the pact. One word fight is spelled out: the Assembly's bid to swap decide for consider was turned down. Other tweaks got a yes. The text is dry as dust. It still shows two young bodies learning to mesh their gears.

Resolution 333, adopted on 22 May 1973 by twelve votes to none with three abstentions, tries to make Rhodesia sanctions work better. Earlier measures since 1966 had not ended the illegal regime, the Council admitted, and some states were still trading with it in breach of the Charter. South Africa and Portugal were condemned for refusing to cooperate with the sanctions effort at all.

The Council approved the recommendations in the sanctions committee's second special report, a list of tightening steps. It asked the committee to keep working on ways to close the gaps. The Assembly's decolonization committee had also written in support. Sanctions were the Council's chosen weapon against Rhodesia, and this is a maintenance order for that weapon.

A Pacific island state, newly independent from Britain, sought a seat at the United Nations in the summer of 1978. Resolution 433, adopted unanimously on 17 August 1978, deals with the application of Solomon Islands. The Council examined the application. It then recommended to the General Assembly that Solomon Islands be admitted to membership in the United Nations. That single recommendation is the whole text of the resolution.

Resolution 733 is the UN Security Council's first response to Somalia's collapse into civil war, adopted unanimously on 23 January 1992. Somalia had asked the Council to take up its situation, and the Secretary-General reported rapid deterioration, heavy loss of life, and widespread damage after the state fell apart.

The resolution asks the Secretary-General to expand humanitarian aid and appoint a coordinator, presses him and regional leaders to contact all factions to end hostilities, and strongly urges an immediate ceasefire. Acting under Chapter VII, it also slaps a total ban on shipments of weapons and military gear into Somalia. It was the opening move of the UN's Somalia involvement of the 1990s.
villon-oeuvres-marot-1533:
Pierre Jannet prepared this French edition of Villon's complete works, with notes and a glossary. The preface admits that little is known of Villon's life beyond what he says himself. His poems, it argues, take Villon himself as their true subject.

Thief, brawler, and the greatest French poet of the 1400s, Villon wrote from Paris taverns and prisons. The Testament and the Ballad of the Hanged Men mix street slang with piercing beauty. Lamants for lost youth run through the work beside sharp satire. An added choice of poems by his followers rounds out the book, and his voice still sounds startlingly alive today.
voltaire-letters-on-the-english-1733:
Voltaire's Letters on England, transcribed here from the Cassell edition of 1894, carries an introduction that tells his life before the letters. Francois Marie Arouet, who called himself Voltaire, was born in 1694. He was the third son of Francois Arouet of Poitou, a Paris notary turned treasurer in the Chambre des Comptes. The boy was born frail and lived to eighty-four. He died just years before the French Revolution he helped to prepare.

At ten he went to the Jesuits at the College Louis-le-Grand. Seven years of training in speech and writing fed his bent for letters. Verses he wrote at eleven, for an invalid soldier, won him the friendship of Ninon de l'Enclos. She urged him on, and left him a legacy at her death. The letters that follow report England to France: its religion, trade, stage, and freedoms, seen by a young exile with sharp eyes.
zadkiel-grammar-of-astrology-1833:
Zadkiel was the pen name of Richard James Morrison, a former naval officer turned London astrologer. His Grammar of Astrology, published in 1833, presents the art's rules in the form of a school grammar. Morrison was Raphael's Victorian rival, and the two men's almanacs fought for the same readers.

The Grammar drills the student in signs, houses, aspects, and the steps of judging a chart, point by numbered point. Morrison claims for astrology a weather-wise certainty, and his forecasts made his name a household word. His work carried the revival Raphael began into the middle of the Victorian age.
